# Technical Specification

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 Executive Summary

### 1.1.1 Project Overview

`hao-backprop-test` is a deliberately minimal, loopback-only Node.js HTTP service maintained as an integration fixture. `README.md` states its purpose in a single line — "test project for backprop integration" — and nothing else in the repository defines what "backprop" is: the repository contains no product description, roadmap, customer segment, pricing, or commercial documentation. The npm manifest (`package.json`) carries the more generic identity: package `hello_world`, version `1.0.0`, description "Hello world in Node.js", author `hxu`, MIT license.

The entire runtime surface is one CommonJS file, `server.js` (29 lines), which instantiates an Express 5 application (`const express = require('express')`, `const app = express()`), enables strict routing (`app.enable('strict routing')`, line 12), registers two literal `GET` routes, and binds a listener to the hardcoded loopback endpoint `127.0.0.1:3000` (lines 3–4, 26–28). Its complete external contract, confirmed both by reading `server.js` and by launching the service and issuing HTTP requests at the current HEAD, is:

| Request | Response | Body |
|---------|----------|------|
| `GET /` (lines 14–18) | `200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain` | `Hello, World!` plus trailing newline — 14 bytes |
| `GET /good-evening` (lines 20–24) | `200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain` | `Good evening` — 12 bytes, no trailing newline |
| Any other path or any non-`GET` method | `404 Not Found` | Express default 404 body |

Every response also carries Express's default `X-Powered-By: Express` header, and the process prints exactly one startup line, `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, to standard output (line 27).

The repository is flat: 19 git-tracked files, of which all but four — `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md`, `Build Prompt.md`, `Project Guide.md`, and `Technical Specifications.md` — sit at the repository root. Beside the runnable service and its two npm manifests, it holds non-runtime artifacts: three minimal Node `http` server scripts with pathological filenames (`Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, and a 170-character `QWYFFGHGHFDDJFDame_…server.js`), an orphan data fixture `phonenumber.csv`, a defect-remediation transcript `Response.txt`, the original requirement note `codebase_context (42).md`, four binary artifacts (`20250304165759.mp4`, `s1.png`, `defect_for_task_1.docx`, `tech_spec.pdf`), and the generated `blitzy/documentation/` artifact set.

The Express-based shape of `server.js` is itself the product of the change set this specification covers. On branch `blitzy-62d685d6-e32c-4f29-bfd6-70d96dfe345a`, commits `b9350e9` ("Add Express ^5.2.1 as first project dependency"), `0fdbfb6` ("Re-platform server.js onto Express with /good-evening route"), `fcbd326` (`.gitignore`), `59adfc5` (`README.md`) and `f2c2ca4` (strict routing) sit on top of base commit `46e6dfe`, which held the earlier native-`http`, single-route, zero-dependency implementation.

### 1.1.2 Core Business Problem

The repository exists to give downstream tooling — the "backprop" integration named in `README.md` — a small, fully deterministic Node.js workload to ingest, analyze, and exercise against a known baseline. Within that purpose, the change set documented here solves four concrete problems.

**Discrete endpoints could not be expressed.** The original implementation (still preserved in the three filename fixtures) used Node's built-in `http` module with one route-agnostic handler: every method on every path received `200 OK` / `text/plain` / `Hello, World!\n`. Such a server cannot model "endpoints" at all. Re-platforming onto Express introduced a routing table — an explicit, declarative mapping from single literal paths to handlers — and with `strict routing` enabled, an explicit `404` for everything unregistered.

**A second greeting had to be added without disturbing the first.** The request (recorded verbatim in `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md`: *"this is a tutorial of node js server hosting one endpoint that returns the response "Hello world". Could you add expressjs into the project and add another endpoint that return the response of "Good evening"?"*) required a new response while explicitly implying the existing one stays intact. The delivered solution preserves the root body byte-for-byte and adds `GET /good-evening` returning `Good evening`.

**The first third-party dependency had to be introduced reproducibly.** `package.json` previously declared no dependencies at all; it now declares `"express": "^5.2.1"`, and `package-lock.json` pins the resolved tree (lockfileVersion 3, 66 package entries including `express@5.2.1` and its 65 transitive packages, each with an `integrity` digest and `registry.npmjs.org` URL). `node_modules/` is excluded via `.gitignore`, so the repository stays source-only while remaining installable with `npm ci`.

**The HTTP contract had to become documentable and verifiable.** `README.md` now records the dependency, both endpoints, the `404` behavior for unregistered paths, and the run procedure, giving reviewers and integration tooling a written contract to test against.

Two open clarifications carry forward from the original ask, both recorded as assumptions in `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2: the path `/good-evening` was chosen because the requester named no path, and the root body remains `Hello, World!\n` even though the requester said "Hello world" and `codebase_context (42).md` asked for a `/hello` endpoint returning `"Hello world"`. Neither `/hello` nor a `"Hello world"` body exists in the code.

### 1.1.3 Key Stakeholders and Users

| Stakeholder | Role and interest | Evidence |
|-------------|-------------------|----------|
| Repository author / maintainer (`hxu`) | Owns and maintains the fixture; approves the dependency introduction | `package.json` `author` field |
| "backprop" integration tooling | The stated downstream consumer; needs a deterministic, small artifact to process | `README.md` line 2 |
| Local developer or operator | Installs dependencies, starts the process, smoke-tests both endpoints and the 404 paths | `README.md` "Running"; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9 |
| Local HTTP clients | The only consumers of the HTTP contract, reachable over loopback only | `server.js` line 3 (`127.0.0.1` binding) |
| Original requester | Authored the natural-language ask for Express plus a "Good evening" endpoint | `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md`; `codebase_context (42).md` |
| Blitzy platform agents | Produced the action plan, implemented the change, and ran the validation recorded in the documentation set | `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md`, `Project Guide.md` |

No end-user segment, paying customer, external API consumer, or operations team is identified anywhere in the repository: the service is not network-reachable beyond the host, has no accounts, and records no user-facing telemetry.

### 1.1.4 Expected Business Impact and Value Proposition

The value of this system is determinism and reviewability at a very small footprint, not feature breadth.

| Value driver | Concrete manifestation |
|--------------|------------------------|
| Deterministic HTTP contract | Two fixed plaintext responses with byte-exact bodies (14 and 12 bytes) and stable status/content-type; unsuitable paths return a stable `404` |
| Reproducible dependency graph | `express` pinned by `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion` 3, 66 packages, SRI digests) and installable with `npm ci`; `node_modules/` kept out of version control |
| Auditable change surface | The entry point is 29 lines; the feature changed exactly five files — `server.js`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.md` — as recorded in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §5 |
| Framework conventions adopted | Express routing (`app.get`, `app.listen`) replaces hand-rolled request handling, so further literal endpoints can be added without URL parsing code |
| Unchanged exposure boundary | The listener remains loopback-only; no authentication, TLS, persistence, or request-input handling was introduced (route callbacks accept `req` but never read it) |
| Tooling-resilience coverage retained | The three pathological-filename scripts remain in the repository as filesystem/tooling fixtures |

The trade-offs the change introduced are equally explicit and are carried through the rest of this specification: the installable dependency count moved from 0 to 66 packages; unregistered paths that previously returned the greeting now return `404`; responses gained the `X-Powered-By: Express` header; the three duplicate scripts are no longer byte-identical to `server.js`; and the service can no longer be started without first installing dependencies.


## 1.2 System Overview

### 1.2.1 Project Context

#### 1.2.1.1 Business Context and Market Positioning

`hao-backprop-test` is not a market-facing product and makes no competitive claim. No pricing, personas, customer segments, service-level commitments, or roadmap exist in the repository; `package.json` carries no `repository`, `homepage`, `bugs`, or `keywords` metadata, and the license is the permissive MIT. Its positioning is internal and instrumental: `README.md` labels it a "test project for backprop integration", which makes the repository a **controlled input artifact** — a workload small enough to be understood exhaustively, running long enough to be observed, and producing output fixed enough to be asserted on.

Two framings coexist in the repository and are worth distinguishing, because they explain the shape of both the code and the requirement history:

- **Tutorial framing** — `codebase_context (42).md` and `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md` describe a Node.js tutorial project serving greetings to an HTTP client. This framing supplies the greeting content and the "add a second endpoint" ask.
- **Fixture framing** — `README.md` (the repository's own name and description) recasts the same code as an integration test bed for "backprop", a term defined nowhere in the repository.

The delivered implementation serves both framings: it is trivial enough to read as tutorial code (29 lines, one file, two routes) and deterministic enough to serve as a fixture.

#### 1.2.1.2 Current System Limitations

The limitations below are observed in the current HEAD. They fall into two groups: limits of the running service, and limits of the repository's documentation and consistency.

**Runtime and architectural limitations**

| Limitation | Detail | Evidence |
|------------|--------|----------|
| Loopback-only, fixed endpoint | Binds `127.0.0.1:3000` from `const` literals; no binding-failure handling, so a port conflict terminates the process with an unhandled `EADDRINUSE` error | `server.js` lines 3–4, 26–28 |
| No configuration layer | No `process.env` reads anywhere in executable code, no `.env` or config module, no CLI arguments; `package.json` `scripts` holds only the untouched npm-init placeholder `test` script | `package.json`; repository-wide text search for `process.env` matched only `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` |
| No resilience features | No server `error` listener, no `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handling, no `try`/`catch` in handlers, no `clientError` handling, no resource cleanup; the process runs until externally killed | `server.js` (whole file); gaps catalogued as proposed features F-101–F-106 in `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §2.3 and `Response.txt` |
| No automated verification | No test files, no framework, no CI configuration, no linter, no container definition; validation in this repository is manual (start the process, issue requests) | `package.json` `test` script exits 1 by design; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Framework-disclosure header | Responses carry `X-Powered-By: Express`, which the earlier native-`http` implementation did not emit; suppression would require an explicit `app.disable('x-powered-by')` | observed in live responses; noted as optional in `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2 |
| Behavioral change for unregistered paths | Paths that previously received the greeting now receive `404`, and `/good-evening/` with a trailing slash is treated as a distinct, unregistered path because strict routing is enabled | `server.js` line 12; `README.md`; verified live |
| Manifest inconsistency | `package.json` declares `"main": "index.js"`, and no `index.js` exists in the repository; the declared entry point is therefore unusable and the file is only ever executed as `node server.js` | `package.json`; file inventory (19 tracked files, no `index.js`) |

**Repository and documentation limitations**

| Limitation | Detail | Evidence |
|------------|--------|----------|
| Documentation describes a superseded state | `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §1 characterizes the system as a 15-line native-`http` server with "zero production dependencies" and a route-agnostic catch-all response; `tech_spec.pdf` renders the same earlier-state specification (68 pages). The checked-in code is the Express implementation with one declared dependency and explicit routing | `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` lines 9–20, 110; `tech_spec.pdf` page 1; `server.js`; `package.json` |
| Drift acknowledged internally | The same specification states that it "reflects the repository state at the time of analysis" and that "any modification to `server.js` invalidates F-001 – F-005 acceptance criteria" | `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §2.7.4 |
| Fixture divergence | The three duplicate scripts were documented as byte-identical copies of `server.js`; they are currently byte-identical to each other (md5 `05576d40…`) but no longer identical to `server.js` (md5 `a423b6d4…`), because they retain the native-`http` implementation | hashes of `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, the 170-character `QWYFFGH…server.js`, and `server.js`; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §5 (F-005) |
| Dormant artifacts | `phonenumber.csv` (15 synthetic `message,phonenumber` rows) is imported by no code; `20250304165759.mp4`, `s1.png`, and `defect_for_task_1.docx` are unreferenced binaries; `Response.txt` describes a hardening programme that was never implemented | repository-wide text search; `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §2.2.6 |

For the two conflicting descriptions of the system — the native-`http`/zero-dependency account in `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` and the Express/one-dependency account in the checked-in code — **the code is authoritative for this specification**. The documentation set predates the change set described in §1.1.1, and its own freshness note concedes that the code change invalidates it.

#### 1.2.1.3 Integration with the Existing Enterprise Landscape

The system integrates with nothing at runtime. It exposes exactly one network interface — the Express listener in `server.js` bound to loopback on port 3000 — and opens no outbound connections, because the route handlers perform no I/O of any kind: they set a status code and a content type and write a fixed string. There are no database drivers, HTTP clients, queue clients, caches, authentication providers, TLS terminators, proxies, log shippers, or instrumentation agents anywhere in the repository.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[Local HTTP client<br/>curl / smoke test]
    Registry[Public npm registry<br/>registry.npmjs.org]

    subgraph NodeProcess[Single Node.js process]
        ExpressApp[Express application<br/>server.js]
        RootRoute["GET / handler<br/>Hello, World!"]
        EveningRoute["GET /good-evening handler<br/>Good evening"]
        DefaultHandler[Express default<br/>404 handler]
    end

    Client -->|"GET /"| ExpressApp
    Client -->|"GET /good-evening"| ExpressApp
    ExpressApp --> RootRoute
    ExpressApp --> EveningRoute
    ExpressApp --> DefaultHandler
    DefaultHandler -->|"404 Not Found"| Client
    Registry -.->|"install time only<br/>66 packages"| ExpressApp
```

The single external touchpoint is **install-time**: `npm ci` or `npm install` fetches `express@5.2.1` and its 65 transitive packages from the public registry whose URLs and integrity digests are recorded in `package-lock.json`. Once installed, the service runs with no network dependency beyond the client's own loopback connection.

Adopting this service inside a larger enterprise landscape would therefore require work that does not exist today: external reachability (reverse proxy or TLS termination), environment-driven configuration, health/metrics surfaces, structured logging, graceful shutdown for orchestrators, and automated tests. Sections 1.3.2.2 and 1.3.2.3 record these as future-phase and uncovered-integration items rather than current capabilities.

### 1.2.2 High-Level Description

#### 1.2.2.1 Primary System Capabilities

| Capability | Implementation | Notes |
|------------|----------------|-------|
| Express application and listener | `const app = express()` (line 6); `app.listen(port, hostname, callback)` (lines 26–28) | Binds `127.0.0.1:3000` for the lifetime of the process |
| Root greeting route | `app.get('/', …)` (lines 14–18) | `200`, `text/plain`, byte-exact `Hello, World!\n` |
| Second greeting route | `app.get('/good-evening', …)` (lines 20–24) | `200`, `text/plain`, byte-exact `Good evening` |
| Explicit routing with strict paths | `app.enable('strict routing')` (line 12) | Trailing-slash variants and unregistered paths fall through to Express's default `404` |
| Startup observability | `console.log` in the listen callback (line 27) | Emits `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` as the only runtime output |
| Declared, locked dependency | `package.json` `dependencies.express` `^5.2.1`; `package-lock.json` `lockfileVersion` 3 | Enables reproducible `npm ci` installs of the 66-package tree |

The system has no other capability: no request parsing, no state, no persistence, no background work, no scheduled tasks, and no administrative surface.

| Component | Path | Responsibility |

| Service entry point | `server.js` | Instantiates Express, registers both routes, enables strict routing, starts the listener |

| Dependency lockfile | `package-lock.json` | Pins `express@5.2.1` plus 65 transitive packages with resolved URLs and integrity digests |

Supporting, non-runtime components:

| Component | Path | Role |
|-----------|------|------|
| Filename fixtures | `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, `QWYFFGHGHFDDJFDame_!@#$%^&(){}long_name_…server.js` | Standalone native-`http` servers retained to exercise filesystem/tooling handling of pathological names |
| Data fixture | `phonenumber.csv` | 15 synthetic `message,phonenumber` rows; not read by any code |
| Requirement history | `codebase_context (42).md`, `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md` | The original `/hello` ask and the verbatim request that produced this change |
| Remediation transcript | `Response.txt` | JSON-wrapped action plan proposing six unimplemented hardening features |
| Documentation set | `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md`, `Project Guide.md`, `Technical Specifications.md` | Requirement IDs, scope decisions, validation results, feature catalogue |

#### 1.2.2.3 Core Technical Approach

- **Language and module format** — JavaScript with CommonJS `require` semantics, one file, no transpilation step; nothing is exported (`module.exports` appears nowhere in the repository).
- **Runtime and framework** — Node.js hosting an Express 5 application. `express` is the project's first and only direct dependency; Express 5 requires Node.js 18 or newer, and the local runtime used during validation was Node 22.
- **Routing model** — A declarative table of two literal `GET` paths. Because `strict routing` is enabled, only the exact strings `/` and `/good-evening` are registered; all other paths, all trailing-slash variants, and all non-`GET` methods fall through to Express's default `404` handler.
- **Response construction** — Handlers deliberately use the low-level pattern `res.statusCode = 200; res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain'); res.end(...)`, which guarantees byte-exact bodies (including the presence or absence of a trailing newline) instead of relying on Express's string-sending defaults.
- **Configuration model** — None. Hostname and port are module-level `const` literals; there are no environment reads, config files, or command-line options.
- **Concurrency model** — The Node.js event loop with synchronous, non-blocking handlers; no promises, streams, timers, or worker threads in application code.
- **State and persistence** — None. Both handlers are pure functions of nothing: they ignore their `req` argument and return fixed strings.
- **Dependency management** — Declared in `package.json` and resolved in `package-lock.json`; installed output lives in `node_modules/`, which is git-ignored, so a fresh checkout must install before it can run.

The request lifecycle of the delivered service is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Operator installs dependencies then runs node server.js]
    Bind[app.listen 3000 on 127.0.0.1]
    Log[console.log startup message]
    Req[Incoming HTTP request]
    Match{Path and method<br/>match a registered route?}
    RootResp[Root handler<br/>200 text/plain 14 bytes]
    EveningResp[Good-evening handler<br/>200 text/plain 12 bytes]
    NotFoundResp[404 Not Found]

    Start --> Bind
    Bind --> Log
    Log --> Req
    Req --> Match
    Match -->|"GET /"| RootResp
    Match -->|"GET /good-evening"| EveningResp
    Match -->|"any other path, slash variant or method"| NotFoundResp
```

### 1.2.3 Success Criteria

#### 1.2.3.1 Measurable Objectives

| Objective | Measurement | Target and observed result |
|-----------|-------------|----------------------------|
| Start and bind successfully | Process starts and prints the startup line | `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`; observed on every launch |
| Preserve the root contract byte-exactly | Status, content type and body of `GET /` | `200`, `text/plain`, `Hello, World!\n` (14 bytes) — matched when re-verified at HEAD |
| Deliver the new contract byte-exactly | Status, content type and body of `GET /good-evening` | `200`, `text/plain`, `Good evening` (12 bytes, no newline) — matched when re-verified at HEAD |
| Reject unregistered requests | Status of an unregistered path and of a trailing-slash variant | `404` for `/does-not-exist`, `/good-evening/`, and `POST /` |
| Introduce the dependency reproducibly | Dependency declared and locked | `express ^5.2.1` in `package.json`; 66 packages pinned in `package-lock.json`; `npm ci` installs cleanly |
| Keep the change minimal | Files changed by the feature | 5 files (`server.js`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.md`), per `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §5 |

The documentation set records the same objectives as a completion ledger: requirement delivery 4/4 (FR-A…FR-D), byte-exact contracts 2/2, in-scope files 5, functional checks 9/9, and 0 npm vulnerabilities across the 66-package tree (`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3, §8).

#### 1.2.3.2 Critical Success Factors

- **A free port 3000 and a working loopback interface** — the service hardcodes `127.0.0.1:3000`, has no fallback port and no binding-error handling, so a conflict is fatal rather than recoverable.
- **Dependencies installed before startup** — `server.js` requires `express` at line 1; since `node_modules/` is git-ignored, `npm ci` or `npm install` is a prerequisite of `node server.js`.
- **A Node.js 18+ runtime** — the minimum for Express 5; the validation environment ran Node 22.
- **Byte discipline in the handlers** — the response bodies, and the presence or absence of a trailing newline, are verified by inspecting raw bytes rather than by eye.
- **Review of the recorded assumptions** — the endpoint path `/good-evening`, the un-normalized root body, and the `X-Powered-By` header are flagged as open confirmations rather than settled requirements (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.6).

#### 1.2.3.3 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)

No formal KPI, service-level objective, or monitoring contract exists: the repository defines no metrics, no targets, no alerting, and no instrumentation. The indicators below are therefore **derived from the observable purpose of the artifact and from the validation the project recorded**, and any future measurement would have to be introduced along with the observability features that do not exist today.

| Indicator | Definition | Target | Basis |
|-----------|------------|--------|-------|
| Contract fidelity | Share of the two registered routes returning byte-exact bodies | 100% (2/2 recorded) | Byte-level comparison of live responses; `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Route coverage under test | Share of documented paths exercised (two routes plus unregistered and trailing-slash cases) | 100% (9/9 functional checks) | Functional harness and `curl` checks reported in `Project Guide.md` §3, §9.5 |
| Startup success | Share of launches that bind and log within the expected time | 100% on a free port | Live launch verification |
| Dependency integrity | Known vulnerabilities in the installed tree | 0 | `npm audit` over the 66-package tree, `Project Guide.md` §5 |
| Determinism | Share of requests that receive an identical response for a given path, method, and header set | 100% — handlers read no request input | Inspection of `server.js` lines 14–24 |
| Change discipline | Number of files touched relative to the intended change set | 5 of 5, no unrelated edits | `Project Guide.md` §5 compliance table |


## 1.3 Scope

### 1.3.1 In-Scope Elements

#### 1.3.1.1 Core Features and Functionalities

**Must-have capabilities.** These are the capabilities the current implementation delivers and therefore the ones this specification covers:

| Capability | Delivered by | Acceptance condition |
|------------|--------------|----------------------|
| Express application and loopback listener | `server.js` lines 1, 3–6, 26–28 | Binds `127.0.0.1:3000` and logs the startup line verbatim |
| Root greeting endpoint | `server.js` lines 14–18 | `GET /` returns `200`, `text/plain`, `Hello, World!\n` (14 bytes) |
| Second greeting endpoint | `server.js` lines 20–24 | `GET /good-evening` returns `200`, `text/plain`, `Good evening` (12 bytes) |
| Explicit routing with strict paths | `server.js` line 12 | Unregistered paths and trailing-slash variants return `404` |
| Declared and locked dependency | `package.json`, `package-lock.json` | `express ^5.2.1` declared; 66 packages pinned; `npm ci` installs cleanly |
| Install hygiene | `.gitignore` | `node_modules/` is ignored and never committed |
| Documented contract | `README.md` | Dependency, both endpoints, `404` behavior, and run steps are recorded |

**Primary user workflows.** The system supports exactly one operational workflow, and it is the workflow every consumer follows:

1. Install dependencies — `npm ci` (reproducible, from the lockfile) or `npm install`, from the repository root.
2. Start the service — `node server.js`; the process binds `127.0.0.1:3000` and prints `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`.
3. Exercise the contracts — `curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/` returns `Hello, World!`; `curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/good-evening` returns `Good evening`.
4. Observe rejection behavior — any other path, a trailing-slash variant such as `/good-evening/`, or a non-`GET` method returns `404`.
5. Terminate — the process runs until it is externally stopped; the service provides no shutdown path of its own.

A secondary, non-runtime workflow exists for tooling: scanning, hashing, or analyzing the repository as a fixture, including its pathological filenames and the documentation artifacts under `blitzy/documentation/`.

**Essential integrations.** The only integration required to operate the system is install-time access to the public npm registry, from which `package-lock.json` resolves `express@5.2.1` and its 65 transitive packages. Runtime integration is limited to two Express-internal collaborations: the router dispatching registered `GET` paths to handlers, and Express's default `404` handler terminating unmatched requests. No other integration is required, and none exists.

**Key technical requirements.**

| Requirement | Value / constraint |
|-------------|--------------------|
| Runtime | Node.js 18 or newer (Express 5 minimum); validated on Node 22 |
| Module format | CommonJS (`require`), single file, no transpilation, no exports |
| Framework | Express, declared as `^5.2.1` and locked at `5.2.1` |
| Routing surface | Exactly two literal `GET` paths: `/` and `/good-evening`; strict routing enabled |
| Response shape | `text/plain` with byte-exact bodies and no dynamic content |
| Network binding | `127.0.0.1:3000`, hardcoded as module constants |
| Configuration | None — no environment variables, config files, or command-line options |
| Repository layout | Flat, single-directory service with `blitzy/documentation/` as the only subtree |

#### 1.3.1.2 Implementation Boundaries

| Boundary dimension | Scope of this system |
|--------------------|----------------------|
| System boundary | One Node.js process executing `server.js` on one host; no child processes, clusters, or supervisors |
| Network boundary | The loopback interface only (`127.0.0.1`); the service is unreachable from other hosts and is not fronted by a proxy or TLS terminator |
| User groups covered | Local operators who start the process, local HTTP clients and smoke tests on the same host, and tooling that consumes the repository as a fixture |
| Data domains included | None. The only data the service handles are two fixed ASCII response strings; there is no persistent store, no cache, no session, and no request payload handling |
| Configuration boundary | Hardcoded constants in `server.js`; no environment or file-based configuration is read by any code path |
| Code boundary | `server.js` plus its npm manifests; the three filename fixtures, `phonenumber.csv`, `Response.txt`, and the binary artifacts are outside the running system |
| Geographic / market coverage | Not applicable — no network-facing deployment exists and no regional or regulatory dimension applies |

### 1.3.2 Out-of-Scope Elements

#### 1.3.2.1 Explicitly Excluded Features and Capabilities

The following capabilities are verified absent from the current implementation and are excluded from this specification's scope. Absence was established by reading `server.js` in full and by text-searching every code-bearing file in the repository.

| Category | Excluded capability and verification |
|----------|-------------------------------------|
| Routing | Methods other than `GET` — `POST /` returns `404`; no method-specific registration exists. Dynamic, parameterized, or wildcard routes — only two literal strings are registered |
| Request processing | Body, query-string, header, and cookie handling — both handlers accept `req` but never read it; no parsing middleware is installed |
| Configuration | Environment variables and config files — no `process.env` or config read exists in executable code; host and port are literals |
| Security | Authentication, authorization, TLS/HTTPS, input validation, rate limiting, and `X-Powered-By` suppression — none implemented; exposure is limited by the loopback binding instead |
| Persistence | Databases, ORMs, migrations, and file I/O — no driver imports and no file access in application code; startup logging writes to standard output only |
| Resilience | Server `error` handling, graceful shutdown, request-handler exception protection, `clientError` handling, and resource cleanup — specified in `Response.txt` as F-101–F-106 but not implemented |
| Observability | Structured logging, metrics, tracing, and health-check endpoints — the only output is one startup `console.log` |
| Lifecycle | Clustering, process managers, container definitions, and orchestrator manifests — none present |
| Tooling | Automated tests (the `test` script is an npm-init placeholder that exits 1), linters/formatters, CI pipelines, and type checking — none configured |
| Data | Consumption of `phonenumber.csv` — the file is present but imported by nothing |
| Entry point | `index.js` — declared as `package.json#main` but absent from the repository |
| Fixtures | The three pathological-filename scripts — deliberately left on the native `http` implementation and not re-platformed onto Express |

#### 1.3.2.2 Future Phase Considerations

Three candidate future phases are documented in the repository; none is implemented, and none changes the scope described above.

| Future phase | Content | Source and constraint |
|--------------|---------|-----------------------|
| Operational hardening (F-101–F-106) | Server `error` handler, `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` graceful shutdown, handler `try`/`catch`, `clientError` handling, `req`/`res` validation, resource cleanup | `Response.txt`; catalogued in `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §2.3. Constrained to no metadata, dependency, port, hostname, or response-content changes |
| Original `/hello` requirement (F-201) | A path-discriminated `/hello` endpoint returning `"Hello world"` exactly as written | `codebase_context (42).md`; recorded as unmet in `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §2.4.1 |
| Optional quality enhancements | Minimal regression suite (`node:test` with `supertest`), `X-Powered-By` suppression, environment-driven host/port parameterization | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3, marked explicitly outside the delivered work |

Both the hardening programme and the original `/hello` requirement predate or sit beside the delivered change; neither was requested by the requester whose prompt produced the current implementation.

#### 1.3.2.3 Integration Points Not Covered

No integration point is active, and none is planned within the current scope. Specifically excluded are database connectivity, message brokers or queues, outbound HTTP clients, authentication/identity providers, TLS termination and reverse proxying, APM and log-shipping agents, service discovery, and any webhook or event-emitter surface. The system neither exposes nor consumes a third-party interface at runtime; the sole external touchpoint is the install-time fetch of npm packages. Any integration work would constitute a new phase, and — as §1.2.1.3 notes — would require configuration, observability, and lifecycle facilities that do not exist today.

#### 1.3.2.4 Unsupported Use Cases

The following use cases are explicitly not supported by the current implementation, and consumers must not assume otherwise:

- **Any externally reachable deployment.** The listener binds loopback only; exposing it requires additional infrastructure (reverse proxy, TLS termination, or networking changes) that lies outside this scope.
- **Production-grade operation.** There is no shutdown handling, no error recovery on bind failure, no health or readiness surface, no metrics, and no automated regression safety net; the artifact is positioned as a tutorial/integration fixture.
- **Multi-tenant or per-caller behavior.** Every request receives the same response for its path regardless of identity, headers, or origin; there is no authentication, authorization, tenancy, or quota concept.
- **Stateful interactions.** No sessions, cookies, tokens, or state tracking exist; nothing is persisted between requests or across restarts.
- **Content negotiation and alternate representations.** `text/plain` is the only media type; `Accept` headers are ignored because handlers do not read request headers.
- **Internationalization or localization.** Response bodies are fixed ASCII English strings compiled into the source.
- **API versioning or contract compatibility guarantees.** No versioning scheme, deprecation policy, or machine-readable contract (for example OpenAPI) exists; `README.md` prose is the only published description.
- **Dynamic or parameterized content.** There is no templating, path parameter, query processing, or file serving; `/good-evening/` and every other unregistered path return `404`.
- **Running the filename fixtures as equivalent servers.** The three duplicate scripts still return the greeting for every path and expose no `/good-evening` route, so they are not interchangeable with `server.js`.
- **Using the dormant artifacts.** `phonenumber.csv`, the media and document binaries, and `Response.txt` play no role in the running service.

# 2. Product Requirements

## 2.1 Feature Catalog

This section catalogues every requirement-bearing capability observable in `hao-backprop-test` at the current HEAD, in three evidence-based classes: **delivered** capabilities present in executable code, **proposed** capabilities documented in `Response.txt` and never implemented, and the **unmet original requirement** recorded in `codebase_context (42).md`. The repository contains no product backlog, ticketing system, roadmap, or test suite, so every priority label and status value below is inferred from the cited artifacts and states its basis.

Two provenance rules govern the catalogue:

The checked-in `server.js` is an Express 5 application with two explicit routes and one declared dependency, so those items are superseded here. That document concedes the drift itself in §2.7.4: "any modification to `server.js` invalidates F-001 – F-005 acceptance criteria."
- **Existing IDs are retained where a capability survives.** F-001 – F-006 and F-101 – F-106 keep the identifiers used by the repository's documentation set so that prior traceability links still resolve; their content is corrected to the Express implementation. ### 2.1.3 Delivered Features (F-001 – F-010)

#### 2.1.3.1 F-001 Express Application Hosting

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Unique ID | F-001 |
| Feature Name | Express Application Hosting |
| Feature Category | Runtime Framework / Request Pipeline |
| Priority Level | Critical (inferred — the application object is the sole request pipeline) |
| Status | Completed |
| Primary Evidence | `server.js` lines 1 and 6; `package.json` line 12 |

| Description Aspect | Detail |
|--------------------|--------|
| Overview | `server.js` line 1 requires the framework (`const express = require('express')`) and line 6 instantiates the application (`const app = express()`). The Express application is the only request pipeline in the service: Express's bundled `router` dispatches registered literal paths to handlers and its bundled `finalhandler` terminates everything else. This replaces the superseded native `http.createServer((req, res) => …)` construction, which had no pipeline at all (still visible in `Test.test..js` lines 6–10). |
| Business Value | Delivers the requester's explicit ask to "add expressjs into the project" and makes `server.js` "actually use Express to serve requests, not merely have it installed" (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.7). Framework conventions replace hand-rolled request handling, so further literal endpoints cost one `app.get` registration instead of URL-parsing code (§0.4.1). |
| User Benefits | The service exposes a declarative routing table that a reader can verify at a glance: two `app.get` calls are the entire request surface. Adding a third greeting is a three-line change with no impact on the existing routes. |
| Technical Context | Express 5.2.1, CommonJS, single file, no transpilation step, nothing exported. No middleware is registered anywhere — a repository-wide text search finds no `app.use` call. Consequently the transitively installed `body-parser`, `serve-static`, `cookie`, `qs` and `mime-types` packages never execute: the handlers read no request input, so no parser is mounted. Framework defaults observed live at HEAD: `x-powered-by` **enabled** (every response carries `X-Powered-By: Express`), `etag` `"weak"` (never exercised, because handlers use `res.end` rather than `res.send`), `query parser` `simple`, `env` `development`, `trust proxy` `false`. |

| Dependency Type | Detail |
|-----------------|--------|
| Prerequisite Features | None — foundational. All other delivered features are realised inside this application object. |
| System Dependencies | Node.js 18 or newer (the minimum for Express 5); a successful `require('express')` resolution at process start, which in turn requires an install from `package-lock.json` because `node_modules/` is git-ignored |
| External Dependencies | The npm package `express` (declared `^5.2.1`, locked at `5.2.1`) and its 65 transitively installed packages |
| Integration Requirements | None beyond the listener established by F-002. No DI container, service registry, database, or configuration layer exists to integrate with (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.1). |

#### 2.1.3.2 F-002 Loopback Listener Lifecycle

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Unique ID | F-002 |
| Feature Name | Loopback Listener Lifecycle |
| Feature Category | Network Transport / Process Lifecycle |
| Priority Level | Critical (inferred — without the listener nothing is reachable) |
| Status | Completed |
| Primary Evidence | `server.js` lines 3–4 and 26–28; live binding verified on port 3000 |

| Description Aspect | Detail |
|--------------------|--------|
| Overview | `app.listen(port, hostname, callback)` binds the Express application to the loopback interface on port 3000. Express creates and returns an underlying Node.js `http.Server`, so the listener's lifetime, error events and `close()` semantics are Node's, not Express's. The process remains running until it is signalled externally. |
| Business Value | Establishes the deterministic, network-reachable surface that the "backprop" integration target consumes (`README.md`), at an address that is stable across restarts. |
| User Benefits | One `node server.js` invocation yields a predictable endpoint at `http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, with no configuration step and no port selection logic to reason about. |
| Technical Context | Hostname `'127.0.0.1'` (line 3) and port `3000` (line 4) are module-level `const` literals; no `process.env` read, no config module, and no CLI-argument handling exists anywhere in executable code. The listen callback (lines 26–28) is the only startup hook. Because no `error` listener is attached to the returned server, a bind failure surfaces as an unhandled `error` event; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.7 records `EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` as a reachable symptom, and the remediation is manual (free the port or edit the literal). Termination is by external signal only: no `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler exists, and a live `kill -TERM` was observed to end the process with exit code `143` and no shutdown output. |

| Dependency Type | Detail |
|-----------------|--------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 — the listener is started on the Express application object |
| System Dependencies | Node.js `http.Server` (created by `app.listen`); `console` global for the startup line; an available TCP port 3000 on the loopback interface |
| External Dependencies | None at runtime |
| Integration Requirements | A free port 3000 and a functional loopback adapter; a supervisor or operator to terminate the process, since the service provides no shutdown path of its own |

#### 2.1.3.4 F-004 Root Greeting Endpoint (`GET /`)

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Unique ID | F-004 |
| Feature Name | Root Greeting Endpoint (`GET /`) |
| Feature Category | Request/Response Handling |
| Priority Level | Critical (inferred — this is the pre-existing contract the change had to preserve) |
| Status | Completed |
| Primary Evidence | `server.js` lines 14–18; live response `200`, `Content-Length: 14` |

| Description Aspect | Detail |
|--------------------|--------|
| Overview | `app.get('/', …)` answers the root path with status `200`, header `Content-Type: text/plain`, and the byte-exact body `Hello, World!` followed by a newline — 14 bytes. |
| Business Value | Preserves, byte for byte, the contract that existed before the framework migration, so the change remains backward compatible for any consumer and for the integration fixture's golden baseline (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2; `Project Guide.md` §5, FR-C). |
| User Benefits | Existing callers and smoke tests keep working unchanged: `curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/` prints `Hello, World!`. |
| Technical Context | The handler deliberately uses the low-level pattern `res.statusCode = 200; res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain'); res.end('Hello, World!\n')` rather than `res.send(...)`, which guarantees the trailing newline is preserved and that no content-type inference or `ETag` computation occurs (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.5.2). The body is a source literal; `req` is accepted but never read. Two deviations from the pre-migration response are recorded and accepted: the framework adds `X-Powered-By: Express`, and the body's wording remains `Hello, World!` although the requester wrote "Hello world" and `codebase_context (42).md` asked for `"Hello world"` (§0.1.2, flagged for requester confirmation). |

| Dependency Type | Detail |
|-----------------|--------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (pipeline) and F-002 (listener) |
| System Dependencies | Express `res` object supporting the Node `statusCode`/`setHeader`/`end` API |
| External Dependencies | None — the body is a literal |
| Integration Requirements | None; consumers need only reach `127.0.0.1:3000` over plain HTTP |

The endpoint's path was likewise not specified by the requester and was assumed to be `/good-evening` (kebab-case) instead of `/evening` or `/goodevening`. Because Express 5 reserves the characters `( ) [ ] ? + & !` in path patterns, the simple literal path avoids the migration pitfalls that changed path matching (§0.2.2). |

#### 2.1.3.6 F-006 Explicit Routing with Strict Path Matching

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Unique ID | F-006 |
| Feature Name | Explicit Routing with Strict Path Matching |
| Feature Category | Routing / Request Dispatch |
| Priority Level | High (inferred — it defines which requests succeed and which are refused) |
| Status | Completed |
| Primary Evidence | `server.js` line 12 (`app.enable('strict routing')`) and lines 14, 20; observed status codes for matched, unregistered, trailing-slash and non-`GET` requests |

| Description Aspect | Detail |
|--------------------|--------|
| Overview | Exactly two literal `GET` paths are registered — `/` and `/good-evening`. Trailing-slash variants are treated as distinct, unregistered paths because strict routing is enabled, and every other path or method falls through to Express's default `404 Not Found` handler. |
| Business Value | Converts the service from a route-agnostic responder into an endpoint model: the routing contract is explicit and enumerable, which is what a fixture must be for downstream tooling to assert against (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.1, §0.4.2). |
| User Benefits | Predictable semantics: a request to a documented path returns content, and any typo, trailing slash, or unsupported method fails loudly with `404` instead of silently receiving a greeting. |
| Technical Context | Strict routing was applied as a QA refinement (commit `f2c2ca4`) after the initial re-platform, so `/good-evening/` returns `404` rather than content (`Project Guide.md` §5, QA Issue 1). Two Express defaults remain in force and are observable: matching is **case-insensitive** (because `case sensitive routing` is not enabled — `GET /GOOD-EVENING` returns `200`), and query strings do not affect matching (`GET /?x=1` returns `200`). Express also answers `HEAD` from the `GET` registration and `OPTIONS` with `200` and `Allow: GET, HEAD`; `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE` and `PATCH` on a registered path return `404`. The `404` response is Express's default HTML body (`Cannot GET <path>`) served with `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. |

| Dependency Type | Detail |
|-----------------|--------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 — the routing table belongs to the Express application object |
| System Dependencies | Express `router` (route matching) and `finalhandler` (default `404`) |
| External Dependencies | None |
| Integration Requirements | Consumers must construct requests against the exact registered literals; the trailing-slash and case behaviours are contract details, not configurable options, because no configuration surface exists |

|--------------------|--------|
| Overview | `package.json` declares exactly one runtime dependency, `"express": "^5.2.1"`, and `package-lock.json` pins the resolved tree: `express@5.2.1` plus 65 transitive packages, 66 package entries in total, each with a `registry.npmjs.org` tarball URL and a `sha512-…` integrity digest. `.gitignore` excludes `node_modules/` so the repository stays source-only. |
| Business Value | Makes the first third-party dependency in the project's history reproducible and auditable: `npm ci` reproduces the exact tree from the committed lockfile, and the pinned digests give each artifact a verifiable identity (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.3.1). |
| User Benefits | A fresh checkout installs deterministically with one command; reviewers can see the full footprint (0 → 66 packages) without inspecting `node_modules/`. |
| Technical Context | The declared range `^5.2.1` permits any 5.x release at or above 5.2.1, so the lockfile — not the manifest — is what guarantees reproducibility; `Project Guide.md` §6 records this as a low, mitigated risk. Express 5.2.1 declares 28 direct dependencies, including `router` (the routing engine behind `app.get`), `finalhandler` (the default `404`), `body-parser`, `qs`, `http-errors`, `statuses`, `accepts`/`type-is`/`mime-types`, `cookie`/`cookie-signature`, and `debug` (§0.3.1). The manifest also carries pre-existing inconsistencies that this feature deliberately left alone: `main` points to `index.js`, which does not exist in the repository, and the `test` script is the unmodified npm-init placeholder. |

| Dependency Type | Detail |
|-----------------|--------|
| Prerequisite Features | None; it is instead a prerequisite of F-001 — `require('express')` cannot resolve until the tree is installed |
| System Dependencies | npm CLI (7 or newer, to install a `lockfileVersion` 3 tree); access to a `node_modules/` path writable by the installing user |
| External Dependencies | The public npm registry (`registry.npmjs.org`) at install time, for all 66 packages |
| Integration Requirements | Install must precede startup, because `node_modules/` is git-ignored and therefore absent from a fresh checkout (`Project Guide.md` §9.3) |

### 2.1.4 Documented but Unimplemented Features (F-101 – F-106, F-201)

The seven features in this subsection are catalogued for completeness and traceability. None is present in executable code: `server.js` contains no `process.on`, no `try`, no `catch`, no `server.on`, and no header-disabling call, and the only route registrations in the repository are the two in F-004 and F-005.

**Provenance and scope note for F-101 – F-106.** All six come from `Response.txt`, a JSON-wrapped Agent Action Plan for a hardening bug fix. That plan targets the superseded native-`http` implementation — its line references (`server.js` lines 6–26) describe `http.createServer`, which no longer exists in `server.js` — and its §0.5 constraints assert that `package.json`, `package-lock.json` and `README.md` must not be modified, that no npm package may be added, and that "Express.js or other frameworks" is out of scope. The delivered change contradicts each of those constraints, and `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2 records the ruling that resolves the conflict: the zero-dependency posture belongs "exclusively to the separate, not-yet-implemented `Response.txt` hardening remediation", and the requester's explicit instruction to add Express governs. The proposals therefore survive as work items, but their assumptions must be re-derived against the Express application before any of them is implemented; the underlying Node.js `http.Server` that `app.listen` returns still emits `error` and `clientError` and still exposes `close()`, so the technical intent remains reachable.

#### 2.1.4.2 F-102 Graceful Shutdown on SIGTERM/SIGINT

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Unique ID | F-102 |
| Feature Name | Graceful Shutdown on SIGTERM/SIGINT |
| Feature Category | Lifecycle / Resilience |
| Priority Level | High (per `Response.txt` §0.1) |
| Status | Proposed (not implemented) |
| Primary Evidence | `Response.txt` §0.4 "Changes #4 and #5"; absence in `server.js`; observed exit code `143` on `SIGTERM` |

| Description Aspect | Detail |
|--------------------|--------|
| Overview | A `gracefulShutdown(signal)` function invoked from `process.on('SIGTERM')` and `process.on('SIGINT')` handlers calls `server.close()` to stop accepting connections, then forces exit after a 10-second timeout if connections do not drain. |
| Business Value | Prevents in-flight request loss on orchestrator-driven termination and on operator `Ctrl+C`. |
| User Benefits | Cleaner restart cycles and predictable termination semantics, including an exit code of 0 on a drained shutdown. |
| Technical Context | Today no signal handler exists, so the runtime's default disposition applies and the process dies immediately with exit code `143`. This feature and F-106 are introduced together, the cleanup hook running inside the `close` callback. |

| Dependency Type | Detail |
|-----------------|--------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-002; F-106 (the cleanup hook executes inside this feature's close callback) |
| System Dependencies | Node.js `process` global; `server.close()`; `setTimeout` for the force-exit guard |
| External Dependencies | None |
| Integration Requirements | An operator or orchestrator that sends `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` |

### 2.1.5 Features Excluded from This Catalogue

Three further candidate enhancements are documented in the repository and are recorded here as **not features of this system**, because the delivering documentation places them explicitly outside the work performed: a minimal automated regression suite (`node:test` with `supertest`) recorded as "Optional, out of AAP scope" (`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.6, §2.3), suppression of the `X-Powered-By` header via `app.disable('x-powered-by')` (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2), and environment-variable parameterisation of host and port (`Project Guide.md` §2.3). None is implemented; each carries documented effort of approximately 2.0h, 0.25h and 1.0h respectively. They are carried forward as maintenance considerations in §2.4.5 rather than as requirements.

## 2.2 Functional Requirements Table

### 2.2.1 Requirement Conventions

Every functional requirement below carries the identifier `<feature-id>-RQ-<NNN>`, so a requirement's parent feature is legible from its ID alone. Priorities use the MoSCoW scale; complexity rates implementation effort for the smallest change that satisfies the requirement.

| Dimension | Values and Meaning |
|-----------|--------------------|
| Priority | **Must-Have** — the delivered or proposed behaviour fails without it; **Should-Have** — a documented property whose loss degrades the contract or its verifiability; **Could-Have** — observed Express default behaviour recorded so a test can rely on it |
| Complexity | **High** — cross-cutting or requiring new lifecycle machinery; **Medium** — more than a literal change or with platform-dependent behaviour; **Low** — a literal, a single call, or a present-or-absent file |
| Verification basis | The repository ships **no automated suite**: the `test` script in `package.json` is the npm-init placeholder that prints `Error: no test specified` and exits `1`. Acceptance criteria are therefore stated as externally observable HTTP, install, or file-system facts and were re-verified against HEAD by launching `node server.js` on Node v22.23.3 and issuing live requests. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 records the parallel 9/9 functional harness and 15/15 total checks. |
| Table format | Requirement detail tables carry four columns (`Requirement ID`, `Description`, `Priority`, `Complexity`). Technical specifications and validation rules are given per feature as an attribute table with two columns. |

### 2.2.2 Delivered Feature Requirements (F-001 – F-010)

#### 2.2.2.1 F-001 Express Application Hosting

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | `server.js` SHALL obtain the framework through CommonJS `require('express')` and create the application by calling the factory once, at module scope | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-002 | The application SHALL register no middleware; request handling SHALL consist solely of literal route registrations and Express's built-in terminal handlers | Should-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-003 | `server.js` SHALL define the whole service in one executed file, exporting nothing and requiring no other project file | Must-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | F-001-RQ-001: `server.js` line 1 is `const express = require('express')` and line 6 is `const app = express()`; the process starts without a module-resolution error once dependencies are installed. F-001-RQ-002: a text search across every `.js` file finds no `app.use` call and no `app.param`; the only Express API calls in the repository are `express()`, `app.enable`, `app.get` (×2) and `app.listen`. F-001-RQ-003: the repository contains exactly four `.js` files, only one of which is the entry point; `server.js` contains no `module.exports` and no `require` of a local path. |
| Input Parameters | None — the factory takes no arguments and no configuration object |
| Output / Response | A configured Express application instance held in the module-level `app` binding; request dispatch delegated to Express's router and default final handler |
| Performance Criteria | Instantiation is synchronous and completes before the listener is created; no framework-internal asynchronous work occurs at construction |
| Data Requirements | None — no configuration file, environment variable, or default-value table is read |
| Business Rules | Framework adoption is the deliverable the requester asked for and must be real, not merely installed: Express must serve the requests (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.7). The single-file, CommonJS convention must be preserved (§0.1.2). |
| Data Validation | None — no request data is parsed, so no validation of parsed input is possible or required |
| Security Requirements | Express defaults are inherited unmodified: `x-powered-by` remains enabled, advertising the framework on every response; `etag` remains `"weak"` but is never exercised because handlers call `res.end` rather than `res.send` |
| Compliance Requirements | MIT licence terms of `express` and of the 65 packages in its resolved tree |

#### 2.2.2.2 F-002 Loopback Listener Lifecycle

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | The listener SHALL bind the loopback host `127.0.0.1` | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-002 | The listener SHALL bind TCP port `3000`, with no fallback port selection | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-003 | The listen callback SHALL execute exactly once on successful bind, and the process SHALL then remain running until externally signalled | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-004 | Process termination SHALL occur through the runtime's default signal disposition, with no shutdown hook of the application's own | Could-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | F-002-RQ-001: an inspecting tool shows the socket bound to `127.0.0.1:3000`, and the host is not reachable from a non-loopback address. F-002-RQ-002: the socket is on port `3000`; starting a second instance while the first runs produces `EADDRINUSE` rather than a shift to another port. F-002-RQ-003: `node server.js` prints the startup line once and the process persists, serving requests indefinitely. F-002-RQ-004: `kill -TERM <pid>` ends the process with exit code `143` and no shutdown output — observed. |
| Input Parameters | None — `hostname` and `port` are module-level `const` literals (`server.js` lines 3–4) |
| Output / Response | An open TCP listener on the loopback interface; the callback returns nothing |
| Performance Criteria | Bind completes during process start-up; no retry, back-off, or timeout logic exists. `Response.txt` §0.6 offers aspirational figures for the superseded implementation (under 50 ms per request, under 50 MB RSS, 100+ concurrent connections); none is a committed objective of this build |
| Data Requirements | None |
| Business Rules | A free port 3000 and a functional loopback interface are preconditions, not guarantees the service can restore: no `error` listener is attached to the server returned by `app.listen`, so `EADDRINUSE` is surfaced as an unhandled error event (`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.7 records it as a known symptom with a manual remedy). Loopback binding is the service's entire exposure boundary. |
| Data Validation | None |
| Security Requirements | Loopback-only binding; plain HTTP with no TLS, no authentication, and no client-address filtering. Any local process can reach the service. |
| Compliance Requirements | None documented |

#### 2.2.2.3 F-003 Startup Console Logging

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-003-RQ-001 | Exactly one line SHALL be written to standard output on successful bind | Must-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-002 | The line SHALL contain the bound host and port | Should-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-003 | No other application log output SHALL be produced: no per-request, error, or shutdown lines | Should-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | F-003-RQ-001/RQ-002: standard output is exactly `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` followed by a newline. F-003-RQ-003: after serving requests and after termination, standard output contains no further line. |
| Input Parameters | None |
| Output / Response | One `console.log` write per process lifetime, emitted from the listen callback (`server.js` line 27) |
| Performance Criteria | Not applicable — a single synchronous write during start-up |
| Data Requirements | The `hostname` and `port` constants, interpolated into a template literal |
| Business Rules | The message is the documented readiness signal; because it is emitted from the listen callback, its appearance implies a successful bind. Log level, destination and format are not configurable. |
| Data Validation | None |
| Security Requirements | The line carries no secret, credential, or personal data: only the public loopback address |
| Compliance Requirements | None |

#### 2.2.2.4 F-004 Root Greeting Endpoint (`GET /`)

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-004-RQ-001 | `GET /` SHALL return status `200` | Must-Have | Low |
| F-004-RQ-002 | The response SHALL carry `Content-Type: text/plain` | Must-Have | Low |
| F-004-RQ-003 | The response body SHALL be byte-exact `Hello, World!` followed by a single `LF` — 14 bytes in total | Must-Have | Low |
| F-004-RQ-004 | The handler SHALL read no request input, so the response is independent of method-adjacent headers, query string and body | Must-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | F-004-RQ-001/RQ-002: a live `GET /` returns `200 OK` with `Content-Type: text/plain`. F-004-RQ-003: `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/ \| od -c` shows `Hello, World!\n` with no additional bytes; `Content-Length: 14`. F-004-RQ-004: `GET /?x=1` returns the same 14-byte body. |
| Input Parameters | The Express request object, accepted by the handler signature and never dereferenced |
| Output / Response | `200`, `text/plain`, 14-byte body; the response also carries `X-Powered-By: Express` and no `ETag` |
| Performance Criteria | Three synchronous statements — status assignment, header set, `res.end` — with no I/O, allocation of dynamic content, or computation |
| Data Requirements | The body is a source literal; nothing is read from disk, memory, or a client |
| Business Rules | The body, including its trailing newline, must not change: it is the pre-migration contract the change was required to preserve byte-for-byte (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2, FR-C; `Project Guide.md` §5). The handler must use `res.statusCode`/`res.setHeader`/`res.end` rather than `res.send`, because `res.send` of a string would infer `text/html` and compute an entity tag (§0.5.2). |
| Data Validation | None on the request; the body is validated by byte comparison in testing |
| Security Requirements | No request data is consumed, removing injection vectors at the handler. `X-Powered-By` advertises the framework; suppression would require `app.disable('x-powered-by')` and is documented as optional, not implemented |
| Compliance Requirements | None |

| F-006-RQ-004 | Requests using `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE` or `PATCH` on a registered path SHALL be answered `404`; `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` SHALL follow Express's defaults | Should-Have | Low |
| F-006-RQ-005 | Path matching SHALL remain case-insensitive and unaffected by the query string | Could-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | F-006-RQ-001: a repository-wide search for route registrations finds exactly `app.get('/')` and `app.get('/good-evening')`. F-006-RQ-002: `GET /good-evening/` returns `404` (observed); the setting is active as `app.get('strict routing') === true` after `app.enable`. F-006-RQ-003: `GET /does-not-exist` returns `404` with a 153-byte `text/html` body reading `Cannot GET /does-not-exist`, plus `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. F-006-RQ-004: `POST /` → `404`, while `HEAD /` → `200` and `OPTIONS /` → `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD`. F-006-RQ-005: `GET /GOOD-EVENING` → `200`, and `GET /?x=1` → `200`. |
| Input Parameters | The request method and path, matched by Express's router against registered literals |
| Output / Response | The matched handler's response, or Express's default `404` HTML body for anything unmatched |
| Performance Criteria | Literal-string matching with two candidates; no regular-expression evaluation and no route-parameter decoding occurs |
| Data Requirements | The registered path table, held in the application object; no external route configuration exists |
| Business Rules | The route table is closed: only the two registered literals serve content, and any other request must fail rather than fall back to a greeting. This behavioural change from the superseded catch-all is documented and accepted (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2; `Project Guide.md` §4). Strict routing was applied as QA Issue 1 after the initial re-platform (`Project Guide.md` §5). |
| Data Validation | Path and method are validated implicitly by the router; no application-level validation exists |
| Security Requirements | Unknown paths and unsupported methods are refused rather than silently answered, which removes the previous ability to probe the service with arbitrary paths and receive a `200`. The `404` response sets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy` by framework default |
| Compliance Requirements | None |

F-007-RQ-003: `npm ci` completes with `added 66 packages` and exit status 0; `npm ls` prints `hello_world@1.0.0` and `└── express@5.2.1` with no unmet peer. ### 2.2.3 Proposed Feature Requirements (F-101 – F-106)

Requirements in this subsection are **not implemented**. Each acceptance criterion below states what the originating plan requires, not what the service does; the "as-built" column of §2.5 states the current position for each. All six are governed by the same recorded constraints, and all six carry the provenance caveat of §2.1.4: the plan targets the superseded native-`http` file and forbids the dependency and route changes that have since been made, so its target must be re-derived against the Express application before implementation.

#### 2.2.3.1 F-101 Server-Level `error` Event Handler

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-101-RQ-001 | An `error` listener on the server SHALL recognise at least `EADDRINUSE` and `EACCES` and log an actionable diagnostic | Must-Have | Low |
| F-101-RQ-002 | After logging, the process SHALL exit with status `1` instead of crashing on an unhandled error event | Must-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | Starting a second instance while port 3000 is held logs an `already in use` message and the process exits with code `1` (`Response.txt` §0.6). |
| Input Parameters | The error object emitted by the server; its `code` property distinguishes the failure class |
| Output / Response | A diagnostic line on standard error, then process termination |
| Performance Criteria | Not specified; the handler runs once per fatal error |
| Data Requirements | The port literal, interpolated into the diagnostic message |
| Business Rules | Logging must use Node built-ins only — the plan forbids adding a logging library (`Response.txt` §0.4, §0.5) |
| Data Validation | The error code is matched against a fixed set; unrecognised codes still log and exit |
| Security Requirements | Messages must not disclose credentials; the plan logs the port number and the error message only |
| Compliance Requirements | None |

#### 2.2.3.2 F-102 Graceful Shutdown on SIGTERM/SIGINT

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-102-RQ-001 | Signal handlers SHALL be registered for both `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` | Must-Have | Low |
| F-102-RQ-002 | `server.close()` SHALL be invoked exactly once per signal, stopping acceptance of new connections | Must-Have | Medium |
| F-102-RQ-003 | A force-exit guard SHALL terminate the process if connections have not drained within 10 seconds | Must-Have | Medium |
| F-102-RQ-004 | A drained shutdown SHALL exit with status `0` | Should-Have | Low |

| Attribute | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Acceptance Criteria | Sending `SIGTERM` prints the signal name and a shutdown start message; on drained connections the process exits `0`; if connections remain open, the guard prints a forced-shutdown line and exits `1` (`Response.txt` §0.6). Currently a `SIGTERM` produces exit code `143` with no output. |
| Input Parameters | The signal name, passed to the shutdown function by each handler |
| Output / Response | Shutdown progress lines on standard output, then process termination |
| Performance Criteria | Connections must be given up to 10 seconds to finish before forced termination |
| Data Requirements | None |
| Business Rules | The process must not terminate while in-flight requests to `/` or `/good-evening` remain unanswered; the shutdown path must remain dependency-free |
| Data Validation | None |
| Security Requirements | Signal handlers are reachable only by local processes with permission to signal the process; they introduce no network surface |
| Compliance Requirements | Container convention: orchestrators send `SIGTERM` and expect a bounded, clean exit |

|-----------|---------------|

| Input Parameters | The thrown error object; the response's `headersSent` flag |
| Output / Response | A `500`, `text/plain`, `Internal Server Error` body when a response is still possible; otherwise a log line only |

| Data Requirements | None |
| Business Rules | The response must not be written twice; the `headersSent` check is mandatory |
| Data Validation | None |
| Security Requirements | The catch block must not echo internal error detail to the client; the plan returns a fixed body |
| Compliance Requirements | None |
