## 2.3 Feature Relationships

### 2.3.1 Feature Dependency Map

The diagram records only relationships visible in the source artifacts. Solid arrows are realised in code at HEAD; dotted arrows are documented proposals that carry no implementation. F-010 (the orphan data fixture) has no edge at all: nothing reads it. F-009 connects to the delivered features only by shared lineage — the fixtures embody the implementation that F-001, F-004 and F-006 replaced.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Platform[Platform and Runtime]
        HTTPMOD["http core module<br/>http.Server"]
        CONSOLE["console global"]
        PROC["process global"]
        NPMREG["npm registry<br/>install time only"]
    end

    subgraph Delivered[Delivered Features]
        F001["F-001 Express Application"]
        F002["F-002 Loopback Listener"]
        F003["F-003 Startup Log"]
        F004["F-004 GET /"]
        F005["F-005 GET /good-evening"]
        F006["F-006 Explicit Routing"]
        F007["F-007 Dependency Graph"]
        F008["F-008 README Contract"]
        F009["F-009 Filename Fixtures"]
        F010["F-010 Orphan CSV"]
    end

    subgraph Proposed[Proposed Features — Not Implemented]
        F101["F-101 error handler"]
        F102["F-102 Graceful shutdown"]
        F103["F-103 try/catch"]
        F104["F-104 clientError"]
        F105["F-105 req/res guard"]
        F106["F-106 Cleanup hook"]
        F201["F-201 /hello route"]
    end

    NPMREG -.->|"express@5.2.1 plus 65 packages"| F007
    F007 -->|"require resolves"| F001
    HTTPMOD -->|"app.listen creates the server"| F002
    CONSOLE --> F003
    PROC -.->|"proposed signal handling"| F102
    F001 --> F002
    F001 --> F006
    F006 --> F004
    F006 --> F005
    F002 --> F003
    F004 --> F008
    F005 --> F008
    F007 -.->|"documents the dependency"| F008
    F004 -.->|"shared lineage, now diverged"| F009
    F002 -.->|"proposed"| F101
    F002 -.->|"proposed"| F104
    F004 -.->|"proposed"| F103
    F005 -.->|"proposed"| F103
    F004 -.->|"proposed"| F105
    F102 -.->|"proposed"| F106
    F006 -.->|"would be one registration"| F201
```

The relationships the diagram encodes, in the order they matter to a reader:

| Relationship | Kind | Evidence |
|--------------|------|----------|
| F-007 → F-001 | Hard prerequisite: `require('express')` cannot resolve until the 66-package tree is installed, so an uninstalled checkout cannot start | `server.js` line 1; `.gitignore`; `Project Guide.md` §9.7 `Cannot find module 'express'` |
| F-001 → F-006 → {F-004, F-005} | Composition: the routing table belongs to the application object, and both endpoints are rows in it | `server.js` lines 6, 12, 14, 20 |
| F-001 → F-002, F-002 → F-003 | Lifecycle ordering: the listener is started on the application object, and the only log line is emitted from the listen callback | `server.js` lines 26–28 |
| F-004, F-005 → F-008 | Documentation obligation: the README describes both responses, so it goes stale the moment either body or path changes | `README.md` lines 9–12 |
| F-004 → F-009 | Historical lineage only: the fixtures preserve the pre-migration implementation, and their byte-identity with `server.js` was deliberately broken | md5 `a423b6d4…` for `server.js` versus `05576d40…` for the three fixtures; `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2 |
| F-101 – F-106 → F-002, F-004, F-005 | Proposed extensions only: the resilience features attach to the listener or wrap the handlers, and none is present | `Response.txt` §0.4; absence of `process.on`, `try`, `catch` and `server.on` in `server.js` |
| F-201 → F-006 | Would-be sibling of the two endpoints, requiring one more `app.get` registration and no other change | `codebase_context (42).md`; observed `404` for `GET /hello` |

Two relationship-level conflicts are recorded rather than resolved. First, the F-101 – F-106 proposals rest on a scope ruling that the delivered change has already broken: their plan forbids modifying `package.json`, `package-lock.json` and `README.md`, forbids adding any npm package, and places "Express.js or other frameworks" out of scope, whereas FR-A, FR-B and the README update were the delivered work. Second, the earlier catalogue's F-005-RQ-001 required the fixtures to remain byte-identical to `server.js`, which the re-platform made impossible; `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2 accepts the divergence, and the superseded requirement is restated as F-009-RQ-004 in §2.2.2.9.

### 2.3.2 Integration Points

The service integrates with nothing at runtime beyond its own loopback socket and standard output. There is no database driver, message broker, outbound HTTP client, cache, identity provider, TLS terminator, proxy, service-discovery entry, log shipper, metrics agent, or webhook surface anywhere in the repository; the sole external touchpoint is an install-time fetch.

| Integration Point | Status | Source |
|-------------------|--------|--------|
| Loopback HTTP listener on `127.0.0.1:3000` | Active — the only network interface | F-002; `server.js` lines 3–4, 26–28 |
| Standard output (single startup line) | Active — the only outbound observability channel | F-003; `server.js` line 27 |
| Public npm registry (`registry.npmjs.org`) | Active at install time only, for 66 packages | F-007; `package-lock.json` `resolved` and `integrity` fields |
| Express router and default `404` handler | Active in-process collaboration | F-006; observed `404` bodies |
| Databases, queues, outbound HTTP, identity providers, TLS terminators, APM agents | Absent — verified by text search across all code-bearing files | §1.2.1.3, §1.3.2.3 |
| Machine-readable API contract (for example OpenAPI) | Absent — `README.md` prose is the only published contract | F-008 |

### 2.3.3 Shared Components

| Shared Element | Sharing Pattern | Features Involved |
|----------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| `hostname` and `port` constants (`'127.0.0.1'`, `3000`) | Declared once at module scope and consumed by both the bind and the startup message, so the logged URL cannot disagree with the bound address | F-002, F-003 |
| `res.statusCode` / `res.setHeader` / `res.end` response pattern | Reused verbatim by both handlers to guarantee byte-exact bodies and to bypass `res.send`'s content-type inference | F-004, F-005 |
| Express `app` object | The single object that owns the routing table and starts the listener | F-001, F-002, F-006 |
| `app.get(path, handler)` registration API | The one extension point for adding an endpoint; no router module, controller, or route file exists | F-004, F-005, F-006, and F-201 if implemented |
| `package.json` and `package-lock.json` | Declare the dependency and pin its resolved tree; both are inputs to the install that makes the service runnable | F-007, F-001 |
| Native-`http` server source | Duplicated byte-for-byte across three fixtures, and no longer shared with `server.js` | F-009; historical lineage to F-001, F-004, F-006 |
| `README.md` | The single prose contract that describes both endpoints and the `404` rule | F-008, F-004, F-005, F-006 |

### 2.3.4 Common Services

| Common Service | Provided By | Features That Depend On It |
|----------------|-------------|----------------------------|
| Node.js HTTP server and socket handling | The `http` core module, instantiated by `app.listen` | F-002, and transitively F-004, F-005, F-006 |
| Request dispatch and unmatched-request termination | Express `router` and `finalhandler`, bundled inside the installed tree | F-006, F-004, F-005 |
| Process lifecycle and signal delivery | The Node.js runtime's default signal disposition, since the application installs no handler | F-002 (current behaviour); F-102 would replace it |
| Standard-output stream | The Node.js `console` global | F-003 |
| Dependency resolution and integrity verification | npm CLI against the public registry, driven by the committed lockfile | F-007, F-001 |

No application-level shared service exists: there is no logging abstraction, no configuration service, no correlation or request-identifier scheme, and no error-classification layer. Every capability above is provided by the runtime or by a dependency rather than by project code.

## 2.4 Implementation Considerations

### 2.4.1 Technical Constraints

| Constraint | Affected Features | Source |
|------------|-------------------|--------|
| Port 3000 must be free; no fallback selection and no `error` listener, so a conflict is fatal | F-002, F-101 | `server.js` lines 4, 26; `Project Guide.md` §9.7 |
| Loopback-only binding — the service is unreachable from any other host and is not fronted by TLS or a proxy | F-002, F-004, F-005, F-006 | `server.js` line 3; §1.3.1.2 |
| Dependencies must be installed before startup: line 1 requires `express`, and `node_modules/` is git-ignored | F-001, F-007 | `server.js` line 1; `.gitignore`; `Project Guide.md` §9.7 |
| Node.js 18 or newer is required by Express 5, yet `package.json` declares no `engines` field, so the constraint is unenforced | F-001, F-007 | `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.2.2; `package.json` |
| Hostname and port are `const` literals; no environment variable, config file, or CLI argument is read anywhere in executable code | F-002, F-003 | `server.js` lines 3–4; repository-wide search for `process.env` |
| CommonJS, single file, no transpilation and no exports — the file is executed, not imported | F-001, F-009 | `server.js`; absence of `module.exports` and of `index.js` |
| `package.json#main` declares `index.js`, which does not exist, so the only working entry point is `node server.js` | F-007, F-008 | `package.json` line 5; no such file in the repository |
| No automated test suite: the `test` script prints `Error: no test specified` and exits `1` by design | All features | `package.json` lines 6–8; `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Response bodies are fixed literals, including the presence of a trailing newline on `/` and its absence on `/good-evening` | F-004, F-005 | `server.js` lines 17, 23 |
| Express 5 reserves the characters `( ) [ ] ? + & !` in path patterns, constraining the naming of any future route | F-006, F-201 | `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.2.2 |
| The hardening proposals forbid adding dependencies, routes, or manifest changes — constraints the delivered change already violated | F-101 – F-106 | `Response.txt` §0.5; `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2 |
| The three fixtures bind the same loopback address and port, so a fixture cannot run concurrently with the service | F-009 | Fixture sources; `server.js` lines 3–4 |

### 2.4.2 Performance Requirements

The repository commits to **no formal performance requirement, service-level objective, or latency budget**. No metric, target, alert threshold or instrumentation exists anywhere in the code or documentation set. The objectives below are therefore derived from the artifact's stated purpose and from the validation the project recorded; they are acceptance signals for correctness and determinism, not throughput commitments.

| Objective | Target | Basis |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Startup succeeds and binds on a free port | 100% of launches | Startup line observed on every launch; `Project Guide.md` §4 |
| Registered routes return byte-exact bodies | 100% (2 of 2) | `od -c` byte comparisons; `Project Guide.md` §3, §5 |
| Determinism: identical response for a given path, method and query | 100% | Handlers read no request input; live re-verification at HEAD |
| Recorded functional checks pass | 15 of 15 | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Response latency | No target. `Response.txt` §0.6 proposes under 50 ms, under 50 MB RSS and 100+ concurrent connections, but those figures belong to the unimplemented hardened variant and are not committed here | `Response.txt` §0.6 |

Handler cost is three synchronous statements with no I/O, no allocation of dynamic content, and no computation, so any request latency is dominated by the Node.js HTTP stack and the client's own loopback round trip. There is no caching layer, no connection pooling, and no timeout configuration to tune.

### 2.4.3 Scalability Considerations

| Dimension | Disposition |
|-----------|-------------|
| Process model | A single Node.js process on one host; no cluster, no worker threads, no child processes, and no process manager |
| Concurrency model | The event loop with synchronous, non-blocking handlers; no promises, streams, timers or asynchronous callbacks in application code |
| Horizontal scaling | Not supported. The loopback binding and hardcoded port prevent running two instances on one host, and nothing allows an upstream load balancer to reach the service |
| Vertical scaling | Bounded only by the runtime; the application adds no memory-resident state beyond the loaded dependency tree of 66 packages |
| Load balancing | Not applicable — no proxying or upstream exists, so there is no scaling axis to balance |
| State and persistence | None. No session, cache, database or shared state, so instances would be trivially interchangeable if the port and binding were parameterised |
| Capacity controls | None. No rate limiting, no maximum-connection setting, no back-pressure, and no queue |

### 2.4.4 Security Implications

The exposure boundary is the loopback binding, not any security control: the service is reachable by every local process, and the application implements no authentication, authorisation, encryption, or input validation.

| Security Consideration | Status | Affected Features |
|------------------------|--------|-------------------|
| Network exposure | Loopback only (`127.0.0.1`); unreachable from other hosts | F-002, F-004, F-005, F-006 |
| Authentication and authorisation | Absent — no account, token, or access-control concept exists | All delivered features |
| Transport encryption | Absent — plain HTTP; no TLS terminator, certificate, or HTTPS listener | F-002 |
| Framework disclosure | `X-Powered-By: Express` is emitted on every response, including `404`s; suppression via `app.disable('x-powered-by')` is documented as optional and is not implemented | F-001, F-004, F-005 |
| Request input handling | No request data is read by any handler and no parsing middleware is mounted, so the injection surface is minimal — but there is likewise no validation, sanitisation, or content negotiation | F-001, F-004, F-005 |
| Availability under failure | A held port yields an unhandled error event, and `SIGTERM` terminates without draining; both are stability risks, and F-101, F-102 and F-104 are the documented, unimplemented remediations | F-002, F-101, F-102, F-104 |
| Dependency supply chain | The surface grew from zero to 66 packages; integrity rests on the pinned `sha512` digests in the lockfile, and `npm audit` reported zero known vulnerabilities when the project was validated — a point-in-time result, not a standing guarantee | F-007, F-001 |
| Sensitive data handling | No credential, secret, personal datum, or token exists in the repository; the only log line carries a public loopback address | F-003, F-010 |
| Dormant artifacts | `phonenumber.csv` (synthetic data), the media and document binaries, and `Response.txt` are unreferenced by code and expose no runtime surface | F-010 |
| Proposed features | F-101 – F-106 improve resilience and error observability and explicitly introduce no authentication, TLS, or authorisation | F-101 – F-106 |

### 2.4.5 Maintenance Requirements

| Maintenance Concern | Current State | Affected Features |
|---------------------|---------------|-------------------|
| Automated regression tests | None. The `test` script exits `1` by design, so contract changes rely on manual `curl` checks | All features |
| Linting and formatting | No linter or formatter configuration exists | All features |
| CI/CD | No `.github/` directory, pipeline file, or automated gate | All features |
| Containerisation | No `Dockerfile` or compose file; deployment is manual process start | F-002, F-102 |
| Type checking | None — plain JavaScript, no `tsconfig.json` | F-001 |
| Runtime version pinning | None — no `engines` field, so Node.js 18+ is a documented rather than enforced requirement | F-001, F-007 |
| Dependency currency | The manifest permits minor and patch upgrades through `^5.2.1`, making lockfile discipline and periodic `npm audit` the only integrity controls | F-007 |
| Contract documentation upkeep | `README.md` is the only published contract, so it must be revised with any change to a body, a path, the dependency, or the bound address | F-008, F-004, F-005, F-006 |
| Specification freshness | The repository's own `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` describes the superseded native-`http`, zero-dependency state and its §2.7.4 concedes that "any modification to `server.js` invalidates F-001 – F-005 acceptance criteria"; the documentation set needs reconciliation with the Express implementation | F-001 – F-008 |
| Fixture upkeep | The three filename fixtures are retained unchanged, deliberately no longer byte-identical to `server.js`; any future requirement for behavioural parity would mean re-platforming all three | F-009 |
| Manifest inconsistencies | `package.json#main` points at an absent `index.js`, and the `test` script is a placeholder; both were deliberately left untouched and remain latent traps for tooling that trusts the manifest | F-007, F-008 |
| Dormant artifacts | `phonenumber.csv`, the media and document binaries, and `Response.txt` are unreferenced; they add repository noise but no runtime obligation | F-010 |
| Documented deferred enhancements | Three candidates are recorded as outside the delivered work: a minimal regression suite (`node:test` with `supertest`, about 2.0h), `X-Powered-By` suppression (about 0.25h), and environment-variable parameterisation of host and port (about 1.0h) | F-001, F-002, F-007, F-008 |
| Deferred hardening initiative | F-101 – F-106 remain unimplemented and, because their plan assumes the superseded implementation, must be re-derived against the Express application before they are attempted | F-101 – F-106 |

### 2.4.6 Per-Feature Consideration Summary

| Feature | Dominant Technical Constraint | Security Implication | Maintenance Obligation |
|---------|-------------------------------|----------------------|------------------------|
| F-001 Express Application Hosting | CommonJS single file; Express 5 needs Node ≥18, unenforced by the manifest | Framework disclosure through `X-Powered-By`; no middleware means no input parsing | Re-derive any change against Express 5 path-matching rules; keep the single-file convention |
| F-002 Loopback Listener Lifecycle | Free port 3000, hardcoded host and port, no bind-error handling | Loopback is the whole exposure boundary; plain HTTP only | Operators must free the port and terminate the process externally |
| F-003 Startup Console Logging | Emitted only from the listen callback | The line carries no sensitive data | The message must stay in step with the bound address if either literal changes |
| F-004 Root Greeting Endpoint | Body must stay byte-exact, including the trailing newline | No request data consumed; `X-Powered-By` present | Any body change must be mirrored in `README.md` |
| F-005 Second Greeting Endpoint | Body has no trailing newline; path and newline are unconfirmed assumptions | Same posture as F-004 | Confirm the three flagged assumptions before treating the contract as final |
| F-006 Explicit Routing with Strict Path Matching | Two literal paths only; trailing slash and case behaviour are framework defaults | Unknown paths and methods are refused rather than answered | Adding a route means updating documentation; reserved characters constrain naming |
| F-007 Declared and Locked Dependency Graph | Install must precede run; caret range permits minor upgrades | 66-package supply chain guarded by pinned digests | Keep the lockfile authoritative and re-audit the tree periodically |
| F-008 Published HTTP Contract Documentation | Prose only; no machine-readable contract | Discloses dependency and address already visible in responses | Must be revised with every contract change |
| F-009 Filesystem Edge-Case Filename Fixtures | Fixtures share the service's port and cannot run concurrently | No added network surface | Retained unchanged; parity with `server.js` is superseded |
| F-010 Orphan Data Fixture | Not read by any code | Synthetic data only; no personal information | None beyond keeping it out of the runtime path |
| F-101 – F-106 Proposed Hardening | Must be re-derived for the Express application; the plan forbids dependencies and manifest edits that the delivered change already made | Improve failure observability and availability without adding authentication or TLS | Unimplemented; would require the test suite that does not exist |
| F-201 Unimplemented `/hello` Route | Awaits requester confirmation of path and body wording | None beyond the platform-wide boundary | Would add a third documented endpoint to maintain |

### 2.5.5 Assumptions, Constraints and Requirement Version Tracking

**Version record.** This catalogue is version 1.1 of the repository's feature inventory. Version 1.0 is the §2 catalogue inside `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md`, which documents the pre-Express, zero-dependency implementation; this version supersedes it for F-001 – F-006 and for F-101 – F-106, retains its identifiers where the capability survives, and adds F-007 – F-010. The superseded document states its own invalidation condition in §2.7.4: "This specification reflects the repository state at the time of analysis; any modification to `server.js` invalidates F-001 – F-005 acceptance criteria."

| Assumption or Constraint | Detail and Consequence |
|--------------------------|------------------------|
| Endpoint path `/good-evening` | The requester specified no path. The kebab-case literal was assumed (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2) and alternatives such as `/evening` or `/goodevening` remain open confirmations; changing it invalidates F-005-RQ-004 and F-008-RQ-001 |
| `Good evening` has no trailing newline | The body matches the requester's wording exactly rather than the root greeting's style; adding a newline would change the 12-byte contract asserted by F-005-RQ-003 |
| Root body stays `Hello, World!\n` | The requester wrote "Hello world" and `codebase_context (42).md` asked for `"Hello world"` at `/hello`; current behaviour is deliberately preserved and flagged for confirmation (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2). F-004-RQ-003 and F-201-RQ-002 record both sides |
| `X-Powered-By: Express` is retained | The header is a framework default that the pre-migration implementation did not emit; suppression is documented as optional and is not implemented, so F-001's security row and F-006's `404` responses both carry it |
| Status and priority labels are inferred | No backlog, ticketing system, or roadmap exists in the repository, so every label in §2.1 derives from the cited artifacts |
| Acceptance is proven by re-run checks, not by a test gate | The `test` script exits `1` by design, so §2.2 criteria are verifiable only by executing the documented `curl`, install and byte-comparison steps |
| `server.js` is the only authoritative implementation | The three fixtures are tooling artifacts; their divergence from `server.js` is accepted, so no acceptance criterion may be satisfied by fixture behaviour |
| F-101 – F-106 remain proposed on a re-based target | Their plan predates the Express migration, forbids the dependency and manifest changes that have since been made, and therefore must be re-derived before implementation |
| Runtime version evidence conflicts | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §5 and §9.1 record Node v20.20.2, and `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.2.2 records Node v22.22.2 as the local runtime; the behaviour asserted in §2.2 was re-verified on Node v22.23.3. All are Express-5-compatible (Node 18 or newer), so the discrepancy does not affect any acceptance criterion |

# 3. Technology Stack

## 3.1 Programming Languages

The repository is written in a single language — JavaScript executed by Node.js — and everything else it contains is data or prose. The checked-in code is the authority for this section: `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` describes a superseded native-`http`, zero-dependency state, so its stack narrative is relied on here only where it agrees with the code at HEAD.

### 3.1.1 Language and Module System by Component

| Component | Path | Language / dialect | Module system | Evidence |
|-----------|------|-------------------|---------------|----------|
| Runtime service (the only process that serves traffic) | `server.js` | JavaScript, conservative ECMAScript 2015 subset, executed directly by Node.js | CommonJS — `require('express')` | `server.js:1`, `:3–4`, `:6`, `:12`, `:14–24`, `:26–28` |
| Filename fixtures (3) | `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, `QWYFFGHGHFDDJFDame_…_server.js` | JavaScript (same subset) | CommonJS — `require('http')`, a Node built-in rather than a package | line 1 of each file; all three byte-identical (sha256 `332fc2d0…`) and distinct from `server.js` (sha256 `a9a9b304…`) |
| Package manifest | `package.json` | JSON | — | 14 lines, single `dependencies` entry |
| Dependency lockfile | `package-lock.json` | JSON, npm lockfile schema version 3 | — | `lockfileVersion: 3`, `requires: true`, 67 `packages` entries |
| Published contract | `README.md` | Markdown | — | one fenced `bash` run block |
| Requirement, plan and specification records | `codebase_context (42).md`; `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md`, `Build Prompt.md`, `Project Guide.md`, `Technical Specifications.md` | Markdown; the specification also embeds JavaScript listings and Mermaid diagram source | — | `blitzy/documentation/` |
| Remediation transcript | `Response.txt` | JSON envelope whose single `sections[0].content` field holds Markdown and JavaScript prose | — | `Response.txt` |
| Data fixture | `phonenumber.csv` | CSV | — | header `message,phonenumber` plus 15 rows |
| Binary artifacts | `s1.png`, `20250304165759.mp4`, `tech_spec.pdf`, `defect_for_task_1.docx` | Not source code; no language | — | tracked, but referenced by no code path |

JavaScript is the only language on the request path. Across the repository, outside `node_modules/`, exactly four `require()` calls exist — `server.js:1` (`express`) and line 1 of each fixture (`http`) — and no other executable source file exists in any language. The tracked inventory is 20 files (`git ls-files`), of which four are JavaScript and the remainder are JSON, Markdown, CSV or binaries, so the absence of any other language is established by enumeration rather than by sampling. `node_modules/` holds dependencies' own sources and is git-ignored (`.gitignore`, sole line `node_modules/`), so it contributes no project source.

### 3.1.2 Justification for the Choice

- **Inherited, not selected.** The language was fixed before the current implementation existed: `codebase_context (42).md` asks for "a nodejs tutorial project", `package.json` describes the package as "Hello world in Node.js", and the delivered change re-platformed the service onto Express while leaving the language and runtime untouched (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.1, FR-B). JavaScript on Node.js is therefore a constraint the stack satisfies, not a decision the stack re-opens.
- **Proportional to the workload.** The entire runtime obligation is to bind a socket and return two fixed strings. Node's standard library supplies the HTTP server, the event loop and the console sink with no compilation step, no additional runtime, and no build artifacts, which is why the whole executable surface is one 29-line file.
- **No toolchain between source and execution.** The same language is written, reviewed and run: `node server.js` (documented in `README.md`) executes the checked-in source directly, so the source file *is* the deployed artifact. There is no transpiler, bundler, type checker, or code generator in the repository to keep in step.
- **Small, deliberately conservative language surface.** `server.js` uses `const`, arrow functions, a template literal for the startup line, string escapes (`'Hello, World!\n'`), and property access on the request and response objects. It contains no `let` or `var`, no classes, no `async`/`await`, no promises, no destructuring, no spread, no optional chaining and no generators. The low feature ceiling keeps the effective runtime floor low and keeps the file readable as the tutorial artifact its prompt asked for.
- **CommonJS because nothing declares otherwise.** `package.json` carries no `type` field, so Node resolves `.js` as CommonJS — consistent with the `require` call at line 1. `module.exports` appears nowhere in the repository, so the file is executed for its side effects rather than imported: there is no module API, and any future `require('./server.js')` would start a listener as a side effect.
- **Trade-offs accepted.** No static type checking, no linter or formatter, and no unit test runner exist, so correctness rests on reading the source and on the manual HTTP checks the project recorded. These are recorded as deferred enhancements in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3 rather than as gaps of the language choice.

### 3.1.3 Version and Compatibility Constraints

No language or runtime version is enforced by the project itself: `package.json` declares no `engines` field, and no `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions` or `.npmrc` file exists, so `engine-strict` is not enabled and npm treats any `engines` declaration as advisory. The binding floor comes from the dependency tree.

| Constraint | Value | Imposed by | Evidence |
|------------|-------|------------|----------|
| Minimum Node.js runtime | 18 | Eleven of the 66 installed packages declare it — `express@5.2.1` (`>= 18`) plus `body-parser`, `content-disposition`, `finalhandler` (`>= 18.0.0`), `merge-descriptors`, `mime-types`, `router`, `send`, `serve-static`, `type-is` and the nested `type-is/node_modules/content-type` (all `>=18`) | `node_modules/express/package.json`; lockfile `engines` entries; the remaining floors are permissive legacy declarations such as `>= 0.4` and `>= 0.8` |
| Project-declared runtime | None | `package.json` has no `engines` key | `package.json` |
| Minimum npm CLI | 7 | The committed lockfile uses `lockfileVersion` 3, the npm 7+ layout | `package-lock.json` |
| Module format | CommonJS | Absence of a `type` field in `package.json` | `package.json`; `require` usage in `server.js:1` |
| Build or transpile step | None required | No bundler, transpiler or type-checker configuration exists | repository inventory (20 tracked files) |
| Runtime used for development and verification in this environment | Node.js v22.23.3, npm 11.21.0 | The environment in which `server.js` was launched and its responses verified | `node -v`, `npm -v` |

Express 5's engines floor names Node 18, and Node 18 reached end of life on 2025-04-30, so the declared minimum is a compatibility floor rather than a supported-version statement. The wider support picture, as of 2026-10-26, is:

| Node.js line | Status | Latest patch in the line | Support window |
|--------------|--------|--------------------------|----------------|
| 26 | Current; becomes Active LTS on 2026-10-28 | 26.12.1 (2026-10-21) | Maintenance from 2027-10-20, EOL 2029-04-30 |
| 24 "Krypton" | Latest LTS | 24.22.1 (2026-10-21) | Active LTS from 2025-10-28; Maintenance from 2026-10-20; EOL 2028-04-30 |
| 22 "Jod" | Maintenance LTS — the line this repository's runtime belongs to | 22.23.4 (2026-10-21) | Active LTS from 2024-10-29; Maintenance from 2025-10-21; EOL 2027-04-30 |
| 18 "Hydrogen" | End of life — the line Express 5 names as its minimum | — | EOL 2025-04-30, no further updates including security patches |

Consequences of the unenforced floor: a host below Node 18 installs the tree (npm reports an `EBADENGINE` warning rather than failing) and then fails when `require('express')` loads a package that uses features the runtime lacks; and no repository mechanism — no `engines` field, no version-manager file, no CI job — pins or checks the runtime. Pinning the effective floor for production would mean adding an `engines` field and a version-manager file, which the delivered change deliberately did not do.

### 3.1.4 Languages Verified Absent

Every default-stack language candidate is absent from the repository. These names appear only as boilerplate prose inside `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §3.1.2, which itself records them as "verified absent" for the superseded implementation; the enumeration below re-establishes the claim against the code at HEAD.

| Language / runtime | Status | Evidence at HEAD |
|--------------------|--------|------------------|
| Python | Absent | No `.py` file among the 20 tracked files; no Python package in the dependency tree; no script invokes an interpreter other than `node` (`package.json` `scripts` holds only `test`) |
| TypeScript | Absent | No `.ts`/`.tsx` file, no `tsconfig.json`; the token occurs only in `Response.txt`'s exclusion list ("TypeScript conversion — Language choice is not part of the error handling requirements") and in the superseded specification's prose |
| Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C | Absent | No native source and no Xcode, Gradle or CocoaPods descriptor anywhere; no native build tooling in the repository |
| Java, Go, C#, Ruby, PHP | Absent | Not present in the tracked inventory, which is exhaustively enumerable at 20 files |
| Desktop and mobile host runtimes (Electron, React Native) | Absent | The dependency tree contains `express` and its closure only; no Electron, React Native or other application host is declared |
| Shell scripting | Absent | No script file with a shell shebang; the only shell text is the fenced `bash` block in `README.md` and command examples inside documentation |

The one non-JavaScript executable surface is the `npm`/`node` command line itself, which is tooling rather than project source and is covered in §3.6.


## 3.2 Frameworks and Libraries

The repository has exactly one framework and no supporting libraries of its own. Express 5.2.1 is the sole declared dependency and the only third-party code on the request path; the three filename fixtures deliberately bypass it and use Node's built-in `http` module instead.

### 3.2.1 Core Framework: Express 5.2.1

| Property | Value | Evidence |
|----------|-------|----------|
| Declared dependency | `"express": "^5.2.1"` — the only entry in `dependencies` | `package.json` lines 11–13 |
| Resolved version | 5.2.1 in the lockfile and on disk in `node_modules/express/` | `package-lock.json` `node_modules/express`; `node_modules/express/package.json` |
| Licence | MIT | `node_modules/express/package.json`; lockfile |
| Runtime requirement | `engines.node` `>= 18` | `node_modules/express/package.json` |
| Published package contents | `LICENSE`, `Readme.md`, `index.js`, `lib/` (no `bin`, no export map, no peer dependencies) | `node_modules/express/package.json`; `node_modules/express/` listing |
| Implementation modules | `lib/application.js`, `lib/express.js`, `lib/request.js`, `lib/response.js`, `lib/utils.js`, `lib/view.js` | `node_modules/express/lib/` |
| Direct dependencies | 28 | `node_modules/express/package.json` `dependencies` |
| Version currency | 5.2.1 installed; 5.3.0 is the current npm `latest` (published 2026-10-09), so the caret range permits an upgrade the lockfile has not taken | npm registry metadata; `package-lock.json` |

Express 5.0.0 reached general availability on 2024-09-10 according to the npm-published version history and the project's GitHub release; the framework's own blog post dates it 2024-09-09, a one-day discrepancy that does not affect this repository, which pins 5.2.1. The 4.x line remains published under a separate `latest-4` tag (4.22.3) and is not installed here.

**Why Express, and why one framework is enough.** The choice was requested rather than evaluated: `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md` and `codebase_context (42).md` frame the work as adding Express to the Node.js tutorial server, and `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.1 records the resulting requirements (FR-A add and lock Express; FR-B replace `http.createServer(...)` with `const app = express()`). The framework earns its place by replacing hand-rolled, route-agnostic request handling with a declarative routing table plus a default 404 handler — the behaviour change that turns the service from a catch-all responder into an endpoint model (§2.1.3.6). The project's earlier zero-dependency posture belongs to the unimplemented hardening plan in `Response.txt`, whose constraints the delivered change overrides (§0.1.2); the accepted cost is that the dependency surface grew from nothing to 66 packages for two literal routes.

### 3.2.2 Framework Surface Actually Used

`server.js` touches five Express APIs, all on the application object; no middleware, template engine, error-handling middleware or sub-application is registered.

| Call | Line | Purpose | Notes |
|------|------|---------|-------|
| `require('express')` | 1 | Load the factory | Resolves from `node_modules/express`; fails at startup if the tree is not installed |
| `express()` | 6 | Create the application | The application owns the routing table and the settings |
| `app.enable('strict routing')` | 12 | Treat trailing-slash variants as distinct paths | Consumed by the router, which receives `strict: this.enabled('strict routing')` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:76`) |
| `app.get('/', …)`, `app.get('/good-evening', …)` | 14, 20 | Register the two literal routes | Dispatch is performed by `router@2.2.0`; unmatched requests fall to `finalhandler@2.1.1` |
| `app.listen(port, hostname, cb)` | 26 | Bind the listener | Creates and starts a Node `http.Server`, which is therefore the object that owns `error`/`clientError` events and `close()` |

The handlers deliberately use the low-level Node response API — `res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, `res.end` — rather than Express's `res.send`, so no response helper performs content-type inference or ETag computation and both bodies are byte-exact, including the trailing newline on `/` and its deliberate absence on `/good-evening`. No `app.use` call exists anywhere in the repository, so the entire middleware layer is unused.

### 3.2.3 Express Defaults in Force

Four framework defaults are observable in the running service and are part of its effective behaviour, whether or not the code names them.

| Setting | Value | Source and effect |
|---------|-------|-------------------|
| `x-powered-by` | Enabled (default) | Every response carries `X-Powered-By: Express`, as confirmed on live `200` responses; suppression would require `app.disable('x-powered-by')`, which is documented as an optional enhancement and is not implemented (§2.4.4) |
| `etag` | `weak` | Set at `node_modules/express/lib/application.js:95`; never exercised, because the handlers call `res.end` and no response helper computes an entity tag |
| `query parser` | `simple` | Set at `application.js:97`, resolved by `compileQueryParser` to Node's built-in `querystring.parse` (`lib/utils.js:164–173`). The `qs` package is loaded by `lib/utils.js:20` but its parser is reachable only under the `extended` setting, which is not configured |
| `trust proxy` | `false` | Set at `application.js:99`; `compileTrust(false)` returns a constant-false function, so `proxy-addr`'s trust-subnet compilation is never invoked, and no handler reads `req.ip`, `req.protocol` or `req.hostname` |
| `env` | `development` | Default environment; no code reads it |

### 3.2.4 Compatibility Requirements

| Requirement | Detail | Consequence if unmet |
|-------------|--------|----------------------|
| Node.js 18 or newer | `express@5.2.1` `engines.node` `>= 18`, matched by ten transitive packages (§3.1.3) | `require('express')` fails at startup; npm warns but does not refuse the install, because no `engines` field and no `engine-strict` setting exist |
| npm 7 or newer | Required to interpret `lockfileVersion` 3 | `npm ci` cannot install the committed lockfile |
| Node's built-in `http.Server` semantics | `app.listen` returns a Node server, so bind failures surface as unhandled `error` events and termination is external | A held port 3000 aborts the process; `SIGTERM` ends it with exit code 143 and no drain (§2.1.3.2) |
| Express 5 path-matching rules | Express 5 reserves the characters `( ) [ ] ? + & !` in path patterns and changed wildcard syntax | Any future route must avoid those characters; the two literals `/` and `/good-evening` are unaffected (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.2.2) |
| Strict-routing and default matching semantics | Strict routing makes `/good-evening/` a distinct, unregistered path; matching stays case-insensitive because `case sensitive routing` is not enabled | Trailing-slash variants and unknown paths return 404 (§2.1.3.6) |
| Framework default disclosure | `X-Powered-By: Express` is emitted on every response | The framework identity is published to any loopback client; the header is advisory only |

### 3.2.5 Runtime Stack Composition and Integration Requirements

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Client["Loopback HTTP client<br/>curl or smoke test"]
    Operator["Operator or log collector<br/>reads stdout"]
    HttpServer["Node.js http.Server<br/>created by app.listen"]
    Console["console.log<br/>startup line"]
    subgraph App["Express 5.2.1 application in server.js"]
        Router["router 2.2.0<br/>literal path dispatch"]
        Root["GET / handler<br/>200 text/plain 14 bytes"]
        Evening["GET /good-evening handler<br/>200 text/plain 12 bytes"]
        Default404["finalhandler 2.1.1<br/>default 404 response"]
    end
    Client -->|"GET /"| HttpServer
    Client -->|"GET /good-evening"| HttpServer
    Client -->|"any other path"| HttpServer
    HttpServer --> Router
    Router --> Root
    Router --> Evening
    Router --> Default404
    Console -.->|"Server running at<br/>http://127.0.0.1:3000/"| Operator
```

Every integration point between components is in-process or install-time; none is a network dependency at runtime.

| Integration | Direction | Contract | Evidence |
|-------------|-----------|----------|----------|
| `server.js` → `express` | Startup, in-process | `require('express')` must resolve from `node_modules/`, so installation precedes execution | `server.js:1`; `.gitignore` excludes `node_modules/` |
| `express` → Node.js | Startup | `engines.node >= 18`; relies on the runtime's `http`, `console`, `process` globals and event loop | `node_modules/express/package.json` |
| `express` → npm registry | Install time only | Resolves the lockfile's 66 packages from `registry.npmjs.org` with pinned `sha512` digests | `package-lock.json` |
| `app` → `router@2.2.0` | Per request | Literal path and method matching over the registered table | `server.js:12, 14, 20`; live `200` responses |
| `router` → `finalhandler@2.1.1` | Per unmatched request | Default 404 body `Cannot GET <path>` with `text/html; charset=utf-8` | live `404` responses (§2.1.3.6) |
| `app.listen` → Node `http.Server` | Startup | Binds `127.0.0.1:3000`; the returned server owns lifecycle events | `server.js:26–28` |
| `console.log` → stdout | Startup | One line, emitted only after a successful bind | `server.js:27` |
| `README.md` → the running contract | Documentation only | Describes both routes, the 404 behaviour, the dependency and the run command | `README.md` lines 4–23 |
| Fixture scripts → Node `http` | Standalone run | Independent servers on the same loopback port, not interchangeable with the Express service | line 1 of each fixture |

### 3.2.6 Supporting Libraries and Non-Selections

- **Supporting libraries: none.** `package.json` declares no `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies` or `peerDependencies`, and no test runner, assertion library, HTTP client, or logging library exists in the tree. Everything the service needs beyond Express is a Node.js global or built-in (`http` in the fixtures, `console` and `process` in the service).
- **Fixtures stay framework-free.** `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js` and the long-named script each call `http.createServer((req, res) => …)` and answer every path, so they are not re-platformed onto Express; the decision to leave them unchanged is recorded in `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2 and their divergence from `server.js` is catalogued as F-009.
- **Web, mobile and desktop frameworks: absent.** No React, TypeScript, TailwindCSS, React Native or Electron dependency exists, and no front-end source file exists — consistent with a service that returns fixed `text/plain` strings and serves no assets (§1.3.2.1).
- **AI and alternative server frameworks: absent.** No Langchain or other AI framework, and no Flask, Django or other non-Node web framework, appears in the dependency tree or in any source file; both names occur only in the boilerplate prose of `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §3.1.2, which records them as verified absent.
- **Unmounted framework internals.** Because no middleware is registered, the parsing and static-serving packages installed as Express dependencies — `body-parser@2.2.2`, `qs@6.15.2`, `raw-body@3.0.2`, `iconv-lite@0.7.2`, `cookie@0.7.2`, `serve-static@2.2.1`, `send@1.2.1`, `mime-types@3.0.2` — never execute. Only `router` and `finalhandler` take part in the observed request path.


## 3.3 Open Source Dependencies

The project declares one open-source dependency and installs 66 packages in total. This subsection records where they come from, how their versions are pinned, exactly which packages are installed, and the current vulnerability and licence posture of that tree.

### 3.3.1 Registry, Declaration and Resolution Semantics

| Aspect | Value | Evidence |
|--------|-------|----------|
| Registry | The public npm registry, `https://registry.npmjs.org` — every lockfile entry resolves to a tarball URL under it | `package-lock.json` `resolved` fields |
| Declared scope | One runtime dependency, `"express": "^5.2.1"`; no `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies` or `peerDependencies` | `package.json` lines 11–13 |
| Semver semantics of the declared range | `^5.2.1` means `>= 5.2.1 < 6.0.0` — minor and patch upgrades are permitted by the manifest | `package.json` |
| Version actually installed | 5.2.1, pinned by the lockfile and confirmed on disk | `package-lock.json`; `node_modules/express/package.json` |
| Dependency depth | 1 direct project dependency (`express`) plus 65 transitive packages: 28 that Express declares directly and 37 deeper in the graph | lockfile; `node_modules/express/package.json` |
| Private or scoped registries | None — no `.npmrc`, no scope configuration, no proxy or mirror | repository inventory (no `.npmrc`) |
| Install commands that work | `npm ci` (reproducible, lockfile-driven) and `npm install` (may resolve newer versions within the caret range and rewrite the lockfile) | `README.md` documents `npm install`; the lockfile is committed |

Because the manifest uses a caret range, the lockfile — not `package.json` — is what guarantees reproducibility: only `npm ci` reproduces the exact 66-package tree, while `npm install` on a clean checkout may legitimately resolve 5.3.0 (the current npm `latest`) and its updated closure.

### 3.3.2 Lockfile Structure and Integrity Guarantees

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Format | npm lockfile version 3, the npm 7+ layout, `"requires": true` |
| Entries | 67 keys in `packages`: the root `""` entry mirroring `package.json` (name `hello_world`, version `1.0.0`, licence MIT, `dependencies.express ^5.2.1`) plus 66 package entries |
| Layout | 65 entries at `node_modules/<package>` plus one nested entry, `node_modules/type-is/node_modules/content-type` at 2.0.0 — a second copy installed because `type-is` requires `>= 2.0.0` while the top level carries `content-type@1.0.5` |
| Integrity metadata | Every package entry carries an exact `version`, a `resolved` tarball URL and a `sha512-…` Subresource Integrity digest; for example `accepts@2.0.0` is bound to `sha512-5cvg6CtKwfgdmVqY1WIiXKc3Q1bkRqGLi+2W/6ao+6Y7gu/RCwRuAhGEzh5B4KlszSuTLgZYuqFqo5bImjNKng==` |
| Optional, peer and development packages | None installed: no entry is marked `optional`, no entry declares `peerDependencies` (`debug@4.4.3` carries `peerDependenciesMeta` only), and no development package exists |
| Installed-tree consistency | The 66 package directories present under `node_modules/` are exactly the 66 packages recorded in the lockfile — the set difference is empty in both directions — and `express` resolves to 5.2.1 in both |
| Executable shims | `node_modules/.bin` is empty: none of the 66 packages ships a CLI |

```mermaid
    end
    Manifest --> Lock
    Lock -->|"npm ci"| Express
    Registry -.->|"61 MIT, 4 ISC, 1 BSD-3-Clause<br/>sha512 integrity per entry"| Express
    Express --> Router2
    Express --> Final
    Router2 --> P2R
    Express --> BP
    Express --> Qs
    Express --> Cookie
    Express --> Static
    Express --> HttpErrors
    Express --> Statuses
    Express --> DebugPkg
    Express --> Mime
    Express --> ProxyAddr
```

Express loads its dependencies eagerly rather than lazily, so the packages above are already in the process once `require('express')` returns: `lib/express.js:15` requires `body-parser`, `lib/express.js:79` requires `serve-static`, `lib/application.js` requires `finalhandler`, `router`, `debug` and `once`, `lib/utils.js:19–20` requires `proxy-addr` and `qs`, and `lib/request.js` requires `proxy-addr`, `accepts`, `type-is`, `fresh`, `parseurl` and others. Being loaded, however, is not the same as being exercised: no middleware is mounted, no query string is parsed (the `simple` parser uses Node's `querystring`, `lib/utils.js:164–173`), no view is rendered, and no request header is read by either handler.

### 3.3.4 Vulnerability Posture

`npm audit` against the installed tree at HEAD reports three advisories — one critical, one high and one moderate — all in transitive packages, and all reported as fixable. The counts returned by npm are `{ "info": 0, "low": 0, "moderate": 1, "high": 1, "critical": 1, "total": 3 }` across 66 installed packages.

| Package | Installed | Affected range | Severity | Advisory and effect | Fix |
|---------|-----------|----------------|----------|---------------------|-----|
| `proxy-addr` | 2.0.7 | 1.1.0 – 2.0.7 | Critical (CVSS 9.1) | `GHSA-jqcg-44mw-7w3h` — IP spoofing via an IPv4-mapped IPv6 trust subnet | Available |
| `body-parser` | 2.2.2 | 2.0.0 – 2.3.0 | High (CVSS 7.5) plus low (CVSS 3.7) | `GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828` — denial of service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body; `GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6` — an invalid `limit` value silently disables size enforcement | Available |
| `qs` | 6.15.2 | 2.2.5 – 6.15.3 | Moderate (CVSS 3.7 and 5.3) | `GHSA-x5fp-wj9c-mxmx` — array-limit bypass via bracket-key comma parsing; `GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g` — denial of service through attacker-controlled `isBuffer` | Available |

Reachability in this service is narrow, and the narrowness is a property of the application rather than of the packages:

- **`body-parser` is never mounted.** No `app.use` call exists in the repository, so no request body is parsed; the denial-of-service path requires body-parser to be installed as middleware.
- **`qs` is never asked to parse.** The configured query parser is `simple`, which resolves to Node's `querystring.parse`; the `extended` parser that calls `qs` is not selected, and no handler reads `req.query`.
- **`proxy-addr` evaluates no trust.** `app.set('trust proxy', false)` is the default, so `proxyaddr.compile([])` builds a function that trusts nothing, and no handler reads `req.ip`, `req.protocol` or `req.hostname`. The advisory's spoofing condition — a configured trust subnet accepting IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses — therefore does not arise in this configuration.

Two records of the same fact must be kept side by side, because they disagree (FA3). `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §6/§8 records "0 npm vulnerabilities" across the 66-package tree, as cited in §2.1.3.7; that was a point-in-time result taken when the tree was validated. The audit run at HEAD on 2026-10-26 returns the three advisories above. Neither record contradicts the other about the tree itself — the installed versions are unchanged — but only the current audit describes the advisories disclosed since. Because no CI job and no dependency-update automation exist (§3.6.4), nothing re-runs that check.

### 3.3.5 Dependency Management Obligations

| Obligation | Current state | Consequence |
|------------|---------------|-------------|
| Reproducible installation | Satisfied — the lockfile pins all 66 packages with integrity digests and `npm ci` reproduces them | A fresh checkout behaves identically after install |
| Currency of the direct dependency | 5.2.1 installed against 5.3.0 on npm; the caret range permits the upgrade but the lockfile holds it back | Advisories fixed upstream remain present until the lockfile is regenerated and the tree re-verified |
| Advisory monitoring | Manual only — `npm audit` is not wired into any script, hook or pipeline | Disclosed advisories stay invisible unless someone runs the command |
| Integrity of installed artifacts | Satisfied by pinned `sha512` digests recorded in the lockfile | Tarball substitution is detectable at install time |
| Committed dependencies | Deliberately excluded — `.gitignore` names `node_modules/`, so the repository stays source-only at 20 tracked files | Installation is a prerequisite of running the service |
| Inventory visibility | Satisfied by the committed lockfile, which lists every package, version, licence and digest without shipping the code | Reviewers see the full footprint (0 → 66 packages) from the manifest and lockfile alone |
| Private-registry or authentication configuration | None exists; every package comes from the public registry | No credential or mirror is needed to install |


## 3.4 Third-Party Services

The service integrates with no third-party service at runtime. Its only external touchpoints are an install-time package fetch and one documentation hyperlink; the running process opens no outbound connection beyond the client's own loopback socket, and nothing outside the host can reach it (§1.2.1.3, §1.3.2.3).

### 3.4.1 Runtime Service Integrations — Verified Absent

| Service category | Status | Evidence |
|------------------|--------|----------|
| Cloud platform (AWS or any other) | Absent | No cloud SDK in the dependency tree; the tree is `express` and its closure only (§3.3.3); no credentials, region or endpoint configuration exists |
| Identity and authentication provider (Auth0 or other) | Absent | No identity library, no client ID, tenant, issuer or callback URL in any file; no request input is read, so no token or session could be validated (§2.4.4) |
| Application performance monitoring or tracing | Absent | No agent dependency and no instrumentation import; the service's entire runtime output is one startup line on standard output |
| Log aggregation or log shipping | Absent | No log shipper, no structured log format, no log destination configuration; `console.log` writes to the process's standard output (`server.js:27`) |
| Error tracking | Absent | No error-reporting client; errors are neither caught nor reported — the handlers cannot throw and no `error` or `clientError` listener exists (§2.1.3.2) |
| Metrics or health endpoints | Absent | The routing table holds exactly two `GET` paths; no `/health`, `/ready` or `/metrics` route is registered |
| Analytics, telemetry or feature flags | Absent | No beacon, SDK or flag client; the only metadata the service emits is the framework's own `X-Powered-By: Express` response header |
| Messaging, queues or event buses | Absent | No broker client (`kafka`, `amqp`, `rabbit`, `nats`, `grpc` and similar names appear nowhere in the lockfile); the process neither publishes nor subscribes |
| Outbound HTTP or API clients | Absent | No HTTP client package exists in the tree, and no handler performs I/O — both handlers set a status code, a content type and a fixed string and return |
| Email, SMS or payment providers | Absent | No such dependency and no such call site; the only data resembling contact information is the unused `phonenumber.csv` fixture |
| CDN, edge or reverse proxy | Absent | No proxy configuration, no asset pipeline and no cache-control headers; the listener binds loopback only and is not fronted by anything |
| Secret management or key vault | Absent | No secret reference of any kind, no `.env` file, and no `process.env` read anywhere in executable code |

### 3.4.2 Install-Time and Non-Runtime Touchpoints

| Touchpoint | When | Detail | Evidence |
|------------|------|--------|----------|
| Public npm registry (`registry.npmjs.org`) | Install time only | Resolves and downloads the 66 packages recorded in the lockfile, each verified against its pinned `sha512` digest. Once installed, no registry call is made | `package-lock.json` `resolved` and `integrity` fields |
| Express documentation site (`https://expressjs.com/`) | Never | A hyperlink in the README's prose naming the framework; not fetched by any code | `README.md` line 6 |
| Git remote (GitHub) | Development time only | Version control transport for the 20 tracked files; not part of the deployed service | `git remote -v`; `git ls-files` |

### 3.4.3 Monitoring and Observability Tooling

The service has no observability tooling, and the absence is structural rather than configured-away: there are no logs beyond startup, no metrics, no traces, no alerts and no dashboards. The single output is `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, written by the listen callback after a successful bind (`server.js:26–28`). Because it is emitted only after the socket is bound, it doubles as the only readiness signal available to an operator or script. Anything that consumes it — a terminal, a file redirect, or a collector outside the repository — lies outside the system's scope; no such consumer is defined here (§2.4.5). The default-stack monitoring tools named in the platform template have no counterpart in this tree: no agent package is installed, and the only runtime telemetry is the readiness line above plus the `X-Powered-By` header on responses.

### 3.4.4 Identity, Secrets and Credential Handling

No authentication or authorisation service is integrated and no credential exists in the repository. There is no account, token, key, certificate or personal datum; the only string resembling contact data is the synthetic `+111111112xx` range in `phonenumber.csv`, which no code reads (§2.1.3.10). Access control is the loopback binding itself: any local process can reach the service, and nothing outside the host can. Consequently there is no secret-rotation, credential-leak or key-management surface to document — and equally, no facility to add one without first building a configuration layer that does not exist (§2.4.5).

### 3.4.5 Integration Requirements If a Service Were Added

The gaps below are consequences of the current stack, not current functionality, and they mirror the future-phase items recorded in §2.4.5:

| Requirement for any third-party service integration | Why it is missing today |
|-----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Configuration and secret injection | Hostname and port are `const` literals; no `process.env` read, no config module, no CLI arguments |
| An outbound client and its dependency surface | The tree contains no HTTP client; adding one grows the dependency graph, which the project's own deferred plan already treats as a review obligation (§3.3.5) |
| Error and failure handling for the integration | No `error` listener, no `try`/`catch`, no retry or timeout policy — F-101, F-103 and F-104 are unimplemented |
| Lifecycle hooks to release the connection | No `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handling and no cleanup hook — F-102 and F-106 are unimplemented; the hook location they would occupy is the comment placeholder in `Response.txt` §0.4 |
| Observability of the integration | No structured logging, metrics or health surface exists to report on it |
| Network reachability | The listener binds `127.0.0.1`; any service-to-service call would be outbound from a loopback-only process and any inbound call would require deployment changes outside this scope |


## 3.5 Databases and Storage

The service uses no database, no cache and no storage service. Both handlers write a fixed string to the response and nothing else, and no file is written at runtime. Persistence in this project is limited to the repository itself and the installed dependency tree.

### 3.5.1 Primary and Secondary Datastores — Verified Absent

| Store category | Status | Evidence |
|----------------|--------|----------|
| Relational database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and others) | Absent | No driver or ORM package in the 66-package tree; no `.sql` file, schema or migration directory among the 20 tracked files; no connection string in any file |
| Document database (MongoDB and others) | Absent | A regex scan of `package-lock.json` for `mongo`, `mongoose`, `pg`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `sqlite`, `redis`, `ioredis`, `knex`, `sequelize`, `typeorm` and `prisma` returns zero matches |
| Key-value store or cache daemon (Redis, Memcached) | Absent | Same scan; no client library and no cache endpoint configuration |
| Search or analytics store (Elasticsearch, DynamoDB and others) | Absent | Same scan (`elastic`, `dynamodb`); no SDK dependency |
| Queue or message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS and others) | Absent | Same scan (`kafka`, `amqp`, `rabbit`, `nats`, `grpc`); no producer or consumer code |
| Embedded or in-process store (LevelDB, SQLite binding) | Absent | No such dependency; no file-opening call exists in application code |

Two further proofs apply across the whole system: the complete installed tree is enumerated in §3.3.3 and contains no data-store client, and the complete `require()` surface outside `node_modules/` is four calls — `server.js:1` (`express`) and line 1 of each filename fixture (`http`) — none of which can open a data connection.

### 3.5.2 Data Persistence Strategy

There is no runtime persistence strategy because the service holds no mutable state. What persists between runs is entirely outside the process:

| Persisted artifact | Location | Role |
|--------------------|----------|------|
| Source, manifest and lockfile | The git repository (20 tracked files) | The system of record for behaviour and for dependency versions |
| Installed dependency tree | `node_modules/`, git-ignored by `.gitignore` | Reproducible install output, recreated by `npm ci`; never committed |
| Process state | Memory only | The Express application object, the two route registrations and the listening socket; discarded at exit |
| Response payloads | Not persisted | Both bodies are compile-time string literals in `server.js` |

No write path exists anywhere: application code imports no filesystem module, opens no file, and logs only to standard output. State across requests is not merely unused but impossible — the handlers accept `req` and never read it, so no request can influence a later response (§1.2.2.3). If a datastore were introduced, it would require a client dependency, a configuration layer for its endpoint, lifecycle hooks to release the connection at shutdown, and a test surface — none of which exists today (§3.4.5).

### 3.5.3 Caching

| Caching layer | Status | Detail |
|---------------|--------|--------|
| HTTP response caching | Absent | The handlers set only the status code, `Content-Type` and the body; no `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `Last-Modified` or `Vary` header is ever written |
| Entity tags | Configured but unreachable | Express's default `etag` setting is `weak` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:95`), but the handlers call `res.end` rather than a response helper, so no validator is generated and conditional requests are never satisfied from cache |
| In-process cache or memoisation | Absent | No cache structure, no memoisation and no retained state; each request re-executes three statements |
| Shared cache (Redis, Memcached) | Absent | No client dependency (§3.5.1) |
| Edge or proxy cache | Absent | The listener binds loopback only and no proxy or CDN fronts it |

Caching is not merely unimplemented but unnecessary for the current contract: both bodies are constants compiled into the source, so there is no computation to cache and no data that can go stale.

### 3.5.4 Storage Services and Data at Rest

No storage service — object store, block volume, network share or managed file service — is referenced by any dependency, configuration or code path. Nothing is uploaded, downloaded or synchronised at runtime.

Data that exists at rest is confined to the repository, and none of it feeds the running service:

| File | Content | Consumed by the service |
|------|---------|-------------------------|
| `phonenumber.csv` | Header `message,phonenumber` plus 15 synthetic rows in the `+111111112xx` range | No — no code imports or reads it (F-010) |
| `README.md` | The published HTTP contract and run procedure | No — documentation only |
| `codebase_context (42).md`, `blitzy/documentation/*.md` (4 files) | Requirement note, build prompt, action plan, project guide and the superseded specification | No — documentation only |
| `Response.txt` | JSON envelope holding the unimplemented hardening plan | No — documentation only |
| `s1.png`, `20250304165759.mp4`, `tech_spec.pdf`, `defect_for_task_1.docx` | Unreferenced binary artifacts | No |
| `package.json`, `package-lock.json` | Dependency declaration and pinned resolution | Yes — read by the npm client at install time, never by the service at runtime |

Because the service consumes no stored data, it has no schema, no data model, no migration path, no backup or restore procedure, no retention policy and no disaster-recovery requirement. Its data-classification surface is minimal for the same reason: the only records in the repository are synthetic fixture rows, and the only runtime output is a public loopback address written to standard output. Introducing a datastore would consequently be a new capability rather than a change to an existing one — it would bring connection management, a configuration surface, credential handling and shutdown cleanup, none of which the current stack provides.


## 3.6 Development and Deployment

Development and deployment in this repository are one and the same act: install the dependencies, then run the single JavaScript file with the system Node.js runtime. No build system, container definition, pipeline or process manager exists to mediate between source and a running service.

### 3.6.1 Development Toolchain

| Tool category | Status | Evidence |
|---------------|--------|----------|
| Language runtime | Node.js — the only runtime required | `server.js` is executed directly by `node`; `README.md` documents `node server.js` |
| Package manager | npm — the only package-management tool | `package.json`, the committed `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion` 3), and `.gitignore`'s `node_modules/` entry; no Yarn or pnpm lockfile exists |
| Runtime and CLI versions observed in this environment | Node.js v22.23.3, npm 11.21.0 | `node -v`, `npm -v` |
| Build, bundling or transpilation tools | None | No bundler, transpiler, minifier or task runner dependency; no configuration file for any of them |
| Type checker | None | No TypeScript dependency, no `tsconfig.json`, no JSDoc-driven checking configuration |
| Linter or formatter | None | No ESLint, Prettier, Biome or EditorConfig configuration; the root holds only `.git` and `.gitignore` |
| Test framework and test files | None | No test dependency and no test file; the sole npm script is the unmodified npm-init placeholder |
| Commit hooks or local automation | None | No `husky`, `lint-staged`, or `.pre-commit-config.yaml`; no `.github/` directory |
| Editor or container tooling configuration | None | No `.editorconfig`, no `.dockerignore`, no `.nvmrc` or `.node-version` |

The only npm script is:

```json
"test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
```

It is the untouched `npm init` placeholder, so `npm test` fails by design and guards nothing. There is no `start`, `build`, `lint` or `dev` script; `npm start` nevertheless runs the service because npm falls back to its implicit default start command for a package whose root contains `server.js` — verified by launching it, which prints `> hello_world@1.0.0 start` / `> node server.js` followed by the expected `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`.

### 3.6.2 Build System and Dependency Installation

There is no compilation step, so the "build" is dependency installation and nothing else.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Build inputs | `server.js`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json` |
| Build command | `npm ci` (reproducible, deleted-and-reinstalled from the lockfile) or `npm install` (may resolve newer versions within the caret range) |
| Build outputs | `node_modules/` only — no `dist/`, `build/`, bundle or generated source; the deployed artifact is the source file itself |
| Ordering constraint | Installation must precede execution, because `server.js:1` requires `express` and `node_modules/` is git-ignored, hence absent from a fresh checkout |
| Determinism | Guaranteed by the lockfile: 66 packages with pinned versions and `sha512` digests (§3.3.2) |
| Known manifest inconsistency | `package.json` declares `"main": "index.js"`, and no `index.js` exists. Tools that resolve the package entry point therefore fail, while `node server.js` and the implicit `npm start` both work |
| Compilation artifacts to clean | None — there is no intermediate output, cache directory or generated code in the repository |

### 3.6.3 Containerisation

Containerisation is absent. No `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore`, image manifest or orchestration manifest (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad) exists anywhere in the repository; the root directory contains only `.git` and `.gitignore` as hidden entries, and no container-related file is tracked. The Dockerfile and Kubernetes references that a reader may encounter are prose inside `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` and `Response.txt` — the former records containerisation as verified absent for the superseded implementation, and the latter mentions Docker and Kubernetes only as illustrative sources of `SIGTERM` signals for an unimplemented shutdown feature. Consequences: the deployment target must supply a Node.js 18+ runtime itself; there is no declared base image, no image-build step, no registry, and no container-level health check; and the loopback binding means a containerised deployment would need its networking addressed before anything outside the container could reach the service.

### 3.6.4 CI/CD

No continuous-integration or continuous-delivery configuration exists: no `.github/workflows/` directory, no pipeline file for any CI provider, no build or deploy script, and no automated gate of any kind. The full commit history is 11 commits on a single branch (`blitzy-62d685d6-…`), and it contains content commits only — the dependency addition, the Express re-platform, `.gitignore`, the README, the strict-routing refinement, and the documentation set. No commit adds or has ever added a pipeline definition.

The practical effect is that every check this project has recorded was manual or transient:

- Contract verification was performed by hand — starting the process and issuing `curl` requests — not by a committed test (§2.1.3.4, §2.1.3.5).
- The strict-routing refinement came from a manual QA pass recorded as a commit message ("Enable strict routing so /good-evening/ returns 404 (QA Issue 1)"), not from an automated assertion.
- Dependency integrity is unmonitored: `npm audit` is not wired into any script or job, so the advisories described in §3.3.4 surfaced only when the command was run explicitly.
- A minimal regression suite (`node:test` with `supertest`, about 2.0 hours) is documented as an optional, out-of-scope enhancement in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3 and is not implemented.

### 3.6.5 Deployment Model and Prerequisites

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Checkout["Fresh checkout<br/>20 tracked files, no node_modules"]
    Install{"Dependencies<br/>already installed?"}
    NpmCI["npm ci from lockfile<br/>or npm install"]
    Run["node server.js<br/>equivalent to npm start"]
    Bind{"Port 3000 free on<br/>127.0.0.1?"}
    Ready["Startup log written<br/>Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/"]
    Serve["Serve GET / and GET /good-evening<br/>404 for everything else"]
    Crash["Unhandled error event<br/>process aborts"]
    Stop["External signal<br/>SIGTERM or SIGINT"]
    End1["Process ends without drain<br/>no cleanup hook"]
    Checkout --> Install
    Install -->|"no"| NpmCI
    Install -->|"yes"| Run
    NpmCI --> Run
    Run --> Bind
    Bind -->|"yes"| Ready
    Bind -->|"no"| Crash
    Ready --> Serve
    Serve --> Stop
    Stop --> End1
```

| Prerequisite | Requirement | Enforced by |
|--------------|-------------|-------------|
| Node.js runtime | 18 or newer | Express 5.2.1's `engines.node`; advisory only, since `package.json` declares no `engines` field and no `engine-strict` setting exists |
| npm CLI | 7 or newer, to read `lockfileVersion` 3 | The committed lockfile |
| Dependencies installed | `npm ci` or `npm install` before first start | `server.js:1`; `.gitignore` excludes `node_modules/` |
| Network address | The loopback interface available and TCP port 3000 free; a conflict is fatal, with no fallback port | `server.js` lines 3–4, 26; §2.4.1 |
| Configuration | None to supply — host and port are `const` literals and no environment variable, config file or CLI argument is read | `server.js` lines 3–4 |
| Termination | An operator or supervisor to signal the process; the service offers no shutdown path, and `SIGTERM` ends it with exit code 143 without draining | §2.1.3.2 |

| Deployment characteristic | State |
|---------------------------|-------|
| Topology | One host, one process, one listener on `127.0.0.1:3000` |
| Artifact deployed | The source tree plus the installed dependency tree; nothing is packaged or published |
| Process management | None — no supervisor, cluster, worker threads or restart policy; the process runs until signalled |
| Health and readiness | Only the startup line on standard output; no health or readiness endpoint |
| Transport security | Plain HTTP; no TLS listener, certificate or terminator |
| External reachability | None — loopback binding; making it reachable requires a reverse proxy or networking change outside this scope |
| Configuration and secrets | None — no environment variables, no config files, no credentials to inject |
| Observability at run time | One line at startup; no per-request logging, metrics or tracing |
| Rollback | Manual — redeploy the previous source revision and re-run `npm ci` |
| Scaling | Not supported as configured: the hardcoded loopback binding and fixed port prevent a second instance on the same host, and nothing allows an upstream balancer to reach the service (§2.4.3) |

### 3.6.6 Version Control and Repository Hygiene

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Version control | Git, with a single branch and 11 commits; the working tree is clean at HEAD |
| Tracked files | 20 — `server.js`, the three filename fixtures, `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.md`, `codebase_context (42).md`, `Response.txt`, `phonenumber.csv`, the four `blitzy/documentation/` Markdown files, and four binary artifacts |
| Ignore rules | `.gitignore` contains one line, `node_modules/`, so installed dependencies are never committed and the repository stays source-only |
| History shape | Discrete, reviewable commits for the delivered change: dependency declaration (`b9350e9`), Express re-platform (`0fdbfb6`), ignore rule (`fcbd326`), README contract (`59adfc5`), strict-routing refinement (`f2c2ca4`), then documentation commits |
| Remote | A GitHub repository, used for version-control transport only; no deployment automation is driven from it |
| Artefacts committed that the service never reads | The four binary files and `phonenumber.csv`; they inflate the checkout without affecting build or run |
