# 4. Process Flowchart

## 4.1 System Workflows

### 4.1.1 Core Business Processes

`hao-backprop-test` executes exactly one process, and that process does three things: it **installs**, it **binds a loopback listener**, and it **answers two literal paths**. Nothing else in the repository executes: the three filename fixtures (`Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, and the 199-character `QWYFFGHGHFDDJFDame_…_server.js`) are standalone scripts that the service never loads, `phonenumber.csv` is read by no code, and no executable file reads any other file — no `fs` usage and no local `require` exists in any of the four `.js` files outside `node_modules/`.

Every flow therefore belongs to one of four end-to-end journeys. Each row maps to the feature identifiers used throughout §2 and §3.

| # | Journey | Trigger | Features | Terminal condition |
|---|---------|---------|----------|--------------------|
| 1 | Dependency installation (install-time) | Fresh checkout on a host with npm 7+ and registry access | F-007 | `node_modules/` holds the 66 locked packages, or npm aborts non-zero and the service cannot start |
| 2 | Process start and bind | `node server.js`, or the implicit `npm start` | F-001, F-002, F-003 | One startup line on stdout with an idle event loop, or a silent zero-status exit |
| 3 | Request handling | Any HTTP request reaching `127.0.0.1:3000` | F-004, F-005, F-006 | A response is written and the socket returns to the keep-alive pool |
| 4 | Termination | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` from an operator, supervisor, or shell | F-002 (RQ-004) | The process ends through the runtime's default signal disposition |

The journeys are not business-domain workflows: both handlers return source literals and read no input, so no approval, pricing, fulfilment, or notification process exists to model. Actor inventory is correspondingly small — **operator** (or supervisor) at install and termination, **npm CLI** at install, **HTTP client** at serve time, and the **Node.js runtime plus Express** as the executing systems. The only user touchpoints in the running service are the two registered URLs and the single startup line.

#### 4.1.1.1 Journey 1 — Dependency installation (F-007)

1. The operator runs `npm ci` (reproducible, from the lockfile) or `npm install` (may resolve newer versions within the caret range) — the run procedure published in `README.md` §Running.
2. npm reads `package.json`, whose only dependency is `"express": "^5.2.1"` (lines 11–13).
3. npm resolves the tree through `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion` 3, 66 package entries, each with a `registry.npmjs.org` tarball URL and a `sha512-…` integrity digest).
4. Tarballs are fetched from the public registry, each verified against its recorded digest.
5. Extracted packages are written to `node_modules/`, which `.gitignore` excludes (single line `node_modules/`), so a checkout is source-only and installation is a precondition of execution.
6. npm exits; the "build" is complete, because there is no compilation, bundling, or transpilation step anywhere in the repository.

**Decision point.** `npm ci` honours the lockfile strictly, `npm install` may float within `^5.x`, so reproducibility rests on the lockfile rather than the manifest.

**Error path.** Without the installed tree, startup aborts at `server.js:1`: running the file in a directory with no `node_modules/` produced `Error: Cannot find module 'express'` (`code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'`, `requireStack: ['…/server.js']`) on stderr, exit status `1`, and nothing on stdout. **Recovery:** re-run the install; no retry, mirror, or offline fallback is configured.

#### 4.1.1.2 Journey 2 — Process start and bind (F-001, F-002, F-003)

Execution is straight-line module evaluation followed by a single bind attempt. Order is significant at step 5.

1. `node server.js` begins; `npm start` reaches the same file because npm falls back to its implicit `node server.js` for a package whose root contains `server.js` (no `start` script is declared; `main` points at the non-existent `index.js`).
2. `const express = require('express')` (`server.js:1`) resolves the framework from `node_modules/`. Failure aborts here, before any output (see Journey 1's error path).
3. `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` and `port = 3000` are bound as module-level `const`s (lines 3–4). No `process.env` read, no config file, and no CLI argument is consulted anywhere in the code.
4. `const app = express()` (line 6) runs `app.init()` → `defaultConfiguration()`: the settings map is created and framework defaults are written — `x-powered-by` **enabled**, `etag` `weak`, `env` `development` (or `NODE_ENV` if set), `query parser` `simple`, `trust proxy` `false`.
5. `app.enable('strict routing')` (line 12) writes `strict routing = true` into the settings map. The router does not exist yet: `app.init` installs a lazy `router` getter that constructs `new Router({ caseSensitive: this.enabled('case sensitive routing'), strict: this.enabled('strict routing') })` **on first access**, and `app.get` is the first accessor. Enabling the setting after the first route registration is therefore ineffective — verified by probe: with the repository's ordering `GET /good-evening/` returns `404`, while enabling strict routing after registering `/` makes the same request return `200`.
6. `app.get('/', …)` (lines 14–18) triggers `lazyrouter()`: the Router is created with `strict: true`, `caseSensitive: false`, and layer L1 is registered for the literal path `/`.
7. `app.get('/good-evening', …)` (lines 20–24) registers layer L2 on the same router. The routing table is now closed: two literal `GET` paths.
8. `app.listen(port, hostname, callback)` (line 26) enters Express's `listen`, which creates the underlying Node `http.Server` over the application, wraps the callback with `once`, registers it as a **one-shot `error` listener** (`server.once('error', done)`), and calls `server.listen(...)`.
9. The runtime attempts to bind TCP `127.0.0.1:3000`.
10. **On success:** the `listening` event invokes the callback, which writes the single line `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` to stdout (line 27). The listener keeps the event loop alive and the process idles.
11. **On bind failure** (`EADDRINUSE`, `EACCES`): the error event is consumed by the one-shot callback registered in step 8. The callback takes no parameters, so it cannot observe the error; it prints the **same** banner and returns. With no further handles the event loop empties and the process exits with status `0` and no diagnostic — observed live: the callback was invoked with one argument `EADDRINUSE` and `this.listening === false`, then the process exited `0`.
12. The server object returned by `app.listen` is **discarded** — line 26 assigns it to nothing — so the application retains no handle through which `server.close()` could ever be called.

**Decision points.** Dependency resolution at step 2; router construction at step 5 (ordering-sensitive); bind outcome at step 9.

#### 4.1.1.3 Journey 3 — Request handling (F-004, F-005, F-006)

1. A client connects to `127.0.0.1:3000` over plain HTTP. No TLS, authentication, or client-address filtering applies: any local process can reach the listener, and loopback binding is the service's entire exposure boundary.
2. Node's HTTP parser reads the request. A syntactically invalid request line or header block raises `clientError`; the repository registers no listener for it, so the runtime's built-in handling answers `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n` and closes that connection while the listener keeps serving — observed live, with nothing written to the application's stdout.
3. The `request` event hands `(req, res)` to `app.handle`: `X-Powered-By: Express` is set (because `x-powered-by` remains enabled), the request/response pair is cross-linked, and the Express `finalhandler` is prepared as the terminal callback.
4. The router dispatches. The query string is removed before matching (Express's `simple` query parser runs lazily and is never consulted), matching is case-insensitive because `case sensitive routing` is **not** enabled, and trailing slashes are significant because `strict routing` **is** enabled. Three outcomes follow:
   - **Registered `GET` path** — `/` (L1) or `/good-evening` (L2) → the handler runs. `HEAD` is answered by the same `GET` layer, so `HEAD /` returns `200` with no body.
   - **Framework-handled method** — `OPTIONS /` returns `200`, `Allow: GET, HEAD`, body `GET, HEAD`, without entering either handler.
   - **Everything else** — unmatched paths (`/nope`, `/hello`, `//`), trailing-slash variants (`/good-evening/`), and non-`GET`/`HEAD` methods on registered paths (`POST /`, `PUT /`) → fall through to step 8.
5. The matched handler executes three synchronous statements and returns: `res.statusCode = 200`, `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')`, `res.end(<literal>)`. `req` is accepted and never dereferenced; there is no branch, loop, I/O, or allocation of dynamic content, so the handler cannot fail for input-dependent reasons.
6. The runtime writes the response: status line, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length` (14 for `Hello, World!\n`, 12 for `Good evening`), `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, and `X-Powered-By: Express`. No `ETag` and no `Cache-Control` are emitted, because `res.end` bypasses the `res.send` path where the `weak` ETag setting would apply.
7. The socket returns to the keep-alive pool for up to 5 seconds of idleness (the runtime's `keepAliveTimeout`), and a reused socket re-enters at step 2.
8. Unmatched requests are terminated by `finalhandler`: `404 Not Found` with Express's default HTML body `Cannot GET <path>`, plus `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`. A plain not-found carries no error object, so nothing is logged.

**User touchpoints.** The HTTP client sees only these responses; the operator sees only the startup line. Every response advertises `X-Powered-By: Express`; no cookie, session, or credential is ever set.

#### 4.1.1.4 Journey 4 — Termination

No application shutdown path exists: a repository-wide search of every `.js` file finds no `process.on` registration, no `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler, no `server.close()`, no `process.exit`, and no cleanup hook. Consequently:

- `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` take the runtime's default disposition and end the process **immediately** — observed: `kill -TERM <pid>` produced exit status `143` (`128 + 15`) with no shutdown output beyond the startup line.
- In-flight responses are dropped, established keep-alive connections are reset, and no drain window exists, so container and orchestrator conventions that expect a bounded, clean exit cannot be honoured (F-102 remains proposed).
- Because the server object is discarded at `server.js:26` (Journey 2, step 12), `server.close()` is not reachable from the current code without first retaining the return value of `app.listen`.
- Unhandled failures inside the runtime's own machinery also end the process: an unhandled `error` event throws out of the event loop, which is exactly what the native-`http` fixtures do on a port conflict (unhandled `EADDRINUSE`, exit `1`, stack trace), in contrast to the silent zero-status exit of the Express implementation.

**Decision points.** None at runtime — termination is unconditional and unobserved by the application.

#### 4.1.1.5 Consolidated Decision Points

| Decision | Condition evaluated | Layers involved | Observed outcome |
|----------|--------------------|-----------------|------------------|
| Is the framework resolvable? | `require('express')` at `server.js:1` | Node module loader | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` → exit `1`, no stdout (verified outside the checkout) |
| Is strict routing active at router construction? | `app.enable('strict routing')` before the first `app.get` | Express settings map → lazy Router getter | Only the repository's ordering makes `/good-evening/` a distinct path (verified both orderings) |
| Did the port bind? | `EADDRINUSE`/`EACCES` on `server.listen` | Node `http.Server`, Express `listen` wiring | Silently swallowed: banner printed, exit `0`, no diagnostic |
| Was the request syntactically valid HTTP? | HTTP parser | Node `http.Server` → `clientError` | Runtime default `400 Bad Request` + connection close; process survives |
| Which route matches? | Literal path equality (case-insensitive, strict trailing slash) + method `GET`/`HEAD` | Express `router` (`strict`/`caseSensitive` options) | L1, L2, `OPTIONS` responder, or `404` |
| Is the response cached or validated? | Not evaluated — `res.end` path | Express `response`, `etag` setting unused | No `ETag`, no `Cache-Control` |
| How does the process end? | External signal only | Node process signal disposition | Immediate exit, no drain (verified `143`) |

### 4.1.2 Integration Workflows

At run time the service integrates with **nothing**: it opens no outbound connection, holds no database session, publishes to no queue, and reads no file. The only cross-system flow in the repository is install-time, and the only interface the service exposes is its two literal HTTP paths. §4.3.1 and §4.3.2 treat the state and error consequences of that isolation.

#### 4.1.2.1 Data Flow Between Systems

| Integration | Direction | Payload | Protocol / contract | Authentication | Evidence |
|-------------|-----------|---------|---------------------|----------------|----------|
| npm CLI → public registry | Outbound, install-time only | Package tarballs requested by name, version, and tarball URL | HTTPS; `package-lock.json` records the resolution and `sha512-…` integrity digests | None (public registry) | `package-lock.json` (66 entries, `lockfileVersion` 3); verified by `npm pack express@5.2.1`, whose `lib/application.js` is byte-identical to the installed copy |
| HTTP client → listener | Inbound, run time | Request line and headers; the body is never read | HTTP/1.1 over loopback `127.0.0.1:3000` | None | `server.js:26`; live requests at HEAD |
| Listener → HTTP client | Outbound, run time | `text/plain` bodies `Hello, World!\n` (14 B) and `Good evening` (12 B), or the default `404` HTML | HTTP/1.1 | None | `server.js:14–24`; live responses |
| Application → stdout | Outbound, once per process | `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | Attached standard-output stream | None | `server.js:27` |
| Signal channel → process | Inbound | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` | OS process signalling | Local process permission only | No handler present; exit `143` observed |

No data flows out of the service other than those two bodies, and no request-derived data is stored, forwarded, or logged: the handlers never read `req`.

#### 4.1.2.2 API Interactions

The published API surface is two literal `GET` paths, documented in `README.md` (lines 9–12) and implemented at `server.js:14–24`. Everything else is framework default behaviour.

- **Transport:** plain HTTP/1.1 on loopback, port 3000. No TLS listener, certificate, or terminator exists; nothing outside the host can reach the service without a proxy or networking change that is not part of this repository.
- **Methods:** `GET` and `HEAD` (answered from the `GET` registration) serve content; `OPTIONS` is answered by Express's built-in responder; `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `PATCH` on a registered path return `404`.
- **Bodies and headers:** no request body is ever parsed — no parsing middleware is registered (no `app.use` exists in any `.js` file) and neither handler dereferences `req`. Content negotiation is absent: the response type is fixed at `text/plain` regardless of `Accept`, and no compression, range, or conditional-request handling is implemented.
- **Versioning and enumeration:** none. There is no API version prefix, no OpenAPI or machine-readable contract, and no discovery endpoint; `README.md` is the de facto contract (F-008).
- **Refusal behaviour:** an unregistered path is a refusal, not a fallback — the framework's `404` replaces the pre-migration route-agnostic greeting, which is the deliberate behaviour change recorded in `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2.

#### 4.1.2.3 Event Processing Flows

All events in the system are emitted by the Node.js `http.Server` or by the Express application. No event bus, message broker, custom `EventEmitter`, or listener registration in application code exists beyond what the framework wires itself.

| Event | Emitted by | Listener at HEAD | Effect |
|-------|-----------|------------------|--------|
| `listening` | Node `http.Server` after a successful bind | The `app.listen` callback (`server.js:26–28`) | Writes the single startup line; process begins serving |
| `error` | Node `http.Server` on bind failure | The same callback, registered by Express as a one-shot `error` listener (`express/lib/application.js:598–606`) | Banner printed, error discarded, process exits `0` — no diagnostic |
| `request` | Node `http.Server` per parsed request | Express `app.handle` | Router dispatch to L1, L2, the `OPTIONS` responder, or `finalhandler` |
| `clientError` | Node `http.Server` on a malformed request | **None** — the repository registers no listener (verified by text search) | Runtime default `400 Bad Request` and connection close; the process survives |
| `SIGTERM` / `SIGINT` | Operating system | **None** — no `process.on` exists | Immediate termination with no drain (exit `143` observed) |

The service is event-driven only in the framework sense: each request is handled synchronously to completion, with no timers, promises, streams, worker threads, or background tasks in application code.

#### 4.1.2.4 Batch Processing Sequences

No batch, scheduled, or asynchronous sequence exists. There is no job runner, cron entry, queue consumer, or `setInterval`/`setTimeout` in application code; no nightly or periodic reconciliation runs; and no build or CI pipeline produces artifacts, since development and deployment are the same act (`npm ci` then `node server.js`, §3.6).

Two repository artifacts resemble batch inputs but are consumed by nothing:

- `phonenumber.csv` (F-010) — a `message,phonenumber` header with 15 synthetic rows, imported by no code path. A repository-wide search finds no file-I/O call in any `.js` file, so no batch ingest or transformation of this data exists.
- The three filename fixtures (F-009) — runnable servers that are never invoked by the service. Each binds the **same** `127.0.0.1:3000` and answers **every** path and method, including `POST /` and `/deep/nested/path`, with `200` and `Hello, World!\n` (14 B, no `X-Powered-By` header, no `404` branch). Because the port is shared, a fixture and `server.js` cannot run concurrently: the fixture additionally crashes on `EADDRINUSE` with an unhandled `error` event (exit `1`, stack trace), while `server.js` exits silently with status `0`.

The only recurring activity in the system is therefore the per-request cycle of §4.1.1.3, repeated once per arriving request.


## 4.2 Flowchart Requirements

### 4.2.1 Per-Workflow Flowchart Elements

Every workflow diagram in §4.4 is built from the same notation, and each element below is traced to the observable behaviour it represents.

| Element | Notation used in §4.4 | Meaning in this system |
|---------|----------------------|------------------------|
| Terminal | Stadium node `(["..."])` or `([...])` | A start or end point: an operator command, a process start, a written response, or process death |
| Process step | Rectangle `["..."]` | A statement or framework action that executes without branching |
| Decision | Rhombus `{...}` | A condition the runtime or framework evaluates, always with labelled outgoing edges |
| System boundary | `subgraph` used as a swimlane | The owner of a step: operator host, npm CLI, registry, Node process, Express application, HTTP client |
| Error edge | Dashed or labelled edge to an error node | A path taken because a condition failed |
| Recovery edge | Edge back to a process step or to the operator | The manual remedy that re-enters the flow |
| Timing annotation | Label on the node or edge | A runtime default or a measured value governing that step |
| Requirement tag | Feature ID in the node label, e.g. `F-006` | The requirement of §2.2 the step satisfies |

The diagrams use Mermaid `flowchart`, `sequenceDiagram`, and `stateDiagram-v2` syntax; the high-level and per-journey flows carry swimlanes for the actors listed above, and every decision diamond is labelled with the condition actually evaluated by the code or the runtime.

#### 4.2.1.1 W1 — Dependency Installation (F-007)

| Element | Specification |
|---------|---------------|
| Start point | Operator shell in a fresh checkout: 20 tracked files, no `node_modules/` |
| End points (success) | `node_modules/` populated with the 66 locked packages; the install command exits `0` |
| End points (failure) | npm exits non-zero with the tree incomplete; the service cannot start |
| Process steps | (1) run `npm ci` or `npm install`; (2) read `package.json` (single dependency `express ^5.2.1`); (3) resolve the tree from `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion` 3, 66 entries); (4) fetch tarballs from `registry.npmjs.org`; (5) verify each against its recorded `sha512` integrity digest; (6) write `node_modules/`; (7) exit |
| Decision diamonds | **Is the lockfile honoured?** `npm ci` → exact tree, `npm install` → caret range may float within `^5.2.1`. **Is the tree complete?** A missing or partial tree makes step 2 of W2 fail with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` |
| System boundaries (swimlanes) | Operator host · npm CLI · public registry · repository filesystem (`.gitignore` excludes `node_modules/`) |
| User touchpoints | The operator's install command and npm's own console output; no application output |
| Error states and recovery | Fetch failure, integrity mismatch, or unwritable target path aborts npm non-zero. Recovery is manual: re-run the install. No retry, back-off, mirror, or offline cache is configured by this repository |
| Timing and SLA | No timeout, budget, or SLA is declared. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 records a completed install of the 66-package tree with `0 vulnerabilities` from `npm audit`; the value is a point-in-time observation, not a commitment |

#### 4.2.1.2 W2 — Process Start and Bind (F-001, F-002, F-003)

| Element | Specification |
|---------|---------------|
| Start point | `node server.js`, or `npm start` (npm's implicit default command for a package whose root contains `server.js`) |
| End points (success) | One line on stdout — `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` — with the event loop held open by the listener |
| End points (failure) | **Missing dependency:** `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at `server.js:1`, exit `1`, nothing on stdout (verified). **Bind conflict:** banner printed, error discarded, exit `0`, no diagnostic (verified) |
| Process steps | (1) `require('express')` (`server.js:1`); (2) bind `hostname`/`port` constants (lines 3–4); (3) `express()` and `defaultConfiguration()` (line 6); (4) `app.enable('strict routing')` (line 12); (5) first `app.get` builds the Router with `strict: true`, `caseSensitive: false` (line 14); (6) second `app.get` (line 20); (7) `app.listen(port, hostname, callback)` creates the `http.Server`, wraps the callback with `once`, registers it as a one-shot `error` listener, and binds (line 26) |
| Decision diamonds | **Is `express` resolvable?** no → process aborts before any output. **Is the bind successful?** no → the one-shot error listener consumes the event and the process exits `0`. **Was strict routing enabled before the first route registration?** no → trailing-slash variants would match (the setting is captured when the Router is constructed) |
| System boundaries (swimlanes) | Operator/supervisor · Node.js module loader · Express application · Node `http.Server` · loopback network interface |
| User touchpoints | The single startup line; no readiness endpoint, health check, or version output exists |
| Error states and recovery | `EADDRINUSE`/`EACCES` are swallowed, so the failure is silent and the banner is misleading. Recovery is manual: free port 3000 or edit the `port` literal, as recorded in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.7. F-101 proposes an `error` listener that logs and exits `1` |
| Timing and SLA | Bind happens during process start-up; no retry, back-off, or fallback port exists. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 records 100 % startup success on a free port and a launch-to-banner interval under one second on this host |

#### 4.2.1.3 W3 — Request Handling (F-004, F-005, F-006)

| Element | Specification |
|---------|---------------|
| Start point | An accepted TCP connection on `127.0.0.1:3000` carrying bytes that may or may not parse as HTTP |
| End points | `200` with a 14-byte or 12-byte `text/plain` body; `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` for `OPTIONS`; `404` with Express's default HTML; `400 Bad Request` plus connection close for malformed input |
| Process steps | (1) parse the request; (2) `app.handle` sets `X-Powered-By: Express` and prepares `finalhandler`; (3) router strips the query string and matches the path case-insensitively with significant trailing slashes; (4) the matched handler assigns `statusCode`, sets `Content-Type`, and calls `res.end(<literal>)`; (5) the runtime writes headers and body, computing `Content-Length`; (6) the socket returns to the keep-alive pool |
| Decision diamonds | **Is the request syntactically valid HTTP?** no → runtime `400` and connection close, process survives. **Does the path match `/` or `/good-evening` exactly (ignoring case, trailing slash significant)?** **Is the method `GET` or `HEAD`?** **Is the method `OPTIONS`?** → framework responder. Otherwise → `404`. Each diamond is evaluated by the router, not by application code |
| System boundaries (swimlanes) | HTTP client · Node `http.Server`/socket · Express router · route handlers and `finalhandler` |
| User touchpoints | The two documented URLs of `README.md` (plus their `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` variants); every response carries the framework-disclosure header |
| Error states and recovery | Malformed request → runtime `400`, connection closed, nothing logged, no application recovery needed because the listener survives (verified). Handler exception → the handlers contain three non-throwing statements, so the state is unreachable; F-103 proposes a `try`/`catch` with a `headersSent` guard for future-proofing. Unmatched request → `404` refusal, logged nowhere |
| Timing and SLA | Runtime defaults govern pacing: `keepAliveTimeout` 5 000 ms (echoed as `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`), `headersTimeout` 60 000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300 000 ms, `server.timeout` 0 (disabled). Measured on this host: 50 sequential keep-alive `GET /` requests between 0.17 ms and 8.93 ms (median 0.46 ms), and 100 concurrent requests completed in 37 ms. No SLA, KPI, or alert threshold is defined (see §1.2.3.3); the figures in `Response.txt` §0.6 (under 50 ms, under 50 MB RSS, 100+ connections) were written for the superseded implementation and are not objectives of this build |

#### 4.2.1.4 W4 — Termination and Failure Paths

| Element | Specification |
|---------|---------------|
| Start point | An external signal, or the end of the failure paths of W1–W3 |
| End points | Process death with exit `143` on `SIGTERM` (observed), `130` on `SIGINT` by the same default disposition, `1` on an unhandled `error` event, or silently `0` on a swallowed bind failure |
| Process steps | None in application code: no `process.on` registration, no `server.close()`, no cleanup, no `process.exit` exists anywhere in the repository's JavaScript |
| Decision diamonds | **Is a signal handler registered?** no → default disposition applies immediately. **Is the listener reference retained?** no → the server object is discarded at `server.js:26`, so `server.close()` is not reachable without a code change |
| System boundaries (swimlanes) | Operator/supervisor · operating system · Node.js process |
| User touchpoints | None — the termination is unobserved by the application, which writes nothing on the way out |
| Error states and recovery | In-flight responses are dropped and keep-alive sockets are reset; recovery is a full restart. F-102 proposes `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handlers with a 10-second force-exit guard and exit `0` on a drained shutdown; F-104 proposes a `clientError` listener; F-106 proposes a cleanup hook inside the close callback |
| Timing and SLA | No drain window exists today; the only proposed bound anywhere in the repository is F-102's 10-second force-exit guard, which is not implemented |

|-------------------------|-------------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|--------------------------|---------------|

| 4.4.5 State transition diagrams | Process/listener lifecycle and single-connection lifecycle | Initial and final states | Guarded transitions | Not applicable | Yes (failure transitions) | Yes (idle timeouts) |

### 4.2.2 Validation Rules

Every validation the system performs is performed **by the runtime or the framework**; the application itself validates nothing. The tables below state each rule, its enforcing layer, and the evidence, and they deliberately mark the rules that are unverifiable by automation because the repository ships no test suite.

#### 4.2.2.1 Business Rules at Each Step

| Step | Business rule | Source | Enforced by | Evidence at HEAD |
|------|---------------|--------|-------------|------------------|
| W1 install | Exactly one runtime dependency may be declared, at `^5.2.1` | F-007-RQ-001, FR-A | `package.json` `dependencies` block | One key, `express` |
| W1 install | The resolved tree must be pinned with registry URLs and `sha512` digests | F-007-RQ-002 | `package-lock.json` | `lockfileVersion` 3, 66 entries |
| W1 install | `node_modules/` must never be committed | F-007-RQ-004 | `.gitignore` | Single line `node_modules/` |
| W2 start | Installation must precede execution | F-007 business rule | Node module loader | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at `server.js:1` without the tree |
| W2 start | The listener binds loopback `127.0.0.1` only | F-002-RQ-001 | `server.js:3`, `app.listen` | Live binding on `127.0.0.1:3000`; no other interface referenced |
| W2 start | The port is `3000` with no fallback | F-002-RQ-002 | `server.js:4` | Port literal; a conflict is not retried or rerouted |
| W2 start | Exactly one startup line is written, on successful bind | F-003-RQ-001 | `console.log` in the listen callback | Verbatim line, one occurrence per launch |
| W2 start | Trailing slashes are significant | F-006-RQ-002 | `strict routing` captured by the Router | `/good-evening/` → `404`; ordering of `enable` before the first `app.get` is load-bearing |
| W3 request | Only the two literal paths serve content | F-006-RQ-001 | Router layer table | Repository search finds exactly `app.get('/')` and `app.get('/good-evening')` |
| W3 request | `GET /` returns byte-exact `Hello, World!` plus one `LF`, 14 B | F-004-RQ-001…003, FR-C | Handler literal and `res.end` | Live response, `Content-Length: 14` |
| W3 request | `GET /good-evening` returns byte-exact `Good evening`, 12 B, no trailing newline | F-005-RQ-001…003, FR-D | Handler literal and `res.end` | Live response, `Content-Length: 12` |
| W3 request | The root contract is byte-preserved from before the framework migration | FR-C, `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2 | `Project Guide.md` §5 | Byte comparison recorded and re-verified |
| W3 request | Case-insensitive matching, query string ignored | F-006-RQ-005 | Express defaults | `GET /GOOD-EVENING` → `200`; `GET /?x=1` → `200` |
| W3 request | Non-`GET`/`HEAD` methods on registered paths are refused | F-006-RQ-004 | Router method matching | `POST /` and `PUT /` → `404`; `OPTIONS /` → `200` `Allow: GET, HEAD` |
| W3 request | No request input may influence the response | F-004-RQ-004, F-005 | Handler code | `req` is never dereferenced; responses are source literals |
| W4 terminate | Termination happens through the runtime's default disposition | F-002-RQ-004 | Absence of signal handlers | `SIGTERM` → exit `143`, no shutdown output |

#### 4.2.2.2 Data Validation Requirements

| Layer | What is validated | Rule | Evidence |
|-------|-------------------|------|----------|
| Node.js HTTP parser | The request line and header block | The message must be syntactically valid HTTP/1.1; otherwise `clientError` fires, the runtime answers `400 Bad Request`, and the connection closes | Observed: `INVALID HTTP\r\n\r\n` returned `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` + `Connection: close`; the server kept serving |
| Express router | Path and method | Literal path equality (case-insensitive, trailing slash significant) and method `GET`/`HEAD`; anything else is refused | Full status matrix observed in §4.1.1.3 |
| Express `OPTIONS` responder | Presence of the method on a matched path | Framework-generated `Allow` header and body | `OPTIONS /` → `200`, `Allow: GET, HEAD`, body `GET, HEAD` |
| Route handlers | Nothing | No input is read, so no schema, type, range, or encoding validation exists; no parsing middleware is mounted, so a request body is never deserialized | No `app.use` in any `.js` file; no `req` dereference in `server.js:14–24` |
| Response construction | Body bytes | Acceptance is defined as byte equality, including the presence or absence of a trailing newline — asserted externally, never in code | `Project Guide.md` §3 records byte-level checks for 14 B and 12 B |
| Install workflow | Artifact integrity | Each locked package carries a `sha512` digest that npm verifies for the fetched tarball | `package-lock.json` entries |

There is no request-validation middleware, no schema library, no sanitisation step, and no rate limiting. The absence is consistent with the interface: neither handler reads a request value, so no injection or type-confusion surface exists inside the handlers themselves.

#### 4.2.2.3 Authorization Checkpoints

**None exist.** No authentication, authorization, session, cookie, token, API key, TLS client certificate, IP allow-list, or CSRF control is present anywhere in the repository, and the framework's cookie and session-adjacent dependencies (`cookie`, `cookie-signature`) are installed transitively but never mounted.

| Checkpoint that would normally apply | Status here | Consequence |
|--------------------------------------|-------------|-------------|
| Client authentication | Absent | Any local process that can reach `127.0.0.1:3000` receives both greetings |
| Authorization / role checks | Absent | There is no privileged operation, resource owner, or user identity to check |
| Transport encryption | Absent | Plain HTTP on the loopback interface; no TLS listener, certificate, or terminator |
| Network admission control | Absent by design of the bind, present by accident of topology | Loopback binding is the only access boundary; there is no proxy, allow-list, or firewall rule in the repository |
| Information disclosure control | Absent | Every response carries `X-Powered-By: Express`; suppression would require `app.disable('x-powered-by')`, which no file contains |

The security posture is therefore "reachable by anything on the host, and by nothing beyond it", which is sufficient for the integration-fixture purpose of the repository (`README.md`) and insufficient for any multi-tenant or network-exposed deployment; §1.3.2 records the hardening work that would be required.

#### 4.2.2.4 Regulatory and Compliance Checks

| Compliance area | Status | Evidence |
|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Regulatory control assertions in code | None | No compliance check, audit-log write, consent flag, or retention rule exists in any `.js` file |
| Personal data handling | No personal data crosses the service | Handlers read nothing; the only data artifact is `phonenumber.csv`, whose 15 rows are synthetic `+111111112xx` numbers with generic messages, read by no code (F-010) |
| Logging of client data | None possible | The single log line is a constant template of the bound host and port; no request data is ever written |
| Licence obligations | Recorded, inherited from the dependency tree | `express` and most transitives are MIT, `inherits`/`once`/`setprototypeof`/`wrappy` are ISC, `qs` is BSD-3-Clause; the project itself is MIT (`package.json`) |
| Supply-chain assurance | Point-in-time only | Pinned versions and `sha512` digests in the lockfile; `npm audit` reported `0 vulnerabilities` when run, and nothing wires that check into a script or pipeline (§3.6) |
| Change control | Manual | 11 commits on one branch, with no protected-branch rule, CI gate, or signed-commit requirement recorded in the repository |

No standard is claimed anywhere in the repository — no SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI scope statement exists — so there is no external obligation for the flowcharts to reflect.

#### 4.2.2.5 Verification Coverage of These Rules

The validation rules above are enforced at run time but are **not covered by any automated test**: `package.json` declares only the npm-init placeholder `test` script, which prints `Error: no test specified` and exits `1` (verified), the repository contains no test file or framework, and no CI pipeline exists. The verification basis is therefore manual and reproducible rather than automated: launch `node server.js`, then issue requests and compare raw bytes — the method used for every observed value in this section, and the same method the repository's own validation ledger records (`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3: 4/4 requirements delivered, 9/9 functional checks). Any change to `server.js` invalidates the observed values in §4.2.1 through §4.2.2, because the contract they describe lives in that single file.


## 4.3 Technical Implementation

### 4.3.1 State Management

The service is stateless in the application sense and stateful only in the framework and runtime sense. Two literal responses are produced from constants, so no request can change what any later request observes.

#### 4.3.1.1 State Inventory

| State | Location | Kind | Lifetime | Mutable at run time? | Evidence |
|-------|----------|------|----------|----------------------|----------|
| `hostname`, `port` | Module scope of `server.js` (lines 3–4) | `const` literals | Whole process | No | Read once for the bind and again for the startup message, so the logged URL cannot disagree with the bound address |
| `app` | Module scope of `server.js` (line 6) | Express application object | Whole process | Only during start-up | Created by `express()`; never exported, never reassigned |
| Express settings map | Internal to the application (`app.settings`) | Key/value configuration | Whole process | Written only at start-up | `strict routing` `true` (line 12), `x-powered-by` `true`, `etag` `weak`, `env` `development`, `query parser` `simple`, `trust proxy` `false`, `subdomain offset` `2` — all framework defaults except the first |
| Empty framework containers | `app.cache`, `app.engines`, `app.locals` created by `app.init` | Objects | Whole process | No writes occur | No view engine, template, or cached-render path is used anywhere |
| Router instance and route table | Retained in the application's closure via the lazy `router` getter | Two route layers plus Router options | Whole process, created on first `app.get` | No — the table is closed after line 20 | `strict: true`, `caseSensitive: false`, captured at construction; a later change to the setting would not affect matching |
| Server object | Returned by `app.listen` and **discarded** (`server.js:26`) | `http.Server` | Whole process | Not reachable from application code | No reference is retained, so `server.close()` cannot be called without a code change |
| Connection and socket state | Node's `http.Server` internals | Per-connection sockets, keep-alive pool | Per connection; idle sockets reaped after 5 s | Managed by the runtime | `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` on responses; `keepAliveTimeout` 5 000 ms |
| Per-request objects | `req`, `res`, and the `finalhandler` closure bound in `app.handle` | Per-request | One request | Yes, but only `res` is written | Created and discarded per request; `req` is never dereferenced |
| Module cache | Node's `require` cache | Loaded module registry | Whole process | No | `express` and its 65 transitives load once, at start-up |

There is **no** application state of any other kind: no counter, sequence, session, user context, job, or in-flight work item. No `let` or `var` binding is mutated at run time, no global is assigned, and nothing is exported.

#### 4.3.1.2 State Transitions

The complete life of a process is a one-way sequence with a single steady state:

| From | To | Guard / trigger | Notes |
|------|----|-----------------|-------|
| (not started) | Module evaluation | `node server.js` | `require('express')` may abort the sequence with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, exit `1` |
| Module evaluation | Application configured | `express()` (line 6) | Framework defaults written into the settings map |
| Application configured | Router built | First `app.get` (line 14) | The Router captures `strict`/`caseSensitive` at this instant — the ordering constraint of §4.1.1.2 |
| Router built | Server created | `app.listen` (line 26) | `http.createServer(app)`; the listen callback is wrapped with `once` and registered as a one-shot `error` listener |
| Server created | Listening / Serving | Successful bind to `127.0.0.1:3000` | Startup line written once; event loop held open by the listener |
| Server created | Terminated | `EADDRINUSE` / `EACCES` | The one-shot listener consumes the event; the process exits `0` with the banner already printed and no diagnostic |
| Serving | Serving (steady state) | Each request | Requests are handled synchronously and independently; no state carries between them |
| Serving | Terminated | `SIGTERM` / `SIGINT` | Default signal disposition: immediate exit (`143` observed), keep-alive sockets reset, in-flight responses dropped |

There is no `Closing`, `Draining`, or `Restarting` state, and none can be entered from the current code: no `server.close()` call exists and the server handle is not retained. The proposed graceful-shutdown feature (F-102) would add exactly those states, and F-106 a cleanup step inside the close callback.

#### 4.3.1.3 Data Persistence Points

| Point | Timing | Persisted artifact | Evidence |
|-------|--------|--------------------|----------|
| Dependency installation | Install-time (once per checkout) | `node_modules/` with the 66 locked packages, git-ignored | `.gitignore` single line `node_modules/`; `package-lock.json` pins the tree |
| Process start-up | Each launch | None | No file, database, or cache write occurs in any code path |
| Request handling | Per request | None | Both handlers assign a status code, set one header, and write a literal; no `fs` usage exists in any `.js` file |
| Termination | Process end | None | Nothing is flushed or checkpointed; no cleanup hook exists (F-106 proposed) |

State therefore lives **only** in process memory and dies with the process, which makes a restart lossless by construction: there is no state to lose, reconcile, or recover. The repository's only durable artifacts are source files, the two manifests, and the documentation set — none of which the running service writes.

#### 4.3.1.4 Caching Requirements

| Cache layer | Status | Detail |
|-------------|--------|--------|
| HTTP response cache directives | None emitted | No `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `Age`, or `Vary` header appears in any response; the service expresses no caching policy |
| Validators | None emitted | No `ETag` and no `Last-Modified`; the `etag` setting is `weak` but never exercised, because both handlers call `res.end` rather than `res.send`, which bypasses the framework's entity-tag generation |
| Conditional requests | Not handled | No `If-None-Match`/`If-Modified-Since` path exists, so a validator can never produce `304`; no handler reads a request header |
| Application-level cache | Not implemented | No in-memory cache, memoisation, or warm-up; the responses are literals, so nothing is expensive enough to cache |
| Framework/runtime caches | Present, structural | The `require` module cache loads `express` and its transitives once at start-up, and the route table is built once; these are process-lifetime structures, not request caches |
| External caches | Outside the repository | npm maintains its own package cache for installs, and any proxy or client cache in front of the service would operate heuristically, since the service supplies no directives or validators |

No cache invalidation, expiry, or stampede control applies, because no cache within the system holds request-derived data.

#### 4.3.1.5 Transaction Boundaries

Neither a database nor a multi-step write exists, so there is no transactional storage to define. The three units of work that do exist are:

| Unit of work | Boundary | Atomicity | Evidence |
|--------------|----------|-----------|----------|
| One HTTP request | From the `request` event to the completion of `res.end` | The handler performs three synchronous statements with no I/O, no `await`, and no callbacks, so it cannot be interleaved with another request; the status, the header, and the body are written in one uninterrupted sequence | `server.js:14–24`; single-threaded event loop |
| Response writing | `res.statusCode` / `setHeader` / `end` | Once the response has been flushed, a second write is impossible — which is exactly the condition F-103's `headersSent` guard is designed to detect, for the exception path that does not occur today | `Response.txt` §0.4 Change #1 |
| Dependency installation | One npm command | The only multi-file write in the repository's life cycle; each package is resolved from a pinned lockfile entry and verified against a `sha512` digest, so a partial tree is detected on the next start-up as `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` | `package-lock.json`; observed abort at `server.js:1` without the tree |

No compensating action, rollback, or retry applies to any of them. A failed bind, a refused route, and a dropped connection all leave the process in exactly the state it was in before the attempt.

### 4.3.2 Error Handling

#### 4.3.2.1 Current Posture

The application contains **no error-handling code**. A text search of all four repository `.js` files for `.on(`, `process.on`, `try`, `catch`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `clientError`, `uncaughtException`, `headersSent`, and `process.exit` returns zero matches. Every failure path below is therefore either the framework's default, the runtime's default, or absent altogether.

| # | Error source | Trigger | Mechanism at HEAD | Observed outcome | Recovery |
|---|--------------|---------|-------------------|------------------|----------|
| 1 | Unresolvable dependency | `require('express')` with no installed tree | Module loader throws at `server.js:1`; nothing registers `uncaughtException` | `Error: Cannot find module 'express'` (`MODULE_NOT_FOUND`) on stderr, **exit `1`**, no stdout (verified outside the checkout) | Manual: run `npm ci` / `npm install`, then restart |
| 2 | Bind conflict or permission failure | Port 3000 already bound (`EADDRINUSE`) or insufficient privilege (`EACCES`) | Express's `listen` wrapper registers the supplied callback with `server.once('error', done)`, so the callback *is* the error listener; it takes no parameters, cannot observe the error, and prints the startup banner | Startup banner printed, **no diagnostic**, **exit `0`** (verified: callback invoked with `EADDRINUSE`, `this.listening === false`) | Manual: free port 3000 or edit the port literal; F-101 proposes a real handler that logs and exits `1` |
| 3 | Unhandled `error` event (native-`http` fixtures) | Same bind conflict, but in `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, or the 199-character fixture | `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` registers no `error` listener at all, so the event throws | `throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event` with the full `EADDRINUSE` stack, **exit `1`** (verified live) | Manual: free the port |
| 4 | Malformed HTTP request | Invalid request line or header block from a client | No `clientError` listener is registered, so the runtime's built-in handling applies | `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` + `Connection: close`, connection closed, listener survives, **nothing logged** (verified with raw socket bytes) | None needed for the service; F-104 proposes an explicit listener on the same event |
| 5 | Route or method not matched | `/nope`, `/hello`, `//`, `/good-evening/`, `POST /`, `PUT /` | Express router falls through to `finalhandler` | `404 Not Found` with default HTML and restrictive security headers; no error object exists for a not-found, so `finalhandler` schedules no `onerror` call and **nothing is logged** | None — a refusal is the designed outcome (F-006) |
| 6 | Exception inside a route handler | Not reachable today: each handler is three non-throwing statements that read no input | Express 5 catches synchronous handler throws and forwards them to its default error handler; with no error middleware registered, the browser-style default response is produced and the error is written to stderr because `env` is `development` | Not exercised — no code path throws | F-103 proposes an explicit `try`/`catch` producing `500 Internal Server Error` only when `headersSent` is `false` |
| 7 | Response already committed | Not reachable: no streaming, no asynchronous write, no double `end` | — | Not applicable | F-103's `headersSent` guard is the designed protection for the future case |
| 8 | Process signal | `SIGTERM` from a supervisor or container stop, `SIGINT` from `Ctrl+C` | No `process.on` registration, so the runtime's default disposition applies | Immediate termination, **exit `143`** on `SIGTERM` (verified), `130` on `SIGINT`; no shutdown output; in-flight responses dropped; keep-alive sockets reset | Manual restart; F-102 proposes `server.close()` with a 10-second force-exit guard, and F-106 a cleanup hook |
| 9 | Exhausted resources (file descriptors, memory, event-loop saturation) | Host-level limits | No limit, back-pressure, or monitoring is configured, and no metric is emitted | Not exercised; the service would simply stop accepting connections | Manual: restart, then investigate host limits |

**Conflicting accounts of source #2.** The repository's documentation describes a bind conflict as fatal: `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §3.6.5 routes the `no` branch of its bind decision to an "Unhandled error event / process aborts" node, and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.7 records `EADDRINUSE` as a reachable symptom. That description fits the native-`http` fixtures (row 3) but not `server.js`: the Express implementation swallows the error and exits silently with status `0` (row 2), because its startup callback is the listener that consumes the `error` event. Both behaviours are recorded here with their paths, and F-101's acceptance criterion (log an `already in use` line, exit `1`) is currently unmet for `server.js`.

#### 4.3.2.2 Retry Mechanisms

None exist. Specifically:

- **No bind retry and no fallback port.** `app.listen` is called once with the literal `3000`; a conflict ends the attempt rather than retrying or shifting ports (F-002-RQ-002).
- **No outbound retry.** The service makes no outbound calls, so no client retry, back-off, jitter, circuit breaker, or timeout configuration exists. The only network retry in the repository's life cycle is npm's own behaviour during installation, which this project does not configure.
- **No request retry or re-drive.** Requests are handled once, synchronously, with no queue, dead-letter path, or idempotency key.
- **The only effective retry is the operator's.** Restarting the process, or re-running the install after a failure, is the entire recovery mechanism; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.7 documents it as such.

#### 4.3.2.3 Fallback Processes

None exist, and the design deliberately refuses rather than substitutes:

- **No greeting fallback.** An unregistered path receives `404`; the pre-migration behaviour of answering every request with `Hello, World!` was intentionally removed (`Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2), so a failed route match cannot degrade into a `200`.
- **No degraded mode.** There is no cached response, no static file served if a handler fails, and no secondary listener.
- **No supervisor-driven fallback.** The process has no health or readiness endpoint for an external watchdog to probe, and no restart policy of its own; the only readiness signal is the single startup line on stdout.
- **No dual-run or failover.** The hardcoded loopback bind and fixed port prevent a second instance on the same host (§3.6.5), so no active/standby arrangement is possible as configured.

#### 4.3.2.4 Error Notification Flows

| Channel | What it carries | When it fires | Evidence |
|---------|-----------------|---------------|----------|
| Standard output | `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` — once per process, from the listen callback | On every launch, including a launch whose bind failed | `server.js:27`; observed on both the successful and the conflict launch |
| Standard error | Runtime diagnostics only: uncaught `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, unhandled `error` events, and — on the Express 5 error path — the framework's `logerror` output, which writes `err.stack` whenever `NODE_ENV` is not `test` | Only when the runtime or framework throws | Verified for rows 1 and 3 of the error table |
| Framework error logging | `finalhandler` schedules `onerror` (Express's `logerror`) via `setImmediate` only when an error object is supplied, which a plain not-found does not carry | Never on a `404`; only on a framework 5xx | `finalhandler/index.js` lines 100–120; observed: a 404 and a malformed request both produced no log line |
| Metrics, traces, alerts, log shippers | Nothing | Never — no instrumentation, agent, or exporter exists anywhere in the repository | No dependency or configuration file for any observability tool |
| Health and readiness probes | Nothing | Never — no health endpoint is registered | Repository search finds only the two `app.get` registrations |

Operationally, the service is effectively **silent**: successes are announced once at start-up, refusals and malformed requests are announced nowhere, and the most damaging start-up failure (a port conflict) is announced as a success. Observability of a running instance depends entirely on an operator tailing the process output, exactly as the repository's own guidance assumes (§3.6.5).

#### 4.3.2.5 Recovery Procedures

| Situation | Signal available | Procedure | Source |
|-----------|------------------|-----------|--------|
| Port 3000 already in use | Startup banner appears and the process exits `0`, or the fixtures print an `EADDRINUSE` stack | Free port 3000, or change the `port` literal and restart | `Project Guide.md` §9.7; verified |
| Dependencies missing after checkout | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at `server.js:1`, exit `1` | Run `npm ci` (reproducible) or `npm install`, then restart | `README.md` §Running; verified |
| Process stopped by a signal | Exit status `143` (`SIGTERM`) or `130` (`SIGINT`) | Restart the process; no drain occurs, so any request in flight at signal time must be re-issued | Verified |
| Requests refused with `404` | HTML body `Cannot GET <path>` | Correct the client's path, method, or trailing slash; the service is behaving as specified | F-006 |
| Malformed request closed with `400` | Runtime status line on the socket, no application log | Fix the client's request framing; nothing to recover on the server | Verified |
| Registry unreachable at install time | npm's own non-zero exit | Re-run the install when the registry is reachable; no mirror or offline fallback is configured | Journey 1 |

#### 4.3.2.6 Resilience Gap Inventory

The six gaps below are catalogued as the proposed features F-101–F-106 in §2.2.3 and remain unimplemented. Each targets a flow described in this section, and each must be re-derived before implementation: the originating plan (`Response.txt`) was written against the superseded `http.createServer` file and forbids the dependencies and routes this repository now has.

| Gap | Missing control today | Proposed feature | Flow it would change |
|-----|----------------------|------------------|----------------------|
| Bind failures are silent and misreported as success | `error` listener on the server returned by `app.listen` | F-101 — log, then exit `1` | §4.1.1.2 step 11; §4.4.3 |
| No drain on shutdown | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handlers calling `server.close()` with a 10-second guard | F-102 (requires retaining the `app.listen` return value) | §4.1.1.4; §4.4.5 |
| Handler exceptions would take the default 500 path | `try`/`catch` with a `headersSent` guard | F-103 | §4.3.2.1 row 6 |
| Malformed requests are handled only by the runtime, silently | `clientError` listener writing a `400` status line | F-104 | §4.1.1.3 step 2; §4.4.3 |
| No guard against a falsy `req`/`res` | Early return on falsy arguments | F-105 | Both handlers |
| No release point for future resources | Cleanup hook inside the close callback | F-106 | §4.3.1.3 |


## 4.4 Required Diagrams

### 4.4.1 High-Level System Workflow

One view of the whole system: the install path that precedes every launch, the start-up path with its single bind decision, the steady-state request path, and the termination path. Each swimlane is the boundary of an actor or an executing system; every decision diamond is labelled with the condition the code or the runtime actually evaluates.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph LaneOperator["Swimlane: Operator or supervisor"]
        OpInstall(["Start: npm ci or npm install"])
        OpRun(["Start: node server.js, or npm start"])
        OpSignal(["Start: SIGTERM or SIGINT sent"])
        OpRemedy["Remedy: free port 3000 or edit the port literal"]
        OpRestart(["End: process restarted"])
    end

    subgraph LaneNpm["Swimlane: npm CLI and public registry (install-time)"]
        NpmRead["Read package.json: one dependency, express ^5.2.1"]
        NpmLock["Resolve the tree from package-lock.json: 66 entries with sha512 digests"]
        NpmFetch["Fetch tarballs from registry.npmjs.org"]
        NpmWrite["Extract into node_modules, which .gitignore excludes"]
    end

    subgraph LaneProcess["Swimlane: Node.js process executing server.js"]
        Dep["require('express') resolves F-001"]
        Cfg["express() applies framework defaults F-001"]
        Strict["app.enable strict routing before the first route registration F-006"]
        Router["First app.get builds the Router with strict true F-006"]
        Table["Second app.get closes the routing table: / and /good-evening F-004 F-005"]
        Listen["app.listen creates http.Server and binds 127.0.0.1:3000 F-002"]
        Ready["Startup line written once to stdout F-003"]
        Idle["Idle event loop: the listener holds the process open"]
    end

    subgraph LaneRuntime["Swimlane: runtime, router, handlers and terminal handler"]
        V{"Valid HTTP syntax?"}
        Decide{"Path and method match a registered route?"}
        Handler["Handler: status 200, Content-Type text/plain, res.end literal F-004 F-005"]
        Options["OPTIONS responder: 200 with Allow GET, HEAD"]
        NotFound["finalhandler: 404 Not Found F-006"]
        Bad["Runtime clientError default: 400 Bad Request, connection closed"]
        Keep["Socket returns to the keep-alive pool, 5 second idle timeout"]
    end

    subgraph LaneClient["Swimlane: HTTP client"]
        Request(["Start: request to 127.0.0.1:3000"])
        Body(["End: 200 with a 14-byte or 12-byte text/plain body"])
        Refused(["End: 404 refusal"])
        Closed(["End: connection closed after 400"])
    end

    OpInstall --> NpmRead --> NpmLock --> NpmFetch --> NpmWrite --> OpRun
    OpRun --> Dep --> Cfg --> Strict --> Router --> Table --> Listen
    Listen --> Ready --> Idle
    Listen -->|"EADDRINUSE or EACCES: the error event is swallowed"| OpRemedy
    OpRemedy --> OpRestart
    Request --> V
    V -->|"no"| Bad
    V -->|"yes"| Decide
    Decide -->|"GET or HEAD on / or /good-evening"| Handler
    Decide -->|"OPTIONS on a registered path"| Options
    Decide -->|"unregistered path, trailing slash variant, or other method"| NotFound
    Handler --> Body
    Options --> Body
    NotFound --> Refused
    Bad --> Closed
    Body --> Keep
    Keep --> Request
    Idle --> Decide
    OpSignal -->|"no signal handler registered"| OpRestart
```

**Reading this diagram.** Solid edges are the normal path; the two failure edges are the silent bind conflict and the runtime-level `400`. The request path is a cycle: the keep-alive pool returns to the next request until the 5-second idle timeout closes the socket. Termination has no application involvement at all, because no signal handler exists. Timing is dominated by three runtime defaults — `keepAliveTimeout` 5 s, `headersTimeout` 60 s, `requestTimeout` 300 s — while the work per request is three synchronous statements.

### 4.4.2 Detailed Process Flows per Core Feature

#### 4.4.2.1 F-007 — Dependency Installation

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start: fresh checkout, no node_modules"]) --> I{"Which install command?"}
    I -->|"npm ci"| C["Resolve the exact tree from package-lock.json, lockfileVersion 3, 66 entries"]
    I -->|"npm install"| N["Resolve express ^5.2.1; may float within the caret range"]
    C --> F["Fetch each tarball from registry.npmjs.org"]
    N --> F
    F --> V{"Fetched tarball matches its recorded sha512 digest?"}
    V -->|"yes"| W["Extract the 66 packages into node_modules"]
    V -->|"no, or the fetch failed"| E(["End: npm exits non-zero, tree incomplete"])
    W --> OK(["End: service can start; exit 0"])
    E --> R["Operator remedy: re-run the install when the registry is reachable"]
    R -.-> S
```

No build, compile, bundle, or transpile step follows; the install is the entire build (`README.md` §Running, §3.6.2).

#### 4.4.2.2 F-001, F-002, F-003 — Process Start, Bind, and Readiness

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start: node server.js, or npm start"]) --> A["Module evaluation begins at line 1"]
    A --> B{"Is express resolvable from node_modules?"}
    B -->|"no"| E1["Uncaught MODULE_NOT_FOUND at server.js:1"]
    E1 --> E1b(["End: exit 1, stack trace on stderr, nothing on stdout"])
    B -->|"yes"| C["Bind the hostname 127.0.0.1 and port 3000 constants, lines 3-4"]
    C --> D["express() runs defaultConfiguration: x-powered-by on, etag weak, env development, query parser simple"]
    D --> F["app.enable strict routing writes the setting only, line 12"]
    F --> G{"Router already built?"}
    G -->|"no, this is the first app.get"| H["Router constructed with strict true and caseSensitive false, line 14"]
    G -->|"yes, a setting change now would be ignored"| H2["Route layer registered on the existing Router"]
    H --> J["Second app.get registers /good-evening, line 20"]
    H2 --> J
    J --> K["app.listen creates http.Server, wraps the callback with once and registers it as a one-shot error listener, line 26"]
    K --> L{"Did the bind to 127.0.0.1:3000 succeed?"}
    L -->|"yes"| M["listening event: the callback writes the startup line once"]
    M --> M2(["End: idle event loop, serving requests"])
    L -->|"no: EADDRINUSE or EACCES"| N["error event consumed by the one-shot listener"]
    N --> O["The same callback prints the startup banner and cannot see the error"]
    O --> O2(["End: no diagnostic, exit code 0 - silent failure"])
    O2 -.-> P["Operator remedy: free port 3000 or edit the literal"]
    P -.-> S
```

**Binding constraint.** The strict-routing setting is only effective because line 12 precedes the first `app.get` at line 14; the Router captures `strict` and `caseSensitive` when it is constructed. Enabling the setting after a route registration leaves `GET /good-evening/` answering `200`.

#### 4.4.2.3 F-004 — Root Greeting Request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start: GET / arrives on 127.0.0.1:3000"]) --> P["Node HTTP parser accepts the request line and headers"]
    P --> Q["Router strips the query string, then matches case-insensitively with significant trailing slashes"]
    Q --> R{"Literal path equal to / ?"}
    R -->|"no"| Next["Continue to the next route layer"]
    R -->|"yes"| M{"Method GET or HEAD?"}
    M -->|"no"| Next
    M -->|"yes"| X["Handler: statusCode 200, Content-Type text/plain, res.end Hello World with one LF"]
    X --> Y["Runtime writes Content-Length 14, Date, Connection keep-alive, Keep-Alive timeout 5"]
    Y --> Z(["End: 200 with the 14-byte body; no ETag and no Cache-Control"])
    Next --> N2["finalhandler answers 404 Not Found with Cannot GET path"]
    N2 --> N3(["End: refusal; nothing is logged"])
```

`HEAD /` takes the same path and returns `200` with the headers but no body. `GET /?x=1` and `GET /` are indistinguishable to the handler, which never reads the request.

#### 4.4.2.4 F-005 — Second Greeting Request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start: GET /good-evening, or a near miss"]) --> Q["Router matches case-insensitively with significant trailing slashes"]
    Q --> D{"Path matches /good-evening ignoring case, with no trailing slash?"}
    D -->|"yes"| M{"Method GET or HEAD?"}
    M -->|"yes"| X["Handler: statusCode 200, Content-Type text/plain, res.end Good evening with no newline"]
    M -->|"other method"| R["finalhandler answers 404"]
    D -->|"no: trailing slash, or a different literal such as /evening"| R
    X --> Y["Runtime writes Content-Length 12 and the keep-alive headers"]
    Y --> Z(["End: 200 with the 12-byte body"])
    R --> R2(["End: 404 refusal"])
```

The trailing-slash distinction is the deliberate behaviour change recorded as QA Issue 1 (commit `f2c2ca4`); case-insensitive matching remains a framework default, so `GET /GOOD-EVENING` returns `200`.

#### 4.4.2.5 F-006 — Routing Decision and Refusal

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start: any request on the listener"]) --> V{"Valid HTTP syntax?"}
    V -->|"no"| B400["Runtime clientError default: 400 Bad Request plus Connection close"]
    V -->|"yes"| M{"Request method"}
    M -->|"GET or HEAD"| G{"Path equal to / or /good-evening, ignoring case, with no trailing slash?"}
    M -->|"OPTIONS"| O["Express OPTIONS responder: 200 with Allow GET, HEAD and body GET, HEAD"]
    M -->|"POST, PUT, DELETE or PATCH"| R["finalhandler: 404 Not Found"]
    G -->|"yes"| H["Registered handler: 200, text/plain, literal body"]
    G -->|"no"| R
    B400 --> E1(["End: connection closed, listener survives, nothing logged"])
    O --> E2(["End: 200"])
    H --> E3(["End: 200 with a 14-byte or 12-byte body"])
    R --> E4(["End: 404 with default HTML, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff and a restrictive CSP"])
```

This is the closed route table: exactly two literal paths serve content, and everything else — including `//`, `/good-evening/`, `/hello`, and `POST /` — is refused rather than answered with a greeting.

#### 4.4.2.6 F-009 — Fixture Server Flow (Contrast)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start: node Test.test..js, or either other fixture script"]) --> L["require http, constants hostname and port, http.createServer with a route-agnostic handler"]
    L --> B["server.listen 127.0.0.1:3000 with no error listener at all"]
    B --> D{"Did the bind succeed?"}
    D -->|"yes"| H["Every request, any path and any method, is answered 200 text/plain Hello World with one LF"]
    H --> E1(["End: no 404 branch, no X-Powered-By header, 14 bytes every time"])
    D -->|"no: port 3000 already bound"| X["Unhandled error event throws EADDRINUSE"]
    X --> E2(["End: exit 1 with an EADDRINUSE stack trace on stderr"])
```

The fixtures share the port with the service and cannot run concurrently; their bind failure **crashes**, which is the behaviour the repository documentation attributes to `server.js` but which the Express implementation replaced with a silent exit (§4.3.2.1).

### 4.4.3 Error Handling Flowchart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph StartupErrors["Startup error paths"]
        A1{"Is express resolvable?"}
        A2["Uncaught MODULE_NOT_FOUND, exit 1, no stdout"]
        A3{"Did the bind to 127.0.0.1:3000 succeed?"}
        A4["One-shot error listener consumes EADDRINUSE or EACCES: banner printed, exit 0"]
```
