```mermaid
    end

    subgraph RequestErrors["Request error paths"]
        B1{"Valid HTTP syntax?"}
        B2["Runtime default: 400 Bad Request, connection closed, nothing logged"]
        B3["F-104 proposed: clientError listener writes the 400 status line to the socket"]
        B4{"Route and method match?"}
        B5["finalhandler 404; no error object, so nothing is logged"]
        B6{"Did a handler throw synchronously?"}
        B7["Express default error handler responds 500 and logs to stderr (env is development)"]
        B8["F-103 proposed: try catch with a headersSent guard"]
    end

    subgraph LifecycleErrors["Lifecycle and process error paths"]
        C1{"Is a signal handler registered?"}
        C2["Default disposition: exit 143 on SIGTERM, 130 on SIGINT, in-flight work dropped"]
        C3["F-102 proposed: server.close with a 10 second force-exit guard"]
        C4["F-106 proposed: cleanup hook inside the close callback"]
    end

    subgraph ManualRecovery["Operator recovery - the only channel today"]
        R1["Free port 3000, or edit the port literal"]
        R2["Run npm ci to restore the dependency tree"]
        R3["Restart the process and re-issue dropped requests"]
    end

    A1 -->|"no"| A2
    A2 --> R2
    A2 --> R3
    A1 -->|"yes"| A3
    A3 -->|"no"| A4
    A4 --> R1
    A4 -.-> A5
    A3 -->|"yes"| B1
    B1 -->|"no"| B2
    B2 -.-> B3
    B1 -->|"yes"| B4
    B4 -->|"no"| B5
    B4 -->|"yes"| B6
    B6 -->|"yes - not reachable in the current code"| B7
    B7 -.-> B8
    B6 -->|"no"| C1
    C1 -->|"no"| C2
    C2 --> R3
    C1 -.-> C3
    C3 -.-> C4
```

Solid edges are implemented behaviour; dashed edges are proposed remediation (F-101, F-103, F-104, F-102, F-106) that no code implements today. Every recovery edge ends in a manual operator action, because the service has no automatic recovery, retry, or drain path.

### 4.4.4 Integration Sequence Diagrams

#### 4.4.4.1 Request Path (F-004, F-005, F-006)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as HTTP client
    participant S as Node http.Server socket
    participant A as Express app.handle
    participant R as Express router
    participant H as Route handler
    participant F as finalhandler

    C->>S: TCP connect to 127.0.0.1:3000, then send the request
    alt Malformed HTTP bytes
        S-->>C: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request, Connection close
        Note over S: No clientError listener is registered, so the runtime default answers and nothing is logged
    else Well-formed request
        S->>A: request event carrying req and res
        A->>R: dispatch after setting X-Powered-By Express
        alt GET or HEAD on / or /good-evening
            R->>H: invoke the matched route layer
            H-->>A: statusCode 200, Content-Type text/plain, res.end literal
            A-->>C: 200 with a 14-byte or 12-byte body, Content-Length, Keep-Alive timeout 5
        else OPTIONS on a registered path
            R-->>C: 200 with Allow GET, HEAD and body GET, HEAD
        else Unregistered path, trailing slash variant, or other method
            R->>F: fall through to the terminal handler
            F-->>C: 404 Not Found with Cannot GET path
        end
        Note over C,S: The socket returns to the keep-alive pool for up to 5 seconds
    end
```

#### 4.4.4.2 Install-Time Data Flow (F-007)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Operator
    participant N as npm CLI
    participant M as package.json and package-lock.json
    participant G as registry.npmjs.org
    participant D as node_modules, git-ignored

    O->>N: npm ci
    N->>M: read the single dependency express ^5.2.1 and the locked tree
    M-->>N: 66 entries, each with a resolved URL and a sha512 digest
    N->>G: fetch each tarball
    G-->>N: tarball bytes
    N->>N: verify each tarball against its recorded digest
    N->>D: extract the 66 packages
    D-->>O: install complete, exit 0
    Note over O,D: Without this step, server.js aborts at line 1 with MODULE_NOT_FOUND and exit 1
```

This is the only cross-system interaction in the repository, and it happens before the service ever runs; after installation the process makes no outbound connection.

#### 4.4.4.3 Termination Path (F-002, RQ-004)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Sup as Supervisor or operator
    participant OS as Operating system
    participant P as Node process
    participant C as HTTP client

    C->>P: request in flight
    Sup->>OS: stop the process
    OS->>P: SIGTERM
    Note over P: No process.on handler exists, so the runtime default disposition applies
    P--xC: connection dropped, response never completed
    OS-->>Sup: exit status 143
    Note over Sup,P: No drain, no cleanup, no shutdown log; F-102 and F-106 remain proposed
```

### 4.4.5 State Transition Diagrams

#### 4.4.5.1 Process and Listener Lifecycle

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ModuleEvaluation : node server.js or npm start
    ModuleEvaluation --> AbortedDependency : express unresolvable, MODULE_NOT_FOUND
    AbortedDependency --> [*] : exit 1 with a stack trace
    ModuleEvaluation --> AppConfigured : express() applies framework defaults
    AppConfigured --> RouterBuilt : first app.get builds the Router, strict true, caseSensitive false
    RouterBuilt --> ServerCreated : app.listen creates http.Server and registers the one-shot error listener
    ServerCreated --> TerminatedSilently : bind fails, EADDRINUSE or EACCES
    TerminatedSilently --> [*] : exit 0 after printing the banner, no diagnostic
    ServerCreated --> Serving : bind succeeds on 127.0.0.1:3000
    Serving --> Serving : request handled synchronously, no state carried over
    Serving --> TerminatedBySignal : SIGTERM or SIGINT, default disposition
    TerminatedBySignal --> [*] : exit 143 or 130, no drain

    note right of Serving
        Steady state. The server object is discarded at line 26, so no Closing
        or Draining state is reachable without retaining the app.listen result.
    end note
```

#### 4.4.5.2 Connection Lifecycle

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Connected : TCP accept on 127.0.0.1:3000
    Connected --> Parsing : request bytes received
    Parsing --> Rejected400 : HTTP syntax invalid
    Rejected400 --> [*] : 400 Bad Request, then connection close
    Parsing --> Dispatched : request event emitted
    Dispatched --> Matched : router matches / or /good-evening with GET or HEAD
    Dispatched --> OptionsResponded : OPTIONS on a registered path
    Dispatched --> Refused404 : no path or method match
    Matched --> Responded : handler writes status, one header and the literal body
    OptionsResponded --> KeepAliveIdle : 200 with Allow GET, HEAD
    Responded --> KeepAliveIdle : socket returned to the pool
    Refused404 --> KeepAliveIdle : 404 written, listener stays up
    KeepAliveIdle --> Parsing : next request within 5 seconds
    KeepAliveIdle --> [*] : 5 second idle timeout reaps the socket
```

Neither diagram has a state that ends in a graceful close: the process states terminate only through a signal or a swallowed bind error, and the connection states terminate through the idle timeout, a protocol error, or the process dying.

#### 4.4.5.3 Diagram-to-Requirement Traceability

| Diagram | Features / requirements illustrated | Failure paths shown |
|---------|-------------------------------------|---------------------|
| 4.4.1 High-level system workflow | F-001 … F-007 | Silent bind conflict, runtime `400`, refusal, termination |
| 4.4.2.1 Dependency installation | F-007-RQ-001 … RQ-004, FR-A | Unreachable registry, digest mismatch |
| 4.4.2.2 Start, bind, readiness | F-001, F-002, F-003, F-006-RQ-002 | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, swallowed `EADDRINUSE`/`EACCES` |
| 4.4.2.3 Root greeting | F-004-RQ-001 … RQ-004, FR-C | Refusal for a non-matching path |
| 4.4.2.4 Second greeting | F-005-RQ-001 … RQ-004, FR-D | Trailing-slash and other-method refusal |
| 4.4.2.5 Routing decision | F-006-RQ-001 … RQ-005 | `400`, `404` |
| 4.4.2.6 Fixture flow | F-009-RQ-002, RQ-003 | Unhandled `error` event, exit `1` |
| 4.4.3 Error handling | F-101 … F-106 (proposed, unimplemented) | All of the above with recovery edges |
| 4.4.4.1 Request sequence | F-004, F-005, F-006 | Malformed request, unmatched route |
| 4.4.4.2 Install sequence | F-007 | Missing tree blocks start-up |
| 4.4.4.3 Termination sequence | F-002-RQ-004, F-102 (proposed) | Dropped in-flight request |
| 4.4.5.1 Process lifecycle | F-001, F-002, F-003 | Silent exit `0`, exit `143`/`130` |
| 4.4.5.2 Connection lifecycle | F-004, F-005, F-006 | `400`, `404`, idle timeout |


### 4.4.4 Integration Sequence Diagrams

#### 4.4.4.1 Request Path (F-004, F-005, F-006)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as HTTP client
    participant S as Node http.Server socket
    participant A as Express app.handle
    participant R as Express router
    participant H as Route handler
    participant F as finalhandler

    C->>S: TCP connect to 127.0.0.1:3000, then send the request
    alt Malformed HTTP bytes
        S-->>C: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request, Connection close
        Note over S: No clientError listener is registered, so the runtime default answers and nothing is logged
    else Well-formed request
        S->>A: request event carrying req and res
        A->>R: dispatch after setting X-Powered-By Express
        alt GET or HEAD on / or /good-evening
            R->>H: invoke the matched route layer
            H-->>A: statusCode 200, Content-Type text/plain, res.end literal
            A-->>C: 200 with a 14-byte or 12-byte body, Content-Length, Keep-Alive timeout 5
        else OPTIONS on a registered path
            R-->>C: 200 with Allow GET, HEAD and body GET, HEAD
        else Unregistered path, trailing slash variant, or other method
            R->>F: fall through to the terminal handler
            F-->>C: 404 Not Found with Cannot GET path
        end
        Note over C,S: The socket returns to the keep-alive pool for up to 5 seconds
    end
```

#### 4.4.4.2 Install-Time Data Flow (F-007)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Operator
    participant N as npm CLI
    participant M as package.json and package-lock.json
    participant G as registry.npmjs.org
    participant D as node_modules, git-ignored

    O->>N: npm ci
    N->>M: read the single dependency express ^5.2.1 and the locked tree
    M-->>N: 66 entries, each with a resolved URL and a sha512 digest
    N->>G: fetch each tarball
    G-->>N: tarball bytes
    N->>N: verify each tarball against its recorded digest
    N->>D: extract the 66 packages
    D-->>O: install complete, exit 0
    Note over O,D: Without this step server.js aborts at line 1 with MODULE_NOT_FOUND and exit 1
```

#### 4.4.4.3 Termination Path (F-002, RQ-004)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Sup as Supervisor or operator
    participant OS as Operating system
    participant P as Node process
    participant C as HTTP client

    C->>P: request in flight
    Sup->>OS: stop the process
    OS->>P: SIGTERM
    Note over P: No process.on handler exists, so the runtime default disposition applies
    P--xC: connection dropped, response never completed
    OS-->>Sup: exit status 143
    Note over Sup,P: No drain, no cleanup and no shutdown log, while F-102 and F-106 remain proposed
```

# 5. System Architecture

## 5.1 High-Level Architecture

### 5.1.1 System Overview

**Architecture style.** `hao-backprop-test` is a **single-process, single-file, stateless, loopback-bound monolith with framework-mediated in-process layering**. Everything that executes lives in one Node.js process running one file (`server.js`, 29 lines); there is no second process, no worker, no database, no queue, no cache tier, and no outbound network call. The apparent layers — application, router, terminal handler, HTTP listener — exist only as objects inside that process: `server.js` creates an Express 5.2.1 application, the application delegates each request to `router@2.2.0`, the router falls through to `finalhandler@2.1.1` when no route matches, and the whole stack is wrapped in a Node `http.Server` created by `app.listen` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-606`).

**Rationale.** The style is dictated by the artifact's purpose rather than by engineering preference. `README.md` describes the repository as a "test project for backprop integration", so the workload must be small enough to read exhaustively and deterministic enough to assert on; and `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md` requests only that Express be added to a Node.js tutorial server and that a second endpoint returning `Good evening` be added. The delivered shape follows from those two inputs:

- **Express replaced a route-agnostic catch-all, not a layered application.** The pre-change file answered *every* path with the same greeting; the change introduced a declarative two-entry routing table and Express's default `404`, which is the whole of the architectural shift (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` FR-B, FR-C, FR-D).
- **The pipeline was left empty on purpose.** No `app.use` call exists in any `.js` file outside `node_modules/`, so the framework's middleware layer — including the parsing and static-serving packages installed as Express dependencies — never executes.
- **Configuration was expressed as code.** Host and port are module-level `const` literals (`server.js:3-4`); no `process.env` read, config file, or CLI argument exists anywhere in the repository.
- **Minimality was the acceptance criterion.** The recorded change set is five files — `server.js`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.md` — with no refactoring of the existing greeting (`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §5).

**Key architectural principles and patterns.**

| Principle or pattern | How it appears | Evidence |
|----------------------|----------------|----------|
| One process, one executable module | All behaviour is `server.js`; the three other root scripts are standalone fixtures the service never loads | `server.js`; `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, the 199-character `QWYFFGHGH…_server.js` |
| Declarative routing table (table-driven dispatch) | Two literal `GET` registrations replace imperative request inspection; dispatch is the framework's | `server.js:14, 20`; `node_modules/router@2.2.0` |
| Empty middleware pipeline | The request path is application → router → handler or terminal handler, with nothing in between | absence of `app.use` repository-wide |
| Low-level response construction for byte control | Handlers use `res.statusCode` / `setHeader` / `res.end`, deliberately bypassing `res.send` and therefore content-type inference and ETag generation | `server.js:15-17, 21-23`; no `ETag` or `Cache-Control` observed on live responses |
| Refusal over fallback | An unregistered path is a `404`, never a substituted greeting — the previous catch-all behaviour was intentionally removed | live `404` for `/nope`, `/hello`, `//`, `/good-evening/`; `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2 |
| Statelessness by construction | Both handlers ignore `req`, hold no state, and perform no I/O; no `let`/`var` binding is mutated at run time | `server.js:14-24`; state inventory in §4.3.1.1 |
| Configuration as compile-time constants | No configuration layer exists to misconfigure, and the logged URL cannot disagree with the bound address | `server.js:3-4, 27` |
| Reproducibility through lockfile pinning | 66 packages resolved from `registry.npmjs.org` with `sha512` integrity digests at `lockfileVersion` 3 | `package.json`; `package-lock.json` |
| Documentation as the published contract | `README.md` documents both endpoints, the `404` behaviour, the dependency, and the run procedure; no machine-readable contract exists | `README.md` lines 4-23 |
| Delegation to the platform for the rest | Failure, lifecycle, and observability behaviour is whatever the Node.js runtime and Express defaults provide, because no application code overrides them | §4.3.2; §5.4 |
| Out-of-band fixtures kept unshared | The native-`http` fixtures solve a different problem (pathological filenames) and were deliberately not re-platformed onto Express | `Agent Action Plan.md` §0.2.1, §0.6.2 |

**System boundaries and major interfaces.**

| Boundary | Direction | Interface and protocol | Notes |
|----------|-----------|------------------------|-------|
| Network | Inbound | HTTP/1.1 over loopback TCP `127.0.0.1:3000`; `GET /`, `GET /good-evening` (plus `HEAD` and `OPTIONS`) | Plain HTTP, no TLS, no authentication, no client filtering; reachable by any local process, unreachable from other hosts |
| Process control | Inbound | POSIX signals `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` | No application handler exists, so the runtime's default disposition applies and the process ends without draining |
| Package supply | Inbound at install time, then in-process | npm resolution of `express` into `node_modules/`, followed by `require('express')` at start-up | Installation is a precondition of execution because `node_modules/` is git-ignored |
| Observability output | Outbound | One line on standard output per successfully started process | `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`; no per-request logging, metrics, or tracing |
| Filesystem | Inbound at start-up | Read-only module resolution and script loading by the Node module loader | No runtime file write occurs in any code path |
| Package registry | Outbound at install time only | HTTPS fetch of locked tarballs from `registry.npmjs.org` | Not a runtime dependency; once installed, the service makes no outbound connection |

*Explicitly outside the boundary:* no database or storage engine, no cache server, no message broker or event bus, no outbound HTTP client, no identity provider, no secrets manager, no TLS terminator or reverse proxy, no metrics or tracing backend, no administrative or health endpoint, and no second runtime instance (the hardcoded loopback address and port prevent one on the same host).

Eight components make up the system: six that participate in its runtime or supply chain, and two that are carried in the repository without executing. The first table states each component's responsibility and dependencies; the second records its integration points and the considerations that constrain it. Component identifiers are local to this section and map to the feature identifiers used in §2 and §3.

### 5.1.3 Data Flow Description

Data flows in this system are short, single-hop, and entirely in memory. Two flows exist end to end: an **install-time supply flow** that happens once per checkout and a **request-time flow** that repeats per request. No other flow exists — there is no batch path, no scheduled job, no publish/subscribe channel, and no inter-service call.

**Primary flow 1 — install-time dependency supply (once per checkout).** npm reads `package.json`, whose only dependency is `express ^5.2.1`, resolves the tree through `package-lock.json` (66 entries at `lockfileVersion` 3), fetches each tarball from `registry.npmjs.org`, verifies it against the recorded `sha512` digest, and writes it into `node_modules/`, which `.gitignore` excludes. The flow terminates there: nothing is compiled, bundled, or published, so the "build" and the deployment artifact are the same source tree plus the installed dependency tree. The only repository file written by this flow is the dependency tree itself.

**Primary flow 2 — request/response handling (per request).** A loopback client connects to `127.0.0.1:3000`; Node's HTTP parser produces `(req, res)` and emits `request`; the handler registered by `app.listen` passes the pair to `app.handle`, which sets `X-Powered-By: Express` and installs `finalhandler` as the terminal callback; the router lowercases the request method, discards the query string, and compares the path against its two literal layers; the matched layer invokes one of the two handlers, which sets the status code, sets `Content-Type: text/plain`, and writes a fixed literal; the runtime writes status line, headers (including `Content-Length` 14 or 12, `Date`, and keep-alive directives) and body onto the socket; the socket returns to the keep-alive pool for up to five idle seconds. If nothing matches, the flow ends at `finalhandler`, which synthesises a `404 Not Found` HTML document and closes the transaction. No request-derived value is retained, logged, forwarded, or stored: the handlers never dereference `req`, so request data affects only the dispatch decision.

**Integration patterns and protocols.**

- **Synchronous in-process call chain.** `http.Server` → `app.handle` → `router` → handler or `finalhandler` is a sequence of ordinary function calls on the event loop, with no serialization, no message envelope, and no inter-process boundary to cross.
- **One protocol on the wire.** HTTP/1.1 in plaintext over loopback, with keep-alive enabled by the runtime (`Keep-Alive: timeout=5`). Request bodies are never read; responses are fixed-length rather than chunked or streamed; there is no compression, no content negotiation, and no conditional-request handling.
- **Event-driven at the runtime edge only.** The only events in play are the runtime's `listening`, `request`, `error`, and `clientError` and the operating system's `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`. The application registers no listener of its own; Express registers a single one-shot `error` listener on the startup callback, which is why a bind conflict is consumed silently.
- **No integration middleware.** With no `app.use` call anywhere, there is no request parsing, no static serving, no cookie or session handling, and no CORS, compression, or logging middleware on the path. The packages Express installs for those purposes (`body-parser@2.2.2`, `qs@6.15.2`, `raw-body@3.0.2`, `iconv-lite@0.7.2`, `cookie@0.7.2`, `serve-static@2.2.1`, `send@1.2.1`, `mime-types@3.0.2`) never execute.
- **Transport encryption, retry, and back-off are all absent.** There is no TLS listener, no outbound client to configure a retry policy for, and no queue to buffer or re-drive a failed unit of work.

**Data transformation points.**

| # | Transformation | Performed by | Effect |
|---|----------------|--------------|--------|
| 1 | Bytes → parsed request | Node `http` parser inside `http.Server` | Produces `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse`; a syntactically invalid request line or header block raises `clientError` instead |
| 2 | Request object → dispatch decision | Express `app.handle` → `router@2.2.0` | Method lowercased (`HEAD` is aliased to `GET` when no `HEAD` layer exists), query string removed before matching, literal path compared case-insensitively with the trailing slash significant |
| 3 | Handler statements → response entities | The two greeting handlers | Status `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and the literal body are written directly to the socket; no templating, escaping, or serialization step applies |
| 4 | Unmatched request → diagnostic document | `finalhandler@2.1.1` | Builds an HTML document from the method and the URL-encoded path (`Cannot GET /hello`), sets `Content-Length`, and adds `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` |
| 5 | Method set → `Allow` list | `router@2.2.0` automatic `OPTIONS` responder | Collects the registered methods, sorts them, and answers `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` and a `GET, HEAD` body without entering either handler |
| 6 | Response entities → wire bytes | Node `http.Server` | Serialises the status line, the header block, and the body, adding `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, and the framework's `X-Powered-By` header |

Transformation stops there: no request field is validated, normalised, enriched, or persisted, and no response is compressed, signed, or cached, because no handler reads an input and no component writes to storage.

**Key data stores and caches.** There are none of either in the application sense. The only structures that hold data are process-lifetime and derived from the source:

| Structure | Kind | Lifetime | Contents |
|-----------|------|----------|----------|
| Node module cache | Runtime in-memory cache | Process | `express` and its 65 transitives, loaded once when `require` runs at start-up |
| Route table | In-memory data structure | Process, built on first `app.get` | Two literal `GET` layers plus the router's captured `strict`/`caseSensitive` options |
| Express settings and container objects | In-memory configuration | Process | `strict routing` (enabled by the code), plus framework defaults `x-powered-by`, `etag: weak`, `env`, query parser, and trust proxy; `app.cache`, `app.engines`, and `app.locals` are created empty and never written |
| Keep-alive socket pool | Runtime connection state | Per connection, idle up to 5 s | Idle sockets held for reuse; all reset when the process ends because no drain exists |
| npm package cache | External, on the developer machine | Across installs | Tarballs keyed by version and digest; the repository configures no custom cache path or offline mirror |

Because both responses are literals, nothing in the system is expensive enough to warrant a cache: there is no response cache, no application-level memoisation, no warm-up step, and no cache invalidation logic to design. The service emits no `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `Age`, `Vary`, `ETag`, or `Last-Modified` header, and no conditional-request path exists, so a client or intermediary can only apply heuristic freshness rules of its own.

### 5.1.4 External Integration Points

The service integrates with nothing at run time. Its only runtime partner is the client on the same host, and the single cross-system flow in its life cycle is the install-time fetch from the public npm registry. The tables below therefore describe boundaries rather than negotiated integrations: for every entry, the "SLA Requirements" column records that no service-level commitment exists in the repository, together with what the system actually does.

| System name | Integration type | Data exchange pattern | Protocol / format |
|-------------|------------------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| Public npm registry (`registry.npmjs.org`) | Install-time, outbound, one-shot per install | Pull: request each locked package tarball by name and version, verify against the recorded integrity digest, extract into `node_modules/` | HTTPS; npm package metadata and gzipped tarballs with `sha512` integrity digests recorded in `package-lock.json` |
| Local loopback HTTP clients (`curl`, smoke tests, any local process) | Runtime, inbound request with outbound response | One request per transaction, synchronous; the request body is never read and the response body is a fixed literal (14 or 12 bytes) | HTTP/1.1 plaintext on `127.0.0.1:3000`; `text/plain` responses; `text/html; charset=utf-8` for framework refusals |
| Operator terminal or log consumer | Runtime, outbound, once per process | Fire-and-forget push of a single startup line | Attached standard-output stream carrying the text `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` |
| Operating-system process signal channel | Runtime, inbound | Edge-triggered signal, no acknowledgement, no drain | POSIX signals `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT`, handled by the runtime's default disposition |
| Node.js runtime and npm CLI | Platform dependency for the process's whole life cycle | In-process hosting of the application, plus a command-driven install or run invocation | Node.js runtime API (built-ins `http`, `console`, `process`, module loader) and the npm CLI reading `lockfileVersion` 3 |
| Local filesystem | Start-up, inbound, read-only | Module resolution and script loading before the listener binds; no write in any code path | POSIX file reads through the Node module loader |
| Git remote (GitHub) | Development-time, outbound on demand | Push and pull of source revisions only; no deployment automation is driven from it | Git transport over HTTPS or SSH |

| System name | SLA requirements | Failure behaviour observed |
|-------------|------------------|----------------------------|
| Public npm registry | None defined. Registry reachability is an unstated precondition of installation; no mirror, offline mode, custom registry, or retry policy is configured, and the repository contains no CI job that would surface a failure | A failed install exits non-zero and leaves the service unstartable; start-up then aborts at `server.js:1` with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and exit `1` |
| Local loopback HTTP clients | None defined. No documented latency, throughput, availability, or concurrency target exists; recorded measurements were 600 keep-alive requests over 100 sockets completing with 0 errors at 0.22 ms average latency on Node v22.23.3, and they are observations rather than commitments | No rate limit, quota, timeout configuration, or contract versioning applies. A client that malforms its request receives `400 Bad Request`; an unregistered path or method receives `404`; neither is logged |
| Operator terminal or log consumer | None defined. The line is unstructured, untimestamped, unlevelled, and emitted only after a successful bind; there is no access logging, log rotation, or retention | If the bind fails, the same success line is printed and the process then exits `0` with no diagnostic, so the log consumer sees a false success |
| Operating-system process signal channel | None defined. No shutdown deadline, drain window, or exit-code contract exists in the repository | `SIGTERM` ends the process with status `143` and `SIGINT` with `130`, immediately and without draining; in-flight responses are dropped and keep-alive sockets are reset |
| Node.js runtime and npm CLI | None committed. `express@5.2.1` declares `engines.node >= 18`, but `package.json` declares no `engines` field, so the requirement is advisory and never enforced at install time | An older runtime fails on `require('express')`; an npm older than 7 cannot read the committed lockfile. Validation ran on Node v22.23.3 with npm 11.21.0 |
| Local filesystem | None defined | A missing dependency tree, an unreadable script, or an inode/descriptor limit surfaces as a start-up exception or a runtime error with no application-level handling |
| Git remote (GitHub) | None defined | Availability affects only the development workflow; the running service neither reads nor writes the repository |


## 5.2 Component Details

### 5.2.1 Express Application Container (C-1)

`server.js` is the only application module in the repository and the container for every architectural decision the service makes. It declares two module-level constants, instantiates the Express application, enables one setting, registers two routes, and binds one listener; it exports nothing and is never imported. Because `package.json` declares `"main": "index.js"` and no such file exists, the only working entry point is `node server.js` (or the implicit `npm start`, which resolves to the same command).

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | Hold the two configuration literals (`hostname = '127.0.0.1'`, `port = 3000`); create the application with `express()`; enable `strict routing` before any route is registered; register `GET /` and `GET /good-evening`; start the listener and print the single startup line from its callback |
| Technologies and frameworks | JavaScript with CommonJS `require` semantics; `express@5.2.1` as the sole dependency; Node.js ≥ 18 runtime; no transpilation, bundler, or type checking |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Inbound: process start (`node server.js`), no arguments, no environment input. Outbound: `express()` factory, `app.enable(setting)`, `app.get(path, handler)` twice, `app.listen(port, hostname, callback)`, `console.log`. Nothing is exported, and no module-level function exists for another module to call |
| Data persistence requirements | None. The module reads no file, holds no state beyond the framework objects created at start-up, and writes nothing to disk |
| Scaling considerations | The module is stateless and side-effect-free apart from the bind, so it would survive being run many times; what blocks horizontal scaling is not the module but its hardcoded loopback address and fixed port, which permit only one instance per host. Startup cost is a single `require` of the 66-package tree plus two route registrations |

Two ordering facts constrain this component. First, `app.enable('strict routing')` at line 12 must precede the first `app.get` at line 14, because the router captures the setting when it is constructed on first access (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:69-80`); reversing the order makes `/good-evening/` match and return `200` instead of `404`. Second, the server object returned by `app.listen` is discarded, so no reference exists through which the listener could later be closed — a prerequisite any graceful-shutdown work would have to satisfy.

### 5.2.2 Route Table and Dispatch Layer (C-2)

Dispatch is entirely delegated to `router@2.2.0`, installed as a transitive dependency of Express. The application contributes two literal path registrations and nothing else; the router owns matching, the method-mapping rules, the automatic `OPTIONS` response, and the decision to fall through.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | Store the two `GET` layers, match an incoming method and path against them, answer `OPTIONS` without entering a handler, serve `HEAD` from the `GET` layer when no `HEAD` layer exists, and hand control back to the terminal callback when nothing matches |
| Technologies and frameworks | `router@2.2.0` with `path-to-regexp@8.4.2` for pattern compilation; router options `{ caseSensitive: app.enabled('case sensitive routing'), strict: app.enabled('strict routing') }` captured at construction; `layer.js` supplies `handleRequest`/`handleError`, and `route.js` performs method-to-layer matching |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Registration side: `app.get(path, handler)`, which builds the router lazily on first access. Runtime side: `router.handle(req, res, done)`, where `done` is the terminal callback supplied by `app.handle`. Matching behaviour: method lowercased, `HEAD` mapped to `GET` when no `HEAD` layer exists (`router/lib/route.js:112`), query string removed before comparison, case-insensitive path comparison, trailing slash significant while strict routing is on |
| Data persistence requirements | None. The route table lives in process memory and closes the moment the second registration returns; there is no serialized route definition, no configuration file, and no persistence of dispatch decisions |
| Scaling considerations | Dispatch is a linear scan of a two-entry table with no dynamic registration, so per-request cost is negligible and no locking or contention exists; any growth in the table would be bounded by Express 5's reserved path characters `( ) [ ] ? + & !`, which constrain how future routes may be written |

A synchronous exception thrown inside a matched layer is caught by `layer.js` and forwarded to the router's error path rather than escaping to the event loop, which is why an unexpected handler failure would produce a framework `500` instead of a process crash. No layer in this repository can throw: both handlers execute three non-throwing statements that read no input.

### 5.2.3 Literal Greeting Handlers (C-3)

The two handler callbacks constitute the system's entire business behaviour. They are grouped as one component because they are symmetric, share one construction pattern, and hold the same contract: each writes a fixed byte sequence and returns.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | Produce the root greeting `Hello, World!\n` (14 bytes) and the second greeting `Good evening` (12 bytes, no trailing newline) with status `200` and `Content-Type: text/plain` |
| Technologies and frameworks | Plain JavaScript arrow functions; the low-level Node `ServerResponse` API (`res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, `res.end`) instead of Express's `res.send`, deliberately, so that no response helper performs content-type inference, charset appending, or ETag computation |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Called by the route layer as `(req, res)`; `req` is accepted and never dereferenced; the observable interface is the HTTP response triple — status, `Content-Type` header, and exact body bytes — plus the `Content-Length` the runtime derives from the body |
| Data persistence requirements | None. The responses are source literals; nothing is read, computed, or stored, and the handlers are pure functions of the request in the trivial sense that their output does not depend on it |
| Scaling considerations | Three synchronous statements with no I/O and no allocation of dynamic content, so the handlers add no measurable cost per request; measured throughput of the whole stack was 600 keep-alive requests in 132 ms with zero errors. Nothing in the handlers limits concurrency, and nothing in them benefits from caching either |

Because `res.end` is used rather than `res.send`, the application's `etag` setting of `weak` is present but never exercised, and no response carries `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, or `Cache-Control`. The presence or absence of a trailing newline differs between the two routes by design, and that difference — 14 bytes versus 12 — is the contract most likely to be broken by a future edit.

### 5.2.4 Loopback HTTP Listener and Connection Layer (C-4)

The listener is a Node `http.Server` created inside Express's `listen` wrapper (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-606`) and bound to `127.0.0.1:3000`. It owns everything below the application: socket acceptance, HTTP parsing, connection reuse, response serialisation, and the events on which the process's operational behaviour depends.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | Bind the loopback address and port, parse HTTP/1.1 request framing, emit `request` per parsed request, emit `error` on bind failure, emit `clientError` on malformed input, serialise responses onto the socket, and hold idle keep-alive connections |
| Technologies and frameworks | Node.js built-in `http` module on the host runtime (validated on Node v22.23.3); no TLS module, no proxy, no connection limiter, and no socket-level configuration from application code |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Bind interface `127.0.0.1:3000` over TCP; events `listening`, `request`, `error`, `clientError`; response control through `http.ServerResponse`; runtime socket defaults `keepAliveTimeout` 5 000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60 000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300 000 ms, `server.timeout` 0; lifecycle operations `listen`, `close`, and `address` available on the server object that the application discards |
| Data persistence requirements | None at rest; per-connection state is transient. Idle sockets persist for up to five seconds of reuse and are reset when the process ends, since no drain path exists |
| Scaling considerations | A single listener on one port with no clustering, worker threads, or child processes, so all requests are served by one event loop and one CPU core; the loopback bind and fixed port make a second instance on the same host impossible, and nothing publishes the service to a balancer. Capacity controls — rate limiting, maximum connections, back-pressure, queues — are entirely absent, so the listener accepts connections until the host runs out of descriptors |

Two runtime behaviours of this layer matter operationally and are invisible in the application source. A malformed request is answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close` by the runtime itself and is not logged, because no `clientError` listener is registered. And because Express registers the startup callback as a one-shot `error` listener, a bind conflict is consumed rather than thrown: the banner is printed, no diagnostic appears, and the process exits `0`.

### 5.2.5 Terminal Not-Found and Error Responder (C-5)

`finalhandler@2.1.1` is the framework's terminal component and the source of every response the two handlers do not produce. Express installs it in `app.handle` as the callback used when the router does not respond, so the application never sees refusals or unhandled errors.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | Terminate a request that no layer handled: produce `404 Not Found` when no error object is supplied, or an error status derived from the error or from `res.statusCode`; add restrictive security headers; schedule `logerror` only when an error object exists; destroy the socket when headers have already been sent |
| Technologies and frameworks | `finalhandler@2.1.1` with `statuses@2.0.1`; Express's own `logerror` (`lib/application.js:615`), which writes `err.stack` to standard error whenever the environment is not `test`; the environment is `development` because `NODE_ENV` is unset |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Created as `finalhandler(req, res, { env, onerror })` and invoked as a callback with an optional error; emits `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, an accurate `Content-Length`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`, and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; body text for a refusal is `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` with the path URL-encoded |
| Data persistence requirements | None. Refusals are generated per request and never recorded: no refusal counter, no error log for a plain not-found, and no dead-letter or audit trail |
| Scaling considerations | The component is invoked only on unmatched or failing requests and performs a small string construction, so it adds no capacity burden; under a flood of unregistered paths it would answer each request with a fresh HTML document and write nothing to disk, which is a logging blind spot rather than a scaling limit |

The distinction between refusals and failures matters for observability: a `404` carries no error object, so `onerror` is not scheduled and nothing is logged; a genuine `5xx` is logged to standard error with a stack trace, but only when a handler actually throws — which no handler in this repository can do.

### 5.2.6 Dependency Supply Chain and Lockfile (C-6)

The dependency tree is a first-class architectural component here because it is 65 packages larger than the application and is the sole precondition for the process starting. `server.js:1` resolves `express` from `node_modules/`, which `.gitignore` excludes, so a checkout without an install cannot run.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | Declare exactly one dependency (`"express": "^5.2.1"` in `package.json`); pin the resolved tree of 66 packages with versions, registry URLs, and `sha512` integrity digests in `package-lock.json` at `lockfileVersion` 3; materialise that tree into `node_modules/` so `require` succeeds; supply the framework on which C-1, C-2, and C-5 all depend |
| Technologies and frameworks | npm ≥ 7 (required to read `lockfileVersion` 3); the public npm registry; Node.js ≥ 18, which `express@5.2.1` declares through `engines.node` and `package.json` does not enforce |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Manifest surface `dependencies.express`; install interface `npm ci` (lockfile-strict) or `npm install` (may float within `^5.x`); module resolution interface `require('express')` → factory function → `express();` the caret range is the interface through which an upgrade could enter, and only the lockfile guards against it |
| Data persistence requirements | The installed tree is the only durable artifact this system writes, once per checkout, to a git-ignored directory. Nothing at runtime reads or writes it again beyond module loading; a partially installed tree is detected on the next start-up as `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` |
| Scaling considerations | Installation cost is fixed and per-checkout, and the tree is identical on every host that installs from the lockfile, so the supply chain is reproducible but not elastic. Two currency risks attach to it: `5.3.0` is the current npm `latest` while the lockfile pins `5.2.1`, and the tree audits with three known advisories at the time of writing, of which the highest is a critical IP-spoofing advisory in `proxy-addr` — a package that never executes here, since `trust proxy` is `false` and no handler reads a client address |

### 5.2.7 Repository-Carried Non-Runtime Artifacts (C-7, C-8)

Two groups of files are tracked and architecturally relevant, yet are never executed or read by the running service. They are documented here because they define the fixture's purpose, hold the published contract, and are the most likely source of confusion for a reader of the repository.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| Purpose and responsibilities | C-7 — three standalone servers (`Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, and the 199-character `QWYFFGHGHFDDJFDame_!@#$%^&(){}long_name_…_server.js`) exercise filesystem and tooling handling of pathological filenames; each answers every path and method with `200` and `Hello, World!\n` and carries no framework header. C-8 — `README.md` publishes the HTTP contract; `blitzy/documentation/` holds the requirement provenance, validation ledger, and a prior specification; `Response.txt` proposes six unimplemented hardening features; `codebase_context (42).md` records the original `/hello` request; `phonenumber.csv` and four binary artifacts are dormant |
| Technologies and frameworks | C-7 uses only Node's built-in `http` module — no Express, no manifest entry, no shared code with the service. C-8 uses Markdown and Mermaid for authoring; no runtime technology applies |
| Key interfaces and APIs | C-7 exposes the same loopback address and port as the service, so the two are mutually exclusive on one host; their response contract differs (route- and method-agnostic `200`, no `X-Powered-By`), which makes them non-interchangeable with `server.js`. C-8 exposes human-readable documentation only — no machine-readable contract, no OpenAPI document, and no interface a tool could consume |
| Data persistence requirements | C-7 persists nothing; C-8 is static text. `phonenumber.csv` is a 16-line `message,phonenumber` fixture with 15 synthetic rows that no code path opens |
| Scaling considerations | Not applicable to either group: nothing in the request path depends on them, and their only cost is checkout size. The fixture scripts are nonetheless retained deliberately rather than deleted, which fixes their port conflict with the service as a permanent property of the repository |

The documentary artifacts are inconsistent with the running code in ways a reader must know: `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` describes the superseded native-`http`, zero-dependency implementation and its §2.7.4 concedes that any change to `server.js` invalidates its acceptance criteria; `Project Guide.md` records zero audit findings at validation time whereas the current tree audits with three; and the fixtures are documented as byte-identical copies of `server.js` although they now differ from it.

## 5.3 Technical Decisions

### 5.3.1 Architecture Style Decision — Single-Process, Single-File, Stateless Monolith

**Decision.** The service is one Node.js process running one CommonJS file that creates an Express application, registers two literal routes, and binds one loopback listener. No tier, service, worker, or module boundary exists inside it beyond the framework's own objects.

**Context.** `README.md` frames the repository as a "test project for backprop integration" and `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md` asks only for Express and a second endpoint on an existing tutorial server; `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.2 fixes "in-place implementation in the repository's flat, single-directory CommonJS single-file convention" as a binding constraint, and §0.7 requires the change to stay minimal.

**Alternatives considered.**

| Alternative | Why it was not taken |
|-------------|---------------------|
| Layered application with separate route, service, and controller modules | The recorded constraints require the flat single-file convention, and two literal responses have nothing to separate |
| Stateless serverless function | No provider account, no handler export, and no packaging or deployment artifact exists; nothing is exported by `server.js` |
| Multi-service or client/server split | The system has one capability and no independently scalable part |
| Containerised service with an orchestrator | No `Dockerfile`, compose file, or orchestration manifest exists; containerisation is recorded as verified absent in §3.6.3 |
| Keep the native-`http` implementation for the service | Explicit routing and a default `404` were the requested capability gain, and the fixture scripts already demonstrate the native alternative |

**Tradeoffs accepted.**

| Benefit realised | Cost accepted |
|------------------|---------------|
| The whole system is readable in 29 lines, so behaviour is auditable and deterministic — the property the fixture exists for | No separation of concerns, no dependency injection, and no seams for unit testing; anything added lands in the same file |
| No state, session, or persistence to migrate, reconcile, or recover; a restart is lossless by construction | Nothing can be remembered between requests: no counters, no rate-limit or audit state, no caching opportunities |
| Startup cost is a single `require` of the dependency tree plus two route registrations | One process on one core, with the loopback bind and fixed port blocking a second instance on the same host |

### 5.3.2 Framework Decision — Express 5.2.1 Rather Than Native `http`

**Decision.** Serve HTTP through `express@5.2.1`, declared as `"express": "^5.2.1"` in `package.json` and pinned with 65 transitive packages in `package-lock.json`.

**Context.** The choice was requested, not evaluated: `blitzy/documentation/Build Prompt.md` says "Could you add expressjs into the project", and FR-A in `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.1.1 records adding and locking it. The repository's earlier zero-dependency posture belongs to the unimplemented hardening plan in `Response.txt`, whose constraints explicitly forbid adding a framework — a conflict resolved in favour of the user's explicit instruction (§0.1.2).

**Rationale.** Express earns its place by supplying exactly what the change needed and nothing that had to be configured: a declarative route table (`app.get`), a default `404` that replaces the previous catch-all behaviour, an automatic `OPTIONS` responder, `HEAD`-to-`GET` aliasing, and the terminal `finalhandler` — all reachable through five application-level API calls.

**Tradeoffs accepted.**

| Benefit realised | Cost accepted |
|------------------|---------------|
| Explicit routing with a refusal path replaces an unconditional greeting; unregistered paths and non-`GET` methods now receive `404` | The dependency surface grew from nothing to 66 packages for two literal routes, with three known audit advisories in the tree at the time of writing |
| Framework defaults cover method handling, refusals, and error termination without a line of code | Every response advertises `X-Powered-By: Express`, which the native implementation did not |
| A caret range plus a lockfile gives one-command reproducible installs | Express 5 raises the runtime floor to Node.js 18, and `package.json` declares no `engines` field to enforce it |
| Five framework calls keep the file at 29 lines | Router options are captured at first route registration, making the position of `app.enable('strict routing')` load-bearing and easy to break |

### 5.3.3 Communication Pattern Decision — Synchronous In-Process Request/Response over Plain HTTP/1.1 on Loopback

**Decision.** Every interaction is a synchronous, single-hop HTTP/1.1 request answered on the same loopback socket. There is no message broker, no publish/subscribe channel, no asynchronous callback chain, no streaming response, and no outbound call of any kind.

**Rationale.** The component chain — `http.Server` → `app.handle` → `router` → handler or `finalhandler` — is a sequence of ordinary function calls with no serialization boundary to design. Responses are fixed-length literals, the request body is never read, and keep-alive reuse is delegated to the runtime, so no framing decision, buffer management, or flow-control policy was required.

**Tradeoffs accepted.**

| Benefit realised | Cost accepted |
|------------------|---------------|
| Predictable, byte-exact responses and negligible latency: 600 keep-alive requests over 100 sockets completed with zero errors at 0.22 ms average | No back-pressure or queueing: the listener accepts connections until host descriptors run out, and there is no rate limiting or maximum-connection setting |
| Zero integration surface to break — no timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, or ordering concerns | Plaintext only: no TLS listener, certificate, or terminator exists, and loopback is the entire reachable scope |
| The runtime's HTTP parser handles malformed input with a `400` and keeps serving | Framing failures are invisible: no `clientError` listener exists, so malformed requests are answered but never logged |

### 5.3.4 Data Storage Decision — No Persistence Layer

**Decision.** The service has no database, no file store, no cache server, and no in-memory domain state. Nothing is written at any point of the process life cycle, and nothing but the dependency tree is written at install time.

**Rationale.** Both handlers return source literals and never dereference `req`, so there is no data to persist; the responses the fixture asserts on depend only on the path, which makes determinism a property of the design rather than a test outcome. A restart is therefore lossless by construction: there is no state to lose, reconcile, or recover.

**Alternatives considered.**

| Alternative | Why it was not taken |
|-------------|---------------------|
| File-backed data (for example, loading `phonenumber.csv`) | No code path opens any file; the CSV is an orphan fixture with 15 synthetic rows and no consumer |
| Embedded or external database | No driver appears in `package-lock.json`, no connection string or schema exists, and no handler reads input that could be stored |
| In-memory domain state (counters, sessions, caches of computed responses) | Nothing is expensive enough to store and no request carries identity; the two bodies are 14 and 12 bytes |

**Tradeoffs accepted:** no audit trail, no request history, no operational counters, and no way to observe usage from inside the process. The observable record of a running instance is exactly one stdout line per process.

### 5.3.5 Caching Strategy Justification — No Application Cache and No Response Validators

**Decision.** No caching layer, no memoisation, and no HTTP validators are implemented. Responses carry no `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `Age`, `Vary`, `ETag`, or `Last-Modified`, and no handler reads a conditional-request header.

**Rationale.** The unit of work is three synchronous statements writing a constant, so there is nothing to amortise and no invalidation problem to solve. The absence of validators is a consequence of the response-construction choice as much as a decision in itself: because handlers call `res.end` rather than `res.send`, Express's `etag: weak` setting is never exercised, so no entity tag is produced even though the setting is present.

**What remains cached.** Only structural, runtime-owned caches exist, and none holds request-derived data:

| Structure | Owner | Purpose |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| Node module cache | Runtime | Holds `express` and its 65 transitives, loaded once at start-up |
| Route table | Application | Two literal layers in memory, built once on first `app.get` |
| Keep-alive socket pool | Runtime | Reuses idle connections for up to five seconds; reset on exit since no drain exists |
| npm package cache | Developer machine | Install-time reuse of tarballs keyed by version and digest; not configured by this repository |

**Tradeoffs accepted:** clients and intermediaries must apply their own heuristic freshness rules, since the service expresses no caching policy; each response is transferred in full with no `304` path, which is immaterial at 14 and 12 bytes. In exchange, the system has no cache-invalidation risk, no stale-response class of defect, and no cache tier to operate.

### 5.3.6 Security Mechanism Selection — Loopback Binding Instead of Authentication, Authorisation, or TLS

**Decision.** The only security control is the network boundary: the listener binds `127.0.0.1`, so the service is reachable by local processes and by nothing else. No authentication, authorisation, transport encryption, input validation, rate limiting, or header hardening is implemented.

**Rationale.** The artifact is a fixture observed from the same host, so no credential scheme, identity provider, or certificate has a consumer. The application also reads no request input at all — the handlers ignore `req`, and no parsing middleware is mounted — so the injection surface is minimal by omission rather than by validation.

| Control area | State at HEAD | Evidence |
|--------------|---------------|----------|
| Network exposure | Loopback only; any local process may connect, no remote host can | `server.js:3, 26`; live requests from localhost only |
| Authentication and authorisation | Absent — no account, token, role, or access-control concept exists | No auth dependency or handler logic anywhere in the repository |
| Transport encryption | Absent — plaintext HTTP/1.1, no TLS listener or certificate | No HTTPS module use; response headers show plain HTTP |
| Input validation | Absent — no request field is read, so nothing is validated, sanitised, or bounded | `server.js:14-24`; no parsing middleware mounted |
| Framework disclosure | `X-Powered-By: Express` on every response, including `404`s; `app.disable('x-powered-by')` is documented as an optional, unimplemented enhancement (~0.25 h) | live response headers; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3 |
| Refusal-response hygiene | Framework refusals do carry `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | `node_modules/finalhandler/index.js`; live `404` headers |
| Supply-chain exposure | 66 packages guarded by pinned `sha512` digests; the tree also audits with one critical, one high, and one moderate advisory at the time of writing, all in packages that never execute here (`proxy-addr` is unreachable because `trust proxy` is `false`) | `package-lock.json`; `npm audit` findings; `application.js:95-99` |
| Secrets and sensitive data | None exist; the only log line carries a public loopback address | repository-wide search for credentials or configuration |

**Tradeoffs accepted:** the boundary is a deployment property rather than an application control, so exposing the service to a network would require TLS termination, authentication, authorisation, configuration, and observability work that does not exist today; and the framework identity is disclosed to every local client.

### 5.3.7 Configuration Decision — Compile-Time Constants Instead of an Environment Layer

**Decision.** Host and port are module-level `const` literals (`server.js:3-4`); no environment variable, configuration file, CLI argument, or secret-injection mechanism is read anywhere in executable code.

**Rationale.** The fixture must be reachable at one predictable address for the assertions around it to hold, and constant literals make the startup message provably consistent with the bound address, since both are derived from the same two bindings. There is nothing environment-specific to vary and nothing secret to inject.

**Tradeoffs accepted.**

| Benefit realised | Cost accepted |
|------------------|---------------|
| No configuration surface to misconfigure; no config file to validate; the logged URL cannot disagree with the bound address | A port conflict cannot be resolved without editing and redeploying the source; there is no fallback port and no way to shift the listener at run time |
| No secret handling, no `.env` parsing dependency, no configuration precedence rules | The service cannot run on a second host or a second instance on the same host, which is the binding constraint on horizontal scaling |
| Deployment prerequisites reduce to "install, then run" | The Node.js ≥ 18 requirement is documented rather than enforced, because `package.json` declares no `engines` field; environment-driven host/port parameterisation is a recorded but unimplemented enhancement (~1.0 h) |

### 5.3.8 Architecture Decision Records

The records below are derived from the decisions observable in the repository at HEAD; the "Status" column distinguishes decisions in force from decisions taken by omission and from documented but unimplemented work.

| ID | Decision | Status | Consequence |
|----|----------|--------|-------------|
| ADR-001 | Single process, single file, stateless service on the flat CommonJS convention | Accepted — implemented | Auditable in 29 lines; no testing seams and no state that survives a restart |
| ADR-002 | Express 5.2.1 as the HTTP framework instead of native `http` | Accepted — implemented | Explicit routing and a default `404`; 66-package dependency tree and `X-Powered-By` disclosure |
| ADR-003 | Two literal `GET` layers with `strict routing` enabled before the first registration | Accepted — implemented | Trailing-slash variants and unregistered paths are refused; the setting's position in the file is load-bearing |
| ADR-004 | Byte-exact bodies via `res.statusCode` / `setHeader` / `res.end` rather than `res.send` | Accepted — implemented | Exact 14-byte and 12-byte contracts; no content-type inference and no ETag, so the `weak` setting is inert |
| ADR-005 | Configuration as compile-time `const` literals | Accepted — implemented | No configuration layer to misconfigure; the port cannot be changed without a code edit |
| ADR-006 | No persistence of any kind | Accepted — implemented | Lossless restarts, no migration or recovery burden, and no audit trail or operational counters |
| ADR-007 | No application cache and no HTTP validators | Accepted — implemented | No invalidation risk; clients fall back to heuristic caching and always transfer the full body |
| ADR-008 | Loopback binding as the entire security boundary | Accepted — implemented | Reachable only from the local host; exposure to any network would require new controls |
| ADR-009 | No application error handling, no graceful shutdown, no signal handlers | Accepted by omission — tolerated, not endorsed | A bind conflict is swallowed with exit `0`; `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` end the process without draining, and the discarded server handle blocks `server.close()` |
| ADR-010 | Lockfile-pinned dependency tree with no test, lint, build, CI, or container tooling | Accepted — implemented | Reproducible installs and no pipeline to maintain; contract verification stays manual and dependency advisories are unmonitored |
| ADR-011 | The three native-`http` fixtures remain unchanged on the service's address and port | Accepted — implemented | Filesystem edge cases stay covered; the fixtures are not interchangeable with the service and cannot run alongside it |
| ADR-012 | `README.md` is the published contract; no machine-readable interface description | Accepted — implemented | A human-readable contract with no drift detection; documentation must be revised with every contract change |
