## 5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns

### 5.4.1 Monitoring and Observability Approach

Observability in this system is a single unstructured line of text. The application contains one logging statement — `console.log` in the `app.listen` callback (`server.js:27`) — and no metric, trace, health, or readiness surface of any kind. There is no instrumentation agent, no exporter, and no monitoring dependency anywhere in the 66-package tree.

| Signal | Availability | Detail and evidence |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|
| Start-up confirmation | Yes | `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` on stdout, once per process, emitted only after a successful bind |
| Bind-failure alarm | Inverted — reports success | A port conflict prints the same banner and exits `0` with no diagnostic, because the startup callback is the one-shot `error` listener registered by `app.listen` |
| Per-request access log | No | After roughly 600 requests plus a malformed request, the process output still held exactly one line |
| Framework diagnostics | Off by default | With `DEBUG=*`, the framework emits 25 stderr lines, including `router dispatching GET /` per request and `finalhandler default 404` per refusal; nothing in the repository sets `DEBUG`, so this visibility is never enabled |
| Application error log | Partial | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on start-up and unhandled `error` events from the fixture scripts reach stderr; Express's `logerror` prints a stack only for a genuine `5xx`; a `404` and a `400` are logged nowhere |
| Metrics, traces, APM | No | No client library, agent, or exporter exists; no counter, gauge, or histogram is emitted |
| Health or readiness endpoint | No | Neither handler responds to a liveness or readiness probe; the only readiness signals are TCP acceptance on port 3000 and the banner |
| Dependency vulnerability monitoring | No | `npm audit` is not wired into a script, job, or pipeline, so the three advisories currently present in the tree surfaced only when the command was run by hand |
| Capacity and saturation signals | No | No resource metric, queue depth, connection count, or event-loop lag measurement is produced |

Because no introspection surface exists, an operator observes the service only from outside the process: tail the startup line, check the exit status (`0`, `143` for `SIGTERM`, `130` for `SIGINT`, `1` for an unresolvable dependency), inspect the listening socket with host tools, and issue requests to the two registered paths. The three recorded observability gaps — a silent bind failure (F-101), no shutdown logging (F-102), and no request-level visibility (F-104) — remain proposed and unimplemented in `Response.txt`.

### 5.4.2 Logging and Tracing Strategy

**Logging.** One statement, one line, one channel. `server.js:27` is the repository's only logging call, and no logging library is declared in `package.json` (`debug@4.4.3` arrives transitively with Express and stays silent unless `DEBUG` is set, which nothing in the repository does).

| Logging aspect | State at HEAD |
|----------------|---------------|
| Format and content | Unstructured single line carrying the loopback URL; no timestamp, level, severity, request identifier, host name, or duration |
| Channels | `stdout` for the startup line; `stderr` for runtime diagnostics (`MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, unhandled `error` events) and for Express's `logerror`, which writes `err.stack` whenever `env` is not `test` — and `env` is `development` |
| Levels and routing | None. No log level, filter, handler, or sink configuration exists; there is no library to configure |
| Request logging | None. Neither handler writes anything, and no middleware is mounted to write on their behalf |
| Refusal and client-error logging | None. A `404` carries no error object, so `finalhandler` schedules no `onerror` call; a malformed request is handled entirely by the Node HTTP parser |
| Retention and rotation | None. The process writes to whatever stream it was given; retention is entirely the operator's concern |
| Sensitive data | None logged, because no request data is ever read |

**Tracing.** There is no tracing strategy, and the architecture gives it nothing to trace: the system has no distributed components, no outbound call, no queue, and no asynchronous chain, so no correlation identifier, span, or propagation header is needed or present. A request's entire life is three synchronous statements on one event loop, and its only record is whatever the framework's disabled `DEBUG` output would have shown.

**Proposed but unimplemented.** No structured logging, request logging, or tracing work is recorded anywhere in the repository's plan; the only observability-adjacent proposals are F-101 (log a bind failure before exiting) and F-102 (log each shutdown phase).

### 5.4.3 Error Handling Patterns

The application contains no error-handling code: a text search of the four repository `.js` files for `.on(`, `process.on`, `try`, `catch`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `clientError`, `uncaughtException`, `unhandledRejection`, `headersSent`, and `process.exit` returns zero matches. Every failure path is therefore the runtime's or the framework's default, and the architectural patterns actually in force are three: **fail fast on an unresolvable dependency**, **delegate everything else to the framework and runtime**, and **refuse rather than substitute**.

| Error class | Mechanism in force | Observable outcome | Owning layer |
|-------------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------|
| Dependency unresolved | Module loader throws at `server.js:1` | `Cannot find module 'express'` on stderr, exit `1`, no stdout | Node module loader — fail fast |
| Bind conflict or permission failure | Express registers the startup callback as a one-shot `error` listener | Banner printed, error discarded, exit `0`, no diagnostic | Framework wiring (`application.js:598-606`) — silent swallow |
| Malformed request | Runtime's built-in `clientError` handling, no listener registered | `400 Bad Request` plus `Connection: close`, connection dropped, nothing logged, listener survives | Node HTTP parser |
| Unmatched path, method, or trailing-slash variant | Router falls through to `finalhandler` | `404 Not Found` with `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` HTML, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; nothing logged | Framework (`finalhandler@2.1.1`) — refusal as designed behaviour |
| Synchronous exception in a handler | Router catches it and forwards to the terminal handler | `500` HTML response plus a stack on stderr via `logerror`; unreachable today because both handlers are literal writes | Framework — untested path |
| Failure after the response is committed | `finalhandler` destroys the socket when headers were already sent; unreachable today | No double-write error is possible | Framework — untested path |
| Process signal | Runtime default disposition, no handler registered | Immediate exit `143` (`SIGTERM`) or `130` (`SIGINT`); in-flight responses dropped, keep-alive sockets reset | Operating system and runtime |
| Resource exhaustion | No limit, guard, or metric | The listener accepts until host descriptors are exhausted; no back-pressure and no alarm | None |

**Patterns deliberately absent:** no `try`/`catch` anywhere, no Express error-handling middleware (no `app.use` of any kind), no `uncaughtException` or `unhandledRejection` registration, no retry or back-off policy, no fallback or degraded mode, no circuit breaker, no dead-letter path, no timeout configuration, and no cleanup hook at process end. Recovery is therefore procedural rather than automated: the operator notices, fixes the cause, and restarts (§5.4.6).

**Proposed remediation.** The six hardening features recorded in `Response.txt` — F-101 server `error` handler, F-102 graceful shutdown on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` with a 10-second force-exit guard, F-103 handler `try`/`catch` with a `headersSent` guard, F-104 `clientError` handler, F-105 `req`/`res` falsy guard, and F-106 resource-cleanup hook — are not implemented. They were written against the superseded native-`http` file and explicitly forbid adding a framework, adding routes, or editing the manifest, so they must be re-derived before implementation; F-102 additionally requires retaining the `app.listen` return value, which the current code discards.

### 5.4.4 Authentication and Authorization Framework

There is no authentication or authorization framework, and no application-level access control of any kind. No identity, credential, session, role, or permission concept exists in the code, and no library in the dependency tree implements one.

| Concern | State | Consequence |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| Identity and authentication | Absent — no credential is requested, validated, or issued | Every request is anonymous; the two routes are indistinguishable from the service's point of view |
| Authorization | Absent and not applicable — both paths are public and have identical posture | There is no protected resource, no role model, and no route guard to add one to |
| Session and cookie management | Absent — no cookie is set or read, and no session store exists | Responses carry no `Set-Cookie`; nothing is remembered between requests |
| Transport security | Absent — plaintext HTTP/1.1 with no TLS listener, certificate, or terminator | Credentials could not be protected even if they were introduced without transport work first |
| Access boundary actually enforced | The operating-system loopback binding to `127.0.0.1`, plus file-system and process permissions on the host | Any local process that can open a TCP connection is authorised; no remote host can reach the service |
| Framework and version disclosure | `X-Powered-By: Express` on every response; `app.disable('x-powered-by')` is documented as an optional, unimplemented enhancement (~0.25 h) | The stack identity is published to local clients |
| Supply-chain trust | The only other trust decision in the system: 66 packages pinned by `sha512` digests in the lockfile | Integrity is verifiable at install time, but no audit or advisory monitoring runs automatically |
| Secrets | None exist in the repository — no key, token, password, certificate, or `.env` file | Nothing to leak, and no mechanism to inject anything either |

The architectural position is therefore explicit: security is delegated to the network boundary, which makes the service safe only while it remains unreachable from other hosts. Any enterprise adoption would require authentication, authorization, and TLS work that has no counterpart in the repository today, along with the environment-driven configuration such a deployment needs.

### 5.4.5 Performance Requirements and Service-Level Objectives

No performance requirement, service-level objective, service-level indicator, alert threshold, or capacity target is defined anywhere in the repository — not in `package.json`, not in `README.md`, and not in the documentation set. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` records validation results rather than commitments, and the per-request figures in `Response.txt` §0.6 (under 50 ms response, under 50 MB RSS, 100+ concurrent connections) belong to the unimplemented hardened variant and are explicitly out of scope for the delivered service.

| Objective | Target | Status |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| Byte-exact contract fidelity for both routes | 100% (2 of 2) | Met — verified by byte comparison at HEAD |
| Determinism: identical response for a given path, method, and query | 100% | Met structurally — neither handler reads request input |
| Start-up success on a free port | 100% of launches, with the banner printed | Met — observed on every launch; a held port is the one exclusion, and it fails silently |
| Refusal of unregistered paths and methods | `404` for unknown paths, trailing-slash variants, and non-`GET` methods | Met — verified for `/nope`, `/hello`, `//`, `/good-evening/`, `POST /`, `PUT /` |
| End-to-end latency | No committed target | Observed: 600 keep-alive requests over 100 sockets completed with zero errors in 132 ms total, 0.22 ms average, on Node v22.23.3 over loopback |
| Resource footprint | No committed target | Observed: approximately 72 MB resident and 1.0 GB virtual for the idle process; the `Response.txt` aspirational figure of under 50 MB is not met |
| Recovery time after a signal | No committed target | Observed: immediate exit (`143`/`130`), with the port released at once |

**Architectural performance characteristics.** Two handlers of three synchronous statements, no I/O, no template rendering, no serialization, and no allocation of dynamic content mean the response cost is dominated by the HTTP stack and the loopback round trip. Three properties shape capacity: the single-threaded event loop bounds throughput to one core and gives no clustering or worker-thread path to scale out; keep-alive reuse (idle timeout 5 s, with `headersTimeout` 60 s and `requestTimeout` 300 s as runtime defaults) removes per-request handshake cost; and there are no tuning knobs in the code at all — no compression, no connection limit, no socket option, no timeout setting, so the only levers available are the Node runtime and the host. The system's scalability position is recorded in §2.4.3: horizontal scaling is blocked by the hardcoded loopback address and fixed port, and vertical scaling is bounded only by the runtime.

### 5.4.6 Disaster Recovery Procedures

There is no disaster-recovery architecture. The service has no replica, no failover target, no backup, no snapshot, no multi-region posture, no supervisor or restart policy, no health probe for an orchestrator to consult, and no automated rollback. What exists instead is a property that makes most of those concerns moot: the service holds no state, so recovery is always a restart, and there is nothing to reconcile, replay, or restore. Recovery of the *artifact* is `git` plus `npm ci`; recovery of the *service* is one command.

| Failure scenario | Impact | Recovery procedure | Notes |
|------------------|--------|--------------------|-------|
| Process killed or signalled (`SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, crash) | Brief total unavailability; in-flight responses dropped, keep-alive sockets reset | Restart with `node server.js`; re-issue any request that was in flight | No drain exists, so a request in flight at signal time is lost; exit statuses are `143` and `130` |
| Port 3000 already held | Launch appears to succeed, then exits `0` with no diagnostic; the caller gets connection refusals | Free port 3000, or edit the `port` literal and restart; no fallback port exists | F-101 would make this failure diagnosable; F-102 requires the retained server handle |
| `node_modules/` missing, partial, or corrupt | Start-up aborts at `server.js:1` with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, exit `1` | `npm ci` from the committed lockfile, then restart | Requires npm ≥ 7 and a reachable registry; no mirror, offline mode, or vendored copy is configured |
| Host loss | Total outage; the service exists nowhere else | Provision a host with Node.js ≥ 18, clone the repository, `npm ci`, `node server.js` | No backup or failover exists; recovery time is provisioning plus install time |
| Registry unreachable during recovery | A new host cannot be prepared | Retry once the registry is reachable; running instances are unaffected | Existing installs keep serving, since the registry is not a runtime dependency |
| Contract drift from an unintended edit | Wrong body, wrong path, or a changed status served silently | Detect by manual `curl` and byte comparison; correct the source and restart | No automated regression suite exists, so detection depends on the operator |
| Dependency advisory or compromise | Unknown exposure until someone audits; three advisories are present today, all in packages off the request path | Re-lock and reinstall; roll back with `git revert` plus `npm ci` | No monitoring is wired into any job, and no rollback automation exists |
| Configuration or secret loss | Not applicable | — | Nothing is configured and no secret exists, so none of these can be lost |

The single point of failure is the single process: there is no bulkhead, retry, fallback, or graceful-degradation path, and the readiness signals an orchestrator would need — a health endpoint and a bounded, drained shutdown — do not exist. Recovery objectives in the conventional sense (RTO, RPO) are therefore not measurable for this system: there is no data to lose, and availability depends entirely on how quickly an operator or supervisor restarts the process.

```mermaid
    Signal{"Termination trigger"} -->|"SIGTERM from a supervisor"| Exit143["Immediate exit 143, no drain,<br/>in-flight responses dropped"]
    Signal -->|"SIGINT from the terminal"| Exit130["Immediate exit 130, no drain"]
    Signal -->|"unhandled error event in a native-http fixture"| Crash["Process aborts, exit 1 with a stack trace"]
    Signal -->|"none, steady state"| Steady["Serving until an external signal arrives"]
    Exit143 --> Proposed["F-102 proposes SIGTERM and SIGINT handlers calling server.close<br/>with a 10 second force-exit guard"]
    Exit130 --> Proposed
    Proposed --> Needs["Requires retaining the app.listen return value,<br/>which is discarded today"]
    Proposed --> Cleanup["F-106 proposes a resource-cleanup hook<br/>inside the close callback"]
```

# 6. SYSTEM COMPONENTS DESIGN

## 6.1 Core Services Architecture

### 6.1.1 Applicability Determination

**Core Services Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

`hao-backprop-test` is a single-process, single-file, stateless monolith whose entire executable surface is one 29-line CommonJS file, `server.js`, hosting an Express 5.2.1 application on two literal `GET` routes bound to `127.0.0.1:3000`. The file exports nothing, is imported by nothing, spawns no second process, holds no data, and makes no outbound connection; the three other JavaScript files at the repository root are standalone native-`http` fixtures that the service never loads. Everything a Core Services Architecture section normally describes — service boundaries, inter-service communication, service discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, retries and fallbacks, auto-scaling, fault tolerance, failover and degradation policy — has no counterpart in this system, because there is no second deployable unit for any of them to relate to.

The section is therefore written as an applicability determination plus a topic-by-topic disposition: §6.1.2 through §6.1.4 record each area the section prompt names as **verified absent**, with the source-level and runtime evidence that fixes the verdict, and §6.1.5 supplies the diagrams the prompt requires, drawn to show the boundary that contains the whole system rather than an empty distributed topology.

| Section prompt topic | Determination | Primary evidence |
|----------------------|---------------|------------------|
| Service components | Not applicable — one process, one module, no peers | `server.js:1-28`; §5.1.2; §6.1.2 |
| Scalability design | Not supported — fixed loopback binding, no scaling mechanism | `server.js:3-4, 26`; §2.4.3; §6.1.3 |
| Resilience patterns | Absent — no handler, supervisor, replica or recovery path | §5.4.3; §5.4.6; §6.1.4 |
| Required diagrams | Supplied as boundary, null-topology and convergence views | §6.1.5 |

#### 6.1.1.1 Basis of the Determination

Five independently verified facts carry the verdict; each is restated here with the evidence it rests on, because the same reasoning recurs in the sub-sections that follow.

1. **One deployable unit, and no internal module boundary.** The only runtime component is `server.js`, which contains two configuration literals, one framework setting, two route registrations and one listener (`server.js:3-28`). It declares no `module.exports` and no internal `require` of repository code, so it cannot be imported, composed or split without rewriting it. Its `package.json#main` points at an `index.js` that does not exist, leaving `node server.js` as the only working entry point.
2. **No second process, worker or supervisor.** A repository-wide text search of every tracked file for `cluster`, `worker_threads`, `fork(`, `pm2`, `systemd`, `nodemon`, `docker`, `kubernetes`, `helm` and `autoscal` returns matches only inside documentation prose; no `Dockerfile`, compose file, orchestration manifest, CI pipeline, process-supervision unit or environment file is tracked at all. The Node process reports a constant seven threads — the JavaScript thread plus the runtime's helper pool — and all requests are served by one event loop (§5.2.4).
3. **No external dependency to communicate with, discover or circuit-break.** The application imports exactly one module, `express`, and performs no outbound call: `fetch`, `axios`, `http.request`, database drivers, cache clients and broker clients are all absent, and the process makes no network connection after installation. §5.1.4 enumerates the integration categories and records each as absent; §5.4.3 records that no retry, back-off, circuit-breaker, dead-letter or fallback pattern exists.
4. **Network reachability is confined to one loopback socket.** The listener binds the literal `'127.0.0.1'` on the literal `3000` (`server.js:3-4, 26-28`), so no remote client and no upstream balancer can reach the service, and the single address is hardcoded rather than discovered. The port is exclusive: a second Express instance launched against the held port prints the startup banner and exits `0` with no diagnostic, and the native-`http` fixture dies on an unhandled `EADDRINUSE` with exit `1`.
5. **There is no state to replicate, rebalance or recover.** Both handlers ignore `req` and write fixed literals, no file is read or written at runtime, and no cache, session store or database exists (§5.2.3, §5.4.6). The only durable write in the system's life cycle is the 66-package dependency tree installed once per checkout into the git-ignored `node_modules/`.

#### 6.1.1.2 Repository Role Context

`README.md` states the project's purpose in two lines: `hao-backprop-test`, a "test project for backprop integration" with an HTTP server built on Express and two documented endpoints. That stated role explains the architecture rather than merely describing it: a fixture intended to be read exhaustively, installed from a lockfile, started by hand and exercised with `curl` needs no service topology, and every capability that would create one was explicitly excluded from the delivered work — testing, linting, CI/CD and containerisation, plus authentication, TLS, configuration files, environment-variable support and persistence (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2). The unimplemented hardening plan recorded in `Response.txt` §0.5 extends the same list of prohibitions to clustering, load balancing, health-check endpoints, metrics collection, database connections and HTTPS/TLS. The one recorded measurement set is a deployment model, not an SLA: §3.6.5 documents manual start as the deployment procedure, and §5.4.5 records that no performance objective, capacity target or alert threshold exists anywhere in the repository.

#### 6.1.1.3 Determinants That Would Otherwise Have Created a Core Services Architecture

The absence is deliberate at every point where a distributed shape could have entered. The two manifests, the published contract and the hardening plan each constrain the surface:

| Determinant | State in this repository | Evidence |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| Deployment unit | One process, one file, one listener; deployment is `npm ci` followed by `node server.js` | `README.md:14-23`; §3.6.5 |
| Dependency graph | One declared dependency (`express ^5.2.1`) expanding to 66 installed packages, all of them framework internals off the request path | `package.json:11-13`; `package-lock.json`; §5.2.6 |
| Configuration | Host and port are `const` literals; no `process.env` read, no config file, no CLI argument, no `.env` | `server.js:3-4`; §2.4.1 |
| Persistence and messaging | No database, cache, queue or broker client; `phonenumber.csv` is imported by no code | §5.2.7; §5.4.6 |
| Planned hardening | F-101–F-106 improve error visibility and shutdown hygiene only; the plan forbids adding dependencies, routes or manifest changes | `Response.txt` §0.5, §0.7 |

#### 6.1.1.4 Conflict With the Repository's Earlier Verdict

The repository already carries a Core Services Architecture section of its own — `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` lines 2781-3113 — which reaches the same "Not Applicable" verdict, and the conclusion is upheld here. Its supporting basis, however, describes a state the repository has since left: that document characterises the system as a 15-line, route-agnostic native-`http` server with **zero** npm dependencies and an empty lockfile (its §6.1.1, §6.1.2), whereas the current tree runs Express 5.2.1 over a 66-package dependency tree, registers two routes with strict path matching, and answers an unregistered path with the framework's `404` rather than the legacy catch-all greeting.

Two of its specific claims are contradicted by observed behaviour, and the observed behaviour governs this specification:

| Claim in `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §6.1 | Observed at HEAD |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| Zero dependencies; lockfile holds only the root self-reference | `package.json` declares `express ^5.2.1`; 66 packages are installed and 66 non-root entries are locked |
| An unhandled `clientError` produces a "connection-level crash" | The runtime answers `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; the process survives and nothing is logged |
| Handler exception crashes the process | The framework's router catches a thrown layer error and routes it to the terminal responder; no handler in this repository can throw (§5.2.2, §5.4.3) |

That document's own §2.7.4 concedes the point of divergence, noting that any modification to `server.js` invalidates its acceptance criteria. The verdict survives the re-platform because the reasons for it do not depend on the framework: the system still consists of one process, one file, one loopback listener, no peers and no state.

#### 6.1.1.5 How Each Required Area Is Documented

| Required area | Treatment in this section |

| Service components | §6.1.2 — boundaries and responsibilities, inter-service communication, discovery, load balancing, circuit breaker, retry and fallback, each recorded as absent with its evidence |

### 6.1.2 Service Components

The system has no service components in the architectural sense: there is no independently deployable unit, no process boundary between capabilities, and no addressable peer. What it does have is a set of in-process components inside one Node.js process, catalogued as C-1 through C-8 in §5.1.2 and detailed in §5.2.1 through §5.2.7. They are restated here only to show what each would have been if the system had been decomposed, and why none of them qualifies as a service.

| In-process component | Responsibility | Why it is not a service |
|----------------------|----------------|-------------------------|
| Express application container (`server.js`) | Holds the two configuration literals, creates the app, enables strict routing, registers both routes, starts the listener | One file, no exports, no internal callers; the whole application |
| Route table and dispatch (`router@2.2.0`) | Matches method and path against two literal layers; answers `OPTIONS`; falls through on no match | A library inside the same process, not an addressable unit |
| Greeting handlers (`server.js:14-24`) | Write the two fixed responses | Functions, not deployables; no I/O, no state |
| Loopback listener (Node `http.Server`) | Binds `127.0.0.1:3000`, parses HTTP/1.1, serialises responses | The process's single listening socket |
| Terminal responder (`finalhandler@2.1.1`) | Synthesises default `404`/`5xx` responses | Framework terminal callback, invoked in-process |
| Dependency supply chain (`package.json`, lockfile, `node_modules/`) | Declares, pins and materialises the 66-package tree | Build-time input, not a runtime service |
| Fixture scripts and documentation | Standalone native-`http` servers and Markdown artifacts | Never loaded or called by the service |

#### 6.1.2.1 Service Boundaries and Responsibilities

Exactly one runtime boundary exists — a single Node.js process on a single host — and it is the thinnest boundary the architecture can express. No capability is allocated to a module of its own, because no second module of repository code exists: `server.js` contains the configuration, the routing table, both handlers and the listener, and exports none of them.

| Boundary dimension | Realization | Evidence |
|--------------------|-------------|----------|
| Process | One Node.js process, 7 threads, one event loop | `server.js`; process inspection at HEAD; §5.2.4 |
| Network | One loopback TCP listener, `127.0.0.1:3000`, plaintext HTTP/1.1 | `server.js:3-4, 26-28`; live responses |
| Module | None — no `module.exports`, no internal `require`, `package.json#main` names an absent `index.js` | `server.js`; `package.json:5` |
| Data domain | None — no write path, no store, no cache, no session | §5.2.3; §5.4.6 |
| Responsibility allocation | Four responsibilities in one file: configuration, route registration, response construction, process lifecycle | `server.js:3-28` |

The consequence for this section is direct: a responsibility cannot be relocated, versioned, scaled or failed over independently, because nothing in the system is independent of anything else. Startup order is the only ordering constraint the code expresses, and it is inside the file — `app.enable('strict routing')` must precede the first `app.get`, because the router captures the setting when it is first constructed (§5.2.1).

#### 6.1.2.2 Inter-Service Communication Patterns

There is no inter-service communication, in either direction. The only communication in the system is an inbound HTTP/1.1 request from a client on the same host, answered by a synchronous in-process call chain: `http.Server` → `app.handle` → `router` → one of the two handlers, or the terminal responder when nothing matches (§5.1.3).

| Communication pattern | State | Evidence |
|-----------------------|-------|----------|
| Inbound transport | HTTP/1.1 plaintext over loopback TCP, keep-alive, request body never read | live responses; §5.1.4 |
| Outbound transport | None — no `fetch`, `axios`, `http.request`, broker or database client anywhere in application code | repository-wide search of all tracked files |
| Inter-process communication | None — no socket pair, pipe, shared memory, RPC or message bus | no second process exists |
| Asynchronous messaging | None — no producer, consumer, topic or queue | §5.4.3 |
| Streaming or server-sent events | None — responses are fixed-length 14-byte and 12-byte literals | live `Content-Length` values |
| In-process call chain | Synchronous function calls on one event loop; no serialization and no envelope | §5.1.3 |

Two framework-mediated behaviours are the closest thing the system has to a protocol contract between layers, and both are internal: the router lowers the request method, aliases `HEAD` to the `GET` layer, drops the query string before matching, and answers `OPTIONS` itself; and a synchronous exception thrown in a matched layer is caught by the router and forwarded to the terminal responder rather than escaping to the event loop (§5.2.2). Neither constitutes communication between services, because no second service exists to receive anything.

#### 6.1.2.3 Service Discovery Mechanisms

Discovery is not merely absent; it is unnecessary, because exactly one address is ever used and it is compiled into the file.

| Aspect | State | Evidence |
|--------|-------|----------|
| Address source | `const hostname = '127.0.0.1'` and `const port = 3000`, read once at listen time | `server.js:3-4, 26` |
| Registry, DNS or mesh lookup | None — no resolver, no registry client, no sidecar, no service-mesh dependency | repository-wide search; `package-lock.json` |
| Published location | `README.md` documents `http://127.0.0.1:3000/`; the startup banner repeats it | `README.md:12, 23`; `server.js:27` |
| Client coupling | Callers must know the literal address and port out of band; nothing advertises or resolves it | `README.md:9-12` |

The operational effect is a fixed, private locator with no indirection: changing the port means editing a source literal and restarting, since no environment variable, configuration file or command-line argument is consulted anywhere in executable code (§2.4.1). Nothing in the system could consume a discovery result even if one were published.

#### 6.1.2.4 Load Balancing Strategy

No load balancer, proxy or upstream of any kind exists, and the binding makes one impossible without a code change: only a local process can reach a listener bound to `127.0.0.1`, so there is no traffic path for a balancer to distribute, and no second instance for it to target. The port is exclusive, which was confirmed by launching a competing process against the held port: the second Express instance printed the startup banner and exited `0` with no diagnostic, and the native-`http` fixture aborted with an unhandled `EADDRINUSE` and exit `1`.

| Balancing concern | State | Evidence |
|-------------------|-------|----------|
| Balancer or reverse proxy | None — no proxy configuration, no upstream group, no TLS terminator | §3.6.5; §5.1.4 |
| Instance multiplicity | Not possible on one host — literal loopback address and fixed port | `server.js:3-4`; §2.4.3 |
| Socket sharing across processes | Not configured — no `SO_REUSEPORT`, no `cluster` module | `server.js`; §5.2.4 |
| Distribution policy | None — one process serves every request it accepts | §5.2.4 |

Load balancing is therefore not a deferred decision but a structurally unavailable one. Making it possible would first require parameterising the bind address and port so that several instances could coexist, and second exposing them behind a listener that remote clients can reach — neither of which is in scope (§2.4.3, §6.1.6).

#### 6.1.2.5 Circuit Breaker Patterns

No circuit breaker exists, and none has a subject. The pattern protects a caller from a failing downstream dependency by tripping after repeated failures; this system has no downstream dependency of any kind — no HTTP client, no database driver, no cache client, no broker client — so no call can fail slowly, fail repeatedly, or be short-circuited. The application's entire request path is three synchronous statements that cannot throw and that touch no external resource (§5.2.3, §5.4.3). The nearest available analogue, the framework's response to an exception thrown inside a route layer, is a single framework `500` handled in-process by the terminal responder, with no threshold, sampling, state machine or half-open probe.

#### 6.1.2.6 Retry and Fallback Mechanisms

Neither exists at any layer: not in the application, not in the framework wiring, and not around the process. The single point where a conventional implementation would apply a retry — failing to bind the port — has no retry, no alternate port and no diagnostic, because `app.listen` registers the startup callback as a one-shot `error` listener (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-606`) whose body is a success log:

```javascript
// server.js:26-28 — the returned server handle is discarded and the
// callback doubles as the one-shot error listener registered by app.listen
app.listen(port, hostname, () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
});
```

| Mechanism | State | Evidence |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| Bind retry or alternate port | None — a held port prints the banner, discards the error and exits `0` | `application.js:598-606`; observed launch |
| Request-level retry or back-off | None — no client, no policy, no timer in application code | §5.4.3 |
| Fallback response path | None — the only outcomes are the two literals, `404`, or a framework `500` | §5.2.5; §5.4.7 |
| Recovery procedure | Manual: free the port, then restart; no supervisor restarts the process | §5.4.6; `Response.txt` §0.5 |

The absence is consequential in one specific way: the silent `exit 0` makes a bind failure indistinguishable from a successful short-lived run to any supervisor, script or operator that consults only the exit status and standard output — a defect the unimplemented feature F-101 was written to correct (`Response.txt` §0.4, Change #2).


### 6.1.3 Scalability Design

No scaling mechanism exists in this system, and none is planned: the repository contains no process supervisor, no cluster module, no worker threads, no container or orchestration manifest, no pipeline, and no metric or health surface a scaler could act on. That disposition is recorded in §2.4.3 as a property of the architecture rather than a backlog item, and §3.6.5 lists scaling as "not supported as configured". The sub-sections below state, for each scaling concern the section prompt names, what exists, what does not, and which of those facts is a limit rather than a choice.

#### 6.1.3.1 Horizontal and Vertical Scaling

| Dimension | Disposition | Evidence |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| Horizontal scaling | Not possible as configured — literal loopback address and fixed port admit one instance per host | `server.js:3-4, 26`; observed launch conflict; §2.4.3 |
| Vertical scaling | Bounded by the Node.js runtime alone; the application adds no resident state beyond the loaded dependency tree | §5.2.4; measured process footprint |
| Concurrency model | One event loop serving synchronous, non-blocking handlers; no `async`, `await`, `Promise`, timer, stream or worker construct in application code | `server.js`; search of all application files |
| Instance interchangeability | Would hold if the address were parameterised — both handlers read no input and hold no state | `server.js:14-24`; §5.2.3 |

The horizontal limit is operational, not theoretical, and it fails in a way that is easy to misread: launching a second instance against the held port prints `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` and exits `0`, because the startup callback doubles as the one-shot `error` listener registered by `app.listen` (§5.2.4), while the native-`http` fixture fails loudly with an unhandled `EADDRINUSE` and exit `1`. The only scaling axis that responds at all is vertical, and it is limited by the fact that the workload is already a single-threaded literal write: a 16-core host contributes nothing to throughput, since nothing in the request path parallelises. Measured on this checkout, one process absorbed 2,000 requests at 100-way client parallelism in 1.718 s with zero errors, and 200 concurrently held sockets each received `200 OK` (200 of 200 responses, 0.021 s for the response phase).

#### 6.1.3.2 Auto-Scaling Triggers and Resource Allocation

There are no triggers, no rules and no controller, because there is no scaling mechanism to govern and no signal to drive one: the service exposes no health or readiness endpoint, emits no metric, and publishes no resource statistic (§5.4.1). The readiness evidence an orchestrator would need reduces to accepting a TCP connection on port 3000 or printing the banner — and a port conflict prints that banner too (§5.4.6).

| Concern | State | Evidence |
|---------|-------|----------|
| Auto-scaling triggers and rules | None — no supervisor, sidecar, orchestrator or autoscaler; no metric to trigger on | §5.4.1; §5.4.6 |
| Health/readiness surface | None — no liveness or readiness route; nothing distinguishes healthy from serving nothing | §5.4.1; §5.4.5 |
| Resource allocation | None — no image, no CPU or memory request or limit, no cgroup, no cpuset | §3.6.3; §2.4.5 |
| Runtime version constraint | Node.js ≥ 18 required by Express, but not enforced: `package.json` declares no `engines` field | `package.json`; §2.4.1 |
| Admission control | None — no rate limit, no request quota, no `maxConnections`, no queue and no back-pressure | §5.2.4; §2.4.3 |

The practical consequence is that the process scales by exhaustion rather than by policy. It holds no resource budget of its own: an idle instance was measured at 63.1 MB resident and, after 2,000 requests plus 200 held connections, at 103.5 MB, with a constant thread count of seven throughout. With no admission control and no timeout configured in application code, the listener accepts until the host runs out of descriptors, and nothing reports the approach (§5.2.4).

#### 6.1.3.3 Performance Optimisation Techniques

The performance posture is not the result of tuning but of subtraction: responses are source literals, the middleware pipeline is empty, and nothing between the socket and the response allocates or computes per-request content.

| Technique | How it is realised | Evidence |
|-----------|--------------------|----------|
| Fixed-literal responses | Three synchronous statements per handler using the low-level `res.statusCode` / `res.setHeader` / `res.end` API; no templating, serialisation or computation | `server.js:15-17, 21-23`; §5.2.3 |
| Empty middleware pipeline | No `app.use` call exists in any application file, so request parsers, static serving, cookie handling and compression never execute | repository-wide search; §5.1.3 |
| No content negotiation or caching work | `res.end` bypasses `res.send`, so no content-type inference, charset appending or ETag computation occurs; no `Cache-Control`, `ETag` or `Last-Modified` is emitted | live response headers |
| Connection reuse | Keep-alive is enabled by the runtime and idle sockets are held for 5 s (`keepAliveTimeout`), with `headersTimeout` 60 s and `requestTimeout` 300 s as runtime defaults | §5.2.4; runtime inspection |
| Trivial dispatch cost | A linear scan of a two-entry route table, with no dynamic registration and no contention | §5.2.2 |
| Absent by design | No compression, no cache layer, no connection pool, no warm-up, no socket-level tuning, and no timeout knob exposed to the operator | §5.3 records that no caching tier exists |

Measured end-to-end behaviour follows from those properties: 2,000 requests at 100-way parallelism completed in 1.718 s wall-clock with zero errors, and an earlier 300-request run at 30-way parallelism completed in 0.255 s, on the same loopback interface and Node v22.23.3 runtime. Because the handlers perform no work and read no input, request cost is dominated by the HTTP stack and the loopback round trip, which means the optimisation ceiling has already been reached for this contract — there is no application-level cost left to remove (§5.4.5).

#### 6.1.3.4 Capacity Planning Guidelines

No capacity commitment exists to plan against. The repository defines no performance requirement, service-level objective, alert threshold or concurrency target in any file, and §5.4.5 records that position explicitly. The figures that circulate in the project's own remediation note — under 50 ms response time, under 50 MB resident memory, 100 or more concurrent connections — were written for the unimplemented hardened variant of the superseded implementation and are not commitments of this build (`Response.txt` §0.6; §2.4.2).

| Capacity aspect | Committed target | Observed at HEAD |
|-----------------|------------------|------------------|
| Request latency | None defined | Single-digit milliseconds over loopback; 2,000 requests in 1.718 s under 100-way load |
| Throughput | None defined | Approximately 1,160 requests per second wall-clock on a 16-core host, from one core |
| Concurrent connections | None defined | 200 simultaneously held sockets, each answered `200 OK` |
| Resident memory | None defined; the aspirational 50 MB figure is not met | 63.1 MB idle, rising to 103.5 MB after load |

The guidelines that can be stated from evidence are therefore constraints rather than budgets. One instance per host, because the address and port are literals and a second launch fails silently. One event loop per instance, so throughput is single-core bound and adding cores to the host changes nothing. Loopback only, so capacity is local to the machine that runs the process and cannot be borrowed from another host without first changing the bind address. Recovery is a restart, not a scale event: because the service holds no state, freeing the port and re-running `node server.js` restores full capacity immediately (§5.4.6). Any capacity plan that assumes horizontal headroom, a balancer or a scaling policy would require the architectural changes catalogued in §6.1.6.


### 6.1.4 Resilience Patterns

Resilience is not designed in this system; it is inherited from the runtime and the framework and stops where their defaults stop. A text search of all four application JavaScript files for `try`, `catch`, `.on(`, `process.on`, `process.exit`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `clientError`, `uncaughtException`, `unhandledRejection` and `headersSent` returns zero matches, and no `app.use` call exists anywhere, so no error-handling middleware is mounted. §5.4.3 states the position canonically — the application has no error-handling paths — and the failure classification below records what actually happens in each case, distinguishing framework defaults from absent mechanisms.

#### 6.1.4.1 Fault Tolerance Mechanisms

| Mechanism | State | Behaviour when the condition occurs |
|-----------|-------|-------------------------------------|
| Dependency resolution guard | Absent, but fail-fast by construction | `require('express')` throws at `server.js:1`; `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on stderr, exit `1`, no banner |
| Server `error` event handler | Absent — the startup callback is the one-shot listener | A held port prints the banner, discards the error and exits `0` with no diagnostic |
| Request-handler exception protection | Absent — no `try`/`catch`, no `app.use` error middleware | Router catches a thrown layer error and passes it to the terminal responder, which returns `500` HTML and logs a stack; unreachable today (§5.2.2) |
| `clientError` handler | Absent — runtime default applies | Malformed bytes are answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; the process survives and nothing is logged |
| Input validation of `req`/`res` | Not applicable — neither handler dereferences `req` | No request-derived value can influence execution |
| Uncaught-exception / rejection handler | Absent | No `uncaughtException` or `unhandledRejection` listener exists; nothing is intercepted |
| Timeouts and limits | Absent in application code | No request timeout, no connection cap, no rate limit; only the runtime's keep-alive (5 s), header (60 s) and request (300 s) defaults apply |
| Health or readiness probe | Absent | No liveness or readiness route exists; TCP acceptance and the banner are the only signals |
| Restart policy or supervisor | Absent | Nothing restarts the process; recovery is manual (§5.4.6) |

Three tolerance properties do hold, and they are properties of the framework and runtime rather than of the application: an unresolvable dependency fails fast and loudly; a genuinely thrown handler error becomes a bounded `500` rather than a process crash; and an unmatched path is refused with `404` rather than answered with a substitute response (§5.2.5, §5.4.3). The net effect is a system that neither degrades nor self-heals: it either serves correctly or stops.

#### 6.1.4.2 Disaster Recovery Procedures

There is no disaster-recovery architecture — no supervisor or restart policy, no replica, no failover host, no backup or snapshot, no rolling-restart strategy, no automated rollback and no health probe for an orchestrator to consult (§5.4.6). What the system has instead is statelessness, which reduces recovery to a restart: because no request-derived value is retained and nothing is written at runtime, there is nothing to reconcile, replay or restore after a failure.

| Failure scenario | Impact | Recovery procedure |
|------------------|--------|--------------------|
| Process killed or signalled | Immediate loss of service; in-flight responses dropped; keep-alive sockets reset | Restart with `node server.js` after freeing the port; exit status was `143` (`SIGTERM`) or `130` (`SIGINT`) |
| Port 3000 already held | The launch appears successful and exits `0`; waiting clients get connection refusals | Free port 3000 or change the `port` literal and restart; no fallback port selection exists |
| `node_modules/` missing or corrupt | Start-up aborts at `server.js:1` with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, exit `1` | `npm ci` from the committed lockfile, then restart |
| Host loss | Total outage; no instance exists anywhere else | Provision a host with Node.js ≥ 18, clone the repository, `npm ci`, `node server.js` |
| Unintended contract drift | A wrong body, path or status is served silently | Detect by manual `curl` and byte comparison; correct the source and restart |
| Dependency advisory in the tree | Unknown exposure until someone audits; no monitoring runs automatically | Re-lock and reinstall; roll back with `git revert` followed by `npm ci` |

Recovery objectives are not measurable for this system in the conventional sense: there is no data to lose, so recovery point is not applicable, and availability is determined entirely by how quickly an operator or an external supervisor restarts the process. The single point of failure is the single process, and nothing in the repository mitigates it.

#### 6.1.4.3 Data Redundancy Approach

No data is processed, so there is nothing to replicate, mirror or restore. The handlers are pure functions of nothing: they read no request input and hold no state between requests (§5.2.3). No runtime file write exists in any code path, no `fs` module is imported, and the two data-carrying artifacts in the repository — `phonenumber.csv` with 15 synthetic rows and the binary documents and media files — are opened by no code (§5.2.7).

| Data class | Location and lifetime | Redundancy posture |
|------------|-----------------------|--------------------|
| Business or request data | None — no store, no cache, no session, no log of request content | Not applicable; nothing to replicate |
| Response payloads | Source literals in `server.js`, recreated per process | Recovered by restarting; identical on every instance |
| Dependency tree | `node_modules/`, git-ignored, written once per checkout | Reproducible from `package-lock.json` (66 pinned entries with `sha512` digests) resolved from the public npm registry |
| Source and fixtures | Tracked files in the Git repository | Replicated only by whatever remote the operator configures; the running service neither reads nor writes them |

The only durable artifact the system produces is its installed dependency tree, and its redundancy is supply-chain redundancy rather than data redundancy: the lockfile pins versions and integrity digests so the same tree can be reconstituted on any host, but nothing runs automatically to verify, back up or re-materialise it.

#### 6.1.4.4 Failover Configurations

No failover path exists. There is one process, on one host, with one listening socket, and no standby, no secondary host, no DNS indirection, no virtual address and no balancer that could redirect traffic (§5.4.6). The one way the system could conceivably have provided a local fallback — the three native-`http` fixture scripts — cannot serve as a substitute, because they bind the same exclusive loopback port and answer a different contract: a route- and method-agnostic `200` with `Hello, World!\n` and no `X-Powered-By` header, whereas the service registers two routes, returns `404` for everything else and identifies itself as Express.

| Failover element | State | Evidence |
|------------------|-------|----------|
| Secondary instance | Not possible on the same host — fixed loopback address and port | `server.js:3-4`; observed silent exit `0` on a held port |
| Standby host or replica | None | §5.4.6 |
| Traffic redirection (DNS, VIP, balancer) | None — unreachable from other hosts by construction | §5.1.4; §2.4.3 |
| Automated promotion or health-gated switch | None — no health endpoint and no controller exists | §5.4.1; §5.4.6 |
| Fixture as substitute process | Not interchangeable — same port, divergent contract | fixture sources; §5.2.7 |

#### 6.1.4.5 Service Degradation Policies

The system has no degraded mode. Degradation requires an alternative path to serve from — a cache to answer with, a queue to buffer work, a read-only mode to fall back to, or a load-shedding rule to apply — and none of those exists: there is no cache at any tier, no queue, no persistence layer, no rate limiting and no connection limit (§5.3, §5.4.3). Every failure resolves to one of three outcomes: a correct response, a refusal, or termination.

| Failure class | Mechanism in force | Observable outcome |
|---------------|--------------------|---------------------|
| Unregistered path, method or trailing-slash variant | Framework terminal responder (`finalhandler@2.1.1`) | `404 Not Found` with `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` HTML; nothing logged |
| Malformed HTTP request | Node HTTP parser default path | `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; process survives; nothing logged |
| Exception thrown inside a route layer | Router error path into the terminal responder | `500` HTML plus a stack on stderr; unreachable, since no handler can throw |
| Port already in use at start-up | One-shot `error` listener registered by `app.listen` | Banner printed, error discarded, exit `0` — a false success |
| `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` | Runtime default disposition; no drain and no cleanup hook | Immediate exit `143` or `130`; in-flight responses dropped; the port is released at once |
| Resource exhaustion (descriptors) | No limit, no guard, no metric | The listener accepts until the host runs out of descriptors; no alarm is raised |

Graceful shutdown — the one degradation policy a reviewer would look for first — is absent, and it cannot be added by configuration: `app.listen` returns the `http.Server`, and `server.js:26` discards it, so no reference exists through which `server.close()` could drain connections without a source change (§5.2.1, §5.4.3). The features that would supply these policies on paper, F-102 (SIGTERM/SIGINT shutdown with a 10-second force-exit guard) and F-106 (a resource-cleanup hook), remain unimplemented and were written against the superseded native-`http` file, so they must be re-derived before they can be applied (`Response.txt` §0.4; §5.4.3). For an orchestrator, the practical meaning is that a rolling update would terminate the process at the first signal with no readiness gate and no drain, and that a port conflict would be indistinguishable from a healthy, short-lived start.


### 6.1.5 Service Interaction, Scalability and Resilience Diagrams

The three diagrams the section prompt requires are supplied below as boundary, null-topology and convergence views. They are not substitutes for diagrams that could not be drawn: they show, explicitly, the single boundary that contains the entire system and the absent edges that a service-interaction, scalability or resilience diagram would otherwise depict.

#### 6.1.5.1 Service Interaction Diagram — One Process, No Peers

This diagram shows every component that can receive or produce a request, and the empty space where peer services, downstream dependencies and platform services would appear. The only edges that carry traffic terminate on the loopback listener; the dashed edge marks the absence of any outbound call.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client["Loopback HTTP client<br/>curl, smoke test, local process"]

    subgraph Host["Single host"]
        subgraph Proc["Single Node.js process, started as node server.js"]
            App["Express application container<br/>server.js: two literals, strict routing,<br/>two route registrations, app.listen"]
            Router["Route dispatch<br/>router 2.2.0, two literal GET layers"]
            Handlers["Greeting handlers<br/>200 text/plain, 14 B and 12 B"]
            Terminal["Terminal responder<br/>finalhandler 2.1.1, 404 and 500"]
            Listener["Loopback listener<br/>Node http.Server on 127.0.0.1:3000"]
        end
        Stdout["Standard output<br/>one startup line"]
    end

    subgraph Absent["No peer, no downstream, no platform service"]
        NoPeer["No second instance or standby<br/>No load balancer or reverse proxy<br/>No service registry, DNS or mesh<br/>No database, cache, queue or broker<br/>No outbound HTTP client or external API<br/>No metrics, tracing or APM backend"]
    end

    Client -->|"HTTP/1.1 request, plaintext, keep-alive"| Listener
    Listener -->|"request event"| App
    App --> Router
    Router -->|"literal path matched"| Handlers
    Router -->|"nothing matched"| Terminal
    Handlers -->|"response bytes"| Listener
    Terminal -->|"404 or 500 document"| Listener
    Listener -->|"response"| Client
    App --> Stdout
    App -.->|"no outbound call exists in any code path"| NoPeer
```

#### 6.1.5.2 Scalability Architecture — Current Topology and the Absent Scaling Path

The upper subgraph is the implemented topology, annotated with measured single-process capacity. The middle subgraph lists the scaling mechanisms that do not exist, and the lower subgraph states what would have to be built before any of them could function; the arrows are prerequisites, not planned work.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CurrentTopology["Current topology — implemented"]
        Solo["One Node.js process on one host<br/>bound to 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>one event loop, one core<br/>measured 2000 requests at 100-way<br/>parallelism in 1.718 s, zero errors"]
    end

    subgraph ScalingAbsent["Scaling mechanisms — absent"]
        LB["Upstream load balancer<br/>or reverse proxy"]
        ClusterNode["cluster module, worker<br/>threads or child processes"]
        OrchestratorNode["Container or orchestrator<br/>no Dockerfile, manifest or pipeline"]
        AutoNode["Autoscaler or scaling policy<br/>no metric, no health endpoint"]
        SupervisorNode["Process supervisor<br/>or restart policy"]
    end

    subgraph Prerequisites["What scaling would require first"]
        Param["Parameterise host and port so<br/>two instances can coexist"]
        Expose["Bind a reachable address and<br/>front it with a balancer"]
        Signals["Publish health and metrics so a<br/>scaler has a trigger"]
        Drain["Retain the server handle to<br/>drain connections on shutdown"]
    end

    Solo -.->|"no scaling path exists"| LB
    LB --> Param
    ClusterNode --> Param
    OrchestratorNode --> Expose
    AutoNode --> Signals
    SupervisorNode --> Drain
```

#### 6.1.5.3 Resilience Pattern Implementation — Convergence to Termination and Manual Restart

Every failure class in this system resolves to one of three outcomes: the process survives because the runtime handled the condition, the process exits silently while reporting success, or the process dies without draining. No path reaches a retry, a fallback, a degraded mode or an automated restart, which is why the diagram converges on manual recovery.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    StartNode(["Failure or refusal event"]) --> Classify{"Failure class?"}
    Classify -->|"Port 3000 already held at start-up"| BindNode["app.listen one-shot error listener<br/>consumes EADDRINUSE"]
    Classify -->|"SIGTERM or SIGINT received"| SignalNode["Runtime default disposition<br/>no handler registered"]
    Classify -->|"Malformed HTTP bytes"| BadNode["Node HTTP parser default<br/>answers 400 Bad Request and closes"]
    Classify -->|"Unregistered path or method"| RefuseNode["finalhandler refusal<br/>404 HTML, nothing logged"]
    Classify -->|"Exception thrown in a route layer"| ThrowNode["Router error path<br/>500 HTML plus stack on stderr"]
    BindNode --> FalseSuccess(["Banner printed, exit 0<br/>false success, no diagnostic"])
    SignalNode --> NoDrain(["Exit 143 or 130<br/>in-flight requests dropped, no drain"])
    BadNode --> Survive(["Process survives,<br/>listener continues serving"])
    RefuseNode --> Survive
    ThrowNode --> Survive
    FalseSuccess --> Manual(["Manual recovery is the only path"])
    NoDrain --> Manual
    Manual --> RestartNode["Free the port, then run node server.js<br/>no supervisor, no replica, no failover"]
    RestartNode --> Restored(["Service restored<br/>no store, cache or session to reconcile"])

    subgraph AbsentPatterns["Absent patterns"]
        NoRetry["No retry or back-off"]
        NoCircuit["No circuit breaker to trip"]
        NoFallback["No fallback response or alternate port"]
        NoProbe["No health or readiness probe"]
        NoShutdown["No graceful shutdown or cleanup hook"]
        NoCatch["No uncaughtException or unhandledRejection handler"]
    end

    AbsentPatterns -.->|"documented but unimplemented:<br/>F-101 through F-106"| Manual
```

The three diagrams together state the architectural position in one view: a request crosses exactly one boundary, capacity cannot leave one core or one host, and no failure has a recovery path that does not pass through an operator.


### 6.1.6 Forward-Looking Considerations

Two classes of change could alter this section: the hardening work already written down but not implemented, and a scope expansion that would create the distributed shape this section currently rules out. The first is bounded and does not move the verdict; the second would.

#### 6.1.6.1 Proposed Hardening Preserves the Monolithic Shape

The six hardening features recorded in `Response.txt` §0.4 improve failure visibility and shutdown hygiene inside the same single process. None introduces a service boundary, an addressable peer, a registry, a balancer, a retry policy or a scaling mechanism, so the determination in §6.1.1 survives them unchanged. They also cannot be applied as written: they were authored against the superseded 15-line native-`http` file and their scope rules forbid the framework, routes and manifest changes that the delivered implementation already made (`Response.txt` §0.5; §2.4.5).

| Feature | What it would add | Effect on this section |
|---------|-------------------|------------------------|
| F-101 server `error` handler | Logs `EADDRINUSE`/`EACCES` and exits `1` instead of exiting `0` silently | Makes a launch failure diagnosable; removes the false-success path in §6.1.4.5 |
| F-102 graceful shutdown | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handlers calling `server.close()` with a 10-second force-exit guard | Introduces a bounded drain, the first degradation policy in §6.1.4.5; requires retaining the `app.listen` handle that `server.js:26` discards |
| F-103 handler exception protection | `try`/`catch` with a `headersSent` guard in the handlers | Makes the framework's existing `500` path explicit; no new component |
| F-104 `clientError` handler | Explicit `400` response for malformed requests | Preserves the runtime behaviour already observed; adds a log line |
| F-105 request/response validation | Falsy checks on `req`/`res` | Defensive only; neither object is dereferenced today |
| F-106 resource cleanup hook | A cleanup point inside the shutdown callback | A placeholder, since the application owns no external resource and performs no file I/O |

#### 6.1.6.2 Conditions That Would Make This Section Applicable

The section becomes applicable only if the project's scope is expanded to permit one or more of the following. Each entry names what the change would require and which sub-section it would activate; none of them is on the current roadmap, and the delivered work explicitly excluded testing, CI/CD, containerisation, configuration externalisation, TLS, authentication and persistence (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2).

| Trigger | What would be required | Sub-section activated |
|---------|------------------------|-----------------------|
| Multi-process execution | `cluster`, worker threads or child processes, plus a supervisor and a port-sharing strategy; clustering was excluded from the hardening scope as well | §6.1.2, §6.1.3 |
| External network exposure | Binding a non-loopback interface, a TLS terminator or reverse proxy, and an access-control decision at the new boundary | §6.1.2, §6.1.4 |
| Decomposition into modules | Extracting handlers, routing or configuration into separate files that import one another, and defining their contracts and lifecycle | §6.1.2 |
| Downstream service dependency | Introducing an HTTP client, database driver, cache client or broker client, with its own timeouts, retry policy and failure budget | §6.1.2, §6.1.4 |
| State or session retention | Introducing a store, session or cache, and with it replication, backup and recovery objectives | §6.1.4 |
| Automated scaling | Health and readiness endpoints, emitted metrics, a scaling controller and externalised host/port configuration | §6.1.3 |
| Deployment beyond a developer host | A container image, orchestrator manifest and pipeline, which would also supply restart policy and lifecycle signals | §6.1.3, §6.1.4 |

#### 6.1.6.3 Recorded Enhancements That Touch These Topics

Three deferred items are recorded in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3 as outside the delivered work, and one of them is the first prerequisite for any scaling discussion: parameterising host and port through environment variables (about 1.0 h), which would remove the single-instance-per-host constraint that §6.1.3.1 and §6.1.2.4 identify as the binding limit. The other two — a minimal regression suite with `node:test` and `supertest` (about 2.0 h) and suppression of the `X-Powered-By` header (about 0.25 h) — touch maintainability and disclosure respectively and change nothing in this section. None of the three is implemented, and the hardening initiative F-101–F-106 remains a separate, unauthorised workstream. Until one of the triggers in §6.1.6.2 is introduced by an explicit scope expansion, the determination recorded in §6.1.1 stands.
