## 6.3 Integration Architecture

### 6.3.1 Applicability Determination

**Integration Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

`hao-backprop-test` requires no integration with any external system or service. Its entire executable surface is one 29-line CommonJS file, `server.js` (870 bytes, md5 `a423b6d4dc1c3156d7abc84f…`), which creates an Express 5.2.1 application, enables strict routing, registers two literal `GET` routes and listens on `127.0.0.1:3000`. The process opens no outbound connection, holds no credential, reads no configuration and speaks to no broker, queue, database or third-party API. The complete `require()` surface outside `node_modules/` is four calls — `require('express')` at `server.js:1` and `require('http')` at line 1 of each of the three native-`http` fixture scripts — and none of them can open a connection to another system.

What the system does have is exactly one interface that a second party crosses: an **inbound** plaintext HTTP/1.1 contract on the loopback adapter, consumed by a client that lives outside this repository. That interface is the whole of the system's integration surface, so it is documented here in §6.3.2 (design of the contract), §6.3.3 (the in-process events that drive it), §6.3.4 (the external systems that do not exist around it) and §6.3.5 (the required diagrams, drawn as boundary views). Every outbound integration category the section prompt names — third-party APIs, identity providers, message brokers, stream processors, batch platforms, API gateways, legacy interfaces, observability backends and cloud services — is **verified absent** with the source-level and runtime evidence recorded below.

This treatment mirrors the precedent set by §6.1 ("Core Services Architecture is not applicable for this system") and §6.2 ("Database Design is not applicable to this system").

| Required topic cluster | Determination | Documented in |
|-----------------------|---------------|---------------|
| API design — protocol, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, versioning, documentation standards | No external API is designed or published; the single inbound contract exists and is documented | §6.3.2 |
| Message processing — event patterns, queues, streams, batch flows, error strategy | Not applicable — no message processing surface of any kind; the only events are the in-process HTTP lifecycle events | §6.3.3 |
| External systems — third-party patterns, legacy interfaces, gateway, service contracts | Not applicable — no external service edge exists in either direction | §6.3.4 |
| Required diagrams — integration flow, API architecture, message flow, key-flow sequence | Supplied as boundary and null-topology views that mark the absent edges explicitly | §6.3.5 |

#### 6.3.1.1 Basis of the Determination

Six independently verified facts carry the verdict. Each is stated with the evidence it rests on, because the same reasoning recurs in the sub-sections that follow.

1. **No outbound client exists in code, in the manifest or in the installed tree.** `package.json:11-13` declares exactly one dependency, `express ^5.2.1`; the lockfile's root `""` entry mirrors that single declaration and its 66 non-root entries are the Express 5.2.1 closure (`router@2.2.0`, `finalhandler@2.1.1`, `send@1.2.1`, `serve-static@2.2.1`, `qs@6.15.2`, `cookie@0.7.2` and their transitive dependencies). No HTTP client, database driver, cache client, broker client, authentication library, limiter or observability agent appears in the lockfile. A 55-pattern scan of every tracked file for outbound-client, auth, rate-limit, queue, broker, streaming, gateway, versioning, API-documentation and telemetry terms (`fetch(`, `axios`, `http.request`, `axios`, `kafka`, `amqp`, `redis`, `jsonwebtoken`, `express-rate-limit`, `helmet`, `cors`, `swagger`, `openapi`, `process.env`, `prometheus`, `sentry` and the rest) returns **zero matches in application code**; the only occurrences anywhere in the repository are in the Blitzy prose artifacts under `blitzy/documentation/` and `Response.txt`.
2. **No handler performs any I/O.** Each route body is three synchronous statements using the low-level response API — set `res.statusCode`, set `Content-Type`, write a fixed literal with `res.end` (`server.js:15-17, 21-23`). Neither handler dereferences `req`: no header, path segment, query parameter, cookie or body is read, so no request-derived value could be forwarded to another system.
3. **No configuration or credential surface exists to parameterise an integration.** Host and port are `const` literals (`server.js:3-4`); there is no `process.env` read, no `.env` file, no configuration file, no command-line argument parsing, and no secret, token, client ID, issuer, endpoint or connection string anywhere in the 19 tracked files. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix E records the environment-variable inventory as `none`.
4. **Reachability is confined to one host, in one direction.** The listener binds the literal `'127.0.0.1'` (`server.js:3, 26`), so nothing off the machine can reach the service and the service cannot be fronted by a gateway, proxy or load balancer on another host. `README.md:12, 23` publishes the same loopback address to its consumers.
5. **No messaging, streaming, scheduling or batch construct exists.** There is no producer, consumer, topic, queue, stream processor, scheduler, worker thread or child process anywhere in the repository; no `EventEmitter` subscription is written in application code (`EventEmitter` appears zero times), and no `app.use` call exists, so no middleware — body parser, cookie parser, limiter, CORS handler or logger — is mounted on the request path.
6. **The two artifacts that look like integrations are not ones.** The three byte-identical native-`http` fixtures (`Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js` and the 170-character-named `…_server.js`, all md5 `05576d40ab8d9f141d1073f784b26e1b`) are never loaded by the service and bind the same exclusive loopback port; `phonenumber.csv` (621 bytes, header `message,phonenumber` plus 15 synthetic rows) is opened by no code path. Neither creates an edge to another system.

The system's only external touchpoints are therefore non-runtime ones: the public npm registry is contacted at install time to resolve and download the 66 pinned packages, and `README.md:6` hyperlinks the Express documentation site, which no code fetches. Both are catalogued in §3.4.

#### 6.3.1.2 The One Integration Interface That Exists

The system is a producer of responses to an inbound request, and that is the only boundary in the architecture. It is worth stating precisely, because it is the reason the API-design topics in §6.3.2 are documented rather than only dismissed: the contract has a defined shape, and a client outside the repository depends on it.

| Interface property | Value | Evidence |
|--------------------|-------|----------|
| Direction | Inbound only — the service is a producer, never a consumer | `server.js:14-24`; repository-wide scan |
| Transport and address | Plaintext HTTP/1.1 over TCP on `127.0.0.1:3000`, loopback only | `server.js:3-4, 26-28`; `README.md:23` |
| Contract published | Two `GET` paths documented with status, content type and body, plus the `404` rule for everything else | `README.md:9-12` |
| Consumer | An out-of-repository client: a shell `curl` call, a smoke test, or the "backprop" tooling named at `README.md:2` | `README.md:1-2, 18-21` |

Nothing in the repository defines that consumer, negotiates with it, authenticates it or meters it: there is no consumer contract, no SLA, no schema the client must satisfy, and no request validation on the server side. The interface is one-directional and stateless in both senses — the server keeps nothing between requests, and the client is expected to know the literal address and the two paths out of band.

#### 6.3.1.3 Repository Role Context

`README.md:1-2` states the project's purpose in two lines: `hao-backprop-test`, a "test project for backprop integration", served by an Express HTTP server. That phrasing names an external development context that consumes the repository as a fixture — it does **not** describe an integration the application performs. The distinction matters for this section: the repository is an artifact built to be read, installed, started and exercised, and a fixture of that kind needs a stable inbound contract rather than a topology. The one column-shaped data file in the tree, `phonenumber.csv`, is the clearest illustration of the fixture posture — it belongs to the surrounding test context and is referenced by no executable path.

The delivered scope reinforces the same reading. `blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2 excludes testing, linting, CI/CD, containerisation, authentication, TLS, configuration files, environment-variable support, logging libraries and persistence from the work, and `Response.txt` §0.5 extends the prohibition list to clustering, load balancing, health-check endpoints, metrics collection, database connections and HTTPS/TLS. No integration capability was deferred by oversight; each was ruled out in writing.

#### 6.3.1.4 Determinants That Would Otherwise Have Created an Integration Architecture

Each determinant through which an integration edge could have entered the design is closed in the tree, and the closure is visible rather than assumed.

| Determinant | State in this repository | Evidence |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| Outbound client and its dependency surface | None — no HTTP, broker, cache or database client in the manifest, the lockfile or any call site | `package.json:11-13`; `package-lock.json`; 55-pattern scan |
| Configuration and secret injection | Absent — `const` literals for host and port; no env var, config file, CLI argument or secret | `server.js:3-4`; Project Guide Appendix E |
| Deployment and network placement | One process on one host, loopback-bound; no image, manifest, proxy or ingress configuration is tracked | `server.js:26-28`; `git ls-files` |
| Inbound contract surface | Two literal `GET` paths with fixed bodies; no dynamic route, parameter, body parser or content negotiation | `server.js:12-24`; `README.md:9-12` |
| Observability of any integration | Absent — the process's total runtime output is one startup line on standard output | `server.js:27`; observed run |
| Planned hardening | F-101–F-106 improve error visibility and shutdown hygiene only, and explicitly forbid new routes, dependencies and TLS | `Response.txt` §0.4, §0.5, §0.7 |

#### 6.3.1.5 Conflict With the Repository's Earlier Verdict

The repository already carries a `## 6.3 Integration Architecture` of its own — `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` lines 3501-4030 — which reaches the same "not applicable" verdict, and the verdict is upheld here. Its reasoning, however, describes a state the repository has since left: that document characterises the system as a 15-line, route-agnostic native-`http` server with **zero** npm dependencies and an empty lockfile (its §6.3.1.1, §6.3.1.3). Five of its load-bearing claims are contradicted by the tree and the behaviour at HEAD, and the observed state governs this specification.

| Claim in the earlier §6.3 | Observed at HEAD |
|---------------------------|------------------|
| "Zero npm dependencies"; the lockfile holds only the root self-reference | `package.json:12` declares `express: "^5.2.1"`; the lockfile pins 66 non-root packages, and 66 are installed |
| "No API contract published"; the README is two lines | `README.md:9-12` documents both paths with status, content type and body plus the `404` rule; `server.js:14-24` registers two literal paths |
| "Method- and route-agnostic handler" that answers every request | Only `GET /` and `GET /good-evening` return content; `GET /unknown`, `POST /` and `GET /good-evening/` return `404`; `OPTIONS /` is answered `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` |
| An unhandled `clientError` produces a "connection-level crash" | A malformed request line is answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; the process survives and nothing is logged |
| A thrown handler exception crashes the process | The router catches a synchronous layer error and hands it to the terminal responder (`finalhandler@2.1.1`); no handler in this repository can throw |
| No framework identity on the wire | Every response carries `X-Powered-By: Express`, emitted because `application.js:94` enables the setting by default and nothing disables it |

What survives the re-platform is the substance of the verdict: the system still has no outbound edge, no peer, no store, no credential, no message processing and no gateway. What changes is the frame — the current service is a framework-hosted application with a registered, strict, case-insensitive route table and a published two-endpoint contract, and it is that contract, not a route-agnostic catch-all, that §6.3.2 documents.

#### 6.3.1.6 Conditions That Would Make This Section Applicable

The section becomes applicable when the repository gains an edge to something outside itself. The conditions are listed so that a reviewer can recognise one if it appears; none is implemented, requested or scheduled.

| Trigger | What it would require first | Sub-sections activated |
|---------|----------------------------|------------------------|
| An outbound dependency (API, database, cache, broker) | A client dependency, a credential or endpoint configuration, a timeout and retry policy, and a shutdown hook to release the connection | §6.3.3, §6.3.4 |
| A published or versioned API contract | A version prefix or negotiation scheme, a machine-readable description, and a compatibility policy | §6.3.2 |
| A second party's traffic across a trust boundary | Binding a non-loopback interface, a TLS terminator or gateway, and an access-control decision at that boundary | §6.3.2, §6.3.4 |
| Asynchronous or scheduled work | A broker or scheduler client plus producer/consumer code, error routing and dead-letter handling | §6.3.3 |
| Observability consumed outside the process | A metrics, tracing or log-shipping agent and a health or readiness surface | §6.3.4 |

Until one of those exists, the determination recorded here stands: the system integrates with nothing, and the only interface to document is the one it serves.


### 6.3.2 API Design

There is no designed, published, versioned API for another system to integrate against — no OpenAPI document, no version scheme, no authentication scheme, no limiter and no gateway sits in front of the service. There is, however, a real inbound contract with a fixed shape that an out-of-repository client depends on, and this sub-section documents it and then disposes of each API-design topic the section prompt names.

#### 6.3.2.1 Protocol Specification

The wire protocol is plaintext HTTP/1.1 over a TCP connection accepted on the loopback adapter. There is no TLS, no HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 negotiation, no ALPN, no compression and no content negotiation: the Node.js HTTP stack parses the request line and headers into `IncomingMessage`, Express dispatches it through `app.handle`, and the handler writes a fixed body with the low-level response API (`server.js:14-24`).

| Protocol attribute | Specification | Evidence |
|--------------------|---------------|----------|
| Transport | HTTP/1.1 over TCP; plaintext, no TLS terminator or certificate | `server.js:26`; observed probe; §3.4 |
| Listener | `127.0.0.1:3000`, literal values, one socket | `server.js:3-4, 26-28` |
| Methods served | `GET` registered; `HEAD` aliased to the `GET` layer; `OPTIONS` answered by the router; other methods fall through to `404` | `server.js:14, 20`; observed `HEAD /`, `OPTIONS /`, `POST /` |
| Path matching | Strict routing — a trailing slash is a distinct path; case-insensitive by default | `server.js:12`; `application.js:75-76`; observed `GET /good-evening/` → `404`, `GET /Good-Evening` → `200` |
| Request input consumed | None — no body parser is mounted, the query string is never read, and neither handler dereferences `req` | no `app.use` call exists; `server.js:14-24` |
| Connection behaviour | Keep-alive with a 5 s idle timeout; runtime-default 60 s header and 300 s request timeouts | observed `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; §6.1.2.4 |
| Caching headers | None emitted — `res.end` bypasses the response helpers, so no `ETag`, `Cache-Control`, `Last-Modified` or `Vary` is produced even though `etag: 'weak'` is configured by default | observed headers; `application.js:95` |

Two framework behaviours complete the protocol contract. Every response carries `X-Powered-By: Express`, because the default configuration enables it and nothing in the application disables it (`application.js:94, 160`); and any unmatched method or path is answered by the terminal responder `finalhandler@2.1.1`, which synthesises an HTML document with `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (`finalhandler/index.js:107, 267-268`).

#### 6.3.2.2 Inbound API Surface

The registered surface is the whole API. The remaining rows are framework-generated outcomes, included because a client observes them.

| Route | Status | Content-Type | Body |
|-------|--------|--------------|------|
| `GET /` | `200 OK` | `text/plain` | `Hello, World!` followed by a newline (14 bytes) |
| `GET /good-evening` | `200 OK` | `text/plain` | `Good evening`, no trailing newline (12 bytes) |
| `HEAD /` | `200 OK` | `text/plain` | None — headers only, no body |
| `OPTIONS /` | `200 OK` | `text/plain` | `GET, HEAD`, with an `Allow` header of the same value (9 bytes) |
| Any other path or method | `404 Not Found` | `text/html; charset=utf-8` | HTML document containing `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` |

Contract details a consumer must honour, all verified over loopback: the two bodies differ in a trailing newline, which makes them distinct byte sequences; `GET /good-evening/` returns `404` rather than the greeting, so callers must use the exact path; the client address is the literal loopback address, so the consumer must run on the same host; and a `200` carries no caching or validation header, so a client cannot revalidate a response.

#### 6.3.2.3 Authentication Methods

No authentication mechanism exists at any layer, and none is reachable by configuration: no middleware is mounted, so there is no pipeline stage in which credentials could be inspected, and no authentication library appears in the 66-package dependency tree.

| Mechanism | Disposition | Evidence |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| HTTP Basic, Digest or Bearer | Absent — no header inspection of any kind | observed probe; `server.js:14-24` |
| API key or custom token header | Absent — no key literal, no comparison in code | repository-wide scan; §6.3.1.1 |
| Session cookie or signed cookie | Absent — `cookie@0.7.2` and `cookie-signature@1.2.2` are present only as Express transitives; no handler reads or writes a cookie | `package-lock.json`; observed absence of `Set-Cookie` |
| Mutual TLS or client certificate | Not possible as bound — the listener is a plaintext loopback socket with no TLS layer | `server.js:26`; §3.4 |
| OAuth 2.0, OIDC or SAML | Absent — no identity library, no issuer, client ID or callback URL in any file | `package-lock.json`; repository-wide scan |

A request carrying `Authorization: Bearer x`, `Cookie: session=abc; user=1` and `X-Api-Key: k` returns exactly the same `200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14` and `Hello, World!\n` body as an anonymous request, confirming that the identity-bearing headers do not influence execution or appear in any output. The only access control in force is the operating system's: any local process may connect, and nothing off the host can.

#### 6.3.2.4 Authorization Framework

There is no authorization decision to make and no framework in which to make it: no role or permission model, no attribute source, no access-control list, no policy engine dependency, no route guard and no per-route restriction. Both routes are registered on the same application with identical handling, and the handlers perform the same three statements regardless of who calls them (`server.js:14-24`). Because no caller identity is established (§6.3.2.3) and no resource is owned by anyone, the concepts an authorization framework expresses — subject, resource, action, decision — have no counterpart in the system. The network boundary documented in §6.3.2.3 remains the only control.

#### 6.3.2.5 Rate Limiting Strategy

No rate limiting, throttling, quota or surge protection exists. There is no limiter package in the dependency tree, no middleware through which a limiter could run (no `app.use` call exists), no counter store for a distributed limit to share, and no `maxConnections`, backlog or timeout setting in application code.

| Limiting concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|------------------|-------------|----------|
| Per-client or per-key limits | Absent — client identity is neither read nor retained | `server.js:14-24`; observed probe |
| Token-bucket, leaky-bucket or fixed window | Absent — no limiter implementation or library | `package-lock.json`; repository-wide scan |
| Concurrency or connection cap | Absent — the listener accepts until host resources are exhausted | `server.js:26-28`; §6.1.3.2 |
| Back-pressure or queueing | Absent — requests are served synchronously on the event loop with no admission control | `server.js:14-24`; §6.1.3.4 |

The practical ceiling is therefore the runtime's, not a policy's: one event loop serves every accepted connection. Measured at HEAD, one process absorbed 2,000 requests at 100-way client parallelism in 1.718 s with zero errors, and 200 simultaneously held sockets each received `200 OK` (§6.1.3.4).

#### 6.3.2.6 Versioning Approach

No versioning scheme is applied to the interface: no `/v1/` prefix on either path, no version header on requests or responses, no media-type or `Accept`-based negotiation, no deprecation policy, no sunset header and no compatibility guarantee published anywhere. `Content-Type` is the fixed literal `text/plain` (no `charset`, no vendor media type), so a client cannot request an alternative representation.

| Versioning mechanism | Disposition | Evidence |
|----------------------|-------------|----------|
| URI-path version prefix | Absent — both registered paths are unversioned literals | `server.js:14, 20` |
| Header or media-type versioning | Absent — no request header is read, and response headers are fixed | observed headers; `server.js:15-17, 21-23` |
| Release version exposed at runtime | Absent — `"version": "1.0.0"` in `package.json:3` is never asserted in a response, header or log line | `package.json`; observed run |
| Deprecation or compatibility policy | None published — `README.md:9-12` states the current contract only | `README.md` |

The only wire-visible version identity is the framework's own `X-Powered-By: Express`, which names the framework and not the release. Contract evolution is therefore managed out of band, through source edits and Git history — 11 commits to HEAD `fdeac01`, of which `0fdbfb6` (re-platform onto Express with the `/good-evening` route) is the one change to the interface. That change was backward compatible for `GET /`, whose body was preserved byte-exact, but not for unmatched paths, which moved from the previous catch-all greeting to `404 Not Found`; the repository records this as a deliberate behavioural consequence of introducing explicit routing (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.4.2).

#### 6.3.2.7 Documentation Standards

`README.md` is the only document that describes the interface, and it does so in hand-written Markdown: the **HTTP Server** section names the framework and dependency, lists both endpoints with status, content type and body, and states that any other path returns `404 Not Found`; the **Running** section gives the install and start commands and the loopback address (`README.md:4-23`).

| Documentation artifact | Disposition | Evidence |
|------------------------|-------------|----------|
| OpenAPI / Swagger description | Absent — no `openapi.yaml`, `swagger.json` or equivalent descriptor | repository-wide scan |
| AsyncAPI, RAML, API Blueprint or GraphQL SDL | Absent — no descriptor and no asynchronous or GraphQL surface exists | repository-wide scan; §6.3.3 |
| Generated API reference | Absent — no documentation generator, no doc script in `package.json#scripts` | `package.json:6-8` |
| Inline API documentation | Only explanatory prose comments (for example the strict-routing note at `server.js:8-11`); no JSDoc/TSDoc tags, since the file exposes no callable interface | `server.js`; repository-wide scan |

What a consumer gets instead of a machine-readable contract is the README plus the route table itself. Neither the manifest nor the lockfile publishes repository, homepage or bug-tracker metadata, and no contract test exists to hold the documented shape in place: the `test` script is the unmodified `npm init` placeholder, `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1` (`package.json:7`), and the README's own smoke steps — `curl` against the two paths and an unregistered path — are the verification of record (`README.md:18-23`).


### 6.3.3 Message Processing

The system processes no messages. There is no producer, no consumer, no topic, no queue, no stream and no batch job anywhere in the repository, and no asynchronous surface of any kind is exposed to a client. What does exist is an event-driven runtime: the Node.js HTTP server emits lifecycle events, Express registers a request listener on it, and those events are the only ones the application participates in. This sub-section documents that in-process event model, then records each message-processing area the section prompt names as verified absent, together with the failure behaviour that stands in for an integration error-handling strategy.

#### 6.3.3.1 Event Processing Patterns

The application subscribes to two runtime events and no others. `app.listen` calls `http.createServer(this)` and passes the Express application as the `'request'` listener (`application.js:598-599`), so every accepted request is dispatched to `app.handle` and then through the two-entry route table. The callback supplied at `server.js:27` receives the `'listening'` event and writes the startup banner; `app.listen` wraps that same callback with `once()` before registering it, which makes it serve double duty as the server's one-shot `'error'` listener (`application.js:602-603`).

| Event or signal | Source | Subscribed in this repository? | Outcome on emission |
|-----------------|--------|-------------------------------|---------------------|
| `'request'` | `http.Server` via `app.listen` | Yes — the application is the listener | Request dispatched through the route table; a fixed response is written |
| `'listening'` | `http.Server` | Yes — the `server.js:27` callback | One banner line on standard output: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` |
| `'error'` | `http.Server` | Only implicitly, as the one-shot listener `app.listen` registers | A failed bind runs the success-logging callback: the banner is printed, the error is discarded, and the process exits `0` |
| `'clientError'` | `http.Server` | No — runtime default applies | Malformed bytes are answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; the process survives and nothing is logged |
| `'close'` | `http.Server` | No — `server.close()` is never called | Never reached; `server.js:26` discards the handle returned by `app.listen` |
| `SIGTERM` | `process` | No | Immediate exit `143`; in-flight responses dropped, no drain, no cleanup |
| `SIGINT` | `process` | No | Immediate exit `130`; same absence of drain and cleanup |
| `'uncaughtException'`, `'unhandledRejection'` | `process` | No | No listener exists; nothing is intercepted |

Two consequences follow, both verified on this checkout. First, a bind failure is indistinguishable from a healthy short run to anything that reads only the exit status and standard output: a second instance launched against the held port printed `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` and exited `0` with no diagnostic on either stream, while the first instance kept serving `200 OK`. Second, no application code emits or listens for domain events: there is no event bus, no publish/subscribe call, no webhook dispatch, no custom `EventEmitter` and no callback registration outside the two above. The application has no `module.exports`, so no second module could subscribe to anything either.

#### 6.3.3.2 Message Queue Architecture

No message queue, broker or event bus is integrated, and none can be without adding a dependency the project does not have. There is no broker client package (`kafka`, `amqp`, `rabbit`, `nats`, `mqtt`, `sqs`, `bull`, `agenda` — zero occurrences across all tracked files and none in the lockfile), no topic or exchange naming, no producer or consumer code, no dead-letter destination and no delivery guarantee to state.

| Queue concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| Broker or event bus integration | Absent — no client library and no connection configuration | `package-lock.json`; repository-wide scan |
| Producer or consumer implementation | Absent — no publish, subscribe, emit or poll call exists | `server.js`; repository-wide scan |
| Topic, exchange, partition or consumer group | Absent — no naming, no offsets, no ordering rule | repository-wide scan |
| Delivery semantics, redelivery, dead-lettering | Not applicable — no message is ever enqueued | §6.3.3.5 |

The only queue-like structure in the running system is the operating system's accept backlog for the single listening socket, which the application neither sizes, monitors nor drains; it is a kernel facility, not an application queue, and it disappears the moment the socket closes.

#### 6.3.3.3 Stream Processing Design

No stream processing exists. The application never imports the Node.js `stream` module, never pipes, never writes incrementally and never holds a long-lived response: each handler calls `res.end` with a fixed string, so every response is a single fixed-length write (14 bytes, 12 bytes, or 9 bytes for the router's `OPTIONS` body). There is no Server-Sent Events endpoint, no `text/event-stream` content type, no WebSocket upgrade, no chunked transfer encoding observed, and no long-polling behaviour.

| Stream concept | Disposition | Evidence |
|----------------|-------------|----------|
| Stream processor (Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming) | Absent — no client library or runtime | `package-lock.json`; repository-wide scan |
| Node.js `stream` use, pipes or incremental writes | Absent — one `res.end` per response with a fixed body | `server.js:14-24`; observed `Content-Length` values |
| Server-Sent Events or WebSocket surface | Absent — no route, no upgrade handling, no protocol library | repository-wide scan; route table holds two `GET` paths |
| Windowing, watermarks, checkpoints, back-pressure | Not applicable — no unbounded data flow exists | §6.3.3.2 |

The nearest behaviour to streaming the framework provides — `send` and `serve-static` in the dependency closure, which can stream a file body — is unreachable here, because no static file is served and no handler uses a response helper.

#### 6.3.3.4 Batch Processing Flows

No batch surface exists. There is no scheduler, no cron entry, no worker thread, no child process and no background job, and the interface offers no way to submit work in bulk: the request body is never read, so a `POST` with a payload is refused with `404` by the router before any handler sees it. Each request is handled synchronously as its own response on the event loop.

| Batch concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| Scheduled jobs (cron, `node-cron`, Agenda, Bull) | Absent — no scheduler dependency and no timer construct in application code | `package-lock.json`; `server.js` |
| Worker threads, child processes or clustering | Absent — one process, one event loop, seven runtime threads | `server.js`; §6.1.3.2 |
| Bulk or multi-record endpoints | Absent — no `POST` layer is registered and no request body is parsed | `server.js:14-24`; observed `POST /` → `404` |
| File-driven intake or ETL | Absent — no file is opened at runtime; `phonenumber.csv` is unreferenced by code | §6.2.2.1 |

The repository's own hardening plan keeps it that way: the proposed features F-101–F-106 add error visibility and shutdown hygiene only, and they forbid new routes, new dependencies and asynchronous machinery (`Response.txt` §0.5).

#### 6.3.3.5 Error Handling Strategy

Because nothing is enqueued, published, streamed or fetched, the conventional integration-error primitives have no subject. There is no outbound call to retry, no slow dependency to circuit-break, no message to dead-letter, no mutation to make idempotent, no alternative response path to fall back to, and no notification channel — no webhook, e-mail, alert or error-tracking client exists, and no error is logged anywhere.

| Integration-error primitive | Disposition | Evidence |
|-----------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Retry, back-off, timeout policy | Absent — no outbound call exists to retry or time out | `server.js:14-24`; repository-wide scan |
| Circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate guard | Absent — no downstream dependency to isolate | §6.3.2.5; §6.1.2.5 |
| Dead-letter queue or poison-message handling | Not applicable — no message processing | §6.3.3.2 |
| Fallback or degraded response path | Absent — one response path per route; the only outcomes are the two literals, `404`, or a framework `500` | `server.js:14-24`; `finalhandler@2.1.1` |
| Error notification, logging or error tracking | Absent — a full run writes one line, the startup banner | `server.js:27`; observed run |

What replaces that strategy is the runtime's default handling of each failure class, all observed at HEAD:

| Failure class | Mechanism in force | Observable outcome |
|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Unregistered path, method or trailing-slash variant | Router falls through to `finalhandler@2.1.1` | `404 Not Found` with an HTML `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` document; nothing logged |
| Malformed HTTP request bytes | Node.js HTTP parser default path | `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; process survives; nothing logged |
| Exception thrown inside a route layer | Router error path into `finalhandler` | `500` HTML plus a stack on standard error; unreachable today, since no handler can throw |
| Port already in use at startup | One-shot `'error'` listener registered by `app.listen` | Banner printed, error discarded, exit `0` — a false success with no diagnostic |
| `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` | Runtime default disposition; no handler registered | Exit `143` or `130` with no drain and no cleanup hook |
| `node_modules/` missing or corrupt | `require('express')` at `server.js:1` throws | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on standard error, exit `1`, no banner |

The integration-relevant reading of this table is that the system neither degrades nor compensates: it answers correctly, refuses, or stops. A client integrating against it receives no retry hint, no error code beyond the HTTP status, and no diagnostic it could act on, and an operator watching standard output learns nothing about failures — including the bind failure that most resembles a successful start.


### 6.3.4 External Systems

No external system is integrated with this application, in either direction. The service calls nothing and nothing calls it from off the host: no outbound request is made by any code path, no third-party service is contacted at runtime, and the only non-runtime touchpoints are the npm registry consulted at install time and the Express documentation hyperlink in `README.md:6`, which no code fetches. §3.4 inventories those absences by service category; this sub-section documents the integration **patterns**, interfaces and contracts the section prompt names, and closes with the repository artifacts that most resemble an integration without being one.

#### 6.3.4.1 Third-Party Integration Patterns

No third-party integration pattern is implemented — not an outbound call, not an inbound callback, not a scheduled exchange, not a sidecar. Every integration category the section prompt implies is verified absent against the same evidence: the dependency tree holds 66 packages, all of them Express internals, and a 55-pattern scan of every tracked file finds no client, credential, endpoint or protocol library in application code.

| Integration category | Disposition | Evidence |
|----------------------|-------------|----------|
| External REST, GraphQL or gRPC APIs | Absent — no HTTP client package and no call site | `package-lock.json`; repository-wide scan |
| Identity providers (OAuth, OIDC, SAML, Auth0) | Absent — no auth library, no issuer or client ID in any file | §6.3.2.3; §3.4.1 |
| Message brokers and queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub) | Absent — no broker client; no publish or subscribe call | §6.3.3.2; §3.4.1 |
| E-mail, SMS or payment providers | Absent — no such dependency and no call site; the only contact-like data is the unread `phonenumber.csv` | §6.3.4.6 |
| CDN, edge or asset providers | Absent — the service ships no static asset and no cache header | `server.js:14-24`; §3.4.1 |
| Webhook senders or receivers | Absent — no inbound callback route and no outbound notification | route table holds two `GET` paths; §6.3.3.5 |
| Cloud-service SDKs (AWS, GCP, Azure) | Absent — no SDK in the tree, no credential, region or endpoint setting | `package-lock.json`; §3.4.1 |
| Error tracking or feature-flag services | Absent — no agent dependency and no instrumentation import | repository-wide scan; §3.4.3 |

The pattern the system uses in place of any integration is a compile-time literal: each handler writes its own body and returns, performs no I/O beyond the socket write, and derives nothing from the request. The framework's dependency closure does supply primitives that would normally belong to an integration layer — `cookie@0.7.2` and `cookie-signature@1.2.2` for cookie handling, `qs@6.15.2` for query parsing, `proxy-addr@2.0.7` for client-address resolution, `etag@1.8.1` and `fresh@2.0.0` for validation — but none of them executes on the request path here: no middleware is mounted, so the request is never parsed, and `proxy-addr` is inert because `trust proxy` defaults to `false` (`application.js:99`).

#### 6.3.4.2 Legacy System Interfaces

No interface of any era exists, legacy or modern. There is no SOAP or XML-RPC client, no flat-file exchange, no FTP/SFTP/SCP job, no mainframe or message-broker bridge, no database link or stored-procedure callout, and no adapter module — the repository contains no `.yml`, `.yaml`, `.xml`, `.sql`, `.ini`, `.conf` or `.sh` file at all, so no bridge configuration could be lurking in one.

| Legacy-interface category | Disposition | Evidence |
|---------------------------|-------------|----------|
| SOAP, XML-RPC or CORBA clients | Absent — no protocol library and no descriptor | repository-wide scan; `package-lock.json` |
| Flat-file or file-drop exchange (FTP, SFTP, SCP) | Absent — no transport library, no watched directory, no file read | `server.js`; §6.2.2.1 |
| Mainframe, MQ or EDI bridging adapters | Absent — no broker client and no adapter module | §6.3.3.2; `git ls-files` |
| Stored procedures, DB links or driver callouts | Absent — no driver in the tree and no connection string in any file | `package-lock.json`; §6.2.1.1 |

The three native-`http` scripts at the repository root (`Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js` and the 170-character-named `…_server.js`) are the closest thing to a second interface in the tree, and they are not one: the service never loads them, they bind the same exclusive loopback port, and they answer any method and any path with `Hello, World!\n` and no `X-Powered-By` header, so they neither extend nor interoperate with the registered contract of §6.3.2.2.

#### 6.3.4.3 API Gateway Configuration

There is no API gateway, reverse proxy, ingress controller, sidecar or TLS terminator associated with the service, and no configuration file in which one could be described. The loopback binding removes the architectural surface a gateway needs: an edge component can only front a listener that remote traffic can reach, and `server.js:3` fixes the address to `'127.0.0.1'`.

| Gateway or proxy concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|--------------------------|-------------|----------|
| API gateway (Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway) | Absent — no configuration, no credential, no published route definition | `git ls-files`; §6.3.2.7 |
| Reverse proxy or TLS terminator (NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy) | Absent — loopback bind precludes an upstream proxy, and no certificate exists | `server.js:3, 26`; §3.4.1 |
| Ingress controller or service-mesh sidecar | Absent — no orchestrator manifest, no mesh dependency, one process | `server.js`; §6.1.2 |
| Edge concerns the gateway would own (rate limiting, auth, routing rules) | Unimplemented at every tier — no limiter, no authentication, two literal routes | §6.3.2.3; §6.3.2.5 |

Introducing a gateway would therefore be a scope change rather than a configuration change: it would require binding a reachable interface, publishing a route definition, and deciding an access-control policy at the new boundary. The repository's own deferred-enhancement list records the prerequisite first — parameterising host and port through environment variables — as unimplemented work outside the delivered scope (`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3). Until then the two endpoints are reachable only from the host that runs the process, and the only metadata a caller learns about the implementation is the framework's `X-Powered-By: Express` header, whose suppression is likewise recorded as a deferred enhancement.

#### 6.3.4.4 External Service Contracts

There is no external service contract in either direction: no upstream consumer has a negotiated agreement, no downstream provider is invoked, and no machine-readable interface description exists for a third party to build against. The one contract that does exist is internal to the repository's own test context — the two-endpoint inbound contract published in `README.md:9-12` and enforced by the route table.

| Contract element | Disposition | Evidence |
|------------------|-------------|----------|
| Upstream consumer agreement (SLA, SLO, support terms) | None — no consumer contract is published, and the only consumer is out-of-repository tooling named by `README.md:2` | `README.md`; §6.3.1.2 |
| Downstream provider agreement | None — no downstream service is called | `server.js`; §6.3.4.1 |
| Schema registry or formal message contract (Avro, Protobuf, JSON Schema) | Absent — no schema file, no serialised payload type; the bodies are plain text literals | `server.js:14-24` |
| Contract testing or consumer-driven verification | Absent — no test runner is configured and the `test` script is the `npm init` placeholder that always fails | `package.json:6-8` |

Nor is there a performance commitment attached to the interface. The repository defines no latency objective, throughput target, availability figure or error budget, and the figures that circulate in its remediation note — under 50 ms per request, under 50 MB resident, 100 or more concurrent connections — were written for the superseded native-`http` variant and are not commitments of this build (§6.1.3.4). Measured at HEAD, the interface is fast but unbounded in any contractual sense: 2,000 requests at 100-way client parallelism completed in 1.718 s from one process, with no admission control limiting what arrives next.

#### 6.3.4.5 Observability Backends and Cloud Services

No observability backend and no cloud service is integrated. The process's total runtime output is the single startup line at `server.js:27`, which no collector consumes, and the only metadata it emits over the wire is the framework header `X-Powered-By: Express`.

| Backend category | Disposition | Evidence |
|------------------|-------------|----------|
| APM and distributed tracing (Datadog, New Relic, OpenTelemetry, X-Ray) | Absent — no agent dependency, no instrumentation import, no exporter configuration | `package-lock.json`; repository-wide scan |
| Log aggregation or shipping (Splunk, ELK, Datadog Logs) | Absent — `console.log` writes to standard output and no destination is configured | `server.js:27`; §3.4.3 |
| Metrics platforms and health probes (Prometheus, StatsD, `/health`, `/ready`) | Absent — no metric is emitted and no health route is registered | `server.js:12-24`; §6.1.4.1 |
| Cloud compute, storage or managed databases (AWS, GCP, Azure) | Absent — no SDK, no credential, no region or endpoint setting, no infrastructure template | `package-lock.json`; `git ls-files` |

Nothing in the system is deployable to a cloud platform as it stands: there is no container image, orchestration manifest, environment file or pipeline in the tree, and the loopback binding would have to change before a platform could route traffic to it. The one readiness signal available to an operator is the startup banner, and §6.3.3.1 records the caveat that a bind failure prints it too.

#### 6.3.4.6 Artifacts That Resemble Integrations

Several tracked artifacts share a vocabulary with integration work — a data fixture that looks like an SMS feed, scripts that look like alternate servers, a remediation transcript about production hardening — and none of them is an interface. Recording why each is not keeps the boundary of this section unambiguous.

| Artifact | What it resembles | Why it is not an integration |
|----------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| `phonenumber.csv` | An SMS or messaging provider extract — header `message,phonenumber` plus 15 rows of synthetic `+111111112xx` numbers | No code path opens or parses it; it is a fixture for the surrounding test context, referenced only in prose |
| `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, `…_server.js` | Alternate server entry points | Never loaded by the service; byte-identical to each other (md5 `05576d40ab8d9f141d1073f784b26e1b`), they bind the same exclusive port and answer a different contract, so they are neither peers nor fallbacks |
| `Response.txt` | A production-readiness specification, including a graceful-shutdown design and performance targets | A remediation transcript for the superseded native-`http` server; its features F-101–F-106 are unimplemented, and its scope rules forbid the framework, TLS and route changes already delivered |
| `codebase_context (42).md` | A requirement naming an integration endpoint (`/hello`) | A 133-character note that no longer matches the delivered routes; no code or consumer implements it |
| `tech_spec.pdf`, `defect_for_task_1.docx`, `s1.png`, `20250304165759.mp4` | Project deliverables | Unreferenced by any code path: the PDF is a documentation specification for a different, TypeScript-based server project (created 2025-11-25), and the DOCX holds 111 characters of unrelated defect text |

Taken together, the disposition of this sub-section is that the system has one interface — inbound, plaintext, loopback, unauthenticated and unversioned — and no counterpart system at all. Every capability that would create one is either absent from the tree or ruled out in writing by the repository's own scope decisions (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2; `Response.txt` §0.5).


### 6.3.5 Required Integration Diagrams

The section prompt requires integration flow, API architecture and message flow diagrams, plus sequence diagrams for key flows. Because the system has no external integration, the first three are drawn as **boundary and null-topology views**: each shows the boundary that contains the whole system, the one edge that carries traffic, and the absent edges marked explicitly, so a reader sees which connections do not exist rather than an empty frame. The sequence diagrams record the two flows a client can actually drive, and the refusal path that answers everything else. The style follows §6.1.5 and §6.2.6.

#### 6.3.5.1 Integration Flow Diagram

The only live edge crosses one boundary — out of the client process, into the loopback listener, and back. Every other edge is absent: there is no peer service, no downstream dependency, no platform service and no second instance. Dashed edges terminate on the named category that does not exist, not on a placeholder.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client["Loopback HTTP client<br/>curl, smoke test, local tooling"]

    subgraph Host["Single host"]
        subgraph Proc["Single Node.js process, started as node server.js"]
            Listener["Loopback listener<br/>Node http.Server on 127.0.0.1:3000"]
            App["Express 5.2.1 application<br/>server.js: two literals, strict routing"]
            RouterNode["Route dispatch<br/>router 2.2.0, two literal GET layers"]
            Handlers["Greeting handlers<br/>200 text/plain, 14 B and 12 B"]
            Terminal["Terminal responder<br/>finalhandler 2.1.1, 404 and 500"]
        end
        Stdout["Standard output<br/>one startup line, no per-request log"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentEdges["Integration edges that do not exist"]
        NoApi["No outbound REST, GraphQL or gRPC client"]
        NoIdentity["No identity provider<br/>OAuth, OIDC, SAML, API keys"]
        NoBroker["No broker, queue or event bus"]
        NoStore["No database, cache or session store"]
        NoGateway["No gateway, proxy, ingress or mesh"]
        NoObservability["No APM, metrics, tracing or log shipping"]
        NoCloud["No cloud-service SDK or credential"]
    end

    Client -->|"HTTP/1.1 plaintext, keep-alive"| Listener
    Listener -->|"request event"| App
    App --> RouterNode
    RouterNode -->|"literal path matched"| Handlers
    RouterNode -->|"nothing matched"| Terminal
    Handlers -->|"response bytes"| Listener
    Terminal -->|"404 or 500 document"| Listener
    Listener -->|"response"| Client
    App -->|"banner on bind"| Stdout
    App -.->|"no outbound call in any code path"| NoApi
    App -.->|"no credential is read or held"| NoIdentity
    Handlers -.->|"no publish or subscribe call"| NoBroker
    Handlers -.->|"no read, no write"| NoStore
    Listener -.->|"loopback bind precludes an upstream"| NoGateway
    App -.->|"no agent is installed"| NoObservability
    App -.->|"no SDK and no region setting"| NoCloud
```

#### 6.3.5.2 API Architecture Diagram

The upper path is the implemented request path: parser, dispatch, literal match, three-statement handler or terminal refusal. The lower band names the layers that a populated API architecture would hold in front of it and that no call in this repository mounts — the reason every API-design topic in §6.3.2 resolves to absent while the contract itself remains real and published.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Caller["Loopback client on the same host"]

    subgraph Contract["Published inbound contract (README.md:9-12)"]
        RespRoot["GET / : 200 text/plain<br/>Hello, World! with newline, 14 B"]
        RespEvening["GET /good-evening : 200 text/plain<br/>Good evening, 12 B"]
        Resp404["Any other path or method : 404<br/>HTML Cannot METHOD path"]
    end

    subgraph Stack["Implemented request path"]
        Parser["Node HTTP parser<br/>request line and headers"]
        Handle["app.handle<br/>Express dispatch"]
        RouterNode["router 2.2.0<br/>strict and case-insensitive match"]
        HandlerNode["Literal handler<br/>statusCode, setHeader, end"]
        Final["finalhandler 2.1.1<br/>default 404 and 500"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentLayers["Layers that exist nowhere in this deployment"]
        NoAuthn["No authentication layer"]
        NoAuthz["No authorization layer"]
        NoLimiter["No rate limiter or quota"]
        NoVersioning["No version negotiation"]
        NoMiddleware["No body parser, CORS or logger middleware"]
    end

    Caller -->|"HTTP/1.1 request"| Parser
    Parser --> Handle
    Handle --> RouterNode
    RouterNode -->|"GET / or GET /good-evening"| HandlerNode
    RouterNode -->|"no layer matched"| Final
    HandlerNode --> RespRoot
    HandlerNode --> RespEvening
    Final --> Resp404
    RespRoot -->|"200 with Content-Length 14"| Caller
    RespEvening -->|"200 with Content-Length 12"| Caller
    Resp404 -->|"404 with CSP and nosniff headers"| Caller
    Parser -.->|"credential headers are never read"| NoAuthn
    RouterNode -.->|"no guard is registered"| NoAuthz
    Handle -.->|"no limiter is mounted"| NoLimiter
    RouterNode -.->|"both paths are unversioned literals"| NoVersioning
    Parser -.->|"no app.use call exists"| NoMiddleware
```

#### 6.3.5.3 Message Flow Diagram

This diagram follows the events the process actually emits, from bind to response, and shows what happens when each event has no handling code — a held port that reports success, and an accepted request that leaves no trace. The dashed band is the messaging tier that does not exist: nothing in the flow reaches a producer, a queue or a consumer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    StartNode(["Process start: node server.js"]) --> BindNode{"Loopback socket binds on 127.0.0.1:3000?"}
    BindNode -->|"bound"| ListeningEvent["listening event fires<br/>banner printed to standard output"]
    BindNode -->|"port already held"| FalseSuccess["One-shot error listener registered by app.listen<br/>consumes EADDRINUSE"]
    ListeningEvent --> RequestEvent["request event fires<br/>the application is the listener"]
    RequestEvent --> Dispatch["app.handle dispatch"]
    Dispatch --> MatchNode{"Literal path matched?"}
    MatchNode -->|"GET / or GET /good-evening"| HandlerMsg["Handler writes a fixed literal<br/>statusCode, Content-Type, res.end"]
    MatchNode -->|"anything else"| RefuseMsg["finalhandler refusal<br/>404 HTML, nothing logged"]
    HandlerMsg --> ResponseBytes["Fixed-length response bytes on the accepted socket"]
    RefuseMsg --> ResponseBytes
    ResponseBytes --> ShutdownPath(["No drain, no cleanup hook and no graceful shutdown exist"])
    FalseSuccess --> ManualPath["Banner printed, error discarded, exit 0"]
    ManualPath --> OperatorRecovery["Operator frees the port and re-runs the process"]
    ShutdownPath --> OperatorRecovery

    subgraph AbsentMessaging["Messaging tier that does not exist"]
        NoProducer["No producer or publisher"]
        NoQueueNode["No queue, topic or consumer group"]
        NoDeadLetter["No dead-letter destination or redelivery"]
        NoStreamNode["No stream, SSE or WebSocket surface"]
        NoBatchNode["No scheduler, worker thread or batch job"]
        NoNotification["No webhook, e-mail or alert egress"]
    end

    HandlerMsg -.->|"no publish call exists"| NoProducer
    NoProducer -.-> NoQueueNode
    NoQueueNode -.-> NoDeadLetter
    HandlerMsg -.->|"one response per request"| NoStreamNode
    HandlerMsg -.->|"synchronous handling only"| NoBatchNode
    RefuseMsg -.->|"no alert is raised"| NoNotification
```

#### 6.3.5.4 Sequence Diagrams for the Key Flows

Two flows can occur, and both are shown. The first is the successful request a client drives against either registered path; the second covers the refusal path and the failure behaviour that stands in for error handling. In both, the notes mark the checkpoints a conventional integration would place — authentication, authorization, rate limiting, versioning, error routing — none of which exists.

**Key flow 1 — a registered route is served**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Loopback HTTP client
    participant Socket as TCP socket on 127.0.0.1:3000
    participant Parser as Node HTTP parser
    participant App as Express application (server.js)
    participant RouterNode as router 2.2.0
    participant Handler as Literal handler

    Client->>Socket: TCP connect, plaintext, no TLS handshake
    Client->>Parser: GET /good-evening HTTP/1.1
    Parser->>App: request event with IncomingMessage
    Note over App: No credential header is read. No authorization,<br/>rate-limit or version check runs. The body is never parsed.
    App->>RouterNode: dispatch with method and path
    RouterNode->>RouterNode: strict, case-insensitive literal match
    RouterNode->>Handler: matched layer for /good-evening
    Handler->>Handler: res.statusCode = 200
    Handler->>Handler: res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')
    Handler->>Handler: res.end('Good evening')
    Handler-->>Client: HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Content-Type text/plain, Content-Length 12
    Note over Client,Socket: The response carries X-Powered-By: Express<br/>and no caching or validation header.
```

**Key flow 2 — an unmatched request is refused, and a malformed one is rejected</**> — the only two outcomes left once no route matches, and both end without logging, notification or retry.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Loopback HTTP client
    participant RouterNode as router 2.2.0
    participant Final as finalhandler 2.1.1
    participant Runtime as Node.js runtime

    Client->>RouterNode: POST / with a body that is never read
    RouterNode->>Final: no layer matched, no error raised
    Final-->>Client: 404 Not Found, Cannot POST / as HTML
    Note over Final: Nothing is logged, no metric or trace is emitted,<br/>and no alert reaches any backend.
    Client->>Runtime: malformed request line
    Runtime-->>Client: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request with Connection: close
    Note over Runtime: The process survives and the listener keeps serving.<br/>No retry, fallback, notification or dead-letter path exists.
```

The four views together state the position in one line each: traffic crosses exactly one boundary and always inward; the contract is two unversioned, unauthenticated literal paths served through an empty middleware pipeline; the only events in play are the runtime's own, and a bind failure reports success; and every failure resolves to a refusal or a termination with no operator-facing diagnostic.

- §6.2 Database Design — §6.2.1.1 for the absence of store clients and connection strings, §6.2.2.1 and §6.2.6.1 for the unread `phonenumber.csv` fixture, and §6.2.6 for the null-topology presentation reused in §6.3.5
- §1.3 Scope and §2.4 Implementation Considerations — the recorded exclusions (testing, CI/CD, containerisation, TLS, authentication, configuration externalisation and persistence) cited in §6.3.1.3 and §6.3.1.4

#### 6.3.6.4 Runtime Evidence

No web source was consulted for this section; every claim rests on repository contents or on behaviour observed at HEAD. The service was launched with `node server.js` on Node v22.23.3 over a loopback connection, and the following were recorded directly from responses: `GET /` returning `200 OK` with `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, `X-Powered-By: Express`, `Connection: keep-alive` and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, body `Hello, World!\n`; `GET /good-evening` returning `200` with `Content-Length: 12` and body `Good evening`; `GET /good-evening/`, `GET /unknown` and `POST /` returning `404` with an HTML `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` document and the `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Content-Type-Options` headers; `OPTIONS /` returning `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` and the body `GET, HEAD`; `HEAD /` returning `200` headers with no body; `GET /Good-Evening` returning `200` with the `Good evening` body, confirming case-insensitive matching; `GET /?q=1` returning the same 14-byte greeting, confirming the query string is ignored; and a request carrying `Authorization: Bearer x`, `Cookie: session=abc; user=1` and `X-Api-Key: k` returning the identical 200 response with no `Set-Cookie`. No response carried `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified` or `Vary`. A malformed request line was answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close` while the process continued serving. A second instance launched against the held port printed the startup banner and exited `0` with nothing on standard error, while the first instance kept answering `200 OK`. `SIGTERM` produced exit `143` and `SIGINT` exit `130`, each with only the startup banner on standard output and no drain or cleanup output. Throughout, standard output contained no per-request line, and dependency facts were read from `package-lock.json` and the installed `node_modules/` listing.


## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Applicability Determination

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

`hao-backprop-test` is a single-process, single-file, stateless HTTP server. Its entire executable surface is `server.js` — 29 lines of CommonJS holding one `require` of `express` (line 1), two configuration literals (lines 3-4), one framework setting (line 12), two route registrations whose handlers write fixed string literals (lines 14-24) and one listener that binds the literal loopback address (lines 26-28). The system has no identity model, no credential surface, no authorization decision to make, no persistence, no secret, no configuration layer and no outbound connection. The three other JavaScript files at the repository root are byte-identical native-`http` fixtures that the service never loads.

What the system does have is exactly one security control: a **loopback-only network binding** (`'127.0.0.1'` on port `3000`), which acts as an implicit security boundary by precluding remote connectivity at the operating-system networking layer. That single control, and a set of standard practices that follow from the system's minimal construction, are the whole of the security posture; every conventional security primitive is **verified absent** below, each with the source-level or runtime evidence that fixes its disposition, and §6.4.6 carries the consolidated control matrix. Section §5.4.4 states the architecture's canonical position: there is no authentication or authorization framework, access control is delegated entirely to the network boundary, and the service is "safe only while it remains unreachable from other hosts."

| Required topic cluster | Determination | Documented in |
|------------------------|---------------|---------------|
| Authentication Framework — identity, MFA, session, token, password | Not applicable — verified absent, no credential surface exists | §6.4.2 |
| Authorization System — RBAC, permissions, resource authorization, enforcement points, audit | Not applicable — verified absent, no protected resource exists | §6.4.3 |
| Data Protection — encryption, key management, masking, secure communication, compliance controls | Not applicable — no data is captured, persisted or transmitted off-host | §6.4.4 |
| Required diagrams — authentication flow, authorization flow, security zones | Supplied as null-topology and boundary views that mark each absent stage | §6.4.5 |
| Standard practices followed instead | Recorded as an explicit policy register with its enforcement point for each rule | §6.4.7 |

#### 6.4.1.1 Basis of the Determination

Eight independently verified facts carry the verdict. Each is stated with the evidence it rests on, because the same reasoning recurs in the sub-sections that follow.

1. **Loopback-only binding is the sole security control.** The listener address is the hardcoded literal `'127.0.0.1'` (`server.js:3`, used at line 26). The listening socket was confirmed in the host's TCP table as exactly one entry in state `0A` (LISTEN) with local address `0100007F:0BB8` — `127.0.0.1:3000`, with no wildcard binding — and a request to the machine's non-loopback address `10.11.0.44:3000` was refused at the transport layer (`curl` exit 7) while `127.0.0.1:3000` answered `200 OK`.
2. **No identity, session or cryptographic library exists in the resolved dependency tree.** `package.json:11-13` declares exactly one dependency, `express ^5.2.1`; the 66 package entries in `package-lock.json` are the Express 5.2.1 closure alone (`router`, `finalhandler`, `send`, `serve-static`, `body-parser`, `cookie`, `cookie-signature`, `qs`, `proxy-addr`, `etag`, `fresh`, `mime-types` and their transitive dependencies). A name scan of all 66 resolves no `bcrypt`, `argon2`, `jsonwebtoken`, `jose`, `jws`, `passport`, `oauth`, `openid`, `saml`, `helmet`, `csurf`, `express-session`, `express-rate-limit`, `node-forge`, `crypto-js`, `keytar`, `dotenv`, `joi`, `validator` or logging/auditing package. The only dependency with a security rationale in its name is `safer-buffer`, a `Buffer`-constructor compatibility shim.
3. **No security construct appears in any repository code.** A case-insensitive keyword scan of all four application JavaScript files for `auth`, `authentication`, `authorization`, `session`, `token`, `jwt`, `cookie`, `password`, `bcrypt`, `hash`, `crypto`, `encrypt`, `tls`, `ssl`, `https`, `helmet`, `cors`, `csrf`, `rate-limit`, `secret`, `credential`, `role`, `permission`, `audit`, `sanitize` and `nonce` returns **zero matches**, as does a scan for the mechanics those features would need: `app.use`, `app.set`, `app.disable`, `process.env`, `req.`, `res.cookie`, `crypto`, `https`, `fs.`, `eval(` and `exec(`.
4. **No credential, secret or key material exists in the repository.** All 19 tracked files were scanned for private-key headers, cloud access-key identifiers, provider tokens and API-key literals: zero matches. No `.env` file, `.pem`, `.key`, `.crt`, `.cer` or `.p12` exists anywhere in the tree, and no `process.env` read appears in executable code, so there is neither a secret to protect nor a mechanism to inject one (§3.4.4).
5. **Transport is plaintext HTTP/1.1 with no TLS layer.** The application never imports `https`, holds no certificate, and creates its listener through Express's `app.listen`, which constructs a `http.Server` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-599`). Responses carry no `Strict-Transport-Security` header, and no TLS-terminating proxy, gateway or ingress is configured anywhere in the repository.
6. **No request input is read, so no request-derived value can reach a security decision or a sink.** The token `req.` appears zero times in application code; both handlers receive `req` and never dereference it. Measured at HEAD, a request carrying `Authorization: Bearer x`, `Cookie: session=abc; user=1`, `X-Api-Key: k` and `X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7` returned a response byte-identical to an anonymous request — `200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, body `Hello, World!\n` — with no `Set-Cookie` and no other change.
7. **No served response carries a security header, and the only framework metadata emitted is the framework's own name.** Both registered routes set exactly one header besides the status line — `Content-Type: text/plain` (`server.js:16, 22`) — and Express adds `X-Powered-By: Express` because `x-powered-by` is enabled by default (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:94`) and nothing in the application disables it. The framework's own refusal documents for `404` and `500` do carry `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (`node_modules/finalhandler/index.js:267-268`), but a successful response carries neither.
8. **No data subject to a compliance obligation is captured, stored, logged or disclosed.** Nothing is persisted, no per-request record is written, and the single line the process emits is the startup banner (`server.js:27`). The only contact-shaped artifact in the tree, `phonenumber.csv`, holds 15 synthetic rows in the `+111111112xx` range under the header `message,phonenumber` and is read by no code path (§6.2.4.3, §3.4.4).

#### 6.4.1.2 The Single Control in Force, and Its Limits

Because the loopback binding is the entirety of the access-control decision, it is worth stating precisely what it does and does not do. It is a network-layer restriction applied by the kernel to a single TCP socket; it is not an identity check, not an authentication step and not an application-level authorization decision, and it is not configurable at runtime.

| Property of the control | Realisation in this system | Evidence |
|-------------------------|----------------------------|----------|
| Mechanism | Kernel-level bind restriction to the loopback interface | `server.js:3, 26`; TCP table showing `0100007F:0BB8` only |
| Coverage | Every request to either route; no per-path or per-method variation | `server.js:14-24`; responses for both routes |
| Effect | Remote hosts cannot establish a connection; the control cannot be bypassed by request content | Refused connection to the non-loopback address |
| Cost | Zero code, zero configuration, zero runtime overhead | `server.js` contains no access-control logic |

Two limits follow, and both are architectural rather than fixable by configuration. First, the control is *coarse*: any process able to open a TCP connection on the same host is fully authorised for both routes, so its strength reduces to the host's own process isolation, file-system permissions and firewall policy — properties the repository neither configures nor can observe. Second, the control is *all-or-nothing*: parameterising the bind address (a deferred enhancement recorded in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3) would remove the only control in existence without adding a replacement, and the repository's hardening plan forbids the compensating work — it rules out adding HTTPS/TLS, authentication or authorization (`Response.txt` §0.5). Section §5.4.4 records the same conclusion in one line: any enterprise deployment would require authentication, authorization and transport-security work that "has no counterpart in the repository today."

#### 6.4.1.3 Repository Role Context

`README.md:1-2` states the project's purpose in two lines: `hao-backprop-test`, a "test project for backprop integration", served by an Express HTTP server with two documented endpoints. That stated role explains the security posture rather than merely describing it: a fixture built to be read exhaustively, installed from a lockfile, started by hand and exercised with `curl` on the machine that runs it requires no identity model, because every plausible caller is the operator. The exclusion lists written into the project's own artifacts confirm the reading — the delivered work explicitly excluded authentication, TLS, configuration files and environment-variable support (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2), and the unimplemented hardening plan extends the same prohibitions to HTTPS/TLS, authentication, authorization, request-parsing middleware, clustering and database connections (`Response.txt` §0.5). No security capability was omitted by oversight; each was ruled out in writing, and each exclusion is the reason the corresponding sub-section below resolves to "verified absent" rather than to a partial implementation.

#### 6.4.1.4 Conflict With the Repository's Earlier Verdict

The repository already carries a `## 6.4 Security Architecture` of its own — `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` lines 4040-4584 — which reaches the same "not applicable" verdict and states the same loopback rationale. The verdict is upheld here; its supporting basis, however, describes a state the repository has since left, and three of its load-bearing claims are contradicted by the tree and by observed behaviour at HEAD. Where the two documents disagree, the observed state governs this specification.

| Claim in the earlier §6.4 | Observed at HEAD |
|---------------------------|------------------|
| The entire executable surface is a "15-line `server.js` using only the built-in `http` core module" | `server.js` is 29 lines and `require`s `express` at line 1; the framework hosts the two routes |
| "`package.json` declares no `dependencies`"; the lockfile holds only a root self-reference | `package.json:12` declares `express: "^5.2.1"`; the lockfile pins 66 non-root packages, all with `sha512` integrity digests, and 66 are installed |
| "No transitive vulnerabilities possible" — no package tree to scan | 66 packages are installed, and `npm audit` at HEAD reports three advisories, one critical, in that tree (§6.4.6.5) |

Four of its security-relevant claims were re-verified independently against the current tree and hold unchanged: no authentication subsystem of any kind exists; no authorization, role or permission logic exists; the bind address is the literal loopback address with no TLS layer; and no secret, credential, `.env` file or `process.env` read exists anywhere in the repository. The verdict survives the re-platform because its reasons do not depend on the framework — the system still has no identity, no authorization decision, no protected resource and no remote reachability. What changes is the frame: the service now runs inside a framework that supplies defaults of its own (`X-Powered-By`, `trust proxy: false`, a `simple` query parser, framework-generated refusal documents), and those defaults are documented as controls or as disclosures in §6.4.6 rather than being invisible.

#### 6.4.1.5 How Each Required Area Is Documented

| Required area | Treatment in this section |
|---------------|---------------------------|
| Authentication Framework | §6.4.2 — identity management, multi-factor authentication, session management, token handling and password policies, each dispositioned against source-level and runtime evidence |
| Authorization System | §6.4.3 — role-based access control, permission management, resource authorization, policy enforcement points and audit logging, including the enforcement points that do exist |
| Data Protection | §6.4.4 — encryption standards, key management, data masking rules, secure communication and data-protection compliance controls, plus an information-disclosure register |
| Required diagrams | §6.4.5 — authentication flow, authorization flow and security-zone diagrams in Mermaid.js, drawn as boundary and null-topology views |
| Security controls and policies | §6.4.6 — the consolidated control matrix (implemented controls, absent controls, coverage by layer, and the dependency-vulnerability register); §6.4.7 — the standard security practices that are followed instead, as a policy register with an enforcement point for each |
| Compliance | §6.4.8 — regulatory applicability, repository-level compliance posture and the triggers that would reopen the scope |
| Forward view | §6.4.9 — the recorded but unimplemented enhancements, and the conditions that would make this section applicable |


### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework — Verified Absent

The system implements no authentication framework of any kind, at any layer, and none is reachable by configuration. Section §5.4.4 states the disposition canonically — no identity, credential, session, role or permission concept exists in the code, and no library in the dependency tree implements one — and §6.3.2.3 records the same finding for the inbound interface. This sub-section extends that position to each authentication topic the section prompt names, with the evidence that fixes it, so that a reviewer can see the absence is a property of the code and the dependency tree rather than an omission from the design.

The one measurement that covers the whole topic is a credentialed request. At HEAD, `GET /` sent with `Authorization: Bearer x`, `Cookie: session=abc; user=1` and `X-Api-Key: k` returned `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, body `Hello, World!\n`, no `Set-Cookie`, and a header set identical to the response to an anonymous request. A credential-bearing request is therefore indistinguishable from an anonymous one in both directions: nothing is inspected, nothing is answered differently, and nothing is remembered.

| Authentication capability | Disposition | Evidence |
|---------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Credential intake (header, cookie, body, query) | Absent — no request input is read | `req.` occurs zero times in application code; identical responses for credentialed and anonymous probes |
| Credential verification | Absent — no comparison, no hash, no provider call exists | Repository-wide keyword scan; no outbound call in any code path (§6.3.1.1) |
| Identity issuance or federation | Absent — nothing is issued, asserted or verified | No identity library in the 66-package tree; no issuer, client ID or callback URL in any file |
| MFA, session and token primitives | Absent — no second factor, no session object, no token format | §6.4.2.2 through §6.4.2.4 below |

#### 6.4.2.1 Identity Management

No identity model exists. The handlers construct no principal, read no actor, and retain no identifier: they receive `req` and write a fixed literal, so there is no point in the request path at which an identity could be established, carried or discarded. There is no user store, no service-account registry, no machine-identity model, no client-certificate trust store and no federated-identity configuration, and the repository contains none of the artifacts such a model would need — no user fixture that code reads, no role or tenant column, no `.env` or configuration file to name an identity provider, and no database in which a subject record could live (§6.2.4.5).

| Identity concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|------------------|-------------|----------|
| User or subject identifier | None — no principal is constructed or retained | `server.js:14-24`; no `req.` dereference |
| Identity store or directory | None — no store of any kind exists | `package.json:11-13`; no datastore client in the lockfile (§6.2.1.1) |
| Service, machine or workload identity | None — no service-account, token or certificate model | No secret, key or certificate file in the tree; no credential literal in any file |
| Identity provider integration (OAuth, OIDC, SAML, Auth0, Okta, Entra ID, Cognito, Keycloak) | None — no client library and no provider metadata | Name scan of all 66 resolved packages; repository-wide keyword scan |

The only identifier-shaped data anywhere in the repository is the unread `phonenumber.csv` fixture, whose 15 rows pair conversational text with synthetic numbers in the `+111111112xx` range. It is not an identity source: no code path opens it, and its presence changes neither startup nor any response (`phonenumber.csv`; §6.2.4.3).

#### 6.4.2.2 Multi-Factor Authentication

Multi-factor authentication is not applicable because no first factor exists. MFA extends a primary credential with a second verification method; with no credential intake, no verification step and no enrolment surface, there is nothing for a second factor to extend. The repository contains no TOTP/HOTP implementation or library, no WebAuthn/FIDO2 relying party, no SMS or e-mail one-time-code path (and no SMS or mail provider dependency, so `phonenumber.csv` implies no messaging capability), no push-notification factor, and no hardware-token enrolment or recovery flow.

| MFA element | Disposition | Evidence |
|-------------|-------------|----------|
| Something the user knows (password, PIN) | Absent — no credential is collected or verified | §6.4.2.5; credentialed probe answered identically |
| Something the user has (token, phone, device) | Absent — no enrolment, binding or challenge exists | No OTP or WebAuthn library in the dependency tree; no route for enrolment |
| Something the user is (biometric) | Absent — no biometric surface and no device trust | No client, no UI and no assertion consumed by either handler |
