| Factor policy (required, step-up, recovery) | Not applicable — no factor exists to require | `server.js:14-24`; no configuration layer exists (§2.4.1) |

#### 6.4.2.3 Session Management

No session lifecycle exists. The handlers are stateless and synchronous: each request is two or three statements ending in `res.end`, no state survives the response, and no per-caller object is created, stored or looked up. The system sets no session cookie — `Set-Cookie` was absent from every response observed at HEAD, including the credential-bearing probe — reads no `Cookie` request header, and operates no session store of any kind, so there is nothing to expire, rotate, invalidate or fixate.

Two packages capable of cookie handling are present in the dependency closure — `cookie@0.7.2` and `cookie-signature@1.2.2` — and both are inert here for a structural reason: Express exposes its cookie, session and body-parsing capabilities as middleware that must be mounted with `app.use`, and no `app.use` call exists anywhere in application code. The same applies to `body-parser` and `raw-body`, which are loaded at `require` time by `node_modules/express/lib/express.js:15` but never enter the request path, because no parser middleware is registered.

| Session primitive | Disposition | Evidence |
|-------------------|-------------|----------|
| Session creation and identifier | None — no session object exists and no identifier is generated | `server.js:14-24`; no `res.cookie` call; no `Set-Cookie` observed |
| Cookie handling (set, read, sign, verify) | Present in the dependency closure, unmounted and never executed | `cookie@0.7.2`, `cookie-signature@1.2.2` in the lockfile; zero `app.use` calls |
| Server-side session store | None — no store, no cache, no datastore | `package.json:11-13`; §6.2.2.1 |
| Expiry, rotation, logout, fixation defence | Not applicable — no session exists to expire or fix | §6.4.2.3 above; `server.js:14-24` |

#### 6.4.2.4 Token Handling

No token is issued, accepted, parsed, validated or logged. The system has no token format (no JWT, no opaque reference, no signed assertion), no signing or verification key, no audience or issuer expectation, no expiry or revocation list, and no place in the code where a token would be read — no `Authorization` header is inspected, and no token library appears among the 66 resolved packages. The `Authorization: Bearer x` header sent in the credentialed probe was ignored in the strongest sense available: it neither changed the response nor produced any log entry, error or downstream effect.

| Token concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| Token issuance, format and claims | None — no token is created and no claim model exists | No `jsonwebtoken`, `jose`, `jws` or `jwa` in the lockfile; no route that could return one |
| Token acceptance or validation | None — no header is read; no parser, key or introspection call exists | `req.` occurs zero times; credentialed probe returned the standard `200` |
| Signing and verification keys | None — no key material of any kind in the tree | 19 tracked files scanned for key headers, tokens and key files: zero matches |
| Revocation, expiry and replay handling | Not applicable — no token exists to revoke or replay | §6.4.2.4 above; no session or state is retained |

#### 6.4.2.5 Password Policies

No password policy exists, and none can be enforced, because the system holds no credential store in which a password could be kept or compared. There is no password field, no registration or password-change route, no login route, no complexity, length, rotation, lockout or history rule, and no account-recovery flow. The repository also contains no password-hashing capability: no `bcrypt`, `argon2`, `scrypt` or `pbkdf2` wrapper appears among the resolved packages, and neither the Node.js built-in `crypto` module nor any hash helper is imported by any repository file. Nothing hashed, salted or encoded appears anywhere in the 19 tracked files.

| Password-policy concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|-------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Credential store and comparison | None — no store, no comparison, no credential field | `server.js`; no datastore and no auth library in the tree |
| Hashing and salting at rest | Not applicable — nothing is stored; no hashing library is present or imported | `crypto` not imported by any file; no `bcrypt`/`argon2` in the lockfile |
| Complexity, rotation, lockout, history | None — no policy file, no configuration layer and no enforcement point | `package.json#scripts` holds only the `npm init` placeholder; no config file exists (§2.4.1) |
| Recovery and reset flows | None — no account concept exists to recover | §6.4.2.1; no route beyond the two literal `GET` paths |

The practical consequence for a reviewer is that the repository is not a system with *weak* authentication controls; it is a system with *no* authentication surface, which is a materially different finding for any risk assessment: there is no credential to steal, phish, replay or brute-force within the application, and equally no mechanism to add access control to the service without first introducing an identity model, a credential store, a transport-security layer and an authorization decision — none of which exists today (§6.4.9.4).


### 6.4.3 Authorization System — Verified Absent

No authorization system exists, and one is not merely unimplemented but structurally unavailable: authorization expresses a decision about a subject, a resource and an action, and this system has no subject (no identity is established, §6.4.2.1), no protected resource (both routes return the same public literals to every caller) and no action beyond reading two constants. Section §5.4.4 records the disposition — access control is delegated entirely to the network boundary, so "any local process that can open a TCP connection is authorised" and no remote host is reachable — and §6.3.2.4 reaches the same conclusion for the inbound interface. This sub-section dispositions each authorization topic the section prompt names, and then documents the enforcement points that *do* act on a request, because those are the only barriers between a caller and a response.

| Authorization capability | Disposition | Evidence |
|--------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Subject, resource and action model | Absent — no principal, no owner and no operation is modelled | `server.js:14-24`; no `req.` dereference in either handler |
| Role, permission or policy store | Absent — no policy file, no database, no configuration layer | `package.json:11-13`; §2.4.1; §6.2.4.5 |
| Enforcement point in the pipeline | Absent — no middleware is mounted, so no stage exists for a check | Zero `app.use` calls in application code; §6.4.3.4 |
| Authorization audit trail | Absent — no decision is recorded because no decision is taken | §6.4.3.5; §5.4.2 |

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control

There is no role model: no role, group, tenant, scope, claim or permission identifier is defined, assigned, resolved or checked anywhere in the repository. Both routes are registered on the same application object with identical handling (`server.js:14-24`), so there are no role-gated paths to distinguish, and there is no caller attribute an RBAC engine could evaluate — the handler never reads a header, a query parameter, a path segment or a cookie. The scans that establish the absence are direct: `role`, `permission`, `scope` and `tenant` return zero matches in all four application JavaScript files; every occurrence of those words in the repository is prose inside the Blitzy artifacts under `blitzy/documentation/` and `Response.txt`.

| RBAC element | Disposition | Evidence |
|--------------|-------------|----------|
| Role or permission definition | None — no role is named or described in executable code | Keyword scan of all four `.js` files: zero matches |
| Role assignment to a subject | None — no subject exists to assign a role to | `server.js:14-24`; §6.4.2.1 |
| Role resolution at request time | None — nothing is resolved, cached or looked up | No middleware, no store, no `req.` dereference |
| Role-gated route or method | None — both routes have identical posture | `server.js:14, 20`; identical `200` responses verified |

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

No permission is defined, granted, inherited, revoked, delegated or reviewed, and no administrative surface exists through which any of those operations could occur: the repository has no administrative route, no management endpoint, no policy endpoint, no user interface and no CLI. Permission management also presumes a configuration or store that can hold grants — and this system has neither, since host and port are the only configuration values and they are `const` literals with no configuration file, no `process.env` read and no command-line argument parsing (§2.4.1). The dependency tree reinforces the point: `casl`, `casbin`, `oso`, `accesscontrol` and comparable policy libraries are absent from all 66 resolved packages.

| Permission-management activity | Disposition | Evidence |
|--------------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Grant creation or change | None — no administrative route, store or interface exists | `server.js:12-24`; route table holds two `GET` paths |
| Effective-permission evaluation | None — no evaluator, no policy and no attributes | No policy library in the lockfile; no `app.use` pipeline |
| Delegation, inheritance, review | Not applicable — no grant exists to delegate or review | §6.4.3.2 above; §5.4.4 |
| Permission configuration source | None — no config file, `.env`, CLI argument or database | `server.js:3-4`; §3.4.5 |

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

No resource is owned, protected or selectively exposed. The two registered routes are public in the strongest sense: they read no input, return the same two compile-time literals to every caller, and make no decision that depends on who is asking or what is being asked for. Object-level authorization has no subject matter here either, because there is no object: no route carries a path parameter, no identifier is accepted, no record is looked up, and no response body is derived from a stored entity — so there is no insecure-direct-object-reference surface, no horizontal or vertical privilege boundary to test, and no ownership check that could be missing. The response bodies are `'Hello, World!\n'` (14 bytes) and `'Good evening'` (12 bytes), both literals in the source (`server.js:15-17, 21-23`).

| Resource-authorization concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|--------------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Protected resource or scope | None — no resource exists that could be gated | `server.js:14-24`; §6.2.2.1 |
| Object-level check (ownership, tenancy) | Not applicable — no object identifier is accepted | No path parameter registered; `req.` never dereferenced |
| Exposure policy per route | Uniform and unconditional — both routes answer every caller identically | Identical `200` for anonymous and credentialed probes |
| Data-exposure surface to abuse | Static literals only — no stored, computed or user-derived content | `server.js:15-17, 21-23`; §6.3.2.2 |

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

The system has no policy enforcement point in the application layer, because it has no policy and no middleware pipeline: no `app.use` call exists in any application file, so a request passes from the TCP socket to a route handler without traversing a single application-controlled check. It does, however, have four enforcement points that act on a request and are worth documenting precisely, because together they are the only barriers between a caller and a response — three of them supplied by the runtime and one by the framework's router.

| Enforcement point | What it enforces | Observed behaviour |
|-------------------|------------------|--------------------|
| Kernel loopback bind | Reachability — only processes on the same host may connect | Non-loopback address refused at the transport layer; sole socket is `127.0.0.1:3000` |
| Node.js HTTP parser | Message well-formedness and header-size limits | Malformed request line answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; a 20 KiB header block answered `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` while 15 KiB was accepted |
| Framework router (`router@2.2.0`) | Path and method match, under `strict routing` | Only `GET /` and `GET /good-evening` return content; `GET /good-evening/` and `POST /` fall through to `404`; `OPTIONS /` is answered `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` |
| Framework terminal responder (`finalhandler@2.1.1`) | Refusal document generation | `404`/`500` documents carry `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` |

Two properties of that table matter for a security review. First, every one of these points is *content-blind*: none inspects a credential, a role or an attribute, because none of those exists to inspect. Second, the parser and header-limit behaviour is a runtime default rather than a project decision — nothing in the repository sets a timeout, a connection cap or a size limit — so it moves with the Node.js version rather than with the code. A fifth control that a reviewer might expect is absent by default: Express's `trust proxy` setting is `false` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:99`), so the framework does not honour `X-Forwarded-For` or `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and a client cannot spoof its own address to the `req.ip` getter through those headers (`node_modules/express/lib/request.js:284-290, 327-330`). Nothing reads that getter either.

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

No audit logging exists, at any layer. The process writes exactly one line in its lifetime — the startup banner produced by the listener callback (`server.js:27`) — and that line is an operational diagnostic rather than an audit record: it has no timestamp, no severity, no actor, no action, no outcome and no correlation identifier, and it is emitted once rather than per event. Nothing is logged for a request that is served, a path that is refused, a malformed message that is rejected or a handled `500`; the framework's `logerror` path writes a stack to standard error only for a genuine server-error response, and the router's `DEBUG` output, which would name each dispatch and refusal, is never enabled because nothing in the repository sets `DEBUG` (§5.4.1, §5.4.2). No audit, ledger, journaling, tamper-evident or log-shipping library appears among the 66 resolved packages, and no log destination, retention rule or rotation policy is configured anywhere.

| Audit element | Disposition | Evidence |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| Security-event log (access, denial, auth) | None — no per-request or per-decision record exists | Observed output after a served request, a `404`, a `400` and a `431`: the banner alone |
| Actor and action attribution | None — no identity is established, so no actor could be recorded | §6.4.2.1; `server.js:14-24` |
| Log integrity, retention and rotation | None — no sink, no retention rule, no rotation, no write to a file | `package.json:11-13`; no `fs` usage in any repository file |
| Alerting on security-relevant events | None — no metric, alert or error-tracking client exists | §5.4.1; §3.4.1 |

The practical consequence is that the system cannot answer any audit question a reviewer would ask — who called, when, from where, and whether the call was permitted — and it cannot detect abuse of the one control it has. Because the loopback binding authorises every local process, unauthorised local access would leave no trace in the application at all; the only evidence would come from host-level tooling outside the repository, which the project neither configures nor documents (§6.4.7).


### 6.4.4 Data Protection

Data protection has no subject in this system: no business data is captured, no record is persisted, no response is derived from stored content, and no bytes leave the host. What the sub-section can document, therefore, is the disposition of each data-protection concern against the evidence, and the one class of finding that is real rather than hypothetical — **information disclosure on the wire**, where the framework's own defaults reveal implementation detail to any caller that can reach the listener. Section §6.2.4.3 records the privacy side of the same position (no data is processed, nothing is written at rest, so no encryption-at-rest control has a subject), and §3.4.4 records that no credential or secret exists to manage.

| Data-protection concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|-------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Data at rest | None exists — no write path, no store, no file output | No `fs` usage in any repository file; the only runtime output is a stdout line (§6.2.3.4) |
| Data in transit | Plaintext HTTP/1.1 over loopback only; no TLS, no certificate, no terminator | `server.js:26`; observed `HTTP/1.1` responses on `127.0.0.1:3000` |
| Cryptographic material | None — no key, secret, certificate or keystore in the tree | 19 tracked files scanned for key material and secret-shaped strings: zero matches |
| Control that does apply | The loopback bind keeps every byte on the host's kernel | Refused connection to the non-loopback address (§6.4.1.1) |

#### 6.4.4.1 Encryption Standards

No encryption standard is applied, in transit or at rest, because nothing is stored and no connection leaves the host. The repository imports no cryptographic module: `crypto`, `tls`, `https` and `node:crypto` appear zero times across all four application JavaScript files, and no encryption, hashing, signing or key-derivation library appears among the 66 resolved packages — the only cryptography-adjacent artifact in the entire checkout is the `safer-buffer` compatibility shim, which performs no cryptographic work. The runtime does make cryptographic primitives available (Node.js ships `crypto` and `https` in the standard library), and Express can be fronted by a TLS server, but neither capability is invoked by any code path: the listener is an `http.Server` created by `app.listen` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-599`), and every response observed at HEAD was served as cleartext `HTTP/1.1`.

| Encryption concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|--------------------|-------------|----------|
| Transport encryption (TLS/HTTPS) | Absent — cleartext HTTP/1.1; no certificate, no HSTS header, no TLS terminator | `server.js:26`; observed cleartext responses; no `Strict-Transport-Security` |
| Encryption at rest | Not applicable — no data is written anywhere | §6.2.3.4; no `fs` usage in any repository file |
| Hashing or signing of any value | None — no hash, MAC or signature is computed | `crypto` not imported; no hashing library in the dependency tree |
| Cryptographic primitive availability | Present in the Node.js runtime but unused by the application | No `crypto`/`https` import in `server.js` or the three fixtures |

#### 6.4.4.2 Key Management

There is no key management, because there is no key. The repository holds no certificate, private key, symmetric secret, API token, database credential, signing key or keystore file — the tree contains no `.pem`, `.key`, `.crt`, `.cer`, `.p12` or `.env` file, no `process.env` read in executable code, and no secret-shaped string in any of the 19 tracked files. There is likewise no secrets manager, key vault, KMS client or hardware-security-module integration among the 66 resolved packages, and no rotation, revocation, expiry or escrow procedure to document, nor any configuration layer through which a secret could be injected (§3.4.4).

The only cryptographic material anywhere in the project is a set of integrity digests, and the distinction matters: `package-lock.json` pins each of the 66 packages to an exact version, a registry URL and a `sha512` integrity value, which is a *tamper check on downloaded code*, not a protection for data or a credential. It is verified by the npm client at install time and serves no role at runtime; nothing in the repository runs an audit or verification job to consume it automatically (§6.4.6.5).

| Key-management concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Key, certificate or secret storage | None — no such artifact exists in the tree | File-pattern scan of the whole checkout; secret-shaped-string scan of all tracked files |
| Secret injection and configuration | None — no `.env`, no config file, no `process.env` read, no CLI argument | `server.js:3-4`; §2.4.1; §3.4.5 |
| Rotation, revocation, expiry and escrow | Not applicable — no key exists to rotate or revoke | §6.4.4.2 above |
| Integrity material actually present | 66 `sha512` package digests in the lockfile, verified at install time only | `package-lock.json`; §3.4.2 |

#### 6.4.4.3 Data Masking Rules

No masking rule is required or implemented, because the system neither captures nor emits data that could be sensitive. Neither handler reads a request field, nothing is logged per request, no response body is derived from an input or a record, and no data file is opened at runtime — so there is no field that could carry personal, financial or health data into a log, a response or storage in the first place. Masking, tokenisation and redaction are controls applied to data *in flow* or *at rest*; here the flow carries two compile-time literals and the store is empty.

The one artifact that would fall under a masking rule if the system ever touched it is the orphan fixture `phonenumber.csv`, which pairs conversational message text with 15 telephone numbers in the synthetic `+111111112xx` range (`phonenumber.csv`; §6.2.4.3). It is a genuine PII *shape* without being a PII *source*: no executable code path opens, parses, serves or logs it, and the numbers are non-routable test values. The rules below are stated anyway, because a reviewer needs to know what would have to become true for masking to matter, and because the first row — log hygiene — is the one rule this system currently satisfies only by accident of never logging.

| Masking or redaction rule | Would apply to | Current enforcement |
|---------------------------|----------------|---------------------|
| Never write request-derived values to a log | Headers, cookies, query strings, bodies, client address | Satisfied trivially — no per-request logging exists and no request field is read (§5.4.2) |
| Mask or omit telephone numbers in output | `phonenumber.csv` `phonenumber` column, if it were ever served or logged | Not applicable today — the fixture is unread by any code path (§6.2.4.3) |
| Omit internals from error responses | Framework error documents and stack traces | **Not satisfied** — with `NODE_ENV` unset the framework returns a full stack in the response body (§6.4.4.5) |
| Mask secrets or credentials in output | Any credential, key or token | Satisfied trivially — no secret exists in the repository (§6.4.4.2) |

#### 6.4.4.4 Secure Communication

Communication is not secured at the transport layer: the listener speaks plaintext HTTP/1.1 over TCP on the loopback interface, with no TLS handshake, no certificate, no cipher negotiation, no mutual authentication and no `Strict-Transport-Security` header. The architectural justification recorded in §5.4.4 and §6.4.1.2 is that the loopback binding substitutes for transport security by construction — traffic never crosses a network medium, so the threats TLS addresses (passive interception and man-in-the-middle on a shared path) have no path to occur on. That reasoning holds only while the address remains loopback, which is why §6.4.1.2 treats re-binding as the trigger that would remove the system's only control.

Two framework defaults shape the rest of the wire behaviour. `trust proxy` is `false` (`node_modules/express/lib/application.js:99`), so the framework does not trust `X-Forwarded-For` or `X-Forwarded-Proto` and a client cannot influence `req.ip` or `req.protocol` through headers — a safe default that happens to be irrelevant here, since no handler reads either. And no permissive cross-origin policy exists: an `Origin` header on a request produces no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` or `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` in the response, and no `Vary` header is emitted, so no origin is granted read access to a response. Because no cookie is ever set and no route changes state, the classic cross-site request-forgery preconditions are absent as well.

| Secure-communication element | Disposition | Evidence |
|-------------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Transport security (TLS, ciphers, certificates) | Absent — cleartext HTTP/1.1 on loopback only | `server.js:26`; observed responses |
| Substituting control | Kernel-level loopback restriction keeping all traffic on-host | TCP table entry `0100007F:0BB8`; refused remote connection |
| Proxy and forwarded-header trust | Not trusted — `trust proxy` is `false`; forwarded headers ignored | `node_modules/express/lib/application.js:99`; `request.js:284-290, 327-330` |
| Cross-origin and state-changing exposure | No CORS grant, no cookie, no `POST` route, no state to change | `Origin` probe returned no `Access-Control-*` headers; `POST /` → `404` |

#### 6.4.4.5 Information Disclosure Register

The only concrete data-protection finding in this system is disclosure of implementation detail, and all of it is produced by framework defaults that the application neither sets nor disables. The most significant entry is the error path: with `NODE_ENV` unset, Express reports its environment as `development` (`app.get('env')` was observed as `development`) and its default error handler returns a `500` document containing the exception message and a full stack trace with absolute filesystem paths — measured at 1,568 bytes in development against 148 bytes for the same failure with `NODE_ENV=production`, where the stack is suppressed in the body but still written to standard error. No handler in this repository can throw, so that path is currently unreachable through the two registered routes; it is nonetheless an inherited default whose exposure depends on an environment variable the project never sets.

| Disclosure | What a caller learns | Severity in this deployment |
|------------|----------------------|------------------------------|
| `X-Powered-By: Express` on every response, including `404`s | The framework identity, and by inference its default behaviours and typical misconfigurations | Low — no version is disclosed; reachable only from the host |
| Framework `500` body containing a stack and absolute paths when `NODE_ENV` is unset | Internal file layout and call structure, if a throwing route is ever added | Low today (unreachable — the handlers cannot throw); would rise if routes were added |
| `404` body echoing the requested method and path | Confirmation of the exact method and path the caller supplied | Informational — the caller already supplied both |
| `OPTIONS /` answering `Allow: GET, HEAD` | The methods the router understands for that path | Informational — the same methods are documented in `README.md:9-12` |
| Absence of security headers on `200` responses | Nothing directly — but no `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` accompanies a `text/plain` body | Negligible — the bodies are static literals and no caller-controlled content is reflected |
| `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` | Server clock and connection policy | Negligible — runtime defaults, no application state behind them |

The framework's own refusal documents behave better than its served responses: `404` and `500` documents carry `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` from `finalhandler` (`node_modules/finalhandler/index.js:267-268`), so the one response class a caller can provoke without credentials is also the better-hardened one. That inversion — hardened error documents, unadorned success documents — is a direct consequence of the handlers using the low-level `res.statusCode`/`res.setHeader`/`res.end` API (`server.js:15-17, 21-23`) instead of a response helper: nothing in the application writes a security header, so the headers a caller sees come from whichever layer generated the response.


### 6.4.5 Required Security Diagrams

The section prompt requires authentication flow, authorization flow and security zone diagrams. Because the system has no authentication framework, no authorization system and no network edge, the first two are drawn as **null-flow views** — each shows the path a request actually takes, marks the checkpoints a conventional implementation would place on that path, and states that none of them exists — and the third is a **zone-boundary view** showing the single zone the system occupies and the boundary that excludes every other one. The style follows §6.1.5, §6.2.6 and §6.3.5.

| Required diagram | What it shows | Where it terminates |
|------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| Authentication flow | The request path with every authentication stage marked absent; anonymous and credentialed callers converge | A single identical `200 OK` for all admitted callers |
| Authorization flow | The four enforcement points that do act, and the absent policy enforcement point | An unconditional allow for any caller the kernel admits |
| Security zone | The one zone the system occupies, its boundary, and the zones with no realisation | A single loopback zone with no path from the off-host network |

#### 6.4.5.1 Authentication Flow Diagram

Every admitted caller converges on the same response. The path on the left is what happens; the dashed edges on the right terminate on the authentication stages that do not exist anywhere in the repository, which is why the two branches of the credential decision are the same branch.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ClientNode(["Caller opens a TCP connection to 127.0.0.1:3000"]) --> Reach{"Kernel loopback bind admits the peer?"}
    Reach -->|"off-host peer"| Refused(["Transport-level refusal, no HTTP response is produced"])
    Reach -->|"on-host peer"| ParserNode{"HTTP message well formed?"}
    ParserNode -->|"no"| BadReq(["400 Bad Request then Connection: close"])
    ParserNode -->|"yes"| CredCheck{"Credential intake stage present?"}
    CredCheck -->|"no such stage exists in the pipeline"| ProbeNode["Authorization, Cookie and X-Api-Key headers are never read"]
    ProbeNode --> Match{"Literal path matched under strict routing?"}
    Match -->|"GET / or GET /good-evening"| Identical200(["200 OK, text/plain, identical bytes for every caller"])
    Match -->|"any other path or method"| NotFound(["404 Not Found from the terminal responder"])

    subgraph AbsentAuthn["Authentication stages with no realisation"]
        NoIntake["No credential intake: no header, cookie or body is read"]
        NoVerify["No verification: no hash, comparison or provider call"]
        NoSession["No session: no Set-Cookie, no store, no expiry"]
        NoToken["No token: nothing issued, parsed, validated or revoked"]
        NoMFA["No second factor: no factor, enrolment, recovery or step-up"]
    end

    CredCheck -.->|"documented as absent"| NoIntake
    NoIntake --> NoVerify
    NoVerify --> NoSession
    NoSession --> NoToken
    NoToken --> NoMFA
```

The measured behaviour matches the diagram exactly: a request carrying `Authorization: Bearer x`, `Cookie: session=abc; user=1` and `X-Api-Key: k` produced `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, body `Hello, World!\n` and no `Set-Cookie` — byte-identical to the anonymous request, with nothing written to standard output.

#### 6.4.5.2 Authorization Flow Diagram

This diagram follows the four enforcement points that do act on a request and shows that none of them evaluates a policy: three are runtime or framework decisions about reachability, well-formedness and path matching, and the fourth is the handler writing a constant. The dashed edges terminate on the authorization decisions that have no realisation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RequestNode(["HTTP request arrives on the loopback socket"]) --> PEP1{"Enforcement point 1: kernel loopback bind"}
    PEP1 -->|"peer is off-host"| Deny1(["Connection refused before any application code runs"])
    PEP1 -->|"peer is on-host"| PEP2{"Enforcement point 2: Node HTTP parser limits"}
    PEP2 -->|"malformed request line"| Deny2(["400 Bad Request, socket closed, nothing logged"])
    PEP2 -->|"header block over 16 KiB"| Deny3(["431 Request Header Fields Too Large, nothing logged"])
    PEP2 -->|"accepted"| PEP3{"Enforcement point 3: router literal path and method match"}
    PEP3 -->|"no layer matched, including POST and trailing slash"| Deny4(["404 document with CSP default-src none and nosniff"])
    PEP3 -->|"GET / or GET /good-evening"| PEP4["Enforcement point 4: handler writes a fixed literal"]
    PEP4 --> Allow(["Admitted caller receives the response unconditionally"])

    subgraph AbsentAuthz["Authorization decisions with no realisation"]
        NoPEP["No application policy enforcement point: no app.use pipeline exists"]
        NoSubject["No subject, role, scope or permission is resolved"]
        NoObject["No resource owner and no object identifier is evaluated"]
        NoAuditNode["No allowed or denied decision is recorded anywhere"]
    end

    Allow -.->|"no policy was evaluated on this path"| NoPEP
    NoPEP --> NoSubject
    NoSubject --> NoObject
    NoObject --> NoAuditNode
```

The security-relevant reading is the last row: the only barrier between an admitted caller and a response is path equality against two literals. There is no decision to deny, so there is no denial to log, and the enforcement points that refuse a request (`400`, `431`, `404`) do so without leaving any record (§6.4.3.5).

#### 6.4.5.3 Security Zone Diagram

The system occupies exactly one zone. Zone 1 is everything off the host, which has no authenticated or unauthenticated path in; Zone 2 is the single host and the single process within it, whose only boundary is the kernel's loopback interface. Multi-zone topologies — DMZ, transport-security termination tier, identity zone, data zone, administrative zone, inspection tier — have no realisation here, and the dashed edges record that each of them is absent rather than merely unpopulated.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph OffHostZone["Zone 1 — off-host network, no path to the service"]
        OtherHosts["Any other host on the local network or the internet"]
        NoEdge["No DMZ, no gateway, no ingress, no TLS termination point"]
    end

    subgraph HostZone["Zone 2 — one host, one Node.js process"]
        KernelNode["Kernel loopback interface: the only boundary traffic reaches"]
        ListenerNode["Listener on 127.0.0.1:3000, plaintext HTTP/1.1"]
        AppNode["Express 5.2.1 application in server.js"]
        HandlerNode["Two literal GET handlers, fixed 14-byte and 12-byte bodies"]
        TerminalNode["Terminal responder: 404 and 500 documents with CSP and nosniff"]
        LocalCallers["Any local process on the same host"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentZones["Zones with no realisation in this architecture"]
        NoIdentityZone["No identity zone: no provider, directory or federation"]
        NoDataZone["No data zone: no database, cache, queue or store"]
        NoAdminZone["No administrative or bastion zone: no management surface"]
        NoInspectionZone["No WAF, IDS, rate limiter or audit collector"]
    end

    OtherHosts -->|"refused at the transport layer, no response"| KernelNode
    LocalCallers -->|"admitted with no identity check"| KernelNode
    KernelNode --> ListenerNode
    ListenerNode --> AppNode
    AppNode --> HandlerNode
    AppNode --> TerminalNode
    KernelNode -.->|"no further zone boundary is crossed"| NoIdentityZone
    AppNode -.->|"no edge leaves the process"| NoDataZone
    AppNode -.->|"no management route exists"| NoAdminZone
    ListenerNode -.->|"no inspection of traffic occurs"| NoInspectionZone
```

Read together, the three diagrams make the section's position concrete: a request crosses exactly one boundary, that boundary is decided by the kernel rather than by the application, every admitted caller is treated identically, and the only zone in which the system operates is the one its own host defines.


### 6.4.6 Security Control Matrix

The matrices below consolidate the security posture into the form a reviewer needs: what is implemented, what is absent, how coverage distributes across the layers of the stack, and which live advisories affect the dependency tree. The disposition of every control rests on the evidence cited in the preceding sub-sections; nothing here introduces a control that has not been observed at HEAD or a gap that has not been verified against the source.

#### 6.4.6.1 Implemented Security Controls

Ten controls are in force. Eight of them are properties of the runtime, the framework or the operating system rather than of any deliberate security work by the project — which is the honest characterisation of the posture: the system is secure to the extent that it is small, unreachable and default-configured.

| Control in force | How it is realised | Evidence |
|------------------|--------------------|----------|
| Loopback-only network exposure | Hardcoded literal `'127.0.0.1'` bound by the single listener | `server.js:3, 26`; sole socket `127.0.0.1:3000`; remote connection refused |
| Host-level access mediation | Only processes on the same host can connect; OS file permissions and host firewall decide the rest | `server.js:3`; §6.4.1.2 |
| No credential or secret surface | No key, certificate, `.env` file, `process.env` read or secret-shaped string exists | Scan of all 19 tracked files: zero matches (§6.4.4.2) |
| No request input consumption | Neither handler dereferences `req`; no body parser is mounted | `req.` occurs zero times; no `app.use` call exists |
| Static, non-reflective responses | Both bodies are compile-time literals written with `res.end` | `server.js:15-17, 21-23`; `Content-Length` 14 and 12 |
| Message well-formedness enforcement | Node.js HTTP parser rejects malformed requests and over-sized header blocks | `400` with `Connection: close`; `431` above 16 KiB, accepted at 15 KiB |
| Path and method restriction | Router matches two literal paths under `strict routing`; everything else falls through | `server.js:12, 14, 20`; `POST /` and trailing-slash variants answered `404` |
| Refusal documents carry security headers | `finalhandler` sets `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | `finalhandler/index.js:267-268`; observed on `404` and `500` |
| Forwarded-header trust disabled | Express default `trust proxy: false`, so `X-Forwarded-*` cannot influence `req.ip` or `req.protocol` | `application.js:99`; `request.js:284-290, 327-330` |
| Dependency integrity pinning | 66 packages pinned to exact versions with `sha512` digests, verified at install time | `package-lock.json`; `node_modules/` git-ignored by `.gitignore` |

#### 6.4.6.2 Absent Security Controls

Each row states a standard control family, its disposition here, and the consequence a risk assessment should record. "Not applicable" means the control has no subject matter in this system; "absent" means the control would have a subject matter if the system were used beyond a fixture, and the gap is therefore a precondition for any wider use.

| Control family | Disposition | Consequence in this deployment |
|----------------|-------------|-------------------------------|
| Authentication (any scheme) | Absent — no credential is requested, read or verified | Every request is anonymous; access decisions are made entirely by the kernel bind |
| Authorization (RBAC, ABAC, ACL, policy engine) | Absent — no subject, role, permission or policy exists | Any admitted caller may reach both routes; no per-route or per-caller restriction is possible |
| Session and cookie management | Absent — no cookie is set or read; no session store exists | Nothing is remembered between requests; no session fixation or hijack surface exists either |
| Transport encryption (TLS, HSTS, certificates) | Absent — cleartext HTTP/1.1 on loopback only | Confidentiality rests solely on traffic never leaving the host |
| Secret management, key management, KMS | Absent — no secret exists and no injection path exists | None required today; any future credential would need a configuration layer first |
| Cryptographic hashing or signing | Absent — no hash or signature is computed | No credential store exists that would require hashing |
| Security headers on served responses | Absent — a `200` carries only `Content-Type` and the framework's `X-Powered-By` | No CSP, HSTS, nosniff, frame or referrer policy accompanies served content |
| Framework fingerprint suppression | Absent — `X-Powered-By: Express` on every response; disabling it is a recorded but unimplemented enhancement | The framework identity is disclosed to any local caller |
| Error hygiene (stack suppression) | Absent — a framework `500` includes a stack and absolute paths unless `NODE_ENV=production`; the project never sets it | Information disclosure, currently unreachable because no handler can throw (§6.4.4.5) |
| Rate limiting, quotas, admission control | Absent — no limiter package, no middleware stage, no connection cap | The listener accepts until host resources are exhausted (§6.1.3.2) |
| Audit logging and security monitoring | Absent — no per-request record, no alert, no metric, no log shipping | Abuse of the loopback boundary would leave no application-level trace (§6.4.3.5) |
| Dependency vulnerability monitoring | Absent — `npm audit` is not wired into any script or job | Three advisories currently sit in the tree unnoticed by the build (§6.4.6.5) |
| CSRF and clickjacking defences | Not applicable — no state-changing route, no cookie, no rendered HTML from the application | No precondition exists for either attack class |
| Input validation and sanitisation | Not applicable — no input is read, so no parsing sink exists | Absence of a sink rather than absence of a control |

#### 6.4.6.3 Coverage by Layer

Coverage is thin and uneven, and the pattern explains the whole posture: the network layer is fully restricted, the runtime supplies defaults the project never had to write, and the application layer contributes no security decision at all.

| Layer | Control in force | Principal gap |
|-------|------------------|---------------|
| Network | Loopback bind on a single socket; no other listener and no outbound connection | No TLS, no gateway, no inspection, no per-client restriction |
| Host | Operating-system process isolation, file permissions and any host firewall the operator maintains | Nothing in the repository configures or verifies these |
| Runtime (Node.js) | HTTP parser validation, 16 KiB header limit, keep-alive, header and request timeouts | No application-set timeout, connection cap or back-pressure |
| Framework (Express 5.2.1) | Strict literal routing, `trust proxy` disabled, hardened refusal documents | `X-Powered-By` enabled, default error document leaks a stack when `NODE_ENV` is unset |
| Application | None — no authentication, authorization, validation or logging code exists | Every control expectation lands on the layers above |
| Supply chain | Pinned versions and `sha512` digests; `node_modules/` untracked | Advisory monitoring absent; three live advisories in the tree |
| Data | Not applicable — no data is captured, stored or transmitted off-host | Would need encryption, access control and retention work the moment data existed |

#### 6.4.6.4 Attack-Surface Summary

The surface that a caller or an operator can influence is small enough to enumerate exhaustively, which is itself the system's strongest security property.

| Surface | Reachable by | Current treatment |
|---------|--------------|-------------------|
| Two literal `GET` routes on `127.0.0.1:3000` | Any process on the host | Uniform, anonymous, unconditional access to two fixed literals |
| Request path and method | Any process on the host | Literal match under strict routing, case-insensitive; all other paths and methods refused `404` |
| Request headers | Any process on the host | Header block capped at the runtime's 16 KiB limit; no header is read by application code |
| Request body | Any process on the host | Never read — no parser middleware is mounted and no non-`GET` route is registered |
| Process lifecycle signals | Operator or supervisor | No handler registered; `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` cause immediate exit with no drain (§6.1.4.5) |
| Dependency tree | Operator at install time | Pinned by version and `sha512` digest; advisories unmanaged (§6.4.6.5) |
| Source and lockfile | Anyone with file-system or Git access | Protected by host and version-control permissions only; no signing or release-verification step exists |

#### 6.4.6.5 Dependency Vulnerability Register

The dependency tree is the one place where the system's security posture has changed since the project's own validation record was written, and it is worth recording precisely. The delivered work introduced the project's first npm dependency (`express ^5.2.1`), expanding the install to 66 packages — every one of them, directly or transitively, code that runs with the process's privileges. Running `npm audit` against the tree at HEAD reports **three advisories: one critical, one high and one moderate**, all transitive, all with a fix available, across 66 production dependencies. The repository's own validation record states the opposite result — `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.2 and §5 record "`npm audit` → 0 vulnerabilities" and §6 records dependency vulnerability risk as passing — which was true when it was written: advisory data changes over time, and nothing in the repository re-runs the audit, so the tree drifted out of its validated state without any signal.

| Package and version | Advisory (severity) | Effect if reached | Reachability in this deployment |
|---------------------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------------------------|
| `proxy-addr@2.0.7` | GHSA-jqcg-44mw-7w3h (critical) | IP spoofing via an IPv4-mapped IPv6 trust subnet, corrupting the resolved client address | Not reachable — `trust proxy` is `false`, so the trust function rejects every address and header values are never trusted; no handler reads `req.ip`; single-host loopback traffic |
| `body-parser@2.2.2` | GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828 (high) | Denial of service through trailing bytes after a compressed request body | Not reachable — Express loads the module at `require` time but mounts no parser middleware, no route accepts a body, and no compression middleware is installed |
| `body-parser@2.2.2` | GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (low) | An invalid `limit` value silently disables body-size enforcement | Not reachable — no parser is configured and no size limit is set by this application |
| `qs@6.15.2` | GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g (moderate) | Denial of service through an attacker-controlled `isBuffer` value | Not reachable — the framework's query parser is `simple` (Node.js `querystring`), so `qs` parses nothing, and no handler reads `req.query` |
| `qs@6.15.2` | GHSA-x5fp-wj9c-mxmx (moderate) | Array-limit bypass via bracket-key comma parsing | Not reachable — same reason: extended query parsing is never configured or invoked |

Three facts complete the picture. All three affected packages are **transitive**, arriving through Express rather than being chosen by the project, and all three sit **off the request path**, since the middleware that would invoke them is never mounted; the audit reports the same conclusion structurally by grouping all three under the critical advisory's dependency chain. All three offer a **fix** (`fixAvailable: true`), which at the time of measurement resolved to a newer lockfile entry rather than to a downgrade. And the mechanism that would have surfaced the change is missing: `package.json#scripts` holds only the unmodified `npm init` placeholder, no CI pipeline or scheduled job exists in the repository, and the manifest declares no `engines` field, no `overrides`/`resolutions` block and no audit gate — so verification depends entirely on an operator running the command by hand (§5.4.1, §6.1.4.2).


### 6.4.7 Standard Security Practices in Effect

When a detailed security architecture is not applicable, the section prompt requires that the standard security practices followed in its place be stated explicitly. The register below does that: each practice is written as a rule this system follows, with the point at which it is enforced and the evidence that it holds. The distinction that matters to a reviewer is recorded in every row — most of these practices are **consequences of the system's construction** rather than deliberately implemented controls, so they survive only as long as the construction does. Two practices are visibly *not* satisfied, and they are listed separately rather than omitted.

#### 6.4.7.1 Network and Exposure Practices

| Policy | Statement | Enforcement point | Evidence |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| Bind to the narrowest interface | Listen on the loopback address only; never bind a wildcard or routable interface | `const hostname = '127.0.0.1'` at the single `app.listen` call | `server.js:3, 26`; socket table shows `127.0.0.1:3000` only; remote connection refused |
| Expose one socket and no egress | Open exactly one listening socket and make no outbound connection | The single listener; no HTTP client, database, cache or broker client in the tree | `server.js:26`; 66-package closure contains no client (§3.4.1) |
| Do not trust client-supplied forwarding headers | Ignore `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` unless a trusted proxy is declared | Express default `trust proxy: false`, never overridden | `application.js:99`; `request.js:284-290, 327-330` |
| Keep the published contract accurate | Document every endpoint, status and refusal behaviour a caller can observe | `README.md` states both routes, their bodies and the `404` rule | `README.md:9-12` |

#### 6.4.7.2 Identity, Secret and Data Practices

| Policy | Statement | Enforcement point | Evidence |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| No credential in source control | Never commit a key, password, token, certificate or `.env` file | Repository and commit inspection; no secret-shaped string in 19 tracked files | Scan of all tracked files: zero matches; no key or secret file exists |
| No configuration secrets to leak | Keep configuration to non-sensitive literals only | Host and port are the only configuration values, both `const` literals | `server.js:3-4`; no `process.env` read anywhere (§2.4.1) |
| Collect no personal data | Read no request field that could carry a data subject's information | Neither handler dereferences `req`; nothing is logged per request | `req.` occurs zero times; observed output is the banner alone |
| Write no data at rest | Perform no file or store write, so no at-rest protection obligation arises | No `fs` usage and no datastore client anywhere | §6.2.3.4; §6.2.4.3 |
| Treat the one data-shaped fixture as inert | Keep `phonenumber.csv` out of every runtime path until a masking rule is defined | No code path opens the file | `phonenumber.csv`; §6.4.4.3 |

#### 6.4.7.3 Code, Runtime and Supply-Chain Practices

| Policy | Statement | Enforcement point | Evidence |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| Keep the dependency surface minimal | Add a package only when the requirement cannot be met by the runtime; one direct dependency today | `package.json#dependencies` holds one entry; no dev dependencies | `package.json:11-13`; all 66 resolved packages are the Express closure |
| Install reproducibly and verifiably | Resolve the tree from the lockfile so every package matches a pinned `sha512` digest | 66 lockfile entries with exact versions, registry URLs and integrity values | `package-lock.json`; §3.4.2 |
| Keep the installed tree out of version control | Ignore the generated dependency directory rather than committing it | `.gitignore` contains `node_modules/` | `.gitignore`; untracked tree confirmed |
| Use no unsafe language constructs | Avoid `eval`, `exec`, dynamic `require`, `child_process`, shell invocation and deserialization of untrusted input | None of these tokens appears in any application file | Keyword scan of all four `.js` files: zero matches |
| Return only constant content | Never reflect, template or interpolate a caller-supplied value into a response | Both bodies are source literals written with `res.end` | `server.js:15-17, 21-23`; both routes byte-verified |
| Rely on the runtime's parsing limits | Let the HTTP parser enforce message well-formedness and header size rather than writing custom parsing | Node.js parser defaults, unbounded by any project setting | `400` for malformed input; `431` above 16 KiB and accepted at 15 KiB |
| Fail fast on a broken install | Terminate immediately rather than start in a degraded state when a dependency is missing | `require('express')` at the top of the module | `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, exit `1`, no banner (§5.4.3) |
| Declare the licence | State the licence under which the code is distributed | `package.json#license` = `MIT` | `package.json`; no separate `LICENSE` file exists |

#### 6.4.7.4 Practices Not Satisfied

Recording these alongside the register keeps the "not applicable" determination from being read as "nothing to do". Each is a genuine, low-severity gap with a cheap remedy, and none of them requires the security architecture this section has found to be inapplicable.

| Practice | Status | Consequence | Remedy identified in the repository |
|----------|--------|-------------|-------------------------------------|
| Suppress framework disclosure | Not satisfied — `X-Powered-By: Express` is emitted on every response | The framework identity is disclosed to any caller that can reach the listener | `app.disable('x-powered-by')`, recorded as an optional enhancement in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3, never implemented |
| Keep dependency advisories current | Not satisfied — three advisories (one critical) sit in the tree, and no audit runs automatically | Exposure is unknown to the build and to the operator until the command is run by hand | Re-lock and reinstall; wire `npm audit` into a script or job (§6.4.6.5) |
| Mark the package non-publishable | Not satisfied — `package.json` declares no `private` field | A package named `hello_world`, version `1.0.0`, could be published accidentally | Add `"private": true` |
| Pin the runtime baseline | Not satisfied — no `engines` field and no `.nvmrc` exists | Express 5 requires Node.js 18 or later, but nothing enforces or records the requirement | Add an `engines` constraint (§2.4.1) |
| Suppress internals in error output | Not satisfied — a framework `500` carries a stack and absolute paths unless `NODE_ENV=production`, which the project never sets | Implementation detail would be disclosed if a throwing route were ever added | Set `NODE_ENV` in the run environment, or add error-handling middleware (§6.4.4.5) |
| Record failures | Not satisfied — a `404`, a `400`, a `431` and a bind failure all leave no diagnostic | Operational and possible security-relevant events are invisible | The unimplemented features F-101 and F-104 propose error logging (§6.4.9.2) |

The register as a whole describes a defensible posture for what this artifact is — an internal fixture, bound to loopback, holding no data and no secret — and an insufficient one for anything else. §6.4.9.4 states the change that would be required before the practices above could stand in for a security architecture rather than merely accompanying its absence.


### 6.4.8 Compliance Requirements

The compliance posture of this fixture is "out of scope" for the conventional regulatory regimes, because no personal, financial, health or otherwise regulated data enters the system: no record is created, none is persisted, none is logged and none is disclosed. Section §6.2.4 dispositions the data-side obligations in full — retention rules, backup and fault-tolerance policies, privacy controls, audit mechanisms and access controls — and this sub-section records the compliance determination itself, the obligations that *do* attach to repository artifacts rather than to runtime data, and the triggers that would reopen the scope.

#### 6.4.8.1 Regulatory Applicability

Each regime below is dispositioned against the same evidence: the handlers read no request field, nothing is written at rest, no outbound connection exists, and the sole data-shaped artifact is an unread fixture of synthetic values in the `+111111112xx` range (`phonenumber.csv`; §6.2.4.3).

| Regime | Applicable? | Rationale in this system |
|--------|-------------|--------------------------|
| GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) | No | No personal data is processed — no controller, no processor role, no data subject record and no transfer |
| CCPA / CPRA (California) | No | No consumer personal information is collected, sold or shared; no request field is read |
| HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) | No | No protected health information is created, received, stored or transmitted |
| PCI-DSS | No | No cardholder data and no payment path; the system is not a payment component |
| SOX §404 and financial-reporting controls | No | No financial data and no financial-reporting workflow is involved |
| SOC 2 Type II | No | The service is not a service organisation in audit scope and processes no customer data |
| FedRAMP / FISMA | No | Not deployed to a government cloud; no authorisation boundary or control baseline is claimed |
| COPPA (15 U.S.C. §6501) | No | No children's data is collected and no user-facing service exists |
| ISO/IEC 27001, NIST SP 800-53, CIS Controls | No | No control framework is adopted, assessed or claimed anywhere in the repository |

The determination is not merely an absence of data. It also reflects the repository's own scope decisions: authentication, TLS, configuration files and environment-variable support were excluded from the delivered work (`blitzy/documentation/Agent Action Plan.md` §0.6.2), and the unimplemented hardening plan forbids adding HTTPS/TLS, authentication, authorization, request-parsing middleware and database connections (`Response.txt` §0.5). Nothing in the repository claims a control framework or an attestation, and no compliance artifact — policy, procedure, control matrix, statement of applicability or audit report — is tracked.

#### 6.4.8.2 Obligations That Would Attach If Regulated Data Appeared

| Obligation family | Applies today? | What would have to exist first |
|-------------------|----------------|-------------------------------|
| Lawful basis, notice and consent records | No — no data subject exists in the system | A collecting endpoint, a storage layer and a purpose record |
| Retention schedule and secure disposal | No — nothing is retained | Any persistence at all; today the only durable artifact is the Git-tracked source (§6.2.4.1) |
| Subject access, correction and erasure | No — no subject data is held | A record keyed to an identifiable person, plus a workflow to reach it |
| Breach detection and notification | No — no log, alert or monitoring surface exists to detect a breach | Request-level logging and an alerting path (§6.4.3.5) |
| Encryption at rest and in transit | No — no data at rest and cleartext loopback transport | A store, a key-management layer and transport security (§6.4.4) |
| Processor and sub-processor agreements | No — no third party processes data on the system's behalf | Any outbound integration, of which there is none (§3.4.1) |
| Data-protection impact assessment | No — no high-risk processing occurs | A processing operation to assess |
| Records of processing activities | No — nothing is processed, so no register is maintained | A processing inventory; none exists |

#### 6.4.8.3 Obligations That Do Attach to the Repository

Two classes of obligation survive the "no data" determination, because they concern the code and its dependencies rather than runtime data: licence compliance, and the duty of care over third-party code that runs with the process's privileges. Both are currently satisfied only partially and by convention rather than by an enforced gate.

| Obligation | Status | Evidence |
|------------|--------|----------|
| Declared licence for the project's own code | Satisfied — `MIT` is declared in the manifest; no separate `LICENSE` file is tracked | `package.json`; `git ls-files` |
| Third-party licence inventory | Derivable but not produced — the lockfile records a licence for every entry: 61 `MIT`, 4 `ISC` (`inherits`, `once`, `setprototypeof`, `wrappy`) and 1 `BSD-3-Clause` (`qs`) | `package-lock.json` |
| Component inventory (SBOM) | Not produced — no SBOM, cyclonedx or SPDX artifact exists; the lockfile is the only usable substitute, listing 66 entries with exact versions, registry URLs and `sha512` digests | `package-lock.json`; no such file in `git ls-files` |
| Known-vulnerability duty of care | Not satisfied as an ongoing control — three advisories (one critical) are present and nothing re-runs the audit automatically | §6.4.6.5; `package.json#scripts` holds only the placeholder `test` script |
| Attribution for bundled dependencies | Not addressed — no notices file, no third-party attribution list | `git ls-files` |
| Runtime version requirement | Not recorded — no `engines` field and no `.nvmrc`, though Express 5 requires Node.js 18 or later | `package.json`; §2.4.1 |
| Security-relevant documentation | Partial — the framework identity and the two routes are documented; the security posture, the loopback boundary and the absent controls are not described to a reader of `README.md` | `README.md:4-23` |

#### 6.4.8.4 Triggers That Would Reopen the Compliance Scope

The disposition above changes the moment the system acquires data, an edge or an identity. Each trigger names the regime it would activate and the architectural precondition it would require, so that a reviewer can recognise one instead of discovering it after the fact.

| Trigger | Regime or obligation activated | Architectural precondition |
|---------|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Binding a non-loopback interface or fronting the service with a proxy | GDPR, CCPA/CPRA and host-security obligations, once any caller data exists | Transport security, access control at the new boundary and request logging |
| Reading any request field into an output or a log | GDPR and CCPA/CPRA, if the field identifies a person; log-protection obligations | Masking and redaction rules with an enforcement point (§6.4.4.3) |
| Introducing any persistence (database, file, cache) | Retention, erasure, encryption-at-rest and backup obligations | A store with access control, key management and a retention policy |
| Introducing authentication or user accounts | GDPR and CCPA/CPRA subject rights; credential-protection obligations | A credential store with hashing, a session lifecycle and transport security |
| Processing payment, health or children's data | PCI-DSS, HIPAA or COPPA respectively | A dedicated control baseline and a compliance programme; neither exists |

Until one of these triggers occurs, the determination stands: no regulatory compliance obligation attaches to this system's runtime behaviour, and the obligations that do attach concern the repository's licence declarations, its third-party inventory and its unmanaged dependency advisories (§6.4.6.5).


### 6.4.9 Forward-Looking Considerations

Two classes of change could alter this section: work already recorded in the repository but not implemented, and a scope expansion that would give the system the identity, data or network edge it currently lacks. The first leaves the determination of §6.4.1 intact; the second would replace it.

#### 6.4.9.1 Recorded but Unimplemented Enhancements

`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3 records three deferred items as outside the delivered work. Only one of them is a security item, and it is the smallest one in the list.

| Enhancement | Security effect | Status |
|-------------|-----------------|--------|
| Suppress the `X-Powered-By` header (~0.25 h) | Removes the framework fingerprint from every response, including `404`s | Not implemented; the header is present on all responses observed at HEAD |
| Parameterise host and port through environment variables (~1.0 h) | **Removes the system's only control** if the new value is not loopback; it is a prerequisite for any deployment, and a deployment needs authentication, authorization and transport security first | Not implemented; both values remain `const` literals |
| Add a minimal regression suite with `node:test` and `supertest` (~2.0 h) | None directly; it would give the contract a guard, since `package.json#scripts` today holds only the always-failing `npm init` placeholder | Not implemented; no test file is tracked |

#### 6.4.9.2 The Unimplemented Hardening Plan

The six features recorded in `Response.txt` §0.4 improve failure visibility and shutdown hygiene. None of them introduces authentication, authorization, transport security, input validation of request content, or any other security primitive, and the plan's own exclusion list forbids HTTPS/TLS, authentication/authorization, request-parsing middleware, health endpoints, metrics collection, database connections and manifest changes (`Response.txt` §0.5). Three of the six are *security-adjacent* in the narrow sense that they make failures visible — which is an operational property with a security benefit — and none of them changes the control matrix of §6.4.6.

| Feature | What it would add | Effect on this section |
|---------|-------------------|------------------------|
| F-101 — server `error` handler | Logs `EADDRINUSE`/`EACCES` and exits `1` instead of reporting a false success | Makes a launch failure diagnosable; adds the first failure record in the system |
| F-102 — graceful shutdown | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handlers calling `server.close()` with a 10-second force-exit guard | Availability hygiene only; requires retaining the handle `server.js:26` discards |
| F-103 — handler exception protection | `try`/`catch` with a `headersSent` guard in the handler | Makes the framework's existing `500` path explicit; would interact with the error-hygiene gap of §6.4.4.5 |
| F-104 — `clientError` handler | An explicit `400` response for malformed requests | Preserves observed runtime behaviour and adds a log line for rejected protocol traffic |
| F-105 — `req`/`res` validation | Falsy checks before use | Defensive only; neither object is dereferenced today |
| F-106 — resource-cleanup hook | A cleanup placeholder inside the shutdown callback | Placeholder only; the application owns no external resource |

The features also cannot be applied as written: they were authored against the superseded 15-line native-`http` file and their scope rules forbid the framework, route and manifest changes the delivered implementation already made, so they must be re-derived before implementation (§5.4.3).

#### 6.4.9.3 Conditions That Would Make This Section Applicable

Each trigger below would require the listed work before a security architecture could be documented rather than dispositioned as absent. None is on the current roadmap, and each would need an explicit scope expansion, since the recorded exclusions name them directly.

| Trigger | What it would require first |
|---------|-----------------------------|
| Reachability from other hosts | A deliberate change to the bind address or a fronting proxy, plus transport security and an access-control decision at the new boundary |
| Any credential or login | An identity model, a credential store with hashing, a session or token lifecycle, transport security and a password policy |
| Per-caller differentiation of access | A subject, a resource and a permission model, with a middleware pipeline to enforce it — none of which the application currently instantiates |
| Persistence of any kind | Encryption at rest, key management, access control, retention rules and an audit trail |
| Security-relevant monitoring | Request logging, an audit trail with integrity protection, and an alerting path |
| Regulatory data | A control baseline, a mapping of obligations to controls, and evidence — none of which is claimed today |

#### 6.4.9.4 What a Non-Fixture Deployment Would Require First

The order matters, because several of these cannot exist before their prerequisites do. The list is a prerequisite graph, not a backlog: item 4 blocks items 2 and 3, and item 1 blocks everything that follows it.

| Prerequisite | Why it must come first |
|--------------|------------------------|
| Decide the trust boundary and the transport | Nothing else can be authorised before it is known who can reach the service and over what; TLS termination or a local-only deployment is a decision, not a default |
| Add a configuration and secret layer | There is no `process.env` read, no configuration file and no CLI argument parsing, so no credential, endpoint or key could be injected (§2.4.1) |
| Introduce an identity model and credential store | No subject exists; hashing, session or token lifecycle and a password policy all follow from it (§6.4.2) |
| Decide authorization per route | Requires the subject of item 3 and a resource model; today both routes are public and identical (§6.4.3) |
| Add request logging and error hygiene | Without a record, no security event can be detected, and error output must stop depending on an unset `NODE_ENV` (§6.4.4.5, §6.4.3.5) |
| Suppress framework disclosure and add security headers | Cheap, independent, and should accompany any exposure beyond loopback (§6.4.6.2) |
| Wire dependency verification into the build | The tree already carries three advisories and nothing re-runs the check (§6.4.6.5) |
| Add a test harness | `package.json#scripts` holds only the always-failing placeholder, so no change today can be verified automatically (§6.4.9.1) |

#### 6.4.9.5 Changes That Would Not Alter the Determination

Three kinds of change would leave §6.4.1 standing. Upgrading the dependency tree to clear the three advisories improves the supply-chain position without adding a security control. Implementing the hardening features F-101–F-106 improves failure visibility and shutdown hygiene while explicitly forgoing authentication, authorization and TLS. And adding tests, documentation or the `private`/`engines` manifest fields closes recorded gaps in §6.4.7.4 without creating an identity, a protected resource or a remote trust boundary. Until one of the triggers in §6.4.9.3 is introduced by an explicit scope expansion, the determination recorded at the head of this section — **Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system**, with the loopback binding as its sole control and the practices in §6.4.7 as its substitute — remains accurate.


### 6.4.10 References

#### 6.4.10.1 Files Examined

- `server.js` — the entire executable surface: `require('express')` at line 1; the `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` and `port = 3000` literals at lines 3-4; `app.enable('strict routing')` at line 12; the two literal `GET` handlers at lines 14-24 writing `'Hello, World!\n'` and `'Good evening'` with `res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader('Content-Type','text/plain')` and `res.end`; and `app.listen` at lines 26-28 with the startup banner. Establishes the loopback bind, the absence of middleware, authentication, authorization, validation and logging code, and the discarded server handle
- `package.json` — the sole declared dependency `express: "^5.2.1"` with no dev dependencies; `license` `MIT`; the placeholder `test` script `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`; `main` naming an absent `index.js`; and the absence of `private`, `engines`, `overrides` and metadata fields
- `package-lock.json` — `lockfileVersion` 3, a root `""` entry mirroring the manifest, and 66 non-root entries with exact versions, registry URLs, `sha512` integrity digests and licences (61 `MIT`, 4 `ISC`, 1 `BSD-3-Clause`); establishes that no identity, cryptographic, session, validation, limiting or audit library exists in the resolved tree, and that `proxy-addr`, `body-parser` and `qs` are present as transitives
- `.gitignore` — one line, `node_modules/`; establishes that the installed tree is untracked and reproducible from the lockfile alone
- `README.md` — the published contract at lines 4-23: the framework and dependency note, both endpoints with status, content type and body, the `404` rule, the run steps, and the loopback address; line 2 supplies the "test project for backprop integration" role discussed in §6.4.1.3
- `phonenumber.csv` — 621 bytes: header `message,phonenumber` plus 15 synthetic rows in the `+111111112xx` range; the only contact-shaped artifact in the repository and the only candidate data class for a masking rule (§6.4.4.3)
- `Response.txt` — the unimplemented remediation transcript for the superseded native-`http` server: the six hardening features F-101–F-106 in §0.4, their graceful-shutdown design, and the §0.5 exclusion list that names HTTPS/TLS support, authentication/authorization, request-parsing middleware, health endpoints, metrics collection, database connections and configuration management as out of scope
- `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js`, `QWYFFGHGHFDDJFDame_!@#$%^&(){}long_name…_server.js` — three byte-identical 14-line native-`http` fixtures bound to the same loopback address and port, answering any method and path with `Hello, World!\n`; establishes that they are never loaded by the service and contain no security code either

#### 6.4.10.4 Runtime Evidence

Every behavioural claim in this section was observed at HEAD on this checkout, with `node server.js` running on Node v22.23.3 with npm 11.21.0 over loopback, and no web source was consulted for any of them. Recorded directly: both registered routes returning `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `X-Powered-By: Express`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` and `Content-Length` of 14 and 12 bytes, and no other header beyond the `Date`; the byte-exact bodies `Hello, World!\n` and `Good evening`; `GET /good-evening/`, `GET /missing` and `POST /` returning `404` with a `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` document carrying `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; `OPTIONS /` returning `200` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` and a matching `nosniff` header; and an `Origin`-bearing request receiving no `Access-Control-*` and no `Vary` header. A request carrying `Authorization: Bearer x`, `Cookie: session=abc; user=1`, `X-Api-Key: k` and `X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7` returned a response byte-identical to the anonymous request, with no `Set-Cookie`; no response in any probe carried `Set-Cookie`, `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy` on a `200`. A malformed request line was answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close` while the process kept serving and logged nothing; a 20 KiB header block was answered `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` and a 15 KiB block accepted with `200`. The host's non-loopback address `10.11.0.44:3000` refused the connection (curl exit 7) while `127.0.0.1:3000` answered, and the listening socket appeared in `/proc/net/tcp` as the single `LISTEN` entry `0100007F:0BB8`. Express defaults were read at runtime (`env=development`, `trust proxy=false`, `x-powered-by=true`, `query parser=simple`) and the error path was probed on a scratch route outside the repository: with `NODE_ENV` unset the framework returned a 1,568-byte `500` document containing a stack trace and absolute filesystem paths, and with `NODE_ENV=production` the same failure returned a 148-byte document while the stack still reached standard error. Dependency facts were read from `package.json`, `package-lock.json` and the installed `node_modules/` listing, file and commit inventories from `git ls-files`, `git log` and `git rev-parse --short HEAD`, and the advisories below from `npm audit` against the public registry.

## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Applicability Determination

**Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

`hao-backprop-test` is a single-process, single-file, stateless HTTP server. Its entire executable surface is `server.js` — 29 lines of CommonJS holding one `require` of `express` (line 1), two configuration literals (lines 3-4), one framework setting (line 12), two route registrations whose handlers write compile-time string literals (lines 14-24), and one listener that binds the literal loopback address (lines 26-28). The system owns no datastore, no cache, no queue, no second process, no outbound connection, no container and no deployment platform to observe. What it emits in its lifetime is one unstructured line of text on standard output, and what it exposes is a TCP socket and a process exit status.

Because there is nothing to instrument, nothing to aggregate and nothing to page anyone about, the section prompt's five required topic clusters resolve as follows.

| Required topic cluster | Determination | Documented in |
|------------------------|---------------|---------------|
| Monitoring Infrastructure — metrics collection, log aggregation, distributed tracing, alert management, dashboard design | Verified absent — no library, agent, exporter, shipper, rule or dashboard exists, and no configuration surface exists to declare one | §6.5.2 |
| Observability Patterns — health checks, performance metrics, business metrics, SLA monitoring, capacity tracking | Not applicable — no probe surface, no metric emission, no business transaction, no committed target and no capacity signal | §6.5.3 |
| Incident Response — alert routing, escalation, runbooks, post-mortems, improvement tracking | Absent as a process — the repository carries an operator guide and a risk register instead, with no routing destination, roster, incident record or tracker | §6.5.4 |
| Required diagrams — monitoring architecture, alert flow, dashboard layout | Supplied as null-topology and boundary views that mark each absent component and the one edge that exists | §6.5.5 |
| Metric definitions, alert threshold matrices, SLA requirements | Registers supplied in the required tabular form; every row resolves to "no metric is emitted", "no threshold is defined" or "no SLA is committed" | §6.5.6 |
| Standard practices followed instead | Recorded as a policy register with the enforcement point and evidence for each rule, plus the practices that are not satisfied | §6.5.7 |

#### 6.5.1.1 Basis of the Determination

Nine independently verified facts carry the verdict. Each is stated with the evidence it rests on, because the same reasoning recurs in every sub-section that follows.

1. **The only observability emission is a single startup line.** `console.log` in the `app.listen` callback (`server.js:27`) writes `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`.
