The distinction that matters to a reviewer is recorded in every row — most of these practices are **consequences of the system's construction**, not deliberately implemented instrumentation — so they survive only as long as the construction does. Seven practices are visibly *not* satisfied, and they are listed separately rather than omitted, because a "not applicable" determination must not be read as "nothing to do".

#### 6.5.7.1 Observation Practices

| Practice | Statement | Enforcement point | Evidence |
|----------|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| Observe from outside the process | Do not rely on in-process telemetry, because none exists; read the process's output, exit status and socket from the host | The operator's terminal, the shell's exit status, and host tooling | §5.4.1; observed: one stdout line, `lsof -i :3000` for socket state, exit status `0`/`1`/`130`/`143` |
| Treat the banner as a startup notice, never as a readiness signal | The banner proves the listener callback ran, not that the bind succeeded | Operator knowledge, recorded in this specification rather than in code | `server.js:26-28`; `node_modules/express/lib/application.js:598-606`; observed banner with exit `0` on a held port |
| Test availability with a real request, not with a socket or a banner | The only trustworthy readiness evidence is a `200` from a registered path | `Project Guide.md` §9.5, the documented verification sequence executed by the operator | `Project Guide.md` §9.5 lists `curl -i` on both routes as the first verification steps |
| Verify the contract byte-exactly, not approximately | Confirm the exact body, including trailing-newline presence or absence, rather than trusting a visual check | `Project Guide.md` §9.5 uses `od -c` on both routes | `Project Guide.md` §9.5: `Hello, World!\n` is 14 bytes and `Good evening` is 12 bytes with no newline |
| Validate the source before restarting | Run a syntax check before starting the process, since a syntax error produces only a loader failure | `Project Guide.md` §9.5 and Appendix F use `node --check server.js` | `Project Guide.md` §9.5; exit `0` expected |
| Capture standard output when running detached | Redirect the process's streams to a file when it is not supervised by a terminal, since nothing else persists them | `Project Guide.md` §9.4 documents `node server.js > server.log 2>&1 &` | `Project Guide.md` §9.4; the only log-retention practice in the project |
| Maintain one process per host, so no aggregation is required | Keep the deployment shape small enough that a single terminal can observe it | The single hardcoded loopback listener; no clustering, forking or worker path exists | `server.js:3, 26`; no `cluster` or worker-thread usage anywhere |

#### 6.5.7.2 Dependency and Change Practices

| Practice | Statement | Enforcement point | Evidence |
|----------|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| Keep the installed tree reproducible | Resolve every package from the lockfile so the tree that is observed is the tree that was validated | 66 lockfile entries with exact versions, registry URLs and `sha512` integrity digests | `package-lock.json`; `Project Guide.md` §9.3 (`npm ci`) |
| Re-run the dependency audit by hand | Check the tree for advisories manually, since nothing does it automatically | `npm audit`, documented in `Project Guide.md` Appendix A | `Project Guide.md` Appendix A lists `npm audit`; at HEAD it reports three advisories, one critical (§6.4.6.5) |
| Verify dependency presence before diagnosing behaviour | Distinguish a missing dependency from a service fault, because both present as "not answering" | `Project Guide.md` §9.7 first troubleshooting row | `Project Guide.md` §9.7: `Cannot find module 'express'` → run `npm ci` |
| Track improvements in the documentation set, deliberately | Record deferred work with effort and priority where a reader will find it, since no tracker is used | `Project Guide.md` §2.2 and §2.3 tables; `Response.txt` §0.4's feature list | `Project Guide.md` §2.3 lists four deferred items with indicative effort; §2.2 lists 1.5 h of human steps with priority |
| Keep the process single-tenant and stateless, so recovery is a restart | Avoid state that would require recovery procedures, reconciliation or replay | The design as delivered: no datastore, no file writes, no session | §5.4.6; §6.5.4.2 |

#### 6.5.7.3 Practices Not Satisfied

Each row is a genuine, low-severity gap with a cheap remedy, and none of them requires the monitoring architecture this section has found to be inapplicable. Recording them keeps the determination from being read as an absence of findings.

| Practice | Status | Consequence | Remedy identified in the repository |
|----------|--------|-------------|--------------------------------------|
| Record failures | Not satisfied — a bind failure, a `404`, a `400` and a `431` all leave no diagnostic anywhere | Start-up and refusal events are invisible, and a held port reports success | `Response.txt` F-101 (log a bind failure and exit `1`) and F-104 (log rejected protocol traffic); both unimplemented (§6.5.8.2) |
| Distinguish readiness from liveness | Not satisfied — the only start-up signal is emitted on a failed bind as well as a successful one | An operator or supervisor reading the banner would treat a dead service as healthy | `Response.txt` F-101; the check list in §6.5.6.2 replaces the banner with a real request |
| Detect anomalies automatically | Not satisfied — no rule, evaluator or notification channel exists | Every failure is found by a human noticing, if at all | None recorded; this is the largest gap and the first item in §6.5.8.3 |
| Measure anything | Not satisfied — no metric, gauge, counter or histogram is produced | No trend, no baseline and no capacity figure can be established | None recorded; §6.5.8.3 makes the telemetry decision the prerequisite for instrumentation |
| Retain and rotate logs | Not satisfied — nothing is written to disk unless the operator redirects the streams, and no rotation rule exists | A crash that writes a stack to an unredirected terminal leaves no durable record | `Project Guide.md` §9.4's redirect practice is the only mechanism; no rotation is documented |
| Monitor dependency drift | Not satisfied — `npm audit` is a manual command and the recorded result is already stale | Three advisories, one critical, sit in the tree unnoticed (§6.4.6.5) | `Project Guide.md` Appendix A documents the command; wiring it into a job or script is not addressed |
| Attribute an event to a caller or a request | Not satisfied — no request identifier, no access record and no audit trail exists | No question about who called, when or whether it was permitted can be answered from the application | §6.4.3.5 records the same finding for the audit dimension; no remedy is proposed in the repository |

### 6.5.8 Forward-Looking Considerations

Two classes of change could alter this section: work already recorded in the repository but not implemented, and a scope expansion that would give the system something worth monitoring — a health surface, a request record, a metric, a target or a second host. The first leaves the determination of §6.5.1 intact and improves the signal surface modestly; the second would replace the determination outright.

#### 6.5.8.1 Recorded but Unimplemented Enhancements

`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.3 records four items as outside the delivered work, with indicative effort. Only one of them adds an automated signal, and even that one is a test rather than a monitor.

| Enhancement | Indicative effort | Effect on monitoring |
|-------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Minimal automated test suite (`node:test` + `supertest`) | ~2.0 h | Would give the contract a repeatable guard in place of the manual `curl`/`od -c` sequence, and would make `npm test` meaningful instead of the always-failing placeholder — a change-detection signal, not a runtime one |
| Suppress the `X-Powered-By` header (`app.disable`) | ~0.25 h | Reduces framework disclosure on every response; no monitoring effect other than removing a field from response inspection |
| Parameterise host and port through environment variables | ~1.0 h | Prerequisite for any deployment-time telemetry configuration, since today there is no configuration surface at all; also removes the only security control if the value is not loopback (§6.4.1.2) |
| `Response.txt` hardening (graceful shutdown, health, error handlers) | Separate initiative | The only recorded item with a direct monitoring effect; dispositioned in §6.5.8.2 |

#### 6.5.8.2 The Unimplemented Hardening Plan and Its Monitoring Effect

Six features are specified in `Response.txt` §0.4 (F-101 through F-106). Together they would add the first failure records and the first shutdown records the system has ever produced, and they remain console-only: the plan adds no library, no shipper, no metric and no endpoint. Its own exclusion list forbids exactly the changes that would make this section applicable — health check endpoints, metrics collection, logging libraries and manifest changes (`Response.txt` §0.5).

| Feature | What it would add | Monitoring effect |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|
| F-101 — server `error` handler | Logs `EADDRINUSE`/`EACCES` to stderr and exits `1` instead of printing a false success | **The highest-value observability change available**: it converts the system's silent, inverted bind failure into a durable stderr record and a non-zero exit status an operator or supervisor can act on |
| F-102 — graceful shutdown | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handlers calling `server.close()` with a 10-second force-exit guard and phase logs | Adds the first shutdown records and bounds in-flight request loss; requires retaining the handle that `server.js:26` currently discards |
| F-103 — handler exception protection | `try`/`catch` with a `headersSent` guard in the handler | Makes the framework's existing `500` path explicit; the stack already reaches stderr through `logerror` because `env` is `development` |
| F-104 — `clientError` handler | An explicit `400` response plus a log line for malformed requests | Makes rejected protocol traffic visible, which is invisible today |
| F-105 — `req`/`res` validation | Falsy checks before use | No monitoring effect; neither object is dereferenced today |
| F-106 — resource-cleanup hook | A cleanup placeholder inside the shutdown callback | No monitoring effect; the application owns no external resource |

Two limitations must accompany the table. First, nothing in the plan introduces a metric, a trace, a health endpoint, a log sink or a notification channel, so even if all six features were implemented the determination at §6.5.1 would stand: the system would still be monitored by reading text. Second, the features cannot be applied as written — they were authored against the superseded 15-line native-`http` file and their scope rules forbid the framework, route and manifest changes the delivered implementation already made, so they must be re-derived before implementation (§5.4.3, §6.4.9.2).

#### 6.5.8.3 Conditions That Would Make This Section Applicable

Each trigger below would create something to monitor and would therefore require the listed work before a monitoring architecture could be documented rather than dispositioned as absent. The order in the second table matters, because several of these cannot exist before their prerequisites do.

| Trigger | What it would create | What it would require first |
|---------|----------------------|-----------------------------|
| A bind address change or a fronting proxy | A reachable service with a real network edge and an availability question | Transport security, an access-control decision, and an availability definition to monitor against |
| A container or orchestrator deployment | Platform probe semantics and platform-side metrics | A liveness and readiness endpoint, and a configuration surface to declare probes |
| Any customer or SLA | A committed target and a reporting obligation | Service-level indicators, a measurement source and a store to aggregate over time |
| Request-level logging | The first per-request record and a log stream to aggregate | A logging library or structured output, a sink, and a retention and rotation rule |
| Any metric instrumentation | Counters, histograms and a scrape or push surface | A metrics library, call sites, an exporter, a store and a dashboard |
| Any persistence or external call | State to measure, latency to trace and dependencies to check | A datastore or client, plus tracing instrumentation and health checks for the dependency |
| Additional routes or request-input reading | Meaningful error rates, refusal rates and input-derived dimensions | Validation, error handling and a status-labelled counter |
| CI, or a published package | An automated quality and security signal | A pipeline or script wiring `npm audit` and the test suite into a gate |

| Prerequisite | Why it must come first |
|--------------|------------------------|
| Decide where telemetry goes and what it is for | The repository defines no monitoring objective and has no recipient for a signal; a destination and a purpose are decisions, not defaults |
| Add a configuration and secret layer | There is no `process.env` read, no configuration file and no CLI argument parsing (§2.4.1), so no collector address, endpoint or credential could be supplied to any agent |
| Add the emission points | No call site exists at which a metric could be created, and no `app.use` pipeline exists in which a middleware-based library could be mounted |
| Add collection and storage | Without a store, nothing can be aggregated, compared over time or alerted on |
| Add rules, thresholds and a notification channel | Requires a signal and a target; §6.5.6.2 shows every row currently ending in a manual step |
| Add a dashboard | Requires a data source; §6.5.5.3 shows every panel empty for want of one |
| Add the process around the tooling | Routing, escalation, runbooks and post-mortems are organizational work that no library supplies, and §6.5.4 records none of it |

#### 6.5.8.4 Changes That Would Not Alter the Determination

Four kinds of change leave §6.5.1 standing. Implementing the hardening features F-101 through F-106 improves failure visibility and shutdown hygiene while remaining console-only, with no metric, trace, health or alerting surface. Upgrading the dependency tree to clear the three advisories improves the supply-chain position without creating a signal. Adding tests, an `engines` constraint, a `.nvmrc`, a `private` flag or reader-facing documentation closes recorded gaps in §6.5.7.3 without producing a metric or a target. And suppressing `X-Powered-By` removes a disclosure without adding an observation. Until one of the triggers in §6.5.8.3 is introduced by an explicit scope expansion, the determination recorded at the head of this section — **Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system**, with a single startup line on stdout as its only observability emission and the practices in §6.5.7 as its substitute — remains accurate. What would change first, and cheaply, is the honest reporting of a start-up failure: a held port that reports success is the one gap in this system that costs an operator real diagnostic time, and §6.5.8.2 records the single feature that closes it.

#### 6.5.9.4 Runtime Evidence

Every behavioural claim in this section was observed at HEAD on this checkout, with `node server.js` running over loopback, and none of it was inferred from documentation. Recorded directly: the process emits exactly one line of standard output — `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` — and zero bytes of standard error across twelve requests spanning both registered routes, six probe paths, a `POST /`, an unmatched path and a malformed request; `GET /` returns `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `X-Powered-By: Express`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` and a `Date` header, and `GET /good-evening` returns the same shape with a 12-byte body; `/health`, `/healthz`, `/metrics`, `/ready`, `/livez` and `/status` each return `404`, and `POST /` returns `404`; a `404` document carries `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a `Cannot <METHOD> <path>` HTML body of 143 bytes, with nothing logged; a malformed request line is answered `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`, with zero bytes on standard error and the process still serving a subsequent `200`. A second instance launched while port 3000 was held printed the success banner, wrote zero bytes to standard error and exited with status `0`; the first instance exited `143` on `SIGTERM` with no shutdown log, and a separate run exited `130` on `SIGINT`. Under `DEBUG=*` the process emitted 25 lines on standard error, including `express:application booting in development mode`, `set "x-powered-by" to true`, `set "etag" to 'weak'`, `set "query parser" to 'simple'`, `set "trust proxy" to false` and per-request `router dispatching GET /` lines; with `DEBUG` unset, nothing but the banner is emitted. Dependency and inventory facts were read from `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `npm ls --depth=0`, a directory listing of all 65 installed top-level packages, explicit existence checks for 19 observability packages, and `find` sweeps for configuration, container, pipeline and ownership files. Search evidence was gathered with recursive text searches over every non-`node_modules` file for logging, metrics, tracing, APM, health-probe, readiness, process-lifecycle and marker vocabularies. Measured tool versions on this checkout were Node.js `v22.23.3` and npm `11.21.0`; `Project Guide.md` Appendix D records Node.js `v20.20.2` and npm `11.1.0` for the validation environment, which is a version difference in the documented versus measured runtime rather than a behavioural claim in this section.

#### 6.5.9.5 External Sources

Four external facts were confirmed for the statements this section makes about signal interpretation, and no external source was used to infer repository behaviour.

- [web] Node.js v22 Process documentation (`https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html`) — confirmed that `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` have default handlers on non-Windows platforms that exit with code `128 + signal number`, that signal exits generally follow the `128 + N` POSIX practice, that `'uncaughtException'` is handled by default by printing the stack trace to standard error and exiting with code `1`, and that installing an `'uncaughtException'` or signal listener removes the corresponding default
- [web] Node.js Errors and Events documentation (`https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/errors.html`, `https://nodejs.org/api/events.html`) — confirmed that an unhandled `'error'` event on an EventEmitter object is thrown as `ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR`, causing the stack trace to be printed and the process to exit, which is why an unhandled server `'error'` event carries exit code `1` rather than `128 + signal`
- [web] Linux `signal(7)` manual page (`https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html`) and the GNU Bash Reference Manual, Exit Status (`https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Exit-Status.html`) — confirmed that `SIGINT` is signal 2 and `SIGTERM` is signal 15, and that a command terminating on a fatal signal whose number is N yields the exit status `128 + N`, which is the source of the observed `130` and `143` values
- [web] Node.js v22 Console documentation (`https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/console.html`) and Command-line API documentation (`https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html`) — confirmed that the global `console` sends its output to `process.stdout` and `process.stderr`, and that writing warnings to a file requires the opt-in `--redirect-warnings=file` flag, supporting the statement that no runtime writes a log file by default and that nothing in this repository persists the startup banner

## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Applicability Determination

**Detailed Testing Strategy is not applicable for this system.**

`server.js` is the repository's only executable application module: 28 lines (870 bytes) of CommonJS that call `express()` once, enable a single setting, register two literal `GET` routes, and start one listener on `127.0.0.1:3000`. It exports nothing, mounts no middleware, keeps no state between requests, and never dereferences the request object — each handler performs three statements and ends with a fixed string literal. A conventional test pyramid has nothing to distribute across that surface: there is one process and one code path per route (Section 4.1), no peer service (Section 6.1), no database (Section 6.2), no external integration (Section 6.3), no authentication or authorization surface (Section 6.4), no monitoring backend (Section 6.5) and no committed service-level objective (Section 5.4.5).

The repository likewise contains no testing infrastructure of any kind. `package.json` declares no `devDependencies`; `node_modules/` holds 65 top-level packages, all of them Express 5.2.1 transitive dependencies, and contains no `node_modules/.bin` directory at all; no `test/`, `tests/`, `spec/` or `__tests__/` directory and no `*.test.js` or `*.spec.js` file exists anywhere in the tree; no test-runner, assertion, mocking, HTTP-client or coverage configuration file is present; and `package.json#scripts.test` is the untouched `npm init` placeholder `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`, which was re-run for this specification and exits with status 1 by design. A repository-wide text search of every non-`node_modules` file for `require('mocha'|'jest'|'chai'|'supertest'|'tap'|'ava'|'sinon'|'nock'|'vitest')`, `describe(`, `it(`, `assert.`, `node:test` and `--coverage` returns no match in any file.

The determination is not a claim that the system is unverified. Verification of record exists and is documented: `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 records a 15-check validation register executed against this build — 9 functional/runtime HTTP-contract checks, 1 static syntax check, 1 dependency install, 1 security audit, 1 dependency-tree check and 2 manifest-validity checks — with 15 passed, 0 failed and a 100% pass rate, corroborated there by an independent re-execution. Those practices are documented in Section 6.6.7, and the minimal automated suite the same document recommends for the future is documented in Section 6.6.2.1.

#### 6.6.1.1 Basis of the Determination

Eight mutually reinforcing facts, each established by inspecting this checkout at HEAD, carry the determination.

1. **Internal fixture, not a product.** `README.md` line 2 identifies the project as `hao-backprop-test`, a "test project for backprop integration". The artefact being documented is itself a verification fixture for an external workflow, so the motivations of a test pyramid — regression protection of business logic, contract validation against consumers, capacity planning under load — are absent together with the context that produces them (Section 6.1.1.2, Section 6.5.1.2).

2. **Trivial executable surface.** The entire executable surface is 28 lines in a single file, auditable from source in seconds (Section 6.6.7.3). Two handlers of three statements each are not a body of logic that coverage instrumentation would meaningfully measure.

3. **Deterministic, input-independent handlers.** Neither handler reads `req` — no method, path, header, query value or body reaches a decision. Each response is a fixed literal, so there is no branch for a unit test to steer and no input space to partition (Section 4.5).

4. **One process, no peers, no state.** A single listener bound to the loopback interface, an empty application cache, nothing persisted, nothing queued, nothing called outwards (Section 6.1.2, Section 6.2).

5. **No test dependency is installed or declared.** The locked closure is Express 5.2.1 plus 65 transitive packages; none is a test runner, assertion library, HTTP test client, mock library or coverage tool, and the manifest has no `devDependencies` block (Section 3.3).

6. **No automation surface exists.** No CI provider configuration, no workflow file, no commit hook, no linter, formatter or type checker, and no gate of any kind; the 11-commit history contains content commits only (Section 3.6.4). There is nowhere for a test command to be wired.

7. **No threshold to enforce.** No coverage target, success-rate requirement, latency budget or quality gate is committed. The only numeric verification figures in the tree are aspirational values in `Response.txt` §0.6 for the unimplemented F-101–F-106 hardening of the earlier native-`http` variant — response under 50 ms, resident memory under 50 MB, 100 concurrent connections, a 10-second forced-shutdown guard — which Section 5.4.5 records as uncommitted and which the Express re-platform has not adopted.

8. **The files that look like tests are fixtures.** `Test.test..js`, `!@#$%^&().js` and the 170-character `QWYFF…_server.js` are byte-identical to one another (MD5 `05576d40ab8d9f141d1073f784b26e1b`, 14 lines each) and differ from `server.js` (MD5 `a423b6d4dc1c3156d7abc84ff3660a67`); they are the filesystem-resilience fixtures of feature F-009, whose value is pathological filenames rather than behavioural parity. A filename-based test-discovery glob would treat `Test.test..js` as a test and start a second listener on the already-occupied port 3000, which is why the repository's only `*test*`-named file is recorded here as a hazard rather than as coverage.

#### 6.6.1.2 Repository Role Context

The fixture role recorded in Section 6.1.1.2 and Section 6.5.1.2 governs this section as well. An internal test fixture — itself a verification artefact for a "backprop integration" workflow — is not the artefact for which a test pyramid, a coverage gate or a delivery pipeline is engineered. Verification of the fixture's own correctness is performed by the operator who runs it, through the probes documented in Section 6.6.8; verification of the *consumer* of the fixture belongs to the consuming system. The two parties meet at the published contract: `README.md` lines 4–12 state both routes, their byte-level bodies and the 404 behaviour, and that text is the only behavioural specification against which a consumer test can be written.

#### 6.6.1.3 Topic Cluster Mapping
