### 8.1.5 How the Conditional Clusters Are Treated

The section prompt makes Cloud Services, Containerization and Orchestration conditional, and permits a single sentence of non-applicability for each. They are documented here with slightly more than one sentence — a stated reason plus an inventory of the artifacts a conventional implementation would carry and this one does not — because that is what makes the absence auditable for a reviewer who must decide whether an infrastructure section is genuinely unnecessary or merely missing. This follows the treatment §6.5.1 and §7.1 already gave to their own not-applicable determinations. The reasoning in every case is the same and rests on the evidence in §8.1.1: no artifact of the category exists, no dependency of the category is installed, and §1.3.2.1 excludes the category from scope.

## 8.2 Minimal Build and Distribution Requirements

As the section prompt directs for a system without deployment infrastructure, this sub-section records the build and distribution requirements the system does have. They are deliberately small: the only transformation between the repository and a running service is dependency installation, and the only delivery mechanism is a copy of the working tree.

### 8.2.1 Build Procedure

There is no compilation step. The "build" is dependency installation and nothing else, because `server.js` is CommonJS source executed directly by `node`.

| Aspect | Detail | Evidence |
|--------|--------|----------|
| Build inputs | `server.js`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json` — nothing else in the checkout is read by the build or the runtime | `server.js:1`; `package.json` |
| Build command | `npm ci` (reproducible, installed from the lockfile) or `npm install` (may resolve newer versions inside the caret range) | `README.md`; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.3 |
| Build outputs | `node_modules/` only — no bundle, no `dist/`, no generated or minified source; the deployed artifact is the source tree plus its installed dependencies | `package.json`; measured `node_modules` size 4.2 MB |
| Determinism | Guaranteed by the lockfile: 66 entries with exact versions, registry URLs and `sha512` integrity digests | `package-lock.json` |
| Ordering constraint | Installation must precede execution, because `server.js:1` requires `express` while `.gitignore` excludes `node_modules/` | `server.js:1`; `.gitignore` |
| Compilation artifacts to clean | None — no intermediate output, cache directory, or generated code exists | Repository inventory |

Two properties of that procedure deserve recording, because both affect automation built on top of it. First, **installation is a prerequisite, not an option**: a fresh checkout contains no `node_modules/`, and `node server.js` fails with `Cannot find module 'express'` until `npm ci` or `npm install` has run (§3.6.2). Second, the manifest carries a **stale entry-point declaration**: `package.json#main` names `index.js`, which does not exist in the repository. It is inert for this system — `node server.js` and the implicit `npm start` both work, because neither resolves the package entry point — but any tool that does resolve it will fail.

### 8.2.2 Distribution Procedure

Distribution is operator-driven and consists of placing the tree on a host and installing. Nothing is packaged, published or registered: there is no npm publish step, no image, no installer, no versioned release artifact and no artifact repository. Git is the transport.

| Step | Operator action | Observed result |
|------|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1 | Place the working tree on a host with a Node.js runtime | 20 tracked files (6.9 MB, dominated by four binaries the service never reads) plus the `blitzy/documentation/` subtree arrive on the filesystem |
| 2 | Install dependencies from the lockfile | `npm ci` installs 66 packages and creates the 65 top-level `node_modules/` directories the runtime needs |
| 3 | Confirm the loopback interface is available and TCP port 3000 is free | No check exists in code; a conflict is not reported as a failure (§8.2.5) |
| 4 | Start the process | `node server.js` — or `npm start`, which resolves implicitly to the same command — prints `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` and serves both routes |
| 5 | Stop the process | External signal only; measured `SIGTERM` exit code `143`, with no drain and no shutdown log |

Because the listener binds `127.0.0.1`, step 1's host is the only host that can reach the service: distribution beyond it would require a reverse proxy or networking change that §1.3.2.4 excludes. There is also no rollback artifact to distribute — recovery is redeploying a previous source revision and re-running the install (§3.6.5).

### 8.2.3 Runtime Prerequisites

| Prerequisite | Requirement | Enforcement at HEAD |
|--------------|-------------|---------------------|
| Node.js runtime | 18 or newer, the floor `express@5.2.1` declares in `engines.node: ">= 18"`; validated on Node 22 | Advisory only — `package.json` declares no `engines` field and no `engine-strict` setting exists |
| npm CLI | 7 or newer, the minimum that reads `lockfileVersion` 3 | The committed lockfile |
| Registry access | Reachable public npm registry for the 66 pinned tarballs | The `resolved` URLs in `package-lock.json` |
| Dependencies installed | `npm ci` or `npm install` completed before the first start | `server.js:1`; `.gitignore` |
| Network address | Functional loopback adapter and TCP port 3000 free | `server.js:3-4`; no fallback port and no bind-error handler |
| Disk | Approximately 4.2 MB for `node_modules/` plus the source tree | Measured `du -sh node_modules/` |
| Configuration | None to supply — no environment variable, config file or command-line argument is read | Zero matches for `process.env` or `process.argv` across the repository's JavaScript |
| Termination | An operator or supervisor to signal the process; there is no in-code shutdown path | No signal handler exists; measured `SIGTERM` exit `143` |

### 8.2.4 Package Manager and Lockfile Notes

npm is the only package-management tool in the repository: no Yarn or pnpm lockfile exists, and `package-lock.json` is `lockfileVersion` 3. Because the manifest declares `express: "^5.2.1"` while the lockfile pins 5.2.1 exactly, the two install paths are not equivalent — `npm ci` reproduces the validated tree, whereas `npm install` on a host without the lockfile may resolve a newer minor. That distinction is not academic at this snapshot: the registry's current `latest` release is a later 5.x minor than the one the lockfile pins, so the caret range admits an upgrade the lockfile does not perform. It is also why the lockfile, not the manifest, is the authoritative record of what the system runs (§3.6.2).

### 8.2.5 Startup Verification

The system's own start-up signal is a single unstructured line written by the `app.listen` callback: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`. It is useful as a start-up notice and **unsafe as a readiness signal**, for a reason that matters to any deployment automation built on it: `app.listen` registers the callback as a one-shot `error` listener, so a bind failure is delivered to it and the success line is printed anyway. Measured at HEAD, a second instance started while port 3000 was held printed the identical banner, wrote nothing to standard error and exited `0`.

The reliable readiness checks are therefore external and procedural: a real request — `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, expecting `200` — and a socket inspection such as `lsof -i :3000` to confirm the listener is bound and released across restarts. Both are documented operator steps in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.5 and Appendix F, and both are the checks §8.7.2 and §8.9.2 assume in place of pipeline gates.

### 8.2.6 Runtime Version Envelope

Nothing in the repository pins a runtime version, so the envelope is set entirely by Express's declared floor. Three external facts frame it.

| Runtime line | Status | Relevance to this system |
|--------------|--------|--------------------------|
| Node.js 18 | End-of-life since 30 April 2025 | It is Express 5's declared floor, and the absence of an `engines` pin means a host may legitimately run the service on an unsupported line that receives no security patches |
| Node.js 22 | LTS, with security support to 30 April 2027 | The runtime in the validated environment (Node v22.23.3 measured; `Project Guide.md` Appendix D records v20.20.2) |
| Node.js 24 | Became Active LTS on 28 October 2025 | A supported upgrade target that nothing in the repository declares or tests against |

The practical consequence is a distribution risk rather than an infrastructure one: because the runtime is neither pinned nor checked, two hosts running the same tree can execute it on different Node.js lines, one of which has reached end-of-life, with no warning at start-up.

## 8.3 Deployment Environment

The deployment environment cluster resolves to a direct-execution model rather than an environment architecture: the operator's own host is the only environment, configuration is source code, and there is no promotion path, no backup mechanism and no recovery automation. Each dimension is dispositioned below against the evidence that fixes it.

### 8.3.1 Target Environment Assessment

#### 8.3.1.1 Environment Type

There is no on-premises configuration, no cloud manifest, no hybrid topology and no multi-cloud reconciliation, because there is no declared deployment target of any class. The system is **host-agnostic**: it requires a runtime that can execute CommonJS `server.js`, a functioning loopback interface and a free TCP port 3000, and nothing else (§1.3.1.2). Development, verification and any operator-run instance share one execution context — the machine on which `npm ci` and `node server.js` were issued — and the artefact is byte-identical on all of them, since no environment-specific configuration exists to vary it. Concretely, the runtime environment consists of: the operating system, the Node.js runtime, the installed `node_modules/` tree, the loopback adapter, and the standard output stream the banner is written to.

#### 8.3.1.2 Geographic Distribution Requirements

**None.** The binding is a module-level constant, `const hostname = '127.0.0.1'` (`server.js:3`), so the listener is reachable only from processes on the same host; §1.3.2.4 records that any externally reachable deployment lies outside scope and would require a reverse proxy, TLS termination or networking changes that do not exist. There is no content delivery network, no edge presence, no multi-region failover, no latency-aware routing and no data-residency question, because there is no external network surface to distribute and no data to place. Measured at HEAD, the port refuses connections as soon as the process exits, so availability is entirely local.

#### 8.3.1.3 Resource Requirements

No formal resource requirement is committed anywhere in the repository. The figures below are measurements taken on the validation host at HEAD; they are observations an operator can size against, not service levels.

| Resource dimension | Specification | Observed basis |
|--------------------|---------------|----------------|
| Compute | None committed; the work is one event loop on one core | No `cluster` or `worker_threads` reference exists in any repository JavaScript file, so throughput is bounded by a single thread |
| Memory | None committed; no ceiling is declared or enforced | Idle process measured 63528-64076 KB RSS (~62 MB) and ~0.97 GB virtual; §5.4.5 records ~72 MB resident as a comparable observation |
| Storage | ~4.2 MB for `node_modules/` (65 top-level packages) plus the source tree; no runtime file I/O | Measured `du -sh node_modules/`; no `fs.` reference appears in any repository JavaScript file |
| Network | Loopback only; no external bandwidth | `server.js:3`; per-request totals measured at 0.0047 s (`GET /`) and 0.00087 s (`GET /good-evening`) |
| Start-up | No target committed | Approximately 130 ms from process exec to the first `200` response on a warm host with dependencies installed |

The sizing consequence is that the service fits comfortably inside any host capable of running a supported Node.js line, and that the binding constraint is not the application but the single-threaded runtime plus the fixed loopback binding — both of which §8.6.2 records as limits on scaling rather than as tunable parameters.

#### 8.3.1.4 Compliance and Regulatory Requirements

No regulated data regime attaches to this system, because it processes no data of any class: both handlers write compile-time string literals and never dereference `req`, `phonenumber.csv` is read by no code path, and no store, cache or session exists. Nothing is transmitted off the loopback interface, and no cryptography is used — a scan of every repository JavaScript file finds no reference to `https`, `tls` or `crypto`.

The compliance burden that does exist is licensing, and it is a distribution-time obligation rather than a runtime one. Across the 66 pinned packages, the lockfile records 61 MIT entries, four ISC entries (`inherits`, `once`, `setprototypeof`, `wrappy`) and one BSD-3-Clause entry (`qs`); `package.json` declares `"license": "MIT"` for the project itself. Notably, **no `LICENSE` file is present in the repository**, so the declared license exists only as a manifest field while the dependency obligations exist only as lockfile metadata. There is no software bill of materials, no attribution file and no license-scanning step — the same gaps §8.7.1 records as absent quality gates. Dependency-security drift is the other compliance-adjacent finding: `npm audit --omit=dev` currently reports three advisories in the resolved closure (one critical, one high, one moderate) and nothing in the repository re-runs it.

### 8.3.2 Environment Management

#### 8.3.2.1 Infrastructure as Code Approach

**No infrastructure-as-code tooling exists.** A search of the entire checkout finds no Terraform (`*.tf`, `*.tfvars`), Pulumi (`Pulumi.yaml`), CloudFormation template, CDK application, Ansible playbook, Chef cookbook, Puppet manifest or SaltStack state file. There is consequently no state backend, no provider configuration, no module registry, no plan/apply workflow and no drift-detection mechanism. The system's entire deployed state is reproducible by reading `server.js`, `package.json` and `package-lock.json` — an audit practice that substitutes for IaC verification here precisely because the surface is three files wide.

#### 8.3.2.2 Configuration Management Strategy

Configuration is hardcoded in source. The complete surface is three `const` literals, and no configuration mechanism of any kind exists to override them.

| Configuration value | Literal | Location |
|---------------------|---------|----------|
| Bind address | `'127.0.0.1'` | `server.js:3` |
| Bind port | `3000` | `server.js:4` |
| Response bodies | `'Hello, World!\n'` and `'Good evening'` | `server.js:14-24` |

The system reads no environment variable, loads no `.env` file, parses no command-line argument, reads no JSON, YAML, TOML or INI file, and consults no configuration service: a text search across every repository JavaScript file for `process.env`, `process.argv`, `app.set` and `app.use` returns zero matches. The consequences for operations are direct and worth stating plainly. Changing the port or bind address requires editing source and restarting; there is no configuration surface into which a deployment could inject a secret, a collector address, a feature flag or an environment name; and because `NODE_ENV` is never set, every instance runs in Express's default `development` mode regardless of where it is deployed, which is why the framework writes error stacks to standard error for a genuine `5xx` (§6.5.2.2).

#### 8.3.2.3 Environment Promotion Strategy

**No environment promotion model exists.** There is no `dev`, `staging`, `qa`, `uat`, `preview` or `prod` designation anywhere in the repository, no environment-specific configuration files, no `NODE_ENV` consumption, no `.env.production`/`.env.development` pairing, and no workspace or values-file stratification. The promotion path is therefore degenerate: whatever tree the operator copies and installs *is* the environment, and the artefact that runs on a development workstation is, file for file, the one that would run anywhere else. The absence is a scope decision rather than an oversight — §1.3.2.1 excludes configuration files and environment variables, and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.2 states that no environment setup is required.

#### 8.3.2.4 Backup and Disaster Recovery Plans

**No backup or disaster-recovery procedure exists.** Because the service holds no state, the recovery objective degenerates to restarting a process, and the only durability mechanism is Git.

| DR primitive | State at HEAD | Operational consequence |
|--------------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Process supervisor (PM2, systemd, forever, nodemon) | None | A crash or an operator logout ends service; nothing restarts it |
| Replica, standby or failover host | None | A single process on a single host is the whole availability story |
| Backup mechanism | Git history only, with a GitHub remote as the transport | Source recovery is `git clone` plus `npm ci`; there is no backup of a running instance because there is no state to back up |
| Rollback procedure | None documented for the current tree | `Response.txt` §0.7 prescribes a `cp server.js.backup server.js` rollback for the superseded native-`http` file, which no longer applies; recovery in practice is redeploying a previous revision and reinstalling |

Recovery-point and recovery-time objectives are undefined, and no measurement mechanism exists for either. The only relevant measured value is the restart cost on a warm host: approximately 130 ms from process start to a served request once `node_modules/` is present. On a cold host the dominant term is the dependency install, which requires registry access. Two termination behaviours belong in the same picture: `SIGTERM` ends the process with exit code `143` without draining in-flight requests, and a start-up that fails to bind reports success and exits `0` — so a supervisor added later would need to check for a served response rather than trust the exit status or the banner (§8.2.5).

## 8.4 Cloud Services

**The system does not use cloud services.** No cloud provider is selected, and no cloud provider is reachable from the application: `npm ls --depth=0` resolves `hello_world@1.0.0 -> express@5.2.1` and nothing else, and the 66 lockfile entries are the Express 5.2.1 closure alone, so no cloud SDK, CLI wrapper or provider agent can be loaded at runtime. §1.3.2.3 records the corresponding scope exclusion — no APM or log-shipping agents, no managed services, no outbound HTTP client — and §1.3.2.4 records that externally reachable deployment is unsupported.

The absence has a structural cause rather than a missing configuration: the system's only network interface is a loopback listener, so there is no workload for a provider to host, no ingress for a managed gateway to route, and no state for a managed service to persist. For completeness, the inventory below dispositions every conventional cloud-service category against that fact.

| Cloud service category | Example services | Disposition |
|------------------------|------------------|-------------|
| Compute (VMs, functions, app platforms) | EC2, Lambda, Cloud Run, App Service | Absent — no provider SDK, no deployment descriptor, no IaC |
| Container compute and registries | ECS, Fargate, EKS, GKE, ECR, ACR | Absent — no image is built (§8.5) |
| Object and block storage | S3, GCS, Blob Storage, EBS | Absent — no SDK, and no runtime file I/O exists |
| Managed databases and caches | RDS, DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, ElastiCache | Absent — no datastore or cache exists |
| Edge and content delivery | CloudFront, Cloud CDN, Cloudflare | Absent — no front-end assets and no public surface |
| Messaging and queues | SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus | Absent — no broker, no queue and no asynchronous work |
| Identity, secrets and key management | Cognito, Secrets Manager, Key Vault, KMS | Absent — no authentication, no credential and no secret to store |
| Monitoring and logging backends | CloudWatch, Cloud Logging, Azure Monitor, Datadog | Absent — the only emission is one stdout line (§8.8) |
| Networking and API management | VPC, API Gateway, Load Balancer, Route 53 | Absent — nothing beyond the OS loopback adapter is used |

Because no cloud service is consumed, there is no high-availability design (no multi-zone placement, no replica, no automatic failover), no cost-optimisation strategy (no rightsizing, no reservations, no autoscaling group) and no provider compliance posture to document. The service's only external touchpoint in its entire lifecycle is the install-time fetch of 66 pinned tarballs from the public npm registry, recorded as `resolved` URLs in `package-lock.json` — a build-time dependency, not a runtime service.

## 8.5 Containerization

**The system does not use containers.** It runs as a native Node.js process in the host's userspace, started by `node server.js`, and no container artefact of any kind exists: a search of the entire checkout for `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `.dockerignore`, Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, `project.toml` buildpack descriptors and registry configuration returns nothing. The only directories outside `node_modules/` and `.git/` are `blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/`, and §1.3.2.1 lists "container definitions, and orchestrator manifests" among the explicitly excluded lifecycle capabilities.

| Container concern | Status | Consequence |
|-------------------|--------|-------------|
| Platform (Docker, Podman, containerd, Buildah, Kaniko) | Absent | No image is built, pushed or run; no runtime socket dependency exists |
| `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore` | Absent | No build recipe, no multi-service definition, no build-context filter |
| Base image strategy (for example `node:*-alpine`, `distroless`, `scratch`) | Not defined | No base image is selected, pinned or scanned, so there is no image-level CVE surface — the supply-chain surface is the npm tree instead |
| Image versioning and registry | Not defined | No tag scheme (semver, Git SHA, `latest`) and no registry exists; distribution remains a copied source tree (§8.2.2) |
| Build optimisation (multi-stage builds, layer caching, dependency caching) | Not applicable | With no image there is no layer to cache; the 4.2 MB install is the only build output |
| Image security scanning (Trivy, Grype, Clair, Snyk Container, Anchore) | Absent | Nothing scans an image, and nothing scans the npm closure either, which is where the three recorded advisories sit (§8.7.1) |

Two structural facts would have to change before containerisation became possible, and both are recorded elsewhere in this specification. First, the bind address is a source literal (`server.js:3`), so a containerised instance would be unreachable even from the host's other processes, and unreachable from outside the container network without a code change or a proxy. Second, `node_modules/` is excluded by `.gitignore` and therefore absent from the tree, so any image build would need an `npm ci` step — and `package.json` declares no `engines` field, so a base image would be the first and only place a runtime version were pinned. Neither gap is addressed, because no container is built.

## 8.6 Orchestration

**The system does not require orchestration.** It is a single foreground process launched by an operator from a shell, with no orchestrator manifest, no process supervisor, no clustering and no service mesh. §1.3.2.1 excludes "clustering, process managers, container definitions, and orchestrator manifests" explicitly, and §1.3.2.4 records that production-grade operation — including restart-on-failure — is unsupported.

| Orchestration concern | Disposition | Evidence |
|-----------------------|-------------|----------|
| Cluster orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad, Docker Swarm) | Absent — no manifests, no chart, no task definition | Repository inventory; §8.5 |
| Process supervisor (PM2, systemd, forever, nodemon) | Absent — no unit file, no ecosystem file, no reload strategy | Repository inventory |
| Node.js clustering or worker threads | Absent — no `cluster` or `worker_threads` reference in any repository JavaScript file | Text scan of all four `.js` files |
| Service mesh or sidecar proxy (Istio, Linkerd, Envoy, Consul Connect) | Absent — no sidecar, no injection annotation, no mesh config | Repository inventory |
| Function-as-a-service runtime (Lambda, Cloud Functions, Container Apps) | Absent — no handler export, no manifest, no provider SDK | `server.js` exports nothing |

The cluster-architecture, scaling and resource-allocation dimensions therefore have no values to record, and the reason is structural rather than unfinished.

| Scaling dimension | State at HEAD | Limiting factor |
|-------------------|---------------|-----------------|
| Cluster topology (nodes, pods, replicas) | One process on one host | No orchestrator and no supervisor exist to place a second replica |
| Deployment strategy (rolling, blue-green, canary) | None | There is no fleet to update gradually; distribution is a tree copy plus a restart (§8.2.2) |
| Auto-scaling triggers and rules | None | No metrics are emitted for a rule to evaluate (§8.8) and no rule engine is installed |
| Resource requests and limits | None | No container and no orchestrator; the only ceiling is the host's own configuration |
| Disruption budgets, affinity, scheduling policy | Not applicable | No pods, nodes or scheduler exist |
| Admission control, rate limiting, connection caps | None | The listener accepts until host descriptors are exhausted; there is no back-pressure path |

Horizontal scaling is prevented by construction rather than merely unconfigured: the bind address and port are `const` literals (`server.js:3-4`), so a second instance on the same host collides on port 3000 — and, as measured at HEAD, that collision is silent: the second process printed the success banner and exited `0`. Vertical scaling is bounded only by the Node.js runtime and the host, because the application exposes no tuning knobs (no compression, no socket options, no application-set timeouts, no connection limit), and the event loop bounds throughput to one core. The service is stateless and would be trivially replicable *if* the bind address were parameterised and a supervisor existed; neither condition holds, and no mechanism in the repository can execute multiple cooperating instances.

## 8.7 CI/CD Pipeline

**The system has no CI/CD pipeline.** No `.github/` directory exists, no pipeline definition for any provider is present, and the Git history — 11 commits on one branch, all dated 2026-06-04 — contains content commits only: the dependency declaration, the Express re-platform, the ignore rule, the README contract, the strict-routing refinement, and four documentation commits. No commit has ever added a pipeline file, a build script, a deploy script or a status check. §1.3.2.1 lists "CI pipelines" among the excluded tooling capabilities.

### 8.7.1 Build Pipeline

| Build-pipeline element | Disposition | Evidence at HEAD |
|------------------------|-------------|------------------|
| Source-control triggers (push, pull request, tag) | None — no CI provider is registered and no workflow file exists to be triggered | Absence of `.github/workflows/` and of any provider marker file |
| Build-environment requirements | Any host with Node.js 18 or newer, npm 7 or newer, and network access to the public npm registry | `express@5.2.1` `engines.node: ">= 18"`; `lockfileVersion` 3; `resolved` URLs in the lockfile |
| Native toolchain requirement | None — no dependency in the resolved closure compiles native code | Search of `node_modules/` finds zero `*.node` binaries and zero `binding.gyp` files, and no `node-gyp`, `node-pre-gyp` or `nan` package is installed |
| Dependency management | `npm ci` reproduces the 66 pinned packages; `npm install` may resolve a newer minor inside the caret range | `package.json`, `package-lock.json` |
| Artefact generation and storage | None — the only build output is `node_modules/` (4.2 MB), which is git-ignored and never stored, published or tagged | `.gitignore`; `git tag` returns zero tags |
| Versioning of the artefact | None — `package.json` stays at `1.0.0` and no release artefact is produced | `package.json` |

The quality-gate row of a conventional build pipeline has no counterpart here: the gates do not exist, and the one npm script that looks like a gate is designed to fail.

| Conventional quality gate | Status | Evidence |
|---------------------------|--------|----------|
| Automated tests | Absent — the `test` script is the untouched `npm init` placeholder `echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1`, so `npm test` fails by design and guards nothing | `package.json`; §3.6.1 |
| Lint and format checks | Absent — no ESLint, Prettier, Biome or EditorConfig configuration exists | Repository inventory |
| Type checking | Absent — no TypeScript dependency and no `tsconfig.json` | Repository inventory |
| Syntax validation | Manual only — `node --check server.js` returns exit `0` and is documented as an operator step, not wired into any script | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.5 |
| Dependency vulnerability scanning | Manual only — `npm audit --omit=dev` reports three advisories (one critical in `proxy-addr`, one high in `body-parser`, one moderate in `qs`) and exits `1`, but nothing runs it automatically | Direct audit at HEAD; §6.5.2.4 |
| Coverage measurement | Absent — no coverage tool is installed and no test suite exists | Repository inventory |
| Commit hooks or local gates | Absent — no `husky`, `lint-staged` or pre-commit configuration exists | Repository inventory |
| Branch protection or required checks | None enforceable — with no pipeline there is no status check to require, and the tree carries no `CODEOWNERS` or review policy | Repository inventory |

The practical effect is that every verification this project has recorded was manual and transient: the functional contract was checked by hand with `curl` and `od -c`, and the one defect found after delivery — the trailing-slash case, fixed by enabling strict routing — was caught by human review and recorded as a commit message rather than by an automated assertion.

### 8.7.2 Deployment Pipeline

There is no deployment pipeline, because there is no deployment automation to sequence and no target environment to sequence it into.

| Deployment-pipeline element | Disposition | Evidence |
|-----------------------------|-------------|----------|
| Deployment strategy (rolling, blue-green, canary) | Not applicable — one process on one host, restarted by hand; there is no fleet to update gradually | §8.2.2; §8.6 |
| Environment promotion workflow | Not applicable — a single execution context exists, so there is no promotion edge to define | §8.3.2.3 |
| Rollback procedures | Manual and undocumented for the current tree — recovery is redeploying a previous revision and re-running the install; the repository's only written rollback procedure describes the superseded native-`http` file | `Response.txt` §0.7; §8.3.2.4 |
| Post-deployment validation | Manual and procedural, executed by the operator | `Project Guide.md` §9.5 |
| Release management (changelog, tags, release notes) | Absent — no `CHANGELOG`, no Git tags, no release notes and no release artefact; commit messages are the only change record | `git tag` returns zero tags; `package.json` stays at `1.0.0` |
| Approval gates or change management | Absent — no workflow engine, no approval step and no change record beyond the commit history | Repository inventory |

Post-deployment validation is the one element with real content, and it is a human checklist rather than an automated stage. Its checks, and the results observed at HEAD, are:

| Validation check | Command | Expected result |
|------------------|---------|-----------------|
| Root greeting intact | `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | `200 OK`, `text/plain`, `Hello, World!\n` (14 bytes) |
| Second route intact | `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/good-evening` | `200 OK`, `text/plain`, `Good evening` (12 bytes) |
| Refusal rule intact | `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/does-not-exist` | `404`, and also `404` for `/good-evening/` |
| Source valid before restart | `node --check server.js` | Exit `0` with no output |

One caveat governs the whole procedure. Because a failed bind reports success and exits `0` (§8.2.5), a validation that only reads the start-up banner or the process status cannot distinguish a serving instance from one that never bound; the reliable evidence is a `200` from a registered route, together with a socket check such as `lsof -i :3000`. Any future pipeline would have to build on that distinction, and would also need the artifacts it lacks today — a test suite and a dependency-audit stage — before its gates could fail meaningfully.

## 8.8 Infrastructure Monitoring

**The system has no infrastructure monitoring.** No host agent, exporter, collector, dashboard, probe or alert rule exists, and no configuration surface exists in which one could be declared. This sub-section records the infrastructure-level dispositions only; §6.5 Monitoring and Observability is the authoritative treatment of the subject, covering the signal surface, the metric and alert registers, the incident-response substitutes and the conditions that would make monitoring applicable. Nothing here restates it.

### 8.8.1 Resource Monitoring

No resource metric is collected at any tier. The process emits one line of standard output per lifetime and nothing else — measured at HEAD, a full request sweep produced zero bytes on standard error — so there is no host-agent stream, no in-process metric, no scrape or push endpoint and no time-series store. What exists instead is host-level visibility that requires no instrumentation: the process table, the socket table and the exit status.

| Monitoring area | Disposition | Evidence or substitute |
|-----------------|-------------|------------------------|
| Host metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) | Absent — no host agent is installed and no collector endpoint is configured | `ps` and `lsof` read by the operator; `Project Guide.md` Appendix F |
| Application metrics (counters, histograms, gauges) | Absent — no instrumented call site exists, and no middleware pipeline exists in which one could be mounted | §6.5.2.1 |
| Runtime metrics (heap, event-loop lag, GC) | Absent — no runtime metrics client is installed | §6.5.2.1 |
| Log aggregation and retention | Absent — one unstructured stdout line, no shipper, no rotation; the only persistence is a shell redirect | §6.5.2.2; `Project Guide.md` §9.4 |
| Distributed tracing | Not applicable — no distributed boundary exists to trace | §6.5.2.3 |
| Alerting and notification | Absent — no rule, evaluator, channel or recipient exists | §6.5.2.4 |
| Dashboards | Absent — no visualization tool, panel definition or data source | §6.5.2.5 |
| Synthetic or uptime probing | Absent — no prober, no second vantage point and no scheduled check | §6.5.2.4 |

The measured figures quoted earlier in this section — approximately 62-64 MB resident and 0.97 GB virtual memory while idle, roughly 130 ms from start to first served request, and per-request totals of 0.0047 s and 0.00087 s — are one-off observations taken with host tools, not values the system reports. None is retained, sampled or compared over time, so no trend, baseline or capacity model can be derived from the system itself.

### 8.8.2 Cost Monitoring and Optimisation

There is nothing to monitor for cost, and nothing to optimise. The system consumes no metered service: no cloud subscription, no managed database, no registry storage, no pipeline minute and no monitoring contract (§8.4; §8.11.3). The only resource consumption is the marginal CPU, memory and disk draw of one idle Node.js process on a host the operator already controls, which is not separately billable and is not measured. Consequently there is no cost dashboard, no budget alarm, no tagging policy, no rightsizing activity and no reserved-capacity decision — and no saving is available to capture, because the external infrastructure spend is already zero.

### 8.8.3 Security Monitoring

No security monitoring exists: there is no SIEM, IDS, IPS, endpoint agent, web application firewall or anomaly detector, and no security event log to feed one. The application produces no access record at all — neither handler dereferences `req`, so no method, path, header, origin or identity is recorded anywhere — and there is no authentication, session, token or privileged operation whose outcome could be audited. §6.4 Security Architecture carries the security disposition; the infrastructure-level findings are these:

| Security-monitoring area | Disposition | Residual exposure |
|--------------------------|-------------|-------------------|
| Access and authentication event logging | Not applicable — no authentication exists and no request field is read | None from this area; there is no credential to attack |
| Network intrusion or anomaly detection | Absent — the loopback binding means no remote traffic can arrive | The service is unreachable from other hosts, which limits rather than monitors the surface |
| Vulnerability and advisory monitoring | Absent — `npm audit` is a manual command and nothing re-runs it | Three advisories sit in the resolved closure (one critical, one high, one moderate) and grow stale between manual checks |
| Runtime tampering or integrity monitoring | Absent — no file-integrity tooling and no signature verification of the installed tree | `package-lock.json` integrity digests protect installs that use `npm ci`, but nothing verifies the installed tree afterwards |
| Configuration drift detection | Not applicable — three source literals are the entire configuration surface | Drift is detectable only by re-reading the source, which is also the only way to know the deployed state |
| Incident notification | Absent — a bind failure is unreported and a termination is unlogged | A silently dead service can persist until an operator issues a request and it refuses |

### 8.8.4 Compliance Auditing

No compliance auditing exists, because no compliance regime is triggered and no audit trail is produced. The system handles no personal, financial, health or payment data — it reads no request input, stores nothing and writes nothing to disk — so no data-protection obligation attaches to its operation (§8.3.1.4). The audit-adjacent gaps that remain are distribution-level rather than runtime ones:

- **No change-approval record.** The Git history is the only record of what changed; there is no approval workflow, no release note and no tag, so the auditability of a deployment rests on identifying the commit that produced the running tree.
- **No licence attribution artefact.** `package.json` declares MIT and the closure carries 61 MIT, four ISC and one BSD-3-Clause entry, but the repository has no `LICENSE` file, no `NOTICE`, no third-party attribution list and no software bill of materials, so the licence obligations of the dependency tree are recorded only as lockfile metadata.
- **No supply-chain attestation.** The lockfile's `sha512` digests make installs reproducible, but there is no provenance verification, no signed artefact and no vulnerability-disclosure policy file.
- **No dependency-drift detection.** Nothing schedules a rescan of the resolved tree, which is why the three recorded advisories are the clearest example in this system of a change that no mechanism would report.

### 8.8.5 What the Operator Can Observe Instead

Every row above resolves to a manual check, and the checks available are the ones the repository's own operator guide documents. They are reproduced here as the infrastructure-level subset, distinct from the functional contract checks in §8.7.2.

| Infrastructure check | Command | What it shows |
|----------------------|---------|---------------|
| Is the process still running | `ps -o pid=,rss= -p <pid>` | Presence and resident memory; no historical value and no ceiling to compare against |
| Is the listener bound | `lsof -i :3000` | One listener on `127.0.0.1:3000` while running, and nothing after the process exits |
| Is the service actually serving | `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | `200` when ready; the only trustworthy readiness evidence given the silent bind failure (§8.2.5) |
| How did the last run end | Shell exit status, or `tail -n 1 server.log` when started with the documented redirect | `0`, `1`, `130` or `143`; the log holds the single banner line and nothing more |
| Has the dependency tree drifted | `npm audit --omit=dev` | The advisory count for the pinned closure; currently three, with `npm audit` exiting `1` |

## 8.9 Required Diagrams

The prompt requires an infrastructure architecture diagram, a deployment workflow diagram, an environment promotion flow and a network architecture diagram. Because the system has no deployment, orchestration, pipeline or monitoring infrastructure, these are drawn as **null-topology views** in the style §6.5.5 and §7.1 established: each shows the one edge that exists, enumerates the components a conventional implementation would place beside it, and records that none of them has a realisation.

### 8.9.1 Infrastructure Architecture

The diagram shows the whole infrastructure topology: one process on one host, one loopback socket, one output stream, and every conventional infrastructure layer reachable only along a dashed "absent" edge.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Operator["Operator on the host<br/>manual launch"]
    LocalClient["Local HTTP client on the same host<br/>curl, smoke test or probe"]

    subgraph Host["Single host - operator workstation, dev box or CI runner"]
        OS["Operating system<br/>any platform that can run Node.js"]
        Runtime["Node.js runtime<br/>Express 5.2.1 floor is 18 or newer, nothing is pinned"]
        Process["Single Node.js process<br/>server.js, 29 lines of CommonJS"]
        Loopback["Loopback socket<br/>TCP 127.0.0.1:3000, plain HTTP"]
        Stdout["Standard output stream<br/>one banner line per process lifetime"]
        OS --> Runtime
        Runtime --> Process
        Process -->|"bind 127.0.0.1:3000"| Loopback
        Process -->|"console.log banner"| Stdout
    end

    Operator -->|"npm ci, then node server.js"| Process
    LocalClient -->|"HTTP GET"| Loopback
    Loopback -->|"200 text/plain, or 404 from the terminal responder"| LocalClient

    subgraph Absent["No realisation at HEAD"]
        NoCloud["Cloud provider<br/>no SDK in the 66-package closure"]
        NoContainer["Container image<br/>no Dockerfile, compose file or registry"]
        NoOrch["Orchestrator or supervisor<br/>no manifest, no PM2 or systemd unit"]
        NoProxy["Reverse proxy or load balancer<br/>the loopback bind precludes fronting"]
        NoPipeline["CI/CD runner<br/>no workflow, hook or build script"]
        NoIaC["Infrastructure as code<br/>no Terraform, Pulumi, CDK or Ansible file"]
        NoMonitor["Metrics, log and alerting backend<br/>no agent, exporter or shipper"]
    end

    Process -.->|"no image is built"| NoContainer
    Process -.->|"no manifest exists"| NoOrch
    Process -.->|"no SDK or credential"| NoCloud
    Process -.->|"no pipeline is registered"| NoPipeline
    Process -.->|"no declarations exist"| NoIaC
    Loopback -.->|"nothing fronts it"| NoProxy
    Stdout -.->|"nothing consumes the line"| NoMonitor
    NoOrch -.->|"no platform probes to collect"| NoMonitor
```

The solid path is the entire architecture: a host, a runtime, a process, one loopback socket and one line of text. Every other node is a statement of absence with the reason attached, and each of those reasons is evidenced in §8.1.1.

### 8.9.2 Deployment Workflow

Deployment is a five-step manual sequence with no automation lane, no quality gate and no traffic-shifting step. The one decision point in the flow is the port check, and its failure branch is the system's most consequential operational quirk: a bind conflict is reported as success.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    StartNode([Operator decides to deploy]) --> Step1["Step 1: place the working tree on a host<br/>20 tracked files, 6.9 MB"]
    Step1 --> Step2["Step 2: install from the lockfile<br/>npm ci, 66 packages, 4.2 MB"]
    Step2 --> CheckPort{"Loopback adapter present<br/>and TCP port 3000 free?"}
    CheckPort -->|"yes"| Step3["Step 3: node server.js<br/>npm start resolves to the same command"]
    CheckPort -->|"no"| SilentFail["Success banner printed, stderr empty, exit code 0"]
    SilentFail --> ManualFix["Operator frees the port by hand<br/>no automation and no alert"]
    ManualFix --> CheckPort
    Step3 --> Running["Serving GET / and GET /good-evening<br/>404 for every other path and method"]
    Running --> Validate["Step 4: validate by hand<br/>curl on both routes and lsof -i :3000"]
    Validate --> Serving(["Step 5: process runs in the foreground until signalled"])
    Serving -.->|"no probe, no canary, no rollback automation, no release record"| NoPost["No post-deployment automation exists"]
    Serving --> Stop{"Operator or supervisor sends a signal"}
    Stop -->|"SIGTERM"| EndSig["Exit 143 with no drain and no shutdown log"]
    Stop -->|"SIGINT"| EndInt["Exit 130 with no drain; in-flight requests are dropped"]
```

Two consequences follow from the flow. The banner is not evidence of deployment success, so the validation step is the only reliable gate; and termination has no graceful path, so a redeploy on a busy host interrupts any request in flight.

### 8.9.3 Environment Promotion Flow

There is exactly one execution context and no promotion edges. The environments a conventional flow would promote between do not exist, and no configuration mechanism exists that could differentiate them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SourceTree["Single source tree<br/>20 tracked files on one branch"] --> Context["Single execution context<br/>the operator's host"]
    Context --> Artifact["Byte-identical artefact on every host<br/>no environment-specific configuration exists"]

    subgraph NotDefined["Environments that do not exist"]
        Dev["dev environment<br/>not defined"]
        Staging["staging environment<br/>not defined"]
        QA["qa or uat environment<br/>not defined"]
        Prod["prod environment<br/>not defined"]
        Dev -.->|"no promotion edge"| Staging
        Staging -.->|"no promotion edge"| QA
        QA -.->|"no promotion edge"| Prod
    end

    Artifact -.->|"no NODE_ENV, no env file, no values overlay, no workspace split"| Dev
```

Because `NODE_ENV` is never set anywhere in the repository, every instance — on a workstation, a CI runner or an operator's server — runs Express's default `development` behaviour, which is why the framework writes error stacks to standard error for a genuine `5xx` regardless of where it is deployed (§8.3.2.2).

### 8.9.4 Network Architecture

The entire network surface is one loopback socket. External networks have no route to it, and no network function exists between them and the listener.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph External["External networks - no route to the service"]
        Internet["Public internet"]
        LAN["Local area network"]
        VPN["VPN or remote access"]
        Peer["Other hosts on the same subnet"]
    end

    subgraph SingleHost["Single host - the only place the service is reachable"]
        subgraph LoopbackZone["Loopback boundary 127.0.0.1"]
            Listener["Express listener on 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>plain HTTP, no TLS terminator"]
            Client["Local process, curl or the operator on the same host"]
            Client -->|"HTTP/1.1 GET"| Listener
            Listener -->|"200 text/plain with a fixed body, or 404"| Client
        end
        TCPStack["Host TCP stack and kernel socket table<br/>no firewall, NAT or policy rule is declared"]
    end

    Internet -.->|"cannot connect: the socket is bound to loopback"| Listener
    LAN -.->|"cannot connect: the socket is bound to loopback"| Listener
    VPN -.->|"cannot connect: the socket is bound to loopback"| Listener
    Peer -.->|"cannot connect: the socket is bound to loopback"| Listener

    subgraph NetAbsent["Network infrastructure with no realisation"]
        NoFirewall["Host firewall rules"]
        NoProxyNode["Reverse proxy or TLS terminator"]
        NoWAF["Web application firewall"]
        NoVPC["Virtual private cloud"]
    end

    TCPStack -.->|"no rules to apply"| NoFirewall
    Listener -.->|"nothing fronts it"| NoProxyNode
    Listener -.->|"no public surface to protect"| NoWAF
    Listener -.->|"no cloud subscription exists"| NoVPC
```

Read together, the four diagrams make the section's position concrete. A deployment is a tree copy, an install and a foreground process; a request crosses a loopback socket, receives a fixed string, and leaves no record; the artefact is identical on every host because no environment exists to vary it; and nothing between the internet and the process — proxy, firewall, balancer, platform probe or monitoring agent — has a node on the solid path.

## 8.10 Standard Infrastructure Practices in Effect

Although no formal infrastructure architecture is implemented, the system observes a small set of infrastructure practices by virtue of its construction. They are recorded here for the same reason §6.5.7 records the monitoring practices in force: a not-applicable determination must not be read as "nothing to do", and these are the practices that hold today together with the maintenance procedures that keep them holding.

### 8.10.1 Source Control and Repository Portability

| Practice | Implementation | Standing |
|----------|----------------|----------|
| Version control | Git, with 11 commits on one branch and a GitHub remote used for transport | Repository is source-of-truth for the deployed state |
| Backup substrate | Git history is the only backup mechanism; there is no other copy, snapshot or archive | Recovery of source is `git clone`; recovery of a running instance is a restart |
| Portability | The tree is flat — 20 tracked files plus the `blitzy/documentation/` subtree — and copies to any host without adaptation | Distribution is a tree copy (§8.2.2) |
| Reproducibility | 66 packages pinned with exact versions and `sha512` integrity digests; `npm ci` reproduces the validated tree | Deterministic install where the lockfile is used |
| Ignore hygiene | `.gitignore` contains one line, `node_modules/`, so the 4.2 MB dependency tree is never committed | The repository stays source-only, and the install step is mandatory |

### 8.10.2 Operating-System Process Visibility

These practices need no application instrumentation; they exploit the host's own facilities, and they are the de facto infrastructure monitoring surface for this system.

| Practice | Implementation | Evidence |
|----------|----------------|----------|
| Process presence | Any process tooling can observe the single `node server.js` process | Measured: RSS 63528-64076 KB and VSZ ~0.97 GB while idle |
| Listener state | The kernel socket table exposes the bound listener and its release on exit | `lsof -i :3000`; measured refusal after the process ended |
| Exit-status propagation | The runtime's own default: `0` clean start, `1` unresolved dependency or uncaught exception, `130` on `SIGINT`, `143` on `SIGTERM` | Measured `143` on `SIGTERM` |
| Functional probing | Any local HTTP client can verify the contract without server cooperation | Measured `200` on both routes, with per-request totals of 0.0047 s and 0.00087 s |
| Start-up timing | Observable from outside by polling until the first `200` | Measured approximately 130 ms on a warm host |

### 8.10.3 Start-Up Confirmation Signal

The `app.listen` callback writes exactly one line, `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` (`server.js:27`). It confirms that the listener callback ran and names the bind address — and that is the limit of what it proves. It is **not** a readiness signal: measured at HEAD, a second instance launched while port 3000 was held printed the identical line, wrote nothing to standard error and exited `0`, because `app.listen` registers the callback as a one-shot `error` listener (§6.5.2.4). Automation that waits for the banner will therefore treat a process that never bound its socket as healthy; the reliable wait condition is a successful request.

### 8.10.4 Supply-Chain Posture

| Practice | Implementation | Standing |
|----------|----------------|----------|
| Declared dependency surface | One direct dependency, `express` at `^5.2.1`, with a resolved closure of 66 packages | Small but no longer zero, which is why the advisory position below matters |
| Install integrity | Every lockfile entry carries a `sha512` integrity digest and a registry URL | `npm ci` verifies digests; the installed tree is not verified afterwards |
| Licence record | Lockfile records 61 MIT, four ISC and one BSD-3-Clause entry; `package.json` declares MIT | No `LICENSE`, notice or attribution file exists in the repository |
| Advisory awareness | `npm audit --omit=dev` is the only check and it is manual | Currently three advisories — one critical (`proxy-addr`), one high (`body-parser`), one moderate (`qs`) — with `npm audit` exiting `1`; nothing re-runs it (§8.7.1) |
| Build-time network exposure | The only external fetch in the lifecycle is the install-time retrieval of the 66 pinned tarballs | No runtime egress exists; the service makes no outbound connection |

### 8.10.5 Maintenance Procedures

The prompt's requirement to document maintenance procedures resolves to a short operator checklist, because every scheduled activity a production system would have — patching windows, certificate renewal, capacity review, failover testing — has no counterpart here. The procedures below are the ones the repository's own operator guide documents, restated with the infrastructure caveats this section established.

| Maintenance activity | Procedure | Trigger |
|----------------------|-----------|---------|
| Start or restart the service | Free port 3000 first (`lsof -i :3000`), then `node server.js`; confirm with a request rather than the banner | After a crash, a host restart or a change |
| Restore dependencies | `npm ci` from the lockfile; confirm with `npm ls --depth=0`, which must resolve `express@5.2.1` | Fresh checkout, or a damaged `node_modules/` |
| Refresh dependencies within the caret range | `npm install` or `npm update`, then review the regenerated lockfile diff | Deliberate upgrade, not scheduled; nothing detects drift |
| Remediate advisories | `npm audit fix` (available for all three current advisories), review the lockfile change, then re-run the manual contract checks | When an audit is run — currently by hand |
| Upgrade the runtime | Unconstrained by the repository: no `engines` field, no `.nvmrc` and no base image pin exist, so the host decides | Host-level change only |
| Recover source | `git clone`, then `npm ci` | Loss of a host or a working tree |
| Handle logs | Redirect the streams when starting detached (`node server.js > server.log 2>&1 &`); nothing rotates or retains the file | When running without a terminal |
| Verify source before restart | `node --check server.js`, expecting exit `0` | Before restarting after a source edit |
| Keep the tree clean | Leave `node_modules/` untracked and out of the repository; treat `.gitignore`'s single rule as invariant | Every install |
| Re-read deployed state | Read `server.js` — three literals are the whole configuration surface, and nothing else records what a host is running | Any doubt about a host's configuration |

## 8.11 External Dependencies, Resource Sizing, and Cost Estimates

### 8.11.1 External Dependencies Inventory

The prompt requires every external dependency to be documented. The list is short, and the reason it is short is that the runtime dependency surface is one package and the infrastructure surface is the operating system.

| Dependency class | Specific dependency | Pinning and control |
|------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Language runtime | Node.js | No repository-level pin: `package.json` declares no `engines` field and no `.nvmrc` exists; the only constraint is Express's floor of Node 18 or newer |
| Package manager | npm | No pin; version 7 or newer is required implicitly by `lockfileVersion` 3 |
| Package registry | Public npm registry, reached at install time | URLs pinned per package in `package-lock.json`'s `resolved` fields |
| Direct library | `express` `^5.2.1`, resolved to 5.2.1 | Caret range in the manifest, exact version plus `sha512` digest in the lockfile |
| Transitive libraries | 65 packages, the Express 5.2.1 closure | Exact versions and `sha512` digests in the lockfile; 4.2 MB installed |
| Operating-system facilities | Loopback adapter, TCP/IP stack on port 3000, standard output, process signals | Provided by the kernel; no configuration is declared |
| Host process tooling | Shell, `ps`, `lsof`, an HTTP client for verification | Used by the operator; nothing in the repository depends on it programmatically |
| Source transport | An HTTPS Git remote on GitHub, used for repository transport only | Credentials are supplied by a token in the remote URL; no credential helper, SSH key or CI integration exists |
| Cloud provider or SDK | None | No SDK in the closure; no provider configuration directory exists |
| Container base image or registry | None | No `Dockerfile`, so no base image is selected or pinned (§8.5) |
| Infrastructure-as-code provider | None | No Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, CDK, Ansible, Chef or Puppet file exists |
| Third-party service, secret store or monitoring backend | None | No SaaS integration, no secret, and no telemetry destination exists |

Two operational notes belong with the inventory. First, the runtime dependency is not optional at install time: `node_modules/` is git-ignored, so the registry is a hard prerequisite of a working deployment and a cold host cannot start the service without network access to it. Second, none of these dependencies is monitored: nothing checks the runtime line, the registry reachability or the installed tree after the fact.

### 8.11.2 Resource Sizing Guidelines

No resource requirement is committed, so the guidance below is derived from measurements at HEAD and marked as informal. It is sufficient to size a host on which this fixture runs comfortably; it is not a service level.

| Resource dimension | Informal guidance | Basis |
|--------------------|-------------------|-------|
| CPU | Any class that can run a supported Node.js line; one core is sufficient and only one is used | Throughput is bounded by a single event loop; no clustering or worker-thread path exists |
| Memory | Allow at least 128 MB headroom for the process | Measured 62-64 MB resident while idle, with ~0.97 GB virtual; no ceiling is declared or enforced |
| Disk | A few tens of MB: 4.2 MB for dependencies, ~6.9 MB of tracked content (mostly unreferenced binaries), plus room for an optional log redirect | Measured `du -sh node_modules/` and repository content |
| Network | Loopback only; no external bandwidth requirement | `server.js:3`; the listener is unreachable from other hosts |
| Start-up budget | Under a second once dependencies are installed | Measured approximately 130 ms from exec to the first served request |
| Process count | Exactly one per host | The fixed port and loopback bind prevent a second instance on the same host (§8.6) |
| Scaling headroom | None available in-process | No tuning knobs exist; the only levers are the Node.js runtime and the host |

### 8.11.3 Infrastructure Cost Estimate

The prompt requires cost estimates. Because no cloud service, managed database, container registry, pipeline minute, monitoring contract or IaC backend is consumed, the external infrastructure cost is zero, and every conventional cost line is zero for the same reason.

| Cost category | Monthly cost | Rationale |
|---------------|--------------|-----------|
| Cloud compute, storage or database | $0 | No provider service is consumed (§8.4) |
| Container registry and image storage | $0 | No image is built or pushed (§8.5) |
| Load balancer, proxy or API gateway | $0 | The loopback bind precludes fronting the listener |
| CI/CD runner minutes | $0 | No pipeline exists to consume minutes (§8.7) |
| Monitoring, logging or APM subscription | $0 | No telemetry is emitted or shipped (§8.8) |
| IaC state storage and secrets management | $0 | No IaC and no secret exists |
| **Total external infrastructure cost** | **$0 per month** | Every category above is absent by construction |

The only cost is the marginal CPU, memory and disk draw of one idle Node.js process on a host the operator already controls — bounded by the sizing guidance in §8.11.2 and not separately billable. There is consequently no cost dashboard, budget alarm, tagging policy or optimisation opportunity: with no spend to attribute, cost monitoring has no subject.

## 8.12 Forward-Looking Considerations

Two classes of change could alter this section: work already recorded in the repository but not implemented, and a scope expansion that would give the system a deployment to operate. The first leaves the determination intact and improves operational hygiene modestly; the second would replace it outright.

### 8.12.1 Recorded but Unimplemented Work

Three sets of deferred work sit in the repository. None adds an infrastructure primitive, and only one of them is a prerequisite for anything infrastructure-shaped.

| Deferred work | Effort recorded | Infrastructure effect |
|---------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| Hardening features F-101 to F-106 (`Response.txt` §0.4) | A separate initiative | Adds a bind-error handler, `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` shutdown with a drain window, handler exception protection, a `clientError` responder, input guards and a cleanup hook — all inside the existing process (`Response.txt` §0.5 forbids new dependencies, health endpoints and metrics) |
| Minimal regression suite (`node:test` with `supertest`) | ~2.0 h | Would give a pipeline something meaningful to run and replace the manual `curl`/`od -c` validation; it is the prerequisite for any quality gate that can fail |
| `X-Powered-By` suppression via `app.disable` | ~0.25 h | Removes a disclosure header; no infrastructure effect |
| Host and port parameterisation | ~1.0 h | The only recorded item with direct infrastructure consequences: it is the prerequisite for containerisation, for orchestration and for any deployment-time configuration. It would also need to preserve the loopback default, since the binding is currently the system's only exposure control (§6.4.1.2) |
| Original `/hello` endpoint requirement (F-201) | Not estimated | No infrastructure effect; it is a routing change |

Two cautions apply. The hardening features were authored against the superseded 15-line native-`http` file and their own scope rules forbid the framework, route and manifest changes the delivered implementation already made, so they must be re-derived before implementation. And several of the deferred items cannot be adopted simultaneously as written: a test suite, an environment-driven port and a suppressed `X-Powered-By` header all require edits that the hardening plan's immutability rules forbid.

### 8.12.2 Constraints That Preserve the Determination

§1.3.2.1 excludes the capability classes this section documents — clustering, process managers, container definitions, orchestrator manifests, CI pipelines and configuration files — and §1.3.2.3 records that no integration point is active or planned. Those exclusions are the reason the determination stands for the current build rather than being a gap to close, and any change to them is a change of scope, not a maintenance task.

### 8.12.3 Triggers That Would Reopen This Section

Each trigger below would create something to deploy, promote, supervise or monitor, and would require the listed work first.

| Trigger | What it creates | Required first |
|---------|-----------------|----------------|
| External exposure (a non-loopback bind or a fronting proxy) | A reachable service, and with it availability, transport security and access-control questions | A configuration surface for the bind address, TLS termination, and an availability definition to operate against |
| Containerisation | An image to build, version, scan and store | A `Dockerfile` with a pinned base image, an install step for the git-ignored `node_modules/`, and a bind address that is not a source literal |
| Orchestrated or supervised execution | Platform-side probes, restart policy and resource limits | A liveness and readiness endpoint, and a start-up signal that is not inverted on a bind failure (§8.2.5) |
| CI/CD adoption | Build, test and deploy stages with gates that can fail | A test suite (the current `test` script fails by design) and a dependency-audit stage |
| Cloud service consumption | A provider to select, size, secure and pay for | A cloud SDK in the dependency tree, credentials, and a configuration surface to inject them |
| Infrastructure as code | Declarative environments and drift detection | A state backend, provider configuration and at least one environment to declare |
| Monitoring or APM adoption | Metrics, log shipping and alerting | Emission call sites (none exist), a middleware stage (no `app.use` exists), and a destination to send data to |
| A committed SLA, or more than one environment | Service levels to measure, and promotion edges to define | Service-level indicators, a measurement source, and `NODE_ENV` or equivalent consumption |

### 8.12.4 Changes That Would Not Alter the Determination

Four kinds of change leave the determination standing. Implementing the hardening features improves termination hygiene and failure reporting while remaining a single unsupervised process. Re-running `npm audit fix` or upgrading Express within the caret range changes the dependency tree without creating an environment, image or pipeline. Adding a `LICENSE` file, an `engines` pin or a `.nvmrc` closes recorded gaps in §8.10.4 and §8.2.6 without producing deployment automation. And suppressing `X-Powered-By` removes a disclosure header without adding an operational surface. Until a trigger in §8.12.3 is introduced through an explicit scope expansion, the determination recorded at the head of this section — **Detailed Infrastructure Architecture is not applicable for this system**, with `npm ci` plus `node server.js` on one host as its entire build, distribution and deployment model — remains accurate.

### 8.13.2 Folders Examined

- Repository root (`""`) — flat, single-directory layout: 20 tracked files, two directories outside `node_modules/` and `.git/` (`blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/`), and hidden entries limited to `.git` and `.gitignore`. A bounded sweep for `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `.dockerignore`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.toml`, `*.tf`, `*.tfvars`, `*.ini`, `*.conf`, `*.cfg`, `.env*`, `Procfile`, `app.json`, `*.sh`, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `Jenkinsfile`, `buildspec*`, `appspec*` and `makefile` returned zero matches. This listing is why the absence claims in §8.1.1, §8.4, §8.5 and §8.7 rest on a directory inventory rather than on a scan alone
- `node_modules/` — 65 installed top-level package directories matching the lockfile's 66 non-root entries, 4.2 MB on disk, with zero `*.node` binaries or `binding.gyp` files and no `node-gyp`, `node-pre-gyp` or `nan` package present. Establishes the install output size and the absence of a native build-toolchain requirement
- `blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/` — one folder holding exactly four Markdown artifacts and no executable code; the source of the scope exclusions, the operator procedures and the superseded earlier Section 8

### 8.13.3 Specification Sections Consulted

- §1.3 Scope — §1.3.1.1 supplies the delivered-capability table and the runtime requirement (Node 18 or newer), §1.3.1.2 the system, network, configuration and geographic boundaries, §1.3.2.1 the explicit exclusions (clustering, process managers, container definitions, orchestrator manifests, CI pipelines, configuration files, tests and linters), and §1.3.2.3 and §1.3.2.4 the record that no integration point is active and that externally reachable deployment, multi-tenant operation and stateful interaction are unsupported
- §3.6 Development and Deployment — §3.6.2 establishes that the "build" is dependency installation and that the source file is the artefact, §3.6.3 the verified absence of containerisation, §3.6.4 the verified absence of CI/CD with the manual checks that substitute for it, §3.6.5 the deployment prerequisites and characteristics table, and §3.6.6 version-control and repository hygiene
- §6.5 Monitoring and Observability — the authoritative treatment of observability, and the source of the findings this section reuses at the infrastructure level: the single stdout emission, the inverted start-up signal on a bind failure, the absent metric, log, trace, alert and dashboard layers, the absence of health and readiness endpoints, and the absence of any committed SLA or capacity target
- §7.1 Applicability Statement — the precedent for stating a determination as a blockquote, dispositioning each required dimension explicitly, and recording a conflict between the repository's earlier documentation and the observed state
- §5.4.5 and §6.4 — consulted through the citations §6.5 carries: §5.4.5 for the recorded latency and memory observations used as comparable figures in §8.3.1.3, and §6.4 for the security disposition and the dependency-advisory register referenced in §8.8.3 and §8.10.4

### 8.13.4 Runtime Evidence

Every behavioural claim in this section was observed at HEAD on this checkout, with the process started over loopback or inspected through an operator command; none was inferred from documentation. Recorded directly: `node -v` returned `v22.23.3` and `npm -v` returned `11.21.0`; `node -p "require('./node_modules/express/package.json').engines.node"` returned `>= 18`; the lockfile parsed to `lockfileVersion` 3 with 67 package entries; `du -sh node_modules/` returned 4.2 MB across 65 top-level directories; `npm ls --depth=0` resolved `hello_world@1.0.0 -> express@5.2.1`; a text search of every repository `.js` file for `process.env`, `process.argv`, `app.set`, `app.use`, `cluster`, `worker_threads`, `https`, `tls` and `fs.` returned zero matches; `node --check server.js` exited `0`; `git tag` returned nothing and the history held 11 commits dated 2026-06-04 on branch `blitzy-62d685d6-e32c-4f29-bfd6-70d96dfe345a` with a GitHub HTTPS remote; the running process printed only `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, answered `GET /` with `200` in 0.0047 s and `GET /good-evening` with `200` in 0.00087 s, and reported RSS 63528-64076 KB with VSZ ~0.97 GB; a second instance launched while port 3000 was held printed the success banner, wrote nothing to standard error and exited `0`; `SIGTERM` ended the first instance with exit code `143` and no shutdown output, after which the port refused connections; `npm start` printed `> hello_world@1.0.0 start` / `> node server.js` and then the banner, resolving implicitly to the entry file; `npm audit --omit=dev` reported three advisories — one critical (`proxy-addr`), one high (`body-parser`) and one moderate (`qs`) — and exited `1`; and the process reached its first served request approximately 130 ms after launch.

### 8.13.5 External Sources

Five external facts were confirmed for the version-envelope and dependency statements; no external source was used to infer repository behaviour.

- [web] npm registry metadata for `express@5.2.1` (`https://registry.npmjs.org/express/5.2.1`) and the Express version-support page (`https://expressjs.com/en/support`) — confirmed the declared minimum runtime `engines.node: ">= 18"` and that Express 5.x requires Node.js 18 or newer
- [web] npm registry version listing for `express` (`https://www.npmjs.com/package/express?activeTab=versions`) — confirmed that the current `latest` tag is a later 5.x minor than the 5.2.1 the lockfile pins (released 9 October 2026), which is why §8.2.4 distinguishes the `npm ci` and `npm install` paths
- [web] Node.js release schedule and end-of-life listings (nodejs/Release `README.md` and `schedule.json`, `https://nodejs.org/en/about/eol`, `https://endoflife.date/nodejs`) — confirmed that Node.js 18 reached end-of-life on 30 April 2025, that Node.js 22 is an LTS line with support to 30 April 2027, and that Node.js 24 became Active LTS on 28 October 2025
- [web] Node.js "Beware of End-of-Life Node.js Versions" (`https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/node-18-eol-support`) — confirmed that lines past end-of-life receive no updates, including security patches, which is the risk §8.2.6 attaches to the absent `engines` pin
- [web] Express 5.x FAQ and release announcement (`https://expressjs.com/en/5x/starter/faq`, `https://expressjs.com/en/blog/2024-10-15-v5-release`) — confirmed that the Node.js 18 floor is a framework-wide requirement rather than a package-specific quirk

The specification, the feature catalogue and the repository's own documentation artifacts use several identifier namespaces, each defined in a different source. The register below is the decoding table for all of them.

| `F-0xx` | `F-001`–`F-010` | Delivered capability in the feature catalogue; F-009 is the fixture set and F-010 the orphan data file | §2.1.2 |
| `F-1xx` | `F-101`–`F-106` | Proposed, unimplemented hardening item carried by `Response.txt` | §2.1.4, §4.3.2.6 |
| `F-2xx` | `F-201` | Unimplemented original requirement for a `/hello` route | §2.1.4.7 |
| `F-xxx-RQ-0xx` | `F-005-RQ-003` | Acceptance criterion belonging to a feature; each states one observable that must be true | §2.2, §2.5.3 |
| `W-0x` | `W-01`–`W-09` | Workflow identifier: W-01 startup, W-02 request/response handling, W-03 external termination, W-04 bind-failure path, W-05–W-08 proposed hardening, W-09 `/hello` | `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §4.1.1, §4.3 |
| `C-x` | `C-1`–`C-8` | Component identifier local to the architecture section, mapping to the feature IDs of §2 and §3 | §5.1.2 |
| `QA Issue n` | `QA Issue 1` | Defect found by review after delivery: the trailing-slash variant returning content, fixed by commit `f2c2ca4` | §6.6.3.3, `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §5 |
| `PA1` | — | Completion methodology used for the project's percentage figures: completed hours over autonomous-plus-manual hours, scoped to the action plan | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.2, §10 footer |
| `Journey n` | `Journey 1` | Install-and-start path used as a referenced recovery narrative | §4.3.2.5 |

No namespace is generated at run time: every identifier is static documentation, and no identifier appears in executable code. That is why the specification can cite requirement IDs for behaviour that has no machine-readable contract and no test that asserts it.

### 9.1.5 Unreferenced and Orphan Artifact Register

Four tracked binaries and one data file are loaded by no code path, no manifest and no configuration file. Their measured properties are recorded here so that a reader can identify them without opening the checkout, and so that the boundary between the running system and its carried payload is explicit.

| Artifact | Bytes | Measured properties | Role in the running system |
|----------|-------|---------------------|----------------------------|
| `20250304165759.mp4` | 5,474,705 | MP4 container; file-type brand `mp42` with a compatible `mp41` brand | None; 76.6% of tracked bytes |
| `tech_spec.pdf` | 648,521 | PDF 1.7 with compressed object streams; its 68-page characterisation in §1.4 could not be re-verified from the byte stream | None; a specification rendered for a different project |
| `defect_for_task_1.docx` | 326,077 | OOXML package containing `word/document.xml` plus two images under `word/media/`; the extracted body text is 111 characters of unrelated defect description | None |
| `s1.png` | 49,680 | PNG image, 1152 × 958 pixels | None; no page, view or asset path exists to serve it |
| `phonenumber.csv` | 621 | CSV with header `message,phonenumber` and 15 synthetic rows whose numbers fall in the `+111111112xx` range | None; `server.js` contains no `fs` usage and no file reference |

Three consequences follow. The service's runtime payload is `server.js` and the `node_modules/` tree it requires, so a deployment can omit all five files without changing any observable behaviour. The repository's size is dominated by material the specification does not describe, which is why §8.11.2's approximation of "~6.9 MB of tracked content" resolves to exactly 7,147,208 bytes with 6,499,604 of them in these five files. And the CSV remains the only fixture of its kind: a data file whose schema is defined by its own header rather than by any consumer.
